A hand-over between bank owners carries no channel. A hand-over to a partner is a separate entry, the HANDOVER of step 3, which holds the partner as PARTNER followed by the partner code.
RWB-E2-034.6: Your code sets this field on every entry, with no person involved. Write RetentionClassResolver to read the Retention classes reference table by ledger event code and return the class, and call it from InteractionLedgerWriter, so no entry is ever appended without one. Until Compliance sets the periods, every event code takes the class ILG-STD. The class is held per entry and set apart from the decision log, because a call note and a decision are kept for different lengths of time. The Compliance and PDPA officer changes a class through a reference data change, so read the table and write no value into code. The retention job itself is out of scope.
RWB-E2-034.7: Your listener writes through the published interface of RWB-E1-066. Call InteractionLedgerWriter.append with each command inside the transaction of the outbox delivery, so the entry and the delivery succeed or fail together; a transaction is a group of writes the database applies all at once or not at all. The writer holds a unique key on idempotency_key, refuses a repeat and counts it under rule R-UNI-40. When the ledger store cannot be written, let the delivery fail so the outbox keeps it with status RETRYING, and raise an incident; the entry is written when the store comes back. After the retry limit, the delivery goes to the exception queue with a task for RW-PLATADM.
RWB-E2-034.8: A person does this, the case owner or any role holding Case record R for a case in their scope. SCR-03 Case record gains a ledger section showing the latest 20 entries, and SCR-04 Case timeline gains filters for channel, source, actor and date range. Build LedgerTimelineSection as the React component behind both. The case owner is the reason the story exists: whoever picks up a case needs to see which number answered and who held the case last, without asking EFS or the partner. A case with no entry yet shows the empty state with MSG-P3-024 in place of a bare empty list.
RWB-E2-034.9: The screen makes this call automatically. The endpoint GET /api/recovery/v1/cases/{caseId}/interactions already exists and takes the case ID in the path and channel, actor, from, to, page and size as parameters. This story adds fields to the Interaction schema it returns: contactPointId, fromHolderRef, toHolderRef, treatmentId, proceedsId and retentionClass, all recorded in the additions file. Extend the schema in the API specification and regenerate the types. A caller without Case record R is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002; a case that does not exist or sits outside the caller's scope is refused with 404 and MSG-P4-003, so scope and absence look the same.
RWB-E2-034.10: The screen renders what the endpoint returned, and no further read happens. Show each entry with its time, channel, the contact point reached, the outcome, any promise amount and date, a link to the linked offer or payment, the holder change on a hand-over, the delivery status on a letter, and the source, EFS or WORKBENCH. Mask the contact point by role, so a role that may not see a phone number gets the reference and not the digits. The first page of a case holding 500 entries has to appear in under 2 seconds, which the index on case and time serves. Keep the ordering rule in one place in the front end.

RWB-E1-002.1: Quartz is the scheduler inside the Workbench that starts jobs by clock time or by a chain. No person starts this. You build CaseListChainListener, a Quartz job listener, which watches JOB-03 for the business date and starts the case list step of JOB-04 as soon as JOB-03 completes. If JOB-03 has not completed, the listener starts the step at the time held in the parameter caselist.allocation.wait.until, 07:15. The step itself is CaseListStepConfig, a Spring Batch step inside JOB-04, and it runs under the service identity SY-DATALOAD. The feature flag rwb.p1.case-list controls it: with the flag off, JOB-04 runs its other steps and skips this one.
RWB-E1-002.2: The step makes this check on its own, with no person involved. LoadRunQuery is the published read interface over the load_run table, built in RWB-E1-003. You call it instead of reading that table directly, because this story may read case and load data only through published interfaces. Pass interface INT-01, which is the account and arrears feed, and the business date. When the answer is COMPLETED, the step carries on. When it is anything else, the step stops before it writes any case list rows, writes a load_run with status REFUSED and the failed check "INT-01 not complete", and sends MSG-P1-001 to the team manager group. The previous extract file in the lake is left as it is.
RWB-E1-002.3: The step writes this row itself. load_run is the run record table from RWB-E1-003; it holds one row per job run with the job code, the product code, the business date, the status and the check results. Open means insert the row with status RUNNING at the start, then set it to COMPLETED, REFUSED or FAILED when the step ends, as section 9 says. Write job code JOB-04 and product code DP03 on the row. Later in the same run you add the four check results named in section 12: COUNT, BELOW_ENTRY, ALLOCATION_COMPLETE and PUBLISHED. The platform administrator reads this row through GET /admin/jobs with type=JOB-04.
RWB-E1-002.4: The step calls this itself. CaseQueryApi is the Java interface published by the case workflow module and built in RWB-E1-018; the case workflow identity SY-CASEWF serves it. Your code may not query recovery_case, case_account or queue, so this call is the only way to reach case data. openCaseAccounts returns a Stream of OpenCaseAccountView, which carries the case ID, case number, account ID, product group, stage code, status, owner user ID, queue code, team code and route code. A Stream is read in pieces as the step works through it, so the whole day of cases is never held in memory at once. Write a contract test against this interface with a stub of synthetic cases. If the call raises an error part way, the step rolls back and the run status is FAILED.
RWB-E1-002.5: The step does this with no person involved. loan_account is the data engine own table, so you read it directly, by the account ID that CaseQueryApi returned. A join here means matching that account ID to loan_account.id and taking three values from the matched row: account_no, total_balance and days_past_due. Some case accounts have no matching row, as exception X7 describes. For those, write the case list row with an empty total balance and empty days past due, and write one dq_exception row with check code CL-01 and the account as the record key. dq_exception is the data quality exception table, so the data steward can see which accounts were short of account data.
RWB-E1-002.6: The step does this on its own. Create case_list_row with migration V1_002__case_list_row.sql and the columns listed in section 13, with the unique key uk_case_list_row on business date, case ID and account ID. Replace means delete every row already held for that business date and insert the new set. A transaction is a group of database changes that either all take effect or none do, so a reader never sees a part-built list, and a rerun for the same date leaves the same row count with no case account twice. Put the time of this run in refreshed_at on every row. CaseListRowRepository owns the delete and the insert, and your first test is the replace of one date of rows.
RWB-E1-002.7: The service CaseListCountCheck does this work with no person involved. Read the threshold from the parameter case.entry.dpd rather than writing 90 into the code. Count the case list rows you just wrote whose days past due reach the threshold. Then build the figure to match: count the loan_account rows at or above the threshold for the business date and subtract the number that the case workflow module excluded when the cases were created, which you get from CaseQueryApi.excludedAccountCount. In AC1, 28,140 accounts less 21 exclusions gives 28,119 to match. Compare the two counts against the parameter recon.caselist.tolerance.pct. Count the rows below the threshold as well, because they are reported as the BELOW_ENTRY check. Unit test the boundary exactly at the tolerance.
RWB-E1-002.8: The step writes the result and sends the alert with no person involved. Put the COUNT check on the load_run row of this run: PASS when the difference is inside the tolerance, FAIL with the difference when it is not. On a FAIL, call LoadAlertNotifier, the alert service built in RWB-E1-003, with MSG-P1-012, so the data steward group and the team manager groups receive the date, the product, the number of accounts and the percentage, as AC4 shows with 25 accounts and 0.09 percent. A failed count check does not hold the list back: the rows stay written and the extract file is still published, as exception X1 says. The recipient groups are configuration values that the platform administrator sets per environment.
RWB-E1-002.9: The step writes the file itself. Build CaseListExtractWriter to produce the CSV with the ten columns in the order AC2 names, plus team, business date and refresh time, under the name case-list/<businessDate>.csv. Hand the file to the outbound file adapter from RWB-E1-007, interface INT-19, and never write to the lake from this code, because the adapter owns every outbound transfer. The lake path is a configuration value set per environment by the platform administrator. When the adapter fails every retry, the run still completes, the PUBLISHED check on the load_run is NO, and the transfer goes to the exception queue with a task for the platform administrator. Test that PUBLISHED check with the adapter forced to fail.
RWB-E1-002.10: No Workbench code runs here. The reporting and BI analyst builds the Power BI data set "Case list v1" on the extract file in the lake and schedules its refresh at 07:30, and the team managers read the report with Reporting R. Your part is the file behind it: the ten columns in the order AC2 names, plus team, business date and refresh time, so the analyst can offer filters on team, queue and product and show the line "Refreshed 1 Dec 2026 07:12, data as of 30 Nov 2026" from the refresh time and the business date. This story builds no Workbench screen, and row-level security by team belongs to RWB-E1-016. The story is done when this data set refreshes in SIT from your extract file.

RWB-E1-014.1: Quartz is the scheduler inside the Workbench, and it starts this job on its own with no person involved. Put the trigger in Quartz as the cron expression 0 0 1 * * ? in the Asia/Bangkok time zone, so the job starts at 01:00 every night. The business date it works on is the previous calendar day, so the run at 01:00 on 1 December copies the entries of 30 November. Build DecisionLogLakeCopyJob as the Quartz job and mark it @DisallowConcurrentExecution, which makes Quartz refuse a second start while a run is in progress. The run, its status and its checks appear in the job monitoring built in RWB-E1-056. The whole job sits behind the feature flag rwb.dataengine.lake-copy.
RWB-E1-014.2: The service reads the row itself; no person is involved. Create the table lake_copy_watermark with a Flyway migration in this story: copy_name varchar(40) as the primary key, last_entry_hash char(64) not null, last_decided_at timestamptz, rows_copied_total bigint not null, business_date date not null, and the standard columns. The same migration inserts a seed row, which is a starting row the migration writes so the first run has something to read: copy_name DECISION_LOG, last_entry_hash of 64 zeros, which the interface calls the genesis hash, and rows_copied_total 0. The watermark is the point the last matched copy reached, held as the hash of the last copied entry and the running total of rows copied. LakeCopyWatermarkRepository reads and writes it.
RWB-E1-014.3: The service makes this call on its own. DecisionLogExport is the interface published by the decision log module in package recovery.decisionlog.api; your code reads the log only through it and never queries decision_log_entry. If the interface is not there yet, it is built in P7 with head() and entriesAfter(), with unit tests on chain order. head() returns a ChainHead holding the live row count, the hash of the last entry and the time of the last decision at the moment of the call. Hold those values for the rest of the run as the cut-off, which is the target this run copies up to. Entries written after the call are left for the next night, and the later match compares the copy against this fixed cut-off.
RWB-E1-014.4: The service runs this loop itself. entriesAfter takes the hash to start after and a page limit, and returns at most that many entries in chain order. Chain order follows the hash chain: each entry holds its own hash and the hash of the entry before it, so the entries come back in the order they were written. Read the page size from the property rwb.dataengine.lake.page-size, which is 5000 per environment, rather than writing the number in the code. Pass the watermark hash on the first call and the last hash of each page on the next, and keep going until you reach the cut-off hash held at step 3. Test the paging with 12,480 synthetic entries. When every call fails, the job ends Failed, MSG-GEN-006 names the decision log, and the watermark is left where it was.
RWB-E1-014.5: LakeFileWriter does this with no person involved. Parquet is a column-based file format that the lake and the reporting tools read. Write the entries into the intake container named by the property rwb.dataengine.lake.container, under the prefix from rwb.dataengine.lake.path-prefix, which is decision-log, in a folder named business_date= and the date. That folder is the partition for the day. Split the entries across files using rwb.dataengine.lake.rows-per-file, which is 50000. Each row carries the 18 DecisionLogEntry fields with the same names they have in api.yaml. Then write _manifest.json in the same folder with the row count, the first hash, the last hash and the cumulative count. On a night with no new entries, write the partition with a manifest of zero rows and the unchanged last hash. Test the writer against an Azurite or local file system container.
RWB-E1-014.6: LakeCopyReconciler does this check itself. Read _manifest.json back from the lake rather than trusting the values your own code held in memory, because a write that stopped part way is only found by reading the result. Compare the cumulative count and the last hash in the manifest with the cut-off taken at the start of the run. The tolerance is zero, so any difference at all fails the check, which is recorded on the job run under the reconciliation code REC-08. On a failure, as AC3 shows when 379 of 380 rows reach the lake, record the break with MSG-P1-019, leave the partition not marked complete, leave the watermark where it is, and alert the data steward. The job tries the same range again the next night.
RWB-E1-014.7: The reconciler does this itself, and only when the check at step 6 matched. Mark the day partition complete, which moves its state from Written to Complete. Then update the single lake_copy_watermark row for copy name DECISION_LOG with the cut-off values: the last entry hash, the time of the last decision, the new total of rows copied and the business date. Write the checks on the job run record as well, so GET /admin/jobs shows the row count and the REC-08 result to the platform administrator and the data steward. Move the watermark nowhere else in the code: a run that did not match leaves it untouched, which is what makes the next night copy the same range again.
RWB-E1-014.8: This runs inside the same job, with no person involved. Read the retention rule row for product DP12 and record class LAKE_COPY from the retention_rule table built in RWB-E1-017, and take retention_months and rule_version from it. The reference data administrator loads that row and Compliance approves it, so the period is never a value in your code. Compare each partition business date with the rule and move only the partitions older than the period to the archive tier, the cheaper storage the lake keeps old data in. The comparison is strict: a partition exactly at its retention age is kept. Write the list of partitions moved, how many there were and the rule version on the job run, as AC2 shows with one partition under rule version RET-2026.11.
RWB-E1-014.9: A person does this, the data steward, who holds Platform administration R. There is no screen in this story, so the data steward reads the result through GET /api/recovery/v1/admin/jobs with type=JOB-13; the interface and job monitor screen SCR-44 arrives in Epic 2. Your work is to make that response carry what the data steward needs: the job ID, type, business date, status, start and end time, and the checks with the row count, the REC-08 result, the number of partitions archived and the rule version. A role without Platform administration R is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002, which is the access test TC-E1-014-09. On a failed run the data steward also receives the operations alert, and the platform administrator reruns the job from the job monitor.

RWB-E1-026.1: A person starts this. The case owner opens the case record screen SCR-03 and selects the Documents tab, which is screen SCR-30. You build that tab as the React component CaseDocumentsTab, with the states listed in section 15: Loading shows skeleton rows while the list and the checklist are fetched, then the list shows the documents, the search bar and the checklist. The other states you build are upload, Empty and Error. The reader needs a role with Documents R and the case inside their scope, or the tab shows no document name. The feature flag rwb.dochub.casedocs controls the whole tab: with the flag off, the tab is hidden and the endpoints answer 404.
RWB-E1-026.2: The browser code makes both calls as soon as the tab opens, with no further action by the user. GET /cases/{caseId}/documents returns a DocumentPage with the items, the page, the size and the total, and only the active version of each document; the default size is 20 and the maximum is 100. GET /cases/{caseId}/document-checklist is new in this story and returns the case ID, the checklist version, which here is the document type table version, and one item per type with its code, label, required flag and present count. Placeholder means the service answers required false for every item, missing count 0 and complete null until RWB-E1-040 sets the required items per case type. Build it as ChecklistPlaceholderService from the document type catalog and the counts per type on the case.
RWB-E1-026.3: A person does this. Build UploadDocumentDialog with a file picker and a document type list taken from LOV-DOC-TYPE, which comes from the document type table in force. Before sending, the dialog compares the file size with the parameter INTAKE_MAX_FILE_MB and shows MSG-P5-017 when the file is larger. The server checks the size as well and answers 413, because the front end check does not replace it. The dialog also sends an Idempotency-Key header, which is a value the client sets so that the same submit arriving twice creates one document only; the key is kept for 24 hours per user and a repeat returns the first response. The Upload choice is shown only to roles that hold Documents C.
RWB-E1-026.4: Server code does this as soon as the submit arrives. Build CaseDocumentUploadService to write the file into the intake container first, then call the malware scan built in RWB-E1-041, because every upload is scanned before it is stored. When the scan finds a threat, answer 422 with MSG-P5-016, leave the file in the quarantine container and write no document row. When the file is clean, call DocumentStore.store with source UPLOAD, which is the only source value a user call may send; any other value is refused with 422. The same service refuses a submit with no document type with 422 and MSG-GEN-001, a type outside the table in force with 422 and MSG-P5-006, and a file type outside PDF, JPG and PNG with 415 and MSG-P5-001.
RWB-E1-026.5: This code already exists from RWB-E1-024, so you call DocumentStore.store and do not write this part again. The order matters. The decision log entry is written first, because a store that cannot be recorded does not proceed; when the decision log write fails, no document row and no file are kept and your dialog shows MSG-P7-003 from the 503 response. The document row is then created and the event DocumentStored is published, and the file is copied last, so the row is in state COPY_PENDING until the copy finishes and STORED after it. Your work here is the call and the error handling, plus the resilience test TC-E1-026-13, which forces the decision log write to fail during an upload and checks that nothing is stored.
RWB-E1-026.6: The browser code does this with no further action by the user. A 201 response means a new document was created, and the tab then calls the list endpoint again so the new document appears at the top of the case document list. A 200 response with the message code MSG-P5-024 means the same file and type is already on the case; for that answer, show the document that already exists and highlight it, and add nothing to the list. The time from submit to the document appearing has to be 5 seconds or less. That is measured by a browser test in SIT, and the story is done when a 2 MB upload shows in the list inside 5 seconds there.
RWB-E1-026.7: The case owner types the filter and the browser sends it. Add dateFrom and dateTo as query parameters on the existing list endpoint. In Epic 1 the date filter works on the stored date of the document, which is the created_at standard column, and not on any date inside the file. Sort newest first and take the page size from the property rwb.dochub.casedocs.page-size, which is 20. CaseDocumentQueryService and CaseDocumentQueryRepository read the document table filtered by case, type, active flag and created_at, using the index ix_document_case_type_created already created in RWB-E1-024. When dateFrom is later than dateTo, answer 422 with MSG-GEN-003 and run no search. When nothing matches, the tab shows the empty state with the sentence "No documents match this search." and the action "Clear the search".
RWB-E1-026.8: A person does this by selecting a row in the list. The panel that shows the document, DocumentDetailPanel, was built in RWB-E1-024, so your work is to open it with the document ID from the row and nothing more. The access check still applies on the way: the reader needs Documents R and the case has to be in their scope, and a case outside the scope is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-003 with no document name shown, which is the test in AC11. Searching across cases, free text search and search on extracted fields are not part of this story; they come in RWB-E1-033. When you log anything about a document, write the document ID in place of the file name.

RWB-E1-039.1: A person starts this. Every bank role generates access events by working normally: signing in, opening a case record, opening a document, listing cases and exporting a list. Those actions are what the rest of this story has to record, each with its own event code from LOV-DECISION: AC-SIGN for a sign-in, AC-READ for a read, AC-EXPT for an export and AC-DENY for a refusal. The data steward loads those codes with this story. There is no code to write for this step alone; it names the points your code has to cover. The measure in section 2 is that 100 percent of reads of the case store and the document store reach the access log.
RWB-E1-039.2: The module serving the read makes this call in its own code, with no person involved. AccessEventPublisher is the interface published in RWB-E1-022, and this story extends it. Your work is to add the publish call to the case read and the list export in the case store module and to the document content read in the document hub, each through the published interface rather than by writing to the log directly. The AccessEvent you pass carries the event code, the actor, the case ID where the action has one, the capability area and right, the result, the field IDs returned with a flag saying which were masked, and, for a list or an export, the filter used and the number of rows. Pass field IDs and the masking position only, never field values. Sign-in, refusal, export and break-glass events carry no case ID.
RWB-E1-039.3: Your code does this; no person is involved. Build AccessLogWriter to turn an AccessEvent into a decision log record and write it through the P7 DecisionLogWriter, inside the transaction the caller already opened for the read. A transaction is a group of database changes that either all take effect or none do, so the entry and the answer to the user succeed or fail together. The entry holds the access event code, the actor, the capability area and right and the result, with the rest of the detail in the actions field: fields returned, filter, row count, and the grant and incident where one applies. The store itself is append only and hash chained from RWB-E1-008, and this story adds no table. When the write fails, return 503 with MSG-P7-003 and no data, and raise an incident to the platform administrator queue.
RWB-E1-039.4: Two people do this, and it happens outside the Workbench. Break-glass means emergency access beyond the rights a role normally holds. The platform administrator raises the request in the bank IAM, naming the open incident, the capability area, the scope and the reason, and the security administrator approves it there. The IAM then adds the platform administrator to the break-glass group for that environment, with an end time; the group name follows DL40 and is RWB-SIT-BREAKGLASS in SIT. You build none of this flow, and the request, approval and review records stay in the IAM. What your code later needs from it is one thing: whether the caller is in the break-glass group, and when that membership ends.
RWB-E1-039.5: A person makes this call. Approval in the bank IAM does not open the grant by itself; the platform administrator has to activate it in the Workbench. Build the activation endpoint to take a BreakGlassActivation holding the incident reference, the IAM request ID, the capability area from LOV-CAPABILITY, the right as C, R or U, the scope from LOV-SCOPE and a reason of 20 to 1000 characters. It answers 201 with a BreakGlassGrant carrying the grant ID, which is the ID of the AC-BGON entry, the incident reference, the area, the right, the scope and the start and end times. The caller needs Platform administration C and membership of the break-glass group. The call takes an Idempotency-Key header.
RWB-E1-039.6: Your service does this with no person involved. Build BreakGlassService with three checks before anything is granted. First, membership of the break-glass group: a caller outside it is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-007, and an AC-DENY entry with reason NO_BREAKGLASS_GRANT is written. Second, the incident reference against the parameter rwb.access.breakglass.incident-pattern; a missing reference gives 422 with MSG-GEN-001 naming the field. Third, the reason length against rwb.access.breakglass.reason-min, with 422 and MSG-GEN-002 below it. Then write the AC-BGON entry, whose entry ID becomes the grant ID. Set the end time to the earlier of the window from rwb.access.breakglass.window-hours and the group end: in AC2, 10:30 plus four hours gives 14:30, which is earlier than the group end of 18:00. A second activation with a new key while a grant is active answers 409.
RWB-E1-039.7: This happens in code while the person works. Build BreakGlassGrantCheck to add the grant right, in its area and scope, to AccessCheck until the grant end time, and to put the grant ID and the incident reference on every decision log entry written for that user while the grant is active. AC8 shows the result: the read at 11:02 carries incident INC0004521 and the two ordinary reads do not. For the screen part, add the break-glass fields to GET /me/session and build the React component BreakGlassBanner, which shows MSG-P4-004 with the end time in the front end shell. This story has no screen of its own, so the banner is the only visible part.
RWB-E1-039.8: No person ends the grant and no job ends it. Check the end time on every request instead, so that from the first request after the end time AccessCheck uses only the letters RW-PLATADM holds in the permission matrix version in force. A call the grant allowed is then refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002, and the refusal is written as an AC-DENY entry. AC2 gives the case to test: the same PATCH on a task is allowed at 14:20 under the grant and refused at 14:31, because RW-PLATADM holds only R in Case record. Test it with a clock fixed at 10:30 and then moved to 14:31, so the end is checked without waiting four hours.
RWB-E1-039.9: A person does this: the security administrator, who holds Platform administration R, and who may not review their own use. The review window comes from the parameter rwb.access.breakglass.review-days, one working day. Your work is the query behind it. Build AccessLogQueryService and the endpoint GET /admin/access-log, mapping the query onto the P7 DecisionLogReader interface rather than reading the log table. The query takes user, from, to, event, page and a size of 1 to 500, and returns AccessLogPage of entries with the time, the actor, the event code, the capability area and the result. Refuse a caller without Platform administration R with 403 and MSG-P4-002, and answer 422 when from is later than to or the size is outside the range. The review itself is recorded in the bank IAM.
RWB-E1-039.10: A person does this. Internal audit reads and changes nothing. The endpoint already exists as the decision log query, and it takes the case ID, the decision code AC-READ, a from date, a to date, the page and the size, returning a page of decision log entries under Decision log right R with scope applied. This answer is complete only because step 3 wrote one entry for every read, so your work here is in the entries rather than the endpoint: actor, time and the field IDs in actions have to be there. AC8 gives the test: three reads of one case on 3 December 2026 come back in time order, and the 11:02 read carries incident INC0004521. The screen for this query, SCR-38, comes in RWB-E2-005.

RWB-E1-051.1: A person does this: the platform administrator, who owns these definitions. Control-M is the bank batch scheduler and ADF is the bank pipeline service. The four definitions are held as JSON in the repository, in ops/control-m/ for the Control-M jobs RWB_ALS_EXTRACT and RWB_EFS_EXTRACT, which extract from ALS and EFS into COLLINS, and in ops/adf/ for the pipelines rwb-ccms-file-move and rwb-svaf-file-move, which move the weekly CCMS and SVAF files. Those four names are proposed until SCB IT issues the bank names. SCB IT gives the platform administrator access to the Control-M folder and the ADF factory for DEV and SIT. Keeping the definitions in the repository is what lets the pipeline check them.
RWB-E1-051.2: The pipeline does this; nobody copies a definition into Control-M or ADF by hand. Your work is the pipeline step that reads the files in ops/control-m/ and ops/adf/ and refuses a definition that is not valid, which is build step 5. The deployment itself follows the bank deployment path into each environment. Keep the times, the folders and the retry window where they belong in configuration: the interface configuration rows hold the inbound path and the file pattern, and the properties rwb.jobs.collins.start, rwb.jobs.collins.last-retry and rwb.jobs.files.weekly-cron hold the times. The story is done when a full week of the four feeds runs in SIT with no manual start.
RWB-E1-051.3: Control-M runs these two extracts on its own, outside the Workbench. The Workbench never calls ALS or EFS directly: both feeds reach it only through the COLLINS daily batch, as interfaces INT-01 and INT-07. Control-M starts the extracts after the COLLINS end of day, and COLLINS finishes its own load before 05:00, which is why the Workbench job in step 5 starts at that time. Nothing in your code starts or waits on Control-M; your code looks for the result of the load at 05:00 and treats a feed with no data as missing. A Control-M job that fails alerts the platform administrator through the bank scheduler, and the Workbench run for that interface is written as MISSING.
RWB-E1-051.4: The two ADF pipelines do this with no person involved. CCMS and SVAF reach the Workbench only as weekly file loads, interfaces INT-10 and INT-11, so there is no direct call from the Workbench to either system. ADF takes the files from the source drop folder and puts them in the Workbench SFTP inbound folder by Sunday 23:00, a time that is still an assumption under DL12. Read the inbound path and the file pattern from the interface configuration rows rather than holding folder names in code. When the ADF pipeline fails, as AC4 describes for CCMS, no file is waiting on Monday, the run row for that interface is written as MISSING and the alert goes out.
RWB-E1-051.5: Quartz inside the Workbench starts both jobs; no person starts them. Build CollinsIntakeJob as the JOB-01 entry point, running daily at 05:00 and retrying each hour until the last retry, with both times read from the properties rwb.jobs.collins.start and rwb.jobs.collins.last-retry. After the 09:00 attempt with no load, write the run rows for INT-01 and INT-07 as MISSING, mark the products stale and show MSG-P1-001 with the date of the load in use. JOB-09 runs weekly on Monday at 04:00 for INT-10 and INT-11 and reads the files through the FileLoadAdapter built in RWB-E1-007; that job entry point also comes from that story. The idempotency key is the interface and the business date, with the file hash added for JOB-09.
RWB-E1-051.6: The job writes this row itself, under the service identity SY-DATALOAD, with no person involved. The interface_run table already exists from RWB-E1-007, so this story needs no migration; you read interface_config and read and write interface_run. Build FeedRunRecorder to write the row at the start of a run and to complete it at the end, and call it from CollinsIntakeJob and from FileLoadJob. The row holds the interface, the business date, the status, the record count and the start and end time, with the status one of LOADED, MISSING, FAILED, REFUSED and DUPLICATE. Keep the row to counts and times, with no customer data. The platform administrator and the data steward read these rows through GET /admin/jobs.
RWB-E1-051.7: The job does this with no person involved. On a failure, write the run row as FAILED or REFUSED and write the event rwb.integration.job.failed to Log Analytics. A structured event is a log record with named fields rather than a line of free text, so an alert rule can match on it. The alert rule itself, JobFailureAlert, is held as code in ops/monitoring/ and emails the data steward and the platform administrator with MSG-P2-004, which names the job, the time, the business date and the run book to follow. The target is 15 minutes from the failure, which is an assumption under DL11. Alerts arrive by email, since this story has no screen. Test the rule with a forced failure in SIT.
RWB-E1-051.8: The merge pipeline runs these tests, with no person involved. Write the four layout files in contracts/ from the interface specifications and the source to target mapping, each naming the field, type, length and whether it is mandatory, and put the synthetic sample files in src/test/resources/contracts/. Build LayoutContractImpl behind the LayoutContract interface to read a layout file and check a sample file against it, returning every field that differs. FeedContractTest is one parameterized test per interface, so one test body covers INT-01, INT-07, INT-10 and INT-11. A field whose name, type or length differs fails the test with MSG-P2-002 naming the field, and the merge is blocked, as AC3 shows for the SVAF field Appraised Value declared as a number of 18 digits with 2 decimals and supplied as text.

RWB-E1-063.1: JOB-15 starts on its own from its Quartz schedule at 01:30 Asia/Bangkok, with no person involved. The job already exists, so your work is one new step added after the ones already there: build AgentRunExtractStep as a Spring Batch step that the job calls for the previous business date. Keep it behind the feature flag rwb.agent.monitor, so that with the flag off JOB-15 runs its other steps and skips this one. The platform administrator can also start a run by hand with POST /admin/jobs/{jobId}/rerun under Platform administration U. The step reads its input through the P10 published interface AgentRunExtractSource rather than from another module tables.
RWB-E1-063.2: The step does this with no person involved. Build AgentMonitorService to read the agent_run rows whose run_at falls on the business date and group them by agent code, policy version, prompt version and model version. For each group work out the number of runs, how many were answered, how many used a fallback, the median and 95th percentile of latency_ms, the tokens from tokens_in and tokens_out, and the cost from cost_thb. The fallback rate is the runs with a fallback divided by the runs, to four decimals, so AC1 reads 0.0750 for 120 runs with 9 fallbacks. Add an index on agent_run (run_at) so the grouping reads one date. Test the aggregates on the fixture of 270 runs that AC1 and AC5 describe.
RWB-E1-063.3: The step does this on its own, in the same pass as the grouping. Read agent_evaluation for each agent and version and take the latest row whose status is DONE, so an evaluation still in progress is left out. Put its score on the group row in the eval_score column of the output table listed in section 12. The evaluation fields the story names are label_key, agreement_rate, precision_value and recall_value. An agent and version with no DONE evaluation leaves the column with no value, which the report then shows as having no score. The dashboard needs this joined here, because the report reads only the data lake table and never the live agent tables.
RWB-E1-063.4: The step writes and checks with no person involved. Write one row per group into the data lake table agent_run_daily, with the columns named in section 12. The write replaces the date: delete the rows already held for that business date in the same transaction as the new insert, so a rerun leaves the same rows and no duplicates. A transaction is a group of changes that either all take effect or none do. Then compare the number of rows written and the sum of runs with the source figures, with zero tolerance. When they differ, as AC3 shows with one row written for two groups, hold the publish, leave the previous day visible with the MSG-P1-001 banner, report the step failed in GET /admin/jobs and alert the data steward and the platform administrator.
RWB-E1-063.5: The step does this itself. Build CostAlertService and read both the cap and the alert role from agent_policy, where RW-COE loads them and RW-RISK approves them, so no cap sits in code. The test is strictly greater than: a cost equal to the cap raises nothing, which AC6 checks at 2,000.0000 baht. Create agent_alert with the migration V10_006__agent_alert.sql, the standard record columns and a unique key on agent code, alert type, segment and business date, so one alert exists per agent, type and date and a rerun writes no second one. The row holds alert type COST_CAP, the business date, the measured value, the threshold, the role sent to and the sent time. Send MSG-P10-004 through the P6 notification interface to the policy alert role and to RW-RISK; when that path is down, leave the sent time empty and let the outbox sender retry.
RWB-E1-063.6: A person does this: the risk and model risk officer, who holds Reporting R, and RW-COE reads the same report. The report is built and maintained by the reporting and BI analyst on the data lake table agent_run_daily, one page per agent with version filters, so no Workbench screen comes from this story; the agent monitor screen SCR-46 arrives in RWB-E2-031. The report has two states: loaded with the figures of the latest published date, and stale with the MSG-P1-001 banner naming the date shown, which is what a held publish looks like to the reader. A role without Reporting R is refused by the workspace with MSG-P4-002. Your part is finished when the page shows the fixture figures for 2026-12-01.

RWB-E2-007.1: Quartz starts this job; no person starts it. The trigger is daily and chained on an event: JOB-01 publishes LoadCompleted, event EV-26, when the ALS load for a business date has passed its checks, and JOB-08 runs after that. An event here is a message one module publishes that another consumes, rather than a direct call. Build BookingMatchJob so it runs for a business date only when that date load passed. A refused or late load means JOB-08 does not run for that date at all, and no missing booking task is raised for it, which AC5 checks with the load refused at DQ-003 Control total. MSG-P1-001 tells the user the product is from the earlier date.
RWB-E2-007.2: The job does this itself, under the service identity SY-DATALOAD. Build BookingMatchService and get the work list by calling TreatmentQuery.approvedNotBooked from RWB-E2-004 with the two treatment types RESTRUCTURE and SETTLEMENT. Read the treatments through that interface and not from the treatment table, because this story may reach treatments, accounts and tasks only through their published interfaces. A treatment stays in this list every night until it is marked booked, which is why a booking that is still missing on the next load needs no new list and raises no second task. The approval date the match uses is recorded by TreatmentApprovedListener, which consumes the TreatmentApproved event.
RWB-E2-007.3: The job makes this check in its own code. IdempotencyGuard comes from RWB-E1-007. Idempotent means that doing the same work a second time leaves the same result as doing it once. The key here is the treatment ID together with the business date, so for each treatment the guard answers whether this pair has already been handled. A treatment already handled for that date is skipped, which gives the behavior AC6 asks for when the platform administrator reruns JOB-08 for 2026-12-16: no second booking, no second TreatmentBooked event and no new task. Build this check before any match work, so a rerun costs nothing and changes nothing.
RWB-E2-007.4: The job reads this itself. Call AccountQuery.forCase in package recovery.data.api with the case ID and the business date, rather than reading loan_account. Read every account of the case, because a restructure counts as booked only when every account matches, and a case with one account booked out of two stays approved. The values the match needs from each account are tdr_flag, last_tdr_date, interest_rate, principal_outstanding, data_as_of, settlement_booked_date and settlement_booked_amount. The last two columns are new on loan_account and are added by P1 with the INT-01 mapping; their ALS source fields are still to confirm with the system owner. The match never calls ALS and works only on the loaded data.
RWB-E2-007.5: The job does this with no person involved. Build BookingMatchRules as a versioned rule table with one row per comparison: treatment type, ALS field, treatment field, comparison and tolerance, loaded by the center of excellence analyst and in force as a version such as BKG-2026.12. Build the comparison evaluator with a test for each row. For a restructure the rows compare tdr_flag, last_tdr_date and principal_outstanding against the offer amount, and the account interest rate against the approved rate; a restructure counts as booked when every account shows tdr_flag true with a last TDR date on or after the approval date. For a settlement the rows compare the settlement booked date and amount against the offer amount. The tolerance on amounts and rates is zero. The result per treatment is booked, missing, partly booked or differing.
RWB-E2-007.6: The job makes the call; the modules do the rest in their own code. Call TreatmentCommands.markBooked with the treatment ID, the business date and the booking reference, which is the account ID together with the business date and holds the account ID rather than the account number. That command writes the decision log entry first and throws DecisionLogUnavailableException when the log is not available; handle it by changing nothing, so the treatment stays APPROVED, no TreatmentBooked event goes out, an incident is raised with MSG-P7-003 and the next load tries the match again. On success the treatment state moves from APPROVED to BOOKED with its booked at date, the payments module publishes TreatmentBooked, and the case workflow module moves the case by rule R-RES-22 or R-SET-13, as AC1 shows from WITH_OPS_SETTLEMENT to AWAITING_PAYMENT.
RWB-E2-007.7: The job raises the task itself. Read the grace from the parameter booking.missing.grace_loads, one ALS load after approval, so a treatment is reported missing only after that many loads have been checked. Raise the task through TaskApi.raiseTask with the case ID, the task code, the owner role RW-RESTRUCT, the message ID and its parameters. That call returns the open task when one already exists for the same case, code and treatment, so the next night raises no second task and the open one stays, as AC7 requires. MSG-P2-011 names the treatment, the load date and the accounts with no booking, which is how the part-booked case in AC4 names account A-0705. The treatment state and the route state are left unchanged.
RWB-E2-007.8: The job does this with no person involved. Call TreatmentCommands.recordBookingDifference with the treatment ID and the list of differing terms; it writes them to the treatment column booking_difference, a jsonb column the treatment owner adds. Then raise one task with code UNMATCHED_EXCEPTION through TaskApi for the role RW-CREDITAD, the Credit Administration officer, with MSG-P2-012, which names the term with its booked value and its approved value. AC3 gives the example: an interest rate approved at 4.2500 and booked at 4.5000. The treatment stays APPROVED, so the next load checks it again. The restructuring officer and the Credit Administration officer see the difference on SCR-14 Treatment record, term by term, and their tasks on SCR-01 My work.
RWB-E2-007.9: The job writes the summary itself. Build BookingRunSummaryWriter to put the four counts, treatments read, booked, missing and differing, into the checks field of the interface_run row for the run. The reconciliation REC-03 compares approved treatments with bookings and reads those counts rather than counting again, so the figures the data steward sees come from this one place. REC-03 is where a treatment missing for more than one load shows up: AC7 has TRT-SYN-0702 on the break list as missing for two days. The target is zero after two days. The story is done when REC-03 over a week in SIT shows every synthetic approved treatment either booked or raised as a task.

RWB-E2-019.1: A person does this, the partner and agency manager, and it happens in the bank IAM rather than in the Workbench. The request names the firm, the partner role and the person business e-mail at that firm. There is no code to write for this step: partner users are requested by the partner and agency manager, approved by the role owner and created by the access administrator, all three in the bank IAM. Your code never creates a partner identity and never holds a partner e-mail, because a partner is referenced by the directory ID of the identity. The same manager also sets the firm panel status in the partner management module, which decides later whether a sign-in is allowed.
RWB-E2-019.2: Two people do this in the bank IAM, so that nobody both asks for access and grants it. The role owner approves the request at level 2 and the access administrator creates the identity at level 3. The identity is created in the partner identity directory, which is separate from bank identities and reachable from the external gateway in SIT and UAT; in production it waits for DL03. The administrator then adds the identity to the group of its partner role, one group per role and environment, for example RWB-SIT-PT-LAWFIRM. Your code builds none of this. What it reads later is the role table: the role code, the role class PARTNER_USER and the Entra group of each partner role.
RWB-E2-019.3: Two people do this. The reference data administrator loads the binding file through the shared reference load endpoint for the table partner_user, and the security administrator approves it, as the parameter rwb.refload.approver.partner_user says. The binding ties one directory identity to one firm and one partner role for a period; an identity with no active binding is refused. Create the table partner_user with the migration V_E2_019__partner_user.sql, holding id, identity_ref, partner_id, role_code, valid_from and valid_to with the standard columns, and a unique index on identity_ref and valid_from. Add no foreign key to partner, which is a column forced to match a row in another table, because partner belongs to the partner management module. Build PartnerUserLoader to check the partner IDs through the S9 interface, to allow partner role codes only, and to refuse an identity bound twice in one period.
RWB-E2-019.4: A person at the partner firm does this. Partners reach the Workbench only through the external gateway, and that route is theirs alone: a bank identity on it is refused, and a partner identity on the bank route is refused as well. The second factor is multi-factor authentication, a second proof of identity beyond the password, and the Workbench reads it from the token rather than asking for it again. Build PartnerSignInPage as the entry screen in the partner portal, with the refusal states for MSG-P4-008 and MSG-P4-001 and no data shown on either. Keep the whole partner route behind the feature flag rwb.access.partner-signin, which stays off in production until DL03 is approved.
RWB-E2-019.5: Code does this on every sign-in, with no person involved. Extend SessionResolver from RWB-E1-022 to tell the partner route from the bank route and to make four checks. The token has to come from the partner directory, so a bank identity on this route is refused with MSG-P4-001 and an AC-DENY entry with reason BANK_IDENTITY_ON_PARTNER_ROUTE. The amr claim, which is the list in the token of how the person proved who they are, has to hold "mfa", or the session is refused with 401 and MSG-P4-005. The identity has to map to exactly one partner role: two partner role groups, or a partner and a bank group together, are refused with MSG-P4-006 and an incident to the security administrator queue. Last, read the active binding from partner_user; with none, refuse with 401, MSG-P4-001 and reason NO_PARTNER_BINDING.
RWB-E2-019.6: Code does this check at sign-in. Build PartnerAccessService to call the S9 published interface for the firm, which returns the panel status and the contract end, and read neither from the partner table, because that table belongs to the partner management module. Allow the session only when the status is ACTIVE or ON_NOTICE and the contract end is today or later. A firm that is SUSPENDED or EXITED, or whose contract end has passed, means the sign-in is refused with MSG-P4-008 and an AC-DENY entry with reason PARTNER_NOT_ACTIVE, as AC3 shows for firm LF-0012 at 11:20. This check is what makes a firm lose access on the day it leaves the panel.
RWB-E2-019.7: Code builds the session, with no person involved. Add the scope type PLACED to ScopeFilter and return it from scopeFor for a partner session, carrying the partner ID and the instruction types of the role. PLACED means the session may see only the cases and instructions placed with that one firm. Take the instruction types from the parameters that name them per role, FILE_SUIT and ENFORCE for a law firm, APPRAISE for a valuer and COLLECT for an agency, owned by the partner and agency manager, so they stay data. Write one AC-SIGN entry in the decision log for the sign-in, in the same way as for a bank user, since the access log applies to partner users as well. GET /me/session returns the partner ID and the scope for the front end.
RWB-E2-019.8: The partner sees this screen; the endpoint behind it belongs to the partner management module, and this story supplies the scope filter it applies. PRT-01 Partner home has two states, Loading while the instructions are fetched and List showing the firm open instructions with their due dates. The S9 repository applies the PLACED filter inside its query, so an instruction of another firm never reaches the response: AC1 returns the 5 instructions of LF-0012 and none of LF-0019, and AC2 returns the 2 APPRAISE instructions of a valuer and not the LIST one. A direct request for an instruction of another firm answers 404 with MSG-P4-003 and no data. Write the repository test for those three cases in S9.
RWB-E2-019.9: Code does this on each request, and no job and no person ends the session. Build PartnerSessionRevalidation to read the binding from partner_user and the firm status from the S9 interface again once the refresh interval has passed, with the interval taken from the property rwb.access.membership-refresh-minutes, five minutes. A firm that changes during an open session therefore loses access at the first request after that interval: AC3 moves LF-0012 to EXITED at 11:00 and ends the session opened at 10:00 at its first request after 11:05. The permission matrix applies on every request as well, so a partner calling an endpoint outside the letters of the partner role, such as the queue list, is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002.

RWB-E2-035.1: The rules component does this with no person involved. A route set is the set of rule rows for a recovery route, and each row holds the from-state, the event, the to_state, the action text, the owner role, the timer and the rule ID and version. The firing rule is the one row whose from-state and event match what just happened on the case. The center of excellence analyst owns the action, owner and timer columns of those rows, and they are loaded as data in RWB-E1-029, so no action text ever sits in your code. There is nothing to build in this step itself. What follows depends on it: your code is handed the firing rule row and copies from it.
RWB-E2-035.2: The case workflow module does this; no person is involved. Your change is one call: from the transition service built in RWB-E1-018, call NextActionAssigner.assign with the case ID, the firing rule and the business date, inside the transaction that already holds the move. A transaction is a group of database changes that either all take effect or none do, so a case never carries its new state with the next action of the old one. Two transitions committing on one case at once are handled by the optimistic lock on the case row, which refuses the second commit against a changed version: it answers MSG-GEN-004, is retried against the new version, and leaves the next action of the rule that committed last.
RWB-E2-035.3: The assigner does this in code, and no person ever types a next action. Add the columns to recovery_case with a migration in the P3 migration folder: next_action_text varchar(1000), next_action_owner_role varchar(20), next_action_due_date date, next_action_rule_id varchar(20) and next_action_waiting boolean not null default false, with the partial index named in section 13 for cases with no due date. Build NextActionAssigner to write the action text, the owner role and the rule ID from the firing rule row onto those columns. For the owner shown to a reader, compare the rule owner role with the role code of the case queue: when they are the same, show the case owner named on the case, and otherwise show the role name read through the P4 reference data interface.
RWB-E2-035.4: Code does this with no person involved. Build TimerSpecResolver as pure functions that take the timer text, the to_state, the date of the move and the holiday list. The patterns are fixed in BR3: "n working days" adds that many working days, "n days" with any label before it adds that many calendar days, "same day" and "immediate" give the date of the move, and "next working day" adds one working day. Any other text, "None" among it, means reading the service levels and timers table for the to_state through the P4 reference data interface. Working days are Monday to Friday, less the dates in the bank holiday list under the configuration key rwb.calendar.bank-holidays. Keep durations for named states out of the parser, which recognizes patterns only. Build the pattern table from the rule rows in force and unit test AC5, AC7 and AC12.
RWB-E2-035.5: The assigner does this in code. Read the owner role through the P4 reference data interface, which returns the role name and the role class, and set next_action_waiting to true when that class is Customer party or Partner user. The screen then shows the text starting "Waiting for" and the owner name before the action text, as AC3 reads: "Waiting for Customer (borrower): Set the payment due date and wait for the money", with the wait ending on 13 January 2027. A wait is a valid next action, so a case in this state raises no exception task and is not on the list of cases with no next action. The flag is a column on the case, so the list and the record both read it from the same place.
RWB-E2-035.6: The assigner does this with no person involved. It happens when the rule timer has no fixed duration and the service levels and timers table holds no row for the to_state, which is AC6 with rule R-DEV-05 moving a case to DEV_WITH_OWNER. Write the action text and the owner role as usual, leave the due date empty, and write one task row with task code NEXT_ACTION_MISSING, element type HUMAN_TASK, discretion REQUIRED and owner role RW-TEAMMGR, for the team manager of the case team. The case record then shows the warning MSG-P2-023 naming that team, and the team manager works the task on SCR-09 Exception queue. At most one open task exists per case, and the task is canceled when the case closes.
RWB-E2-035.7: This runs as a step in an existing job, with no person involved. Build NextActionCheckStep inside JOB-05 Timer check, which runs every five minutes, and have it select active cases whose next action rule ID or due date is empty, using the partial index on the case table. For each such case, call the P7 decision log query for the latest state change, which returns the rule that last moved the case, and fill the next action fields from that rule. AC11 is the case to test: three active cases moved by R-RES-04 on 11 December 2026 come out with the due date of 15 December 2026 after a run on 14 December. Where no rule can be found, raise the NEXT_ACTION_MISSING task, once only. A case the run misses is picked up by the next run.
RWB-E2-035.8: A person opens the case record and the browser makes the call. Build NextActionController for the new endpoint and NextActionPanel for the SCR-03 header. The response holds the action text, the owner role, the owner name, the owner user ID where the case owner is the one shown, the due date, and the flags for waiting, overdue and missing, with the rule ID and version. The panel shows the action, its owner and its due date, or the waiting text with the wait end date, marks an overdue action with the word Overdue, and shows MSG-P2-023 when the action is missing. A reader without Case record R is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002, which is the access test, and a case outside their scope answers 404 with MSG-P4-003.
RWB-E2-035.9: A person reads this, and the work is in the list and export responses. Add nextAction, nextActionOwner, nextActionDueDate and nextActionOverdue to each Case item returned by the case list endpoint and to each row of the export, read from the same columns on the case, with the authorization and errors left as RWB-E2-033 set them. An action is overdue when its due date is earlier than today and the case is not closed, so in AC4, read on 16 December 2026, the case due 15 December is marked Overdue and the case due 13 January 2027 is not. With the feature flag rwb.casewf.next-action off, these columns and the panel are hidden. The story is done when the report of active cases with no next action reads zero on the SIT data set after JOB-05 has run.

RWB-E1-003.1: Migration: creates the tables, columns and keys listed in section 11.
RWB-E1-003.2: Build: creates the entities, repositories, mapper/check/service classes listed in section 13.
RWB-E1-003.3: Build: registers the endpoint and published-interface contracts.
RWB-E1-003.4: Deferred: job scheduling, load execution and validation; see the data load reference.

RWB-E1-015.1: Nothing new is built at this step. It is the moment a load job finishes its write and commits, and it happens on its own. JOB-01 is the COLLINS load check and intake built in RWB-E1-003, and JOB-09 loads the weekly and monthly file products. Commit means the database has accepted every row of that load as one unit of work. The stamp of step 2 has to be written inside that same unit, so each load job needs a hook at its commit point rather than a call that runs afterward. Every Epic 1 load job has to call recordLoad, which is part of the done condition of this story.
RWB-E1-015.2: The load job calls this; no person types the times. Build FreshnessStampService.recordLoad with product code, business date, source extract time and load time, and a Flyway migration for data_product_load holding id, product_code, source_system, business_date, source_extracted_at, loaded_at, status, stale_flagged_at, duplicate_count and the standard columns, unique on product_code and business_date, with an index on product_code and loaded_at descending. Flyway applies versioned SQL files in order, so every environment reaches the same schema. The source extract time is when the source system took the data, read from the COLLINS control record; the load time is when the Workbench wrote it. A repeat for the same product and date adds 1 to duplicate_count and writes no second row.
RWB-E1-015.3: This runs on a schedule, not on request. Build FreshnessCheckStep and create one Quartz trigger per product from the data_product rows, each firing at that product's expected_by time in Asia/Bangkok. DP01 is daily at 08:00 and DP06 is weekly at Monday 08:00. The step reads data_product, then looks for a data_product_load row for the expected business date. Cycles and times are data rows, so a new product or a changed time needs no code change. A weekly product inside its cycle has to be left alone on the days between loads, which is AC8. Tests run against a fixed test clock rather than the real clock.
RWB-E1-015.4: The same scheduled step does this. When no load for the expected business date is present, set status STALE and stale_flagged_at on the product's latest data_product_load row, raise one data quality exception row with the product code and check FRESHNESS in the list built in RWB-E1-006, and send the alert to the channel named by the property rwb.dataengine.freshness.alert-channel. Loaded rows are never changed or removed, so the previous load stays in use for every reader. A rerun after a failure must not raise a second exception for the same product and day, so look for an open exception for that product and date before writing one.
RWB-E1-015.5: This is event driven and needs no person and no clock. Build a listener on LoadRefused, EV-27, which the load job of RWB-E1-003 publishes when a check refuses a load, and set the product STALE as soon as the event is handled rather than waiting for the expected-by time. AC4 sets DP01 stale from 05:20, the time of the refusal. The listener is idempotent on the event ID, which means handling the same event twice leaves the same result and writes nothing a second time, so keep the event ID and check it before acting. The stamp for the business date already in use stays in use.
RWB-E1-015.6: Other modules and the front end read the stamp here; no person acts. Build the published interface FreshnessQuery in package recovery.dataengine.freshness.api with stampFor, stampForRow and stampsFor, and FreshnessController for GET /data-products/freshness with optional product and asOf query values. The response is DataProductFreshness with productCode, productName, businessDate, sourceExtractedAt, loadedAt, status and staleSince. Authorization is Case record R and no case scope applies, because the stamp holds no case data. A malformed product code or date answers 400 with MSG-GEN-001. P3 and P7 read stamps only through this interface and never read data_product_load.
RWB-E1-015.7: A person reads this on the screen. Build DataFreshnessPanel, a React component in the data panel of SCR-03 Case record, showing each product with its business date and its load time. When a product is STALE the panel shows MSG-P1-001 beside it, in the form Account and arrears is from 2026-11-30. Today's load has not arrived. The Loading state shows skeleton rows while the call runs. The reader needs Case record R, so case roles such as the case owner and the team manager see it, and the Thai text of the message follows decision DL10.
RWB-E1-015.8: The decision log writer does this while it records a decision. The inputs_ref column on decision_log_entry points at a snapshot of the values a decision read, and this step adds the freshness of each of those products to that snapshot. Pass the set of product codes to stampsFor, which returns one stamp per code in a single call, then write each stamp into the snapshot. The snapshot itself belongs to RWB-E1-027; the work here is the interface and the call. AC3 expects the snapshot to list DP01 and DP06 with their load times and status LOADED. This story writes no P7 table.
RWB-E1-015.9: The arriving load does this through the same recordLoad call. A load that commits after the product was flagged sets status LOADED on the row for that business date with the new load time, clears the stale flag and closes the open FRESHNESS exception for that product and day. AC6 has DP01 flagged at 08:00 on 2026-12-01 and the load committing at 08:40, after which the status reads LOADED with load time 08:40. The row is found by the unique key on product_code and business_date, so this changes the existing row rather than adding another one.

RWB-E1-027.1: The calling module does this, not the code of this story. A module such as the case workflow module under identity SY-CASEWF fills a DecisionLogRecord with the case, the decision code, the rule ID and rule version, the inputs reference, the actor, the final call, decidedAt and an idempotency key, while its own transaction is open. Build Epic1DecisionRecords with one builder per Epic 1 event: case created, owner assigned, case transferred and document attached. Each builder takes its decision code from the parameter catalog keys rwb.decision.code.CASE_CREATED, OWNER_ASSIGNED, CASE_TRANSFERRED and DOCUMENT_ATTACHED, so no decision code is written in Java. The idempotency key is the event ID the calling module already holds.
RWB-E1-027.2: The caller makes this call. Wire JOB-02, JOB-03, the transfer engine of RWB-E1-021 and document attach of RWB-E1-032 to call the published interface DecisionLogWriter.write in package recovery.decision.writer. The call is placed last so that everything the action changes is already in the transaction when the record is written, which lets a failed write take the whole action back with it. An architecture test has to fail the build when any class outside recovery.decision writes to decision_log_entry, which keeps this interface the only write path. The method hands back a DecisionLogEntryRef with entryId, chainSeq, entryHash and a repeated flag.
RWB-E1-027.3: The writer does this first, with no person involved. Mark the write method @Transactional with Propagation.MANDATORY. MANDATORY means the method joins the caller's open transaction and never starts one of its own, so Spring raises IllegalTransactionStateException when a caller has no transaction and nothing at all is written. That setting is what makes a refused record stop the action: the entry and the action share one unit of work, which either commits together or rolls back together. Build DecisionLogWriterService in folder recovery/decision/writer and test the refusal with a caller that has no transaction open, which is AC6.
RWB-E1-027.4: The writer does this before any write. Add Flyway migration V_E1_027__declog_idempotency.sql with the column idempotency_key varchar(80) on decision_log_entry and the unique index uk_declog_idempotency. Idempotent means the same call made twice leaves the same single result. Look the key up through DecisionCenterAndLogRepository; on a hit, hand back the first entry's reference with repeated set to true and add 1 to the repeat count, which is exposed as the metric decision_log_repeats_total in the monitoring of RWB-E1-056. AC5 sends the document attached event twice with key EV-7f3a-0001 and expects one entry and the first entry's ID in the reply.
RWB-E1-027.5: The validator runs inside the writer. Build DecisionLogRecordValidator for the three rules of section 8. BR2 needs a decision code that is in LOV-DECISION, the inputs reference, the final call, decided at and the actor, plus the case unless the decision code is an access event. BR3 needs at least one of rule version, model version and agent version, and a rule ID always needs its rule version. BR4 needs an approval level from LOV-APPROVAL-LEVEL on any record that names an approver. A failure throws DecisionLogRecordInvalidException carrying MSG-P7-009 and the field name, and the writer logs the case ID with that field name alone.
RWB-E1-027.6: The writer calls the store that RWB-E1-008 built. That store appends hash-chained entries: each row carries chain_seq and a hash computed over the previous entry, so a later change to an entry can be found. Nothing of the chain is built here; this story only appends through it and reads back the entry reference. When the store cannot be written, the append raises DecisionLogUnavailableException, which carries MSG-P7-003. The columns chain_seq, corrects_entry_id and actor_user_id already exist in that store, so pass the values from the record through instead of adding columns.
RWB-E1-027.7: The writer does this in the same breath as the append. Build DecisionRecordedPublisher to write EV-08 DecisionRecorded, with entryId, caseId, decisionCode and approver, into the ACE outbox of RWB-TE-006. The outbox is a table in the same database, so the event row joins the caller's transaction: a rollback leaves no event and a commit leaves exactly one. Test the rollback case and check the outbox is empty, as section 13 build step 4 asks. The ledger and reporting consume the event later, and nothing is sent to a broker from inside the write.
RWB-E1-027.8: The calling module commits, and the database writes the action's own changes, the decision log entry and the outbox event as one unit. No code of this story runs at this point. AC1 shows the result: two entries for the case with final calls CASE_CREATED and OWNER_ASSIGNED, the second carrying rule ID ALLOC-MTG-BKK-01, rule version ALLOC-2026.11, actor SY-CASEWF and an inputs reference, with two DecisionRecorded events in the outbox. Both entries also have to pass the schema check, so the validator of step 5 and the commit here are tested together in TC-E1-027-01.
RWB-E1-027.9: The writer throws and does nothing else. It never retries; the caller's job or request is what tries again. The exception travels out through the caller's transaction, which rolls back, so the action does not happen: in AC4 the case owner stays empty and the case status stays New. An incident goes to the platform administrator queue through the monitoring of RWB-E1-056. The caller chooses what a user sees, either MSG-P7-003 for a store failure or its own message, such as MSG-P3-013 on the allocation summary when a case was not allocated.

RWB-E1-040.1: Two people are involved and nothing starts on its own. The reference data administrator, RW-REFADM with Reference data C, sends a multipart request to POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/reference-loads with the file, table set to DOCUMENT_CHECKLIST and a validFrom date. A second person holding Reference data A approves it, and the response of the load itself is 201 ReferenceLoad. No role holds Reference data A in the permission matrix today, so the right is assumed granted to the legal counsel as co-owner of the checklist under DL01. The version for this release is CHK-2026.11. Stages, routes and required types stay rows, never code.
RWB-E1-040.2: The loader runs on its own when a file arrives. Build ChecklistLoader against the ReferenceTableLoader interface for table DOCUMENT_CHECKLIST. Check each row: the stage is in LOV-STAGE, the route is in LOV-ROUTE or empty, the document type is in the document type table in force from RWB-E1-025, and no row repeats. One bad row refuses the whole file, nothing is written, and the version already in force keeps serving. Row errors answer 422 with MSG-P3-027 naming the row and the error, and a version already loaded answers 409 with the same message. AC7 is the test, with type POWER_OF_ATTORNEY absent from the type table.
RWB-E1-040.3: The evaluator runs on events, with no person pressing anything. Build ChecklistEvaluator plus two listeners, DocumentStoredChecklistListener for DocumentStored, EV-16, and CaseStateChangedChecklistListener for CaseStateChanged, EV-05. Each listener keeps the event ID so a second delivery of the same event is ignored and counted, and after the retry limit the event goes to the exception queue with the platform administrator as owner. The evaluator asks the P3 published interface CaseDirectory for stage_code, route_code and owner, and never reads the P3 tables. The third trigger is the job step of step 8. The evaluator only reports and never blocks a case from moving stage.
RWB-E1-040.4: The evaluator does this as part of each recompute. Read from document_checklist_item the rows whose table_version is in force on the business date and whose stage_code matches the case stage. Where rows exist for the case route, use those; where none exist for the route, use the rows with an empty route. Index ix_checklist_stage on stage_code and valid_from supports the read. A version takes effect on its valid_from date with no deployment, so the date decides which rows apply rather than a release. When the stage has no rows at all, the result is the empty checklist of exception path X1, which AC6 tests at stage DEBT_SALE.
RWB-E1-040.5: The evaluator writes the result; no person edits it. Count documents on the case by document_type where is_active is true, counting each type once even when the case holds several versions of one document, so an appraisal report at version 2 with version 1 inactive counts as one present. Write one case_document_check row per case, unique on case_id, holding checklist_version, required_count, present_count, missing_types as jsonb, complete, checked_at and last_event_id. The complete flag is false while a required type is missing, true when every required type is present, and empty when the stage has no checklist. AC3 expects complete false, missing count 1 and missing type SETTLEMENT_AGREEMENT.
RWB-E1-040.6: A person reads the result here. Extend the endpoint that RWB-E1-026 built as a placeholder so GET /api/recovery/v1/cases/{caseId}/document-checklist returns DocumentChecklist with caseId, checklistVersion, stageCode, items holding documentType, label, required and presentCount, plus missingCount and complete. Build DocumentChecklistPanel, the React component that replaces the placeholder on SCR-30, with skeleton rows in its Loading state and MSG-P5-023 above the list when a type is missing. Authorization is Documents R with scope applied, so a role without the right is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002, and a case outside the reader's scope with MSG-P4-003.
RWB-E1-040.7: The case owner reads this, and the count comes from the stored flag rather than a fresh count per row. Build the published interface DocumentChecklistService with forCase and missingCounts, where missingCounts takes up to 500 case IDs in one call and returns the missing count per case. The P3 case list calls it, because P3 never reads case_document_check itself. Build MissingDocumentsBadge for the SCR-02 rows, showing nothing when the count is 0, and let the list be filtered to cases with one or more missing documents. AC3 expects the owner to see 1 missing for the deed in lieu case.
RWB-E1-040.8: The job step runs on a schedule. Add ChecklistRefreshStep to JOB-12 Document intake. Each run looks for checklist versions whose valid from date has been reached since the previous run, then recomputes case_document_check for the cases sitting at the stages those versions change. Without this step a case already at its stage would keep its old counts until its next document or stage event. AC2 is the test: version CHK-2026.12 adds GUARANTOR_NOTICE for DEED_IN_LIEU from 1 December 2026, and the case opened that day shows four items, with no code deployed between 30 November and 1 December 2026.

RWB-E1-052.1: The caller is the case workflow module under SY-CASEWF, or a person later through the endpoint of RWB-E2-021. Epic 1 has no endpoint at all, so build the published interface NoticeApi in package recovery.comms.notices with generate taking a NoticeGenerationRequest of caseId, noticeType, partyId, language, requestedBy and businessDate, and returning NoticeResult with noticeId, state, documentId, holdReason, templateVersion and messageCodes. The method throws TemplateNotApprovedException, PartyNotOnCaseException and DecisionNotRecordedException. NoticeGenerationService sits behind the interface and carries out steps 2 to 9 without any further input from the caller.
RWB-E1-052.2: The service does this on its own. Call CaseWorkflowApi.getCaseSummary for the case number, product group and status, and CaseWorkflowApi.getCaseParties for the parties on the case. Both are P3 published interfaces, and this module reads neither recovery_case nor case_party directly. The product group decides which template applies in step 3, and the party list is what makes the check of exception path X7 possible: a party that is not on the case is refused with MSG-P4-003, which AC8 tests with party P-0999 on case RC-2026-000123.
RWB-E1-052.3: The service reads the catalog built in RWB-E1-046; no person picks a template. TemplateCatalog returns the version that is Approved and current for that notice type, product group and language on the business date. Two outcomes end generation here. With no Approved version the call is refused with MSG-P6-005 naming the template and version, and no notice row and no document are created, which AC2 tests with RECALL-HP version 1 in Draft. With the current version Withdrawn and no later approved version, write the notice in state Held with hold reason TEMPLATE_WITHDRAWN and raise a task to the litigation officer team with MSG-P6-003.
RWB-E1-052.4: The service resolves the values; nobody keys them. Build MergeValueResolver.
