If any check from steps 3 to 5 failed, refuse the load whole and name every failing row and test case in the Problem detail with MSG-P3-027; the version takes status REFUSED and the version in force keeps working. If everything passed, write the rows to rule_row with rule_table, row_order and target_queue_code, and write the rule_version header with status LOADED, in one transaction, which is a single unit of database work that either completes in full or leaves both tables untouched. That header is the change log: version label, author, load time, check result and dry run counts. Only P4 code writes rule_row.
RWB-E1-029.7: A second person has to approve, and it cannot be the person who loaded. RW-RISK calls POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/rule-versions/{versionId}/approve with the Rules and parameters A right, and the version moves from LOADED to APPROVED. Compare the approver user ID with the author on the rule_version header: when they match, answer 409 with MSG-P7-002 and leave the status at LOADED. The same answer applies when the version is not in LOADED status. Approval alone changes no decision; it clears the version for its valid-from date. RW-REFADM may prepare load files and may never approve.
RWB-E1-029.8: No one triggers this. RuleEffectiveDateJob runs daily at 00:01 and sets every APPROVED version whose valid-from date is today to IN_FORCE, marking the version it replaces SUPERSEDED, which flips is_active on the rule_row rows. From that moment RuleTableReader.rowsInForce answers with the new rows for that table and date, cached per version, and every new decision uses them. A case already decided keeps the rule version recorded on its decision log entry, so a case allocated under ALLOC-2026.13 still shows that label after a later version arrives. The partial index ix_rule_table_version over rule_table and rule_version where is_active serves this read.
RWB-E1-029.9: A person calls this once and the code does the rest. POST /admin/rule-versions/{versionId}/rollback is a new endpoint you build; it takes a required reason in the body, an Idempotency-Key header, and the Rules and parameters U right. In one transaction, set is_active false on the rolled-back version and true on the previous one, so readers never see a moment with no version in force. Record the rollback in the change log with the caller, the time and the reason. When the table has no earlier version, answer 409 with MSG-P3-015, as with TRANSFER holding only TRF-2026.11. A missing reason answers 422 with MSG-GEN-001.

RWB-E1-042.1: A squad member does this as a code change. The parameter is a line added to config/parameter-catalog.csv with key, kind, type, unit, range, default, scope, required flag, owner role, environments and the packages that use it. The pull request goes to the owner named on the line for review, following the code owner rule. Your work is the column set, because two build tools and a generated migration read this file. An environment setting and a secret each get a catalog line as well; the value of a secret lives only in the ACE secret store and never in the file. The Epic 1 lines include case.entry.dpd with default 90.
RWB-E1-042.2: The build does this, not a developer by hand. ParameterKeysGenerator reads config/parameter-catalog.csv and writes the ParameterKeys class, giving each catalog line a typed constant such as ParameterKeys.CASE_ENTRY_DPD of type ParameterKey<Integer>. Application code then reads a value only through ParameterService.get with one of those constants and a business date. Because the constants are generated, a key the catalog does not list will not compile, and the type on the key stops an integer parameter being read as text. Wire the generator into the build so the class is written again whenever the catalog file changes.
RWB-E1-042.3: Both checks run in the pipeline on every pull request. RwbMagicNumberCheck scans the recovery packages for numeric and text business literals; 0, 1, -1 and test code are allowed. When it finds one it fails the build and names the file, the line, and any catalog key whose default equals that literal, so a hard-coded 90 points at case.entry.dpd. CatalogCompletenessCheck compares the keys that services read through ParameterService with the lines in the catalog file and fails on a key that is missing, or on a catalog line with no owner or no default. Both live in build-tools/rwb-checks.
RWB-E1-042.4: This happens at deployment with nobody present. Flyway is the migration runner: it applies numbered SQL files to each environment in order and records which ones have run. V042_1__parameter_catalog.sql creates parameter_catalog, keyed on param_key, and parameter_value, which holds one row per key, environment, product group and version number. V042_2__parameter_seed.sql is generated from the catalog file and inserts the seed rows, meaning the first rows a table needs in order to work: the catalog lines themselves and their default values. The schema name in both files comes from the Flyway placeholder, so the same files run in every environment.
RWB-E1-042.5: A person loads the new value. RW-COE calls POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/reference-loads with table set to PARAMETER and a file whose rows hold key, environment and value, plus the valid-from date. The example sets case.entry.dpd to 91 for PROD from 2026-12-10. The caller needs the Reference data C right. The idempotency key is the table, the valid-from date and the content hash of the file together, so sending the same file again returns the load that already exists instead of making a second one. This story builds the PARAMETER handler behind that existing endpoint.
RWB-E1-042.6: Your checks run automatically when the file arrives. ParameterLoadChecks reads the catalog line for each key in the file and verifies that the key is listed, that the value parses as the declared type, that it falls inside min_value and max_value, that the environment is one the line allows, and that a required parameter ends up with a value. One bad row refuses the whole load; nothing partial is written. A value of 400 for case.entry.dpd answers 422 with MSG-GEN-002 naming 1 and 365, and a value of ninety answers MSG-P1-002 with the check that the value is not INTEGER. The version already in force keeps serving.
RWB-E1-042.7: A second person approves, and the author cannot. The owner named on the catalog line calls POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/reference-loads/{loadId}/approve with the Reference data A right; where the change moves a threshold or a limit, RW-RISK approves instead. Compare the approver with the author of the load and answer 409 with MSG-P7-002 when they are the same user, leaving the version at VALIDATED. Approval moves the version to APPROVED. Approval changes no value yet: the version waits for its valid-from date, which is why a version approved on 2026-12-05 still answers with the old value on 2026-12-09.
RWB-E1-042.8: This is all code. ParameterService resolves a read by key, environment and the business date passed in, so an approved version starts answering on its valid-from date with no deployment and no restart. Each instance keeps a cache of values; publish ParameterVersionApproved to the outbox when a version is approved, carrying the keys, the version number and the valid-from date, and have every instance reload those keys when it receives the event. The cache also expires on its own after config.cache.ttl-seconds, which is 60, so an instance that missed the event still picks the value up. The result carries the version number.
RWB-E1-042.9: The engines do this as part of their own work. A read answers with a ParameterValue holding the key, the typed value, the version number, the valid-from date and the environment, and the caller writes that version number into the inputs it records on its decision log entry. The entry decision in the acceptance criteria records parameter version 1 alongside the value 90. This is what lets a decision be explained later: the inputs name the version in force when the decision was taken, and a decision already taken keeps that version after a newer one starts. Pass the business date on every call.
RWB-E1-042.10: Any role holding the Rules and parameters R right calls this, and you build the endpoint. GET /admin/parameters takes optional key prefix, kind, owner and environment filters and answers with one entry per parameter: key, kind, type, unit, min, max, default, scope, required flag, owner, environments, usedBy, secret flag, the value in force, its version number and its valid-from date. ParameterCatalogController leaves the value out when the line is marked secret, so ace.db.password shows its owner, environments and usedBy with no value anywhere in the response. A role without the right gets 403 with MSG-P4-002.

RWB-E1-054.1: A person opens the screen. SCR-31 Document review queue is new in this story, built as the React component ReviewQueuePage with four states: skeleton rows while the queue loads, the list itself, the state after an item is resolved, and the empty state showing the text No documents are waiting for review. The officer holds RW-LITOFF with the Documents CRU rights and team scope. The screen appears only when the feature flag rwb.dochub.review is on; with the flag off, the queue is hidden and the items waiting in it are left untouched.
RWB-E1-054.2: The list is assembled by code as soon as the screen opens. ReviewQueueService answers GET /review-items and brings three groups into one list: intake items that carry a review_reason and no case, shown to the review team named in the document_hub_parameter row REVIEW_TEAM_UNATTACHED; intake items whose candidate cases fall in the officer's scope; and stored documents with review_status PENDING on cases in scope. Order by the time received, oldest first, and page at REVIEW_PAGE_SIZE, which is 50. Each row carries the reason, the proposed type, the type candidates with their confidence, and the age. Two partial indexes in your migration serve these reads.
RWB-E1-054.3: The officer picks a row, and the detail arrives from two endpoints you build. GET /intake-items/{intakeItemId} answers with the item: source, time received, review reason, predicted type and candidates, the candidate cases with their status, the page text, and the extracted fields with their state. GET /intake-items/{intakeItemId}/content answers with the file itself for the viewer. Mark every field whose state is REVIEW so the officer sees what needs a decision. Field values are masked for roles that may not see them. An item on a case outside the officer's scope answers 404 with MSG-P4-003 rather than revealing that it exists.
RWB-E1-054.4: The officer chooses, and your code reacts. Keeping the type needs no call. Choosing another type is POST /intake-items/{intakeItemId}/resolve with action SET_TYPE, and you check the chosen type against the type version in force through DocumentTypeCatalog; a type outside that list answers 422 with MSG-P5-006 naming the value, as with PAYSLIP. For a type that is in force, call FieldExtraction.extractIntake so extraction runs again for the new type, then show the new field set with every field in state REVIEW. The fields of the old type are no longer offered: a demand letter changed to a guarantor notice shows the four guarantor notice fields.
RWB-E1-054.5: The officer supplies the case. The candidate cases already on the item come from the matching step; when none of them is right, the officer types a case number and your code resolves it with CaseDirectory.findByCaseNo, a published P3 interface. Use that same call to read the case status, because a closed case is refused later with MSG-P5-005. Never query the case tables directly; the case module owns them and CaseDirectory is the only way in. The case chosen here also decides whose scope the item falls in.
RWB-E1-054.6: Field by field, the officer decides and your endpoint saves. Confirm keeps the extracted value; Correct replaces it. Both go through PATCH /api/recovery/v1/documents/{documentId}/fields/{fieldId} with an If-Match header holding the document version the officer loaded, which lets the server refuse a save made against an older version. Validate the entered value against the field data type, and a date against the document_hub_parameter rows REVIEW_DATE_MIN and REVIEW_DATE_MAX, which hold 2000-01-01 and 2100-12-31, so a Buddhist year such as 2569-12-16 falls outside and answers 422 with MSG-GEN-002. An empty value on a Correct answers 422 with MSG-GEN-001. Keep the original in extracted_value and write the officer into confirmed_by.
RWB-E1-054.7: The officer presses Attach and a chain of checks runs before anything is stored. Refuse with 422 when a field is still in state REVIEW (MSG-GEN-001), when the type is not in force (MSG-P5-006), or when the chosen case is closed (MSG-P5-005). When the file hash already belongs to a document on that case, link the item to the existing document instead of storing a second one and show MSG-P5-024. Otherwise call DocumentStore.store from RWB-E1-024 with the case, the type and the fields; it writes the document, its fields and the DOCATT decision log entry, and places a legal type in the write-once container. A failed decision log write stores nothing and answers MSG-P7-003.
RWB-E1-054.8: This is bookkeeping your code does inside the same unit of work as the attach. Set review_outcome to ATTACHED on the intake item, with resolved_by and resolved_at, and set the document review_status: CONFIRMED when the type, the case and every value were kept as extracted, CORRECTED when any of them changed. Then publish DocumentFieldsExtracted, event EV-17. The four columns review_outcome, resolved_by, resolved_at and discard_reason are added to document_intake by the migration V1_5_054__review_outcome.sql in this story. An item with an outcome drops out of the queue, which is why the queue index looks for a review_reason with no review_outcome.
RWB-E1-054.9: This is the second kind of item in the queue, and the officer works it the same way. For a document already stored whose field is in state REVIEW, the officer confirms or corrects with the PATCH call from step 6, then finishes with POST /documents/{documentId}/review carrying action COMPLETE and the document version. Refuse with 422 and MSG-GEN-001 while any field is still in REVIEW, and with 409 and MSG-GEN-004 when the version sent is older than the stored one. On success set review_status to CONFIRMED or CORRECTED by the same rule as step 8. RWB-E2-017 reuses this action for generated drafts.
RWB-E1-054.10: Nobody clicks this; another module pulls the data. Build LabeledSetReader as a published P5 interface with resolvedSince(since, limit), answering with each resolved item as a labeled example: the intake or document ID, the predicted type, the confirmed type, and per field the name, the extracted value, the confirmed value, the confidence and the extractor version. The model evaluations in RWB-E1-060 call it; those evaluations are out of scope here, so your part ends at the interface and its tests. The examples hold real field values, so they stay inside the bank and go into no log and no prompt.

RWB-E1-066.1: A person records the call. POST /api/recovery/v1/cases/{caseId}/interactions is the existing P3 endpoint API-P3-015, so you change its handler rather than add a route. The case owner sends the channel CALL, the direction OUTBOUND, the contact result RIGHT_PARTY and a summary, and the example also carries a promise of 25,000.00 baht for 2026-12-15. The caller needs the Case record C right and the case in scope. Epic 1 has no screen for this; the case record view SCR-03 shows the entries later through RWB-E1-068. A successful call answers 201 with the stored Interaction.
RWB-E1-066.2: The handler runs the access checks first and then opens the unit of work the whole step depends on. Check the Case record C right and the case scope: a missing right answers 403 with MSG-P4-002, and a case that does not exist or sits outside the scope answers 404 with MSG-P4-003. Then open a database transaction, which is one unit of work that either commits in full or leaves the database unchanged, and call InteractionLedgerWriter.append inside it. The writer is marked Propagation.MANDATORY, meaning it refuses to run unless a caller has already opened such a transaction. The entry and the action it records therefore commit together.
RWB-E1-066.3: Validation is the first thing inside the writer, before any lock or insert. Check that the case ID is present, that the event code is a value of the list LOV-LEDGER-EVENT, which holds CONTACT, LETTER, PROMISE, PAYMENT, HANDOVER, CASE_CREATED, CASE_ALLOCATED, CASE_TRANSFERRED, CASE_ESCALATED, DOCUMENT_ATTACHED, DECISION_TAKEN and CORRECTION, and that the occurred time, the actor type, the actor reference, the source system and the source reference are all there. A missing value answers 422 with MSG-GEN-001 naming the field and writes nothing, as in the test where append is called with no event code. The reference data administrator loads that list.
RWB-E1-066.4: The writer assigns the position in the case history itself. Take a transaction-level advisory lock on the case ID with pg_advisory_xact_lock: an advisory lock is a lock on a number of your choosing rather than on a row, and a transaction-level one is released when the transaction ends. While it is held, no other transaction can be assigning a sequence number for the same case. Read the highest case_seq for that case and add 1. The unique key over case_id and case_seq catches any clash, so retry once on a unique key violation. Two appends at the same moment therefore take 7 and 8, with no gap.
RWB-E1-066.5: The insert happens in code with no person involved. Write one interaction row carrying the event code, the actor type and actor reference, the source system and source reference, and the case_seq from step 4. Channel and direction go in where the event has them; a Workbench event such as CASE_CREATED has neither, which is why the migration drops NOT NULL on those two columns. For a decision, put the decision log entry ID in decision_log_id and leave the rule, the version and the inputs to the decision log itself. A correction carries corrects_entry_id naming the entry it corrects, since no entry is ever edited.
RWB-E1-066.6: The handler finishes the work it opened in step 2. Commit once: the action the user asked for and the ledger entry both sit in the transaction opened before the writer was called, so either both are saved or neither is. Then answer 201 with the Interaction object holding id, caseId, partyId, occurredAt, channel, direction, actionCode, contactResult, promiseAmount, promiseDate, summary, conductCheck and sourceSystem. The idempotency key is built from the request ID header, so a repeated request answers with the entry already written rather than a second one. After the commit the case has one more entry and the next case_seq is free.
RWB-E1-066.7: These paths are code, not people, and they use the same writer. The EFS history load, the ALS payment load and notice dispatch each call append within their own transactions, setting source system to EFS or WORKBENCH and filling source_ref with the key the sending system used. They pass their own event codes from the same list, so an EFS history row and an officer's call land in one ordered sequence per case. The architecture test in the build steps holds this in place: no class outside recovery.dataengine.ledger may use InteractionRepository, so there is no second way to write an entry. The EFS history load of RWB-E1-004 has to go through append before this story is done.
RWB-E1-066.8: This path runs on its own when the insert fails. Translate the database error into LedgerWriteException so the transaction rolls back; the user action is undone with it, which is the point, since no contact may be saved without its ledger entry. The API answers 503 with MSG-P1-022, telling the caller the entry was not saved and to try again in a few minutes. Then call IncidentRecorder.raise from RWB-E1-027 with incident code LEDGER_WRITE_FAILED, the case ID and a detail holding the error class. The platform administrator receives that incident. Keep the summary and every other personal value out of the detail and out of the log.

RWB-E2-010.1: No person starts this. The stage 2 step is a new part of JOB-01, wired in after the COLLINS load for business date D has passed its own checks, so it runs daily before 07:00. You build Stage2ProductStep for that position in the job. When the step fails, the platform administrator restarts it from the job monitor with POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/jobs/{jobId}/rerun, and a rerun for the same business date replaces the rows rather than adding to them. The business date carried into the step is what every later part of the flow keys on.
RWB-E2-010.2: Stage2ProductService makes this call itself. TreatmentQuery is a published interface of the treatment module from RWB-E2-004, so treatments never come from its tables. changedBetween takes a window, and the window for business date D runs from the start of D up to the start of D plus one day, which puts a treatment changed at 2026-12-14T23:59:59+07:00 in that day and one changed a second later in the next. Each TreatmentView carries the treatment fields including installments, which the ACE restructure calculation produced. An error from the interface fails the step with MSG-GEN-006 and leaves the previous day's rows in place.
RWB-E2-010.3: The same service makes a second interface call, for guarantee claims changed on D. GuaranteeClaimQuery belongs to the guarantee module, which is built in Epic 4; until then the interface answers with an empty list, so write the step to treat no claims as a normal day rather than an error. Each GuaranteeClaimView carries the claim type, the claim deadline, the claimed and paid amounts, the filing time and the status. The 5 TCG claims in the test data each name an existing case and each produce one row later in the flow.
RWB-E2-010.4: This is code filling in the contract reference. For each case behind a treatment or a claim, call CaseScopeQuery.linksInScope with a system context rather than a user, because the job has no user whose scope could narrow the answer. From the links take the case's primary account, then read contract_no and contract_date from loan_account, a P1 table your own module owns. Those two values go onto every dp_treatment row beside the treatment fields. A case that does not resolve is held back in the next step rather than written with an empty contract.
RWB-E2-010.5: Two outcomes, both automatic. A row whose case does not resolve is not written; record it instead through DataQualityExceptions with product DP04 and check References, and leave it for the next day's load to pick up. Everything else goes to dp_treatment and dp_guarantee_claim, both new tables in this story's Flyway migration along with their sys_objects and sys_fields entries. Write by record ID and business date: the unique key over those two columns means a second run for 2026-12-14 updates the same rows, so the count holds at 40 instead of doubling. dp_treatment also carries business_date, contract_no and contract_date.
RWB-E2-010.6: The service checks its own work before anything is published. Count the active treatment rows it just wrote and compare that with TreatmentQuery.countActive from the owning module. The tolerance is zero: 40 rows against a count of 41 holds the publish, so DP04 gets no freshness stamp for that business date and a break naming the two numbers goes to the data steward with MSG-P1-002. The data store therefore never shows a day as complete while it disagrees with the module that owns the records. On a match the step moves to the stamp.
RWB-E2-010.7: FreshnessStampService writes the stamp, and only a matching count reaches it. The stamp is a data_product_load row for DP04 and business date D with status LOADED, built in RWB-E1-015, and it is what tells every reader how current the product is. DP04 carries an expected-by time of 08:00; when no stamp for the day has arrived by then, the stale check flags DP04 with MSG-P1-001 naming the date of the last load it does have. Call the existing service rather than writing the row yourself.
RWB-E2-010.8: A person reads the product, through an endpoint that already exists from RWB-E1-016. GET /api/recovery/v1/data-products/DP04/records with a caseId answers with that case's treatments, plan terms, contract reference and guarantee claims. Two things have to be true for the read to pass: the caller holds the Case record R right with the case in scope, and the caller's role has a DP04 row in data_product_access, version DPA-2026.12, which covers RW-CASEOWN, RW-RESTRUCT, RW-GUARANT, RW-CREDITAD, RW-COE and RW-AUDIT. A role with no DP04 row, such as RW-PHONECOL, gets 403 with MSG-P4-002, and the refusal is logged with the user and the product.
RWB-E2-010.9: The owner of the product checks it after the run, by hand. The data steward reads the DP04 catalog entry through GET /admin/data-products, where it shows the system of record Workbench, the owner RW-DATASTEW and the fields of treatment and guarantee_claim, and reads the breaks and References exceptions through GET /api/recovery/v1/admin/data-quality/exceptions with the Platform administration R right. From Epic 2 the same lists appear on SCR-45 Data quality in its loading and breaks states. Rows held with check References keep their place in the list until a later load resolves their case.

RWB-E2-023.1: Nothing here is manual. JOB-04 Daily reconciliation is already scheduled on Control-M from RWB-E1-051 and runs after JOB-02 for business date D; your work is EfsReconStep, a new step inside it. The step keys on the business date, and its idempotency key is the text INT-07 followed by that date, which is what makes a second run for the same day harmless. When JOB-02 did not run for D because the load was late, there is no reconciliation for that date at all; the day counts as not clean and MSG-P1-001 explains that today's load has not arrived.
RWB-E2-023.2: EfsReconService reads one side of the comparison through a published interface. EfsHandoverQuery.handedOver in P1 recovery.data.api takes the business date and answers with the account IDs that EFS handed over at 90 days past due on that date; the count is the size of that list. Call the interface rather than reading loan_account or any other module's table yourself. For the first test day, 2026-12-14, that call answers with 104 accounts. The service identity running the step is SY-DATALOAD, so no user scope narrows the answer.
RWB-E2-023.3: The other side of the comparison comes from the hand-over run that JOB-02 already recorded. Call HandoverRun.summary in P2 recovery.integration.handover.api, built in RWB-E2-001, with the same business date; it answers with the cases created and the accounts linked for that date. For 2026-12-14 that is 98 cases created and 4 accounts linked, which is 102 accounts on cases. Read the summary rather than counting the cases again, so both sides describe the same run. An absent summary is the late-load case covered in step 1.
RWB-E2-023.4: The comparison is code. Match the two lists on account ID and keep every account that appears on one side only. Give each difference a reason: the account was handed over and has no case, the account was held in the data quality exception list, or a case carries the account with no hand-over on that date. The difference count divided by the number of accounts handed over gives the percent used in step 6, so 3 differences in 2,000 accounts is 0.15 percent and 1 in 2,000 is 0.05 percent. A day with no difference at all is a clean day.
RWB-E2-023.5: Two writes, both automatic. Each difference goes in through DataQualityExceptions.add with product DP05, check EFS hand-over reconciliation, the account ID as the record key, the business date and the reason from step 4; a rerun adds only differences not already listed for that date, so the three listed for 2026-12-15 remain three. The day result goes onto the run record in interface_run.checks: the two counts, the difference percent, and whether the day was clean. CleanDayCounter reads those day results later, counting back from the last business date and breaking the run at a missing day.
RWB-E2-023.6: The step sends the alert, not a person. Read the threshold from the parameter recon.efs.alert_pct, which is 0.1 percent, and compare the percent from step 4 with it. Above the threshold, alert both the data steward and the platform administrator with MSG-P2-013, which names the number of hand-overs with no case, the date and the percent, and points at the data quality exceptions; those alerts arrive by email. At or below the threshold, list the differences and send nothing, and still record the day as not clean when the difference is above zero. Send one alert per business date, even after a rerun.
RWB-E2-023.7: A person decides this, once the days support it. The data steward calls POST /admin/interfaces/{interfaceCode}/manual-retirement, a new endpoint, with a note of up to 500 characters and the Reference data U right. The required run of clean days is the parameter recon.efs.clean_days_required, which is 10, and CleanDayCounter counts them back from the last business date. With 7 clean days the call answers 409 with MSG-P2-014, naming the count reached and the count needed, and the manual path keeps running. The platform administrator, who holds no Reference data U, is refused with MSG-P4-002.
RWB-E2-023.8: The rest is code inside ManualRetirementService. Check the clean days again rather than trusting the caller, then write the sign-off row to interface_signoff with interface ID INT-07, the first and last dates of the clean run, the number of clean days, the user and the time. The migration V2026_12_23__p2_interface_signoff.sql creates that table with a unique constraint on interface_id, which is what makes a second sign-off impossible and answers 409 with MSG-P2-019. Then switch rwb.integration.efs-manual-upload off for the environment through FeatureFlagService, write the ACE audit entry, and answer with MSG-P2-015.

RWB-E2-029.1: A person starts the run. RW-COE calls POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/agent-evaluations with the Rules and parameters C right, naming the agent SCREENING and the sample SCREEN-S2 version 1. That sample holds the business analysts' review of 500 shadow cases: for each case, which of the deviation codes X1 to X7 the analysts judged to be present. Shadow means the agent has been running on real cases without its output reaching anyone, which RWB-E1-062 put in place. The evaluation compares the agent's output on those cases with the analysts' judgement, and nothing happens to the cases themselves.
RWB-E2-029.2: The scoring is code. For each code X1 to X7, count the true positives, false positives and false negatives against the sample, then store precision and recall on agent_evaluation with label_key set to the code and sample_size 500. Precision is true positives divided by every case the agent flagged with that code; recall is true positives divided by every case the sample says carries it. For X1 with 41 true positives, 4 false positives and 5 false negatives, that gives 0.9111 and 0.8913. Keep four decimal places, because the promotion conditions in step 3 compare against values at that precision.
RWB-E2-029.3: A person loads the proposal and a second person approves it. RW-COE calls POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/agent-configs with policy SCREENING version P2: autonomy mode L1 for segment product group MORTGAGE and segment region BKK, the ID of the evaluation run from step 1, the promotion conditions, the fallback and the measures. RW-RISK then approves through POST /admin/agent-configs/{versionId}/approve with the Rules and parameters A right. The policy loader checks the stated conditions against that evaluation run, so a condition of recall at least 0.75 for every code refuses the load with 422 and MSG-P10-001 naming X4 at 0.6000. On a clean load the version reaches status LOADED.
RWB-E2-029.4: The agent runs on an event, with no one asking. ScreeningShadowListener already consumes EV-01 CaseCreated and EV-16 DocumentStored; extend it to read the autonomy mode from the policy in force for the case rather than running every case in shadow. Compare the case product_group and region_code with segment_product_group and segment_region_code on agent_policy: a Mortgage case in BKK runs in mode L1, and every other case keeps running in shadow with its output reaching no user. Record the mode and the segment on the agent_run row. With the flag rwb.agent.screening-l1 off, every segment runs in shadow.
RWB-E2-029.5: The officer opens the case and the proposals are already there. Build ProposedDeviationsPanel on SCR-03 Case record, fed by GET /api/recovery/v1/cases/{caseId}/agent-outputs, which answers with the SCREENING proposals: the code, the reasons, the source references, the preceding contact, the confidence, a low confidence flag and any feedback already given. ScreeningOutputFilter prepares that list: drop any code already open as a deviation on the case, and set the low confidence flag when the confidence falls under the floor 0.80, which the panel shows as the marker Low confidence. Every proposal carries the marker Agent output, and reasons shown on the panel hold masking tokens in place of personal data.
RWB-E2-029.6: The officer confirms, and the agent itself raises nothing. On a confirmation, call DeviationService.raise from RWB-E2-015 with the case, the code, the reason, any document IDs, raisedBy set to SCREENING_AGENT and the agent run ID; it answers with the deviation ID and the ID of the decision log entry it wrote. S8 applies R-DEV-01, which pauses the stage clock and routes the case, so the case status becomes On hold and the flag shows on SCR-03 and in SCR-08 Deviation queue. S8 publishes EV-06. Two confirmations of the same proposal leave one deviation; the second answers 409 with MSG-GEN-004.
RWB-E2-029.7: Your code writes the feedback row after S8 answers. Insert one agent_feedback row with the agent run ID, item_key set to the code such as X1, verdict ACCEPTED, the user and the time, and decision_log_id set to the entry ID that DeviationService.raise returned. One row per run and item: a repeat is refused rather than counted twice. This row is what ties the officer's judgement back to the agent output, so the error rate per flag can be measured later. The endpoint carrying the verdict is POST /api/recovery/v1/agent-runs/{runId}/feedback, which needs the Case record U right.
RWB-E2-029.8: A rejection is also a decision, and the order of writes matters. The same feedback endpoint takes verdict REJECTED with a reason, and an empty reason answers 422 with MSG-P7-005. Write the decision log entry first, through the P7 DecisionLogWriter, holding the code as the decision, the agent version SCREENING@P2/PR2, the final call REJECTED and the officer's reason; only then insert the agent_feedback row with verdict REJECTED. When the decision log write fails, store nothing at all: answer 503 with MSG-P7-003 and raise the incident, leaving no feedback row behind. No deviation is raised and the case status does not change.

RWB-E1-006.1: Nobody starts this run by hand. It begins when a load step finishes. Your work is to call the runner from two places: the end of each load step in JOB-01 and JOB-09, and the end of the case list step of JOB-04 for data product DP03. The call is the internal method DataQualityRuleRunner.runFor with the product code and the load run ID of the step that has just finished, so each run knows which rules to read and which load to attach its results to. A data product is one named set of recovery data, for example DP01 for accounts and DP03 for the case list. The feature flag rwb.p1.dq-rules controls it; with the flag off, loads finish as before and no rule runs.
RWB-E1-006.2: The runner takes its work from database rows and not from Java code. DqRuleRepository selects the dq_rule rows whose product_code matches the data product of this run and whose dates cover the business date: valid_from on or before it, and valid_to empty or on or after it. In force means approved and inside those dates. A rule whose valid to date has passed or whose valid from date is still in the future is left out, which is exception path X5, and it then appears nowhere in the load run results. Build step 1 in section 13 asks you to test this date query on its own, because every later step depends on reading the right set of rules for the right day.
RWB-E1-006.3: Each rule row holds a rule type and parameters, so the runner has to turn the row into a SQL statement. RuleTypeTemplates holds one template per rule type, seven in all: NOT_NULL, UNIQUE_ACROSS, RANGE, SUM_EQUALS, EXISTS_LINK, MAX_AGE_DAYS and FIELD_BEFORE. The template supplies the shape of the statement. Table and column names come only from sys_fields, the data dictionary of the P1 owned tables, and the values in rule_params go in as bound parameters, which means the database receives them as values and never as text it executes. No rule text is run as SQL. A rule naming a field that sys_fields does not hold is refused at load time with MSG-P1-005, so the runner never meets one.
RWB-E1-006.4: This happens inside the runner with no person present. DataQualityRuleRunner executes each built statement and keeps the records it returns, which are the rows that fail that rule. Each rule has a limit of 60 seconds. When one rule passes that limit or fails for another reason, the runner marks that rule as ERROR on the load run, carries on with the remaining rules, and alerts the data steward group with MSG-P1-015. One slow or broken rule therefore does not stop the others. Build step 4 in section 13 covers the per rule limit, the ERROR result and the clear step together, so write them as one service.
RWB-E1-006.5: The runner writes the failing records to dq_exception, one row per failing record, filling check_code and reason_code with the rule code, plus the rule version, the record key and the business date. The insert has to be idempotent, which means running it again gives the same result instead of a second row. The unique constraint uk_dq_exception on load_run_id, check_code and record_key gives you that, and DqExceptionRepository inserts with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so a repeat of the same run adds nothing, which is exception path X4. record_key holds an account key or a record ID. Never put a name or a contact value in it.
RWB-E1-006.6: An exception row carries a status. A row raised earlier is OPEN until the record passes its rule again, and the runner then sets that row to CLEARED with cleared_on set to the business date. It does this by matching the same rule code and the same record key. Nothing is deleted, so the history of the break stays readable. AC9 is the test: an OPEN DQ01 exception for case account ACC0000777 raised on 2026-11-27 becomes CLEARED with cleared_on 2026-11-30 once the case has an owner. The cleared_on column is new and comes with the rule_version column in migration V1_006__dq_rule.sql.
RWB-E1-006.7: The runner also writes a count for each rule it ran into check_results on the load_run row, which is the record of that load. This is what the data steward reads to see how many records failed each rule, for example DQ02 equal to 3 in AC1. A rule that failed at run time appears there as ERROR, and a rule outside its valid dates appears not at all, as AC8 states for DQ07. load_run already exists from RWB-E1-003, so you add content to check_results and create no table for this.
RWB-E1-006.8: The daily reconciliation job JOB-04 has a publish step, and this story adds DataQualityExtractWriter to it. The writer selects the exceptions that are open and the ones raised on the business date, and writes them to the data lake extract, which is the file the reporting layer reads. Each row carries the rule code, the rule name, the data product, the business date and the record key, as AC2 requires with its 19 rows. No person triggers this. The reporting and BI analyst builds the Power BI data quality report on top of the extract and owns the report layout.
RWB-E1-006.9: The data steward reads the result in one of two ways. The first is the endpoint GET /admin/data-quality/exceptions, which you build as a method on RecoveryDataEngineController with the query parameters product, from and to, returning id, product, check, record and raisedOn per row. The method needs the capability check for Platform administration R with scope All, so a role without it receives 403 with MSG-P4-002, as test TC-E1-006-10 asks. The second way is the Power BI data quality report built from the extract of step 8. The endpoint is read only and changes nothing in the data.

RWB-E1-018.1: Your story does not build this step. JOB-01 loads the COLLINS data, runs its load checks, and publishes the event LoadCompleted, which carries the source and the business date. Publishing means writing the event once so that other parts of the system can react to it. The event arrives only when every load check has passed, which is why no case can be created from a refused or late load (BR7). When the load is refused, JOB-01 publishes nothing, your job never starts for that date, and the job monitor shows MSG-P1-001 (AC9). Treat the event as the one trigger of your job and read the business date from it.
RWB-E1-018.2: You build CaseCreationJob as a listener on LoadCompleted for source COLLINS, scheduled as JOB-02 after JOB-01. No person starts it. Its first action is to read the entry threshold from the parameter service built in RWB-E1-042, under the key case.entry.dpd, whose value is 90. Read the value on every run and keep no copy of 90 in Java code, because the threshold is data and the center of excellence owns it. The feature flag rwb.p3.casecreation turns the job off, and with it off JOB-02 creates no case. Build step 5 in section 13 pairs the listener with the skip rule that makes a second run harmless.
RWB-E1-018.3: The job asks P1 for the accounts that qualify instead of querying the account tables itself. Call RecoveryDataQuery.accountsAtOrAbove with the threshold and the business date. The call returns AccountEntrySnapshot records holding the account ID, the primary party ID, the product group, the region code, days past due, the total balance, the data as of date and the flags for restructuring, dispute, deceased, bankruptcy and fraud. Accounts already sitting on an open case are left out, which means no open case_account link for that account. An account at 89 days past due is not returned and comes back into view the next day once the load moves it to 90 (AC7).
RWB-E1-018.4: EntryRuleEvaluator runs inside the job as the service identity SY-RULES, with no person involved. It reads the exclusion rows, which are rule rows with rule table EXCLUSION, through RuleTableReader in P4, and applies them to each account snapshot. The five reason codes are DECEASED, FRAUD, BANKRUPTCY, ACTIVE_PLAN and OPEN_DISPUTE. When a row matches, the account gets no case, and you write one case_entry_exclusion row holding the account ID, the business date, the reason code, the rule ID and the rule version, for example ACTIVE_PLAN with version EXCL-2026.11 in AC2. The unique key on account_id and business_date keeps a repeated run from writing a second exclusion row.
RWB-E1-018.5: CaseGrouping takes the accounts that passed the entry rule and groups them by primary customer and product group. One group becomes one case, so a customer with two hire purchase accounts at 95 days past due receives a single case with both accounts linked (AC3), and a customer with a mortgage and a hire purchase account receives two cases (AC12). Before creating anything the service looks for an open case for the same customer and product group through CaseRecordService.findOpenCase and links the new account to it. The partial unique index ux_case_open_customer_product enforces this in the database. A partial index applies only to the rows matching its WHERE clause, here the cases with no closed date.
RWB-E1-018.6: CaseNumberIssuer produces the case number. It draws the next value from the yearly database sequence case_no_seq_YYYY and formats it as RW, the entry year and six digits, for example RW-2026-000123. A sequence is a database object that hands out each number once, which is what keeps a number from being used again after a case closes (AC4). The issuer refuses a value above 999999: creation stops for the rest of that year, the job record carries MSG-P3-025 and an incident goes to the platform administrator (AC11). The job creates the next year sequence each December, so case_no_seq_2026 and case_no_seq_2027 both come with migration V018_1__case_creation.sql.
RWB-E1-018.7: CaseCreationService writes the case in one transaction, which means the database keeps every write of that case or none of them. Inside it you write the recovery_case row with status NEW, the case_account rows for the linked accounts with the primary account marked, the case_party row with role BORROWER for the primary customer, and the CaseCreated event row in the outbox. The outbox is a table in the same database: writing the event there inside the same transaction means the event exists only when the case exists, and delivery happens after the commit. Status NEW is read from the list LOV-CASE-STATUS through CaseStatusCatalog, so write no Java enum of statuses.
RWB-E1-018.8: The last call before the commit is DecisionLogWriter.write from RWB-E1-027, with decision code D6, final call CASE_CREATED, the entry rule version and the inputs that led to the case. The writer runs inside the same transaction as the case. When it throws DecisionLogUnavailableException the whole transaction rolls back, which means every write of step 7 is undone: no case, no account links, no party link and no outbox row. The job record then lists that account as failed with MSG-P7-003 and the next run takes the account again (AC10). Test TC-E1-018-14 forces the decision log write to fail for a whole run.
RWB-E1-018.9: At the end of the run the job writes its counts on the job record: accounts read, excluded, linked, created and failed. The platform administrator reads these in the job monitor and reruns the job from there when needed. A rerun has to be harmless, so the job skips any account already linked or excluded for that business date and takes only the failed ones again; the second run issues no case number (AC8). The entry decision is keyed on account ID and business date for exactly this reason. JOB-03 is scheduled after JOB-02 and starts once it completes, so set the job completion correctly.
RWB-E1-018.10: A person reads the result. The case owner, or any role holding Case record R, opens the case with GET /api/recovery/v1/cases/{caseId} and its accounts with GET /api/recovery/v1/cases/{caseId}/accounts. You build both methods on CaseAndWorkflowController, plus the caseNo query parameter on GET /cases for the case number search in AC4. Each method applies the right and the scope: 403 with MSG-P4-002 when the role has no Case record R, and 404 with MSG-P4-003 when the case is outside the caller scope. RW-REFADM holds no Case record right and is refused, which is access test TC-E1-018-13. The full read only case view comes later in RWB-E1-023.

RWB-E1-030.1: Quartz is the scheduler inside the service, so no person starts this. You configure a daily trigger for JOB-06 at 06:30 and a condition on JOB-03: when JOB-03 has not completed for the business date at 06:30, the job waits and starts once JOB-03 completes. The platform administrator can rerun it through POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/jobs/{jobId}/rerun, which needs Platform administration U and answers 409 while the job is running. A role without that right is refused with MSG-P4-002, which is access test TC-E1-030-11. The feature flag rwb.p3.rebalance turns the moves off while the snapshot of steps 7 and 8 still runs.
RWB-E1-030.2: RebalanceJob collects two work lists from the database. The first is the cases in each queue with no owner and status NEW or ASSIGNED, read from recovery_case by queue_id, owner_user_id and status. The second is the owners whose open case count is above their capacity, which comes from counting open cases per owner_user_id against queue_member.capacity and queue.capacity_cap. A queue with no cap loaded is still listed for the snapshot and no case in it is moved (AC5), so treat a missing cap as no move. The caps and member capacity come from RWB-E1-019 and are data values (DL23), so read them on every run.
RWB-E1-030.3: RebalanceService decides which cases leave an owner above the cap. It orders that owner open cases by assignment time, newest first, and takes them from the top until the owner count is back inside the cap. Rule R-UNI-19 sets this order, so the oldest work stays with the person who has held it. An owner holding exactly the cap loses no case, for example 150 against a cap of 150 in AC10. An owner at 153 loses 3. The selection runs in the service with no person involved, and build step 1 asks for unit tests on it with AC8 and AC10.
RWB-E1-030.4: Two fields on the case block a move: deviation_open and legal_hold. When either is true the case stays with its owner, whatever its assignment time. RebalanceService checks both as it walks the ordered list, skips the held cases and goes on to the next newest, so an owner at 152 whose two newest cases have deviation_open true loses the two after them instead (AC8). The check reads recovery_case and needs no call to another module. Rules R-UNI-20 and R-DEV-01 are the source, and a move never resets the stage clock or the prescription date.
RWB-E1-030.5: AssignmentEngine from RWB-E1-020 chooses the receiving owner, so this story calls it and repeats none of that logic. It is given the queue and picks a member below the cap by the method on the queue row, queue.assignment_method, which is LOWEST_LOAD for TDR-BKK-CO in AC1. Ties go to the member first in the queue list, which is how the 12 cases with no owner split 8 to U-61 at 140 cases and 4 to U-62 at 144. When no member of the queue has capacity, those cases keep no owner and the team manager receives MSG-P3-011 with the count (AC4). The engine is called for selected cases and for cases with no owner alike.
RWB-E1-030.6: Each move is one transaction, case by case, so a failure on one case leaves the other moves in place. The transaction holds the decision log write through the writer from RWB-E1-027, the end of the current assignment row, the new assignment row with reason REBALANCE, the new value of recovery_case.owner_user_id, and the CaseTransferred event in the outbox, which is a table in the same database whose rows are delivered after the commit. When the decision log write fails, that case is not moved, the job record lists it with MSG-P7-003, and the run carries on with the next case (AC6). BR7 requires a log entry for every move.
RWB-E1-030.7: QueueMeasureService runs once at the end of the job and writes one queue_measure row per queue, all read at a single time so the numbers agree with each other. The snapshot holds depth, the number of cases with no owner, age in days counted from the case entry date as an average and a maximum, the lowest and highest open case count per owner, and the count of SERVICE_LEVEL timers with status EXPIRED. The read runs in one REPEATABLE READ transaction, which means every query inside it sees the same picture of the database. The row starts with status TAKEN, and the unique key on queue_id and as_of keeps a rerun from writing a second row for the same time.
RWB-E1-030.8: Before anything is published the service checks itself. For each queue it compares the depth it just counted with the case count for the same queue at the same time, and only when every queue matches does it set the rows to PUBLISHED. One difference holds the whole set: the rows stay HELD, nothing reaches the reporting layer, and the data steward receives MSG-P3-029 naming the check, as AC9 shows with depth 88 against a count of 87 for DIL-BKK-CO. GET /api/recovery/v1/cases filtered by queue gives the second count in the test. DL25 and REC-01 are the source of the zero difference rule.
RWB-E1-030.9: JOB-15 is the reporting extract job owned by the reporting and BI analyst and it already runs nightly, so you do not build it. It copies the published snapshot to the data lake, and the Power BI queue page shows the numbers the next morning: the snapshot of 2026-12-02 appears on 2026-12-03. Your part is the hand over in build step 7. P9 reads the snapshot through the published interface QueueMeasureService.latestPublished for a business date and never queries queue_measure directly. A snapshot held at step 8 is not copied, so the report keeps the last published numbers.
RWB-E1-030.10: TimerBreachNotifier is a listener, so it reacts to an event instead of running on a schedule. JOB-05 raises TimerBreached when a case passes its service level, and the listener counts the breaches for that queue and sends MSG-P3-028 to the team manager of the team, for example count 1 for queue TDR-BKK-CO in AC3. The case itself does not move and its owner does not change (BR8). The same breach appears in the next snapshot inside the breached count, which is how the Power BI queue page shows it. Build step 6 covers the listener and test AC3.

RWB-E1-043.1: A person starts this. The reference data administrator uploads one file for one table through POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/reference-loads, sending multipart form data with the file as CSV or XLSX with one sheet, the table code, and the valid from date on which the new values take effect. The endpoint belongs to P4 and is already deployed, so your work begins at step 2. The caller must hold Reference data right C; a role with read only is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002, which is test TC-E1-043-11. One load covers one table, and that table code has to be a value of the list LOV-REF-TABLE.
RWB-E1-043.2: The P4 handler writes nothing itself. It calls the method recordVersion on the published interface of this story, in package recovery.casewf.refdata.api, passing the file rows as a list of maps, the table code, the valid from date, the user ID of the caller as the author, and the load ID. Your work in build step 7 is to wire the handler to that interface and to map the exceptions it throws onto the error responses of section 12, for example 422 with MSG-P3-027 for a failed check. P4 reaches this module only through the interface and never reads reference_version or reference_row, which the boundary test RWB-TE-001 checks.
RWB-E1-043.3: The service runs every check before it writes anything. The table code must be in LOV-REF-TABLE, read through the P4 list interface. The rows are checked against ReferenceTableSchemas, which holds the column names, types and key columns per table and comes from the parameter catalog of RWB-E1-042, so the text five in the numeric column limit_days fails with MSG-P3-027 naming row 12 and that column (AC4). Row keys must be unique. The valid from date must not be before the business date (AC6). A file with no data rows fails with MSG-GEN-001. The service also computes the content hash, a SHA-256 over the rows sorted by key, and the next version number, one above the highest version of that table.
RWB-E1-043.4: Writing happens on its own once the checks pass. The service writes one reference_version row with status VALIDATED and one reference_row row per file row, holding row_key and row_data as jsonb, in one transaction, which means the version and all its rows appear together or not at all. A load with any failed check writes no version and no rows (BR5). When the same file arrives again for the same table and valid from date, the unique key on table_code, valid_from and content_hash matches, the service returns the existing load and writes nothing, so there is still one version 5 and no version 6 (AC7).
RWB-E1-043.5: A second person has to act before the values are served. The approver calls POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/reference-loads/{loadId}/approve with no body. This is the separation of duty that control CTL-08 requires: one person prepares the load and a different person releases it. The approver holds Reference data right A, which section 10 assumes is RW-RISK, the risk and model risk officer, because no role holds that right in the permission matrix today. The same person may not hold RW-REFADM and RW-RISK. Until the approval arrives the version stays VALIDATED and the engines keep reading the earlier version, as AC5 shows with HOLIDAY version 1.
RWB-E1-043.6: The service checks the approver and then records the approval. The approver must be present, must not be the author of the load, and must hold the approve right, which is checked through the ACE access check. It then sets status to APPROVED and fills approver_user_id and approved_at. The database backs this with a CHECK constraint that refuses an approver equal to the author. Build step 4 adds an optimistic lock on the version column, which means the update carries the row version it read and fails when another thread changed the row first, so two approvals arriving together give one success and one refusal with MSG-GEN-004 (AC8). An author approving their own load receives 409 with MSG-P7-002.
RWB-E1-043.7: The same approve call closes the version it replaces. The service sets valid_to on the previous approved version of that table to the day before the new valid from date, so approving a version valid from 2026-12-01 sets the earlier valid_to to 2026-11-30 (AC1). The old version and its rows stay readable, which is what lets an open case show the values it was decided under. valid_to is one of the few columns an update may change on reference_version; the update trigger refuses changes to anything else and refuses every change to reference_row. A trigger is database code that runs on each write and can reject it.
RWB-E1-043.8: The engines read the values with no person involved. The case service, the allocation engine and the timer engine call ReferenceDataService.rows with a table code and a business date, at start up and again each time their cache entry expires. The service answers with the approved version whose valid from is the latest on or before that date (BR3), so EXPOSURE_BAND returns version 3 for business date 2026-11-30 and version 4 for 2026-12-01. ReferenceRowCache keys entries by table code and business date and takes its lifetime from refdata.cache.ttl-seconds, 300 seconds. The cache never holds a version that is not APPROVED. When no approved version applies, rows throws NoVersionInForceException and the engine does not run (AC9).
RWB-E1-043.9: Each engine writes one line per table it read, carrying the table code, the version number and the business date. You build ReferenceVersionLogger for this and call it from the start up hook of the case service, the allocation engine and the timer engine, which is build step 6. The line holds no row content and no party identifier, which AC3 tests on captured log lines. This is what lets anyone say later which version of QUEUE, SERVICE_LEVEL or HOLIDAY a run used, and it is the measure named in section 2.

RWB-E1-055.1: Quartz starts JOB-10 every day at 16:00 Bangkok time with no person involved. WinNoticeFileJob selects the notices to send: those in a dispatch eligible state with no sent date. The eligible states are configuration, rwb.comms.dispatch.eligible-states set to GENERATED in Epic 1, so read the value and keep no state name in code. The index ix_notice_state_sent on state and sent_date supports the query. A notice already written into an unacknowledged file of the same date is skipped, which is how a rerun from SCR-44 writes no notice twice (AC8). The platform administrator can rerun the job from that screen.
RWB-E1-055.2: WinNoticeFileWriter builds one file per run to the INT-14 layout. Each record carries the contract number of the case primary account, the addressee, the address, the notice type, the template version and the document reference. The contract number comes through the P1 and P3 interfaces, from the case_account row marked is_primary and loan_account.contract_no, with no direct read of another module tables. The address is held as a token, so call PiiService.detokenize to put the real value into the outbound file stream only and keep it out of every log line. The file ends with a trailer, a final record holding the count of records, which lets WIN check that nothing was lost in transit.
RWB-E1-055.3: The system hands the finished file to the P2 integration adapters by calling WinFileGateway.send, and the adapters place it on the SFTP path agreed with the WIN owner. No code in this story talks to WIN directly (REQ-DRI-006). For each notice in the file you then write dispatch_file_id with the file ID and add one to dispatch_attempts, both new columns from migration V1_055__notice_dispatch.sql. The notice state does not change yet and stays Generated until WIN acknowledges. The attempt count is what the limit rwb.comms.dispatch.max-attempts, set to 3, is measured against.
RWB-E1-055.4: WIN answers with an acknowledgment file, and the P2 adapters deliver it by calling WinAcknowledgmentHandler.onAcknowledgment, a published interface you implement in P6. The acknowledgment holds one entry per contract number with the sent date, the barcode and the sent type, following the s2t mapping of INT-14. The sent date arrives as DDMMYYYY, so 26112026 has to be parsed into 2026-11-26 before it is stored. When no acknowledgment arrives, the notices stay Generated with their file sent and the next JOB-10 run writes them again; after the third attempt a task goes to the litigation officer team with MSG-GEN-006 naming WIN (AC4).
RWB-E1-055.5: The handler applies the acknowledgment. For each entry it sets the notice state to Sent and fills sent_date, barcode and sent_type. The unique index ux_notice_barcode keeps one barcode on one notice. It then writes an outbound LETTER entry to the interaction ledger through InteractionLedgerApi.record from RWB-E1-066, and writes NoticeDispatched to the outbox through NoticeEventPublisher, so the event is delivered after the change is committed. The case record then shows MSG-P6-004 with the notice type and the date. AC1 covers the whole step with barcode RR123456789TH and sent date 2026-11-26.
RWB-E1-055.6: JOB-09 runs weekly on Monday at 04:00, or on file arrival, and loads the INT-15 proof of delivery file. You build WinProofOfDeliveryStep as a Spring Batch step inside that job, running checks DQ-085 to DQ-091 on the file. A file failing any one of them is refused in full: nothing is written, the delivery data already on the notices stays as it is, and the message is MSG-P1-002 naming the check, for example a trailer saying 40 records against a body of 39 (AC5). A file for a business date that has already loaded is refused the same way (AC7). A corrected file is loaded whole.
RWB-E1-055.7: DeliveryMatcher ties each record in the file to a notice. It matches on the barcode first, and when that finds nothing it matches on the contract number together with the sent date. On a match the system sets callback_date from the call back date in the record, delivery_status to DELIVERED and the notice state to Delivered. A record matching no notice on either key is held on the exception list with check References, and the other records in the same file still load, so 29 of 30 records update their notices (AC6). The data steward sees the held records on SCR-45.
RWB-E1-055.8: Two writes follow each matched delivery. The system records the delivery in the interaction ledger through the ledger writer, and publishes NoticeDelivered to the outbox with the delivery date. P3 consumes that event and starts the NOTICE_PERIOD timer from the delivery date, so the notice period counts from the day the letter arrived (CTL-15). P3 already holds that consumer from RWB-E1-028, so your part is the event and the delivered date on it. A later file repeating a delivery already recorded leaves the notice unchanged, publishes no second event, and counts the repeat under R-UNI-40 (AC10).
RWB-E1-055.9: BarcodeReconciliation is a daily job you build, running after JOB-01. It compares the notices written to WIN files with the barcodes that have come back, which is reconciliation REC-05, and lists any notice still without a barcode three days after it was sent. The three days come from rwb.comms.dispatch.barcode-break-days, so the number is configuration. The breaks go to the platform administrator on SCR-45 Data quality, as AC9 shows with notice N-0002 sent on 2026-11-25 and listed on 2026-11-28. The same job marks the notice data product stale one business day after an INT-15 file was due, which produces MSG-P1-001 on the case (AC11).

RWB-E1-067.1: This is not your code. Each publishing module, for example the case creation story RWB-E1-018, commits its own change and writes the event row to the outbox inside the same transaction. The outbox is a table in the same database as the change, and writing both together means an event exists only for a change that was kept, and a change is never kept without its event. Your story depends on six of these events: EV-01 CaseCreated, EV-02 CaseAllocated, EV-04 CaseTransferred, EV-08 DecisionRecorded, EV-16 DocumentStored and EV-19 TimerBreached. The event header carries the event ID, the idempotency key, the schema version, the time it happened and the actor.
RWB-E1-067.2: The outbox delivers each event to your listener after the publishing transaction commits. LedgerEventListener is the consumer you build, subscribed to the six events; it runs inside the service and not as a scheduled job. Delivery is at least once, so the same event can arrive more than once, and step 7 handles that. Delivery for one case keeps the order in which the events were written, which RWB-TE-006 provides, so the ledger entries of a case follow that order in case_seq: CASE_CREATED at 1 and CASE_ALLOCATED at 2 (AC6). An event not yet processed is delivered again after a restart.
RWB-E1-067.3: The listener checks the schema version in the event header before it does anything else. A schema version is the number of the event payload layout, and a consumer accepts the current one and the one before it (BR6). When CaseTransferred is at schema version 2 and accepts version 1, an event at version 3 is not written: it goes to the exception queue with owner RW-PLATADM and a reason naming the version, and nothing reaches the ledger (AC4). Build step 3 covers the listener with this check, and test TC-E1-067-04 sends a CaseTransferred event at schema version 3.
RWB-E1-067.4: LedgerEventMapper turns one event into one LedgerEntryCommand, which is the input the ledger writer takes. The pairing is EV-01 to CASE_CREATED, EV-02 to CASE_ALLOCATED, EV-04 to CASE_TRANSFERRED, EV-19 to CASE_ESCALATED, EV-16 to DOCUMENT_ATTACHED and EV-08 to DECISION_TAKEN. Read it from configuration, the property rwb.dataengine.ledger.event-map, so the map is data and not a switch in Java. For EV-08 the command also carries the decision log entry ID into decision_log_id. Everything the entry needs comes from the event payload, so the mapper queries no assignment, document or decision table.
RWB-E1-067.5: The mapper fills the fields that say where the entry came from. actor_type and actor_ref come from the event header and hold either a user ID, for example u-teammgr-03, or a service identity, for example SY-RULES. The source system is always WORKBENCH. source_ref is built as the owning module followed by the event ID and name, which gives P3 case and workflow, EV-02 CaseAllocated for an allocation (AC2). The event idempotency key is copied onto the entry as idempotency_key, which is what step 7 uses. No personal data goes into any of these fields; the events carry codes and references only.
RWB-E1-067.6: InteractionLedgerWriter.append writes the entry, and it comes from RWB-E1-066 rather than from this story. It appends the row and sets case_seq, the per case sequence number that gives the case history its order. The writer checks that the calling identity holds Case record C and throws AccessDeniedException otherwise, mapped to MSG-P4-002, so the listener has to run as SY-CASEWF. Build step 5 adds that identity check. SY-AGENT holds read only and is refused, which is access test TC-E1-067-09. An event naming a case that does not exist writes no entry and goes to the exception queue (AC8).
RWB-E1-067.7: Appending the same event twice has to leave one entry, which is what idempotent means: doing it again changes nothing. The unique constraint on interaction.idempotency_key makes the second insert fail, and LedgerDuplicateService catches that clash and upserts a processed_event row instead, adding one to hit_count and setting last_hit_at. Run that upsert in a new transaction, because the failed insert is rolling its own transaction back and the hit has to survive it. processed_event is a new table in this story, keyed on idempotency_key with first_interaction_id, hit_count and last_hit_at. The same event on two consumer threads at once gives one entry and one hit (AC7).
RWB-E1-067.8: The outbox marks the event processed for the ledger consumer, which stops it being delivered again. Mark it only once the entry has been written, the repeat counted, or the event moved to the exception queue. A guardrail in section 17 states this: the listener never acknowledges an event it has not written or moved. An event left unmarked is delivered again after a restart, and the duplicate rule of step 7 keeps that harmless. Each consumer has its own processed marker, so marking an event for the ledger leaves other consumers of the same event untouched.
RWB-E1-067.9: When the ledger write fails the event is kept. The outbox retries it with the retry limit of 3 from the outbox settings, so an event is delivered four times in all before it stops (AC5). After that it goes to the exception queue with owner RW-PLATADM, and the system raises the incident LEDGER_WRITE_FAILED for the case, carrying MSG-P1-022. The platform administrator sees these events on SCR-09 Exception queue. Build step 6 covers the path, and test TC-E1-067-05 forces every ledger insert to fail.

RWB-E2-011.1: A person starts this. The case owner picks My queue from the menu, which opens the My queue view of SCR-02. The menu item appears only when the feature flag rwb.p3.queue-views is on; with the flag off both My queue and Team queues are hidden. You build the screen as the React component MyQueuePage, and its first state is Loading with skeleton rows while the call of step 2 runs. The signed in person needs Case record R with scope Own, which RWB-E1-037 sets, and the list then holds the open cases whose owner is that person (BR1).
RWB-E2-011.2: The front end asks the existing case endpoint for the data. It calls GET /cases with owner set to me, sort set to serviceLevelDueAt, and any filters kept for the session. Both the sort value and the route filter are new, and you add them to the endpoint in build step 2. Filters live in browser session storage through the useSessionFilters hook: wrap every read and write in try and catch, because storage can be blocked, and the page has to work without it. Session storage also means the filter survives opening a case and coming back, and is gone after sign out and sign in (AC3). The server stores nothing about filters (BR8).
RWB-E2-011.3: The case service answers with one page of cases and no person is involved. CaseListQueryService applies the caller scope, the filters, the age range and the sort, and CaseListRepository runs one SQL query joining recovery_case with the SERVICE_LEVEL timer of each case. Three fields are computed instead of stored: ageDays, the calendar days from entry_date to the business date; serviceLevelDueAt from the timer; and serviceLevelState as BREACHED, RUNNING, PAUSED or NONE. The sort has four groups in that order, breached first, then running by due date earliest first (BR2). A page size outside 1 to 200 is refused with MSG-GEN-002, and an age range with age from above age to with MSG-GEN-003. The header X-Data-As-Of carries the business date of the case data.
RWB-E2-011.4: The front end draws what came back. With rows it shows the List state, each row holding the case number, product group, stage, status, age in days from the entry date and the service level due date. With no row for this person and these filters it shows the Empty state with MSG-P3-017, which reads that there are no cases in this queue (AC4). MSG-P3-017 is a new message recorded in the additions file, and its Thai text follows DL10. Build step 5 asks for all four states of the page, Loading, Empty, List and Filtered, so write the empty state together with the list.
RWB-E2-011.5: The case owner sets the stage filter, for example to Litigation, and the front end reloads the list in the Filtered state showing only those cases (AC3). The stage values come from the list LOV-STAGE through the P4 list interface, with LOV-ROUTE and LOV-CASE-STATUS for the route and status filters, so no label or code sits in the front end. The chosen filter is written to session storage by useSessionFilters and sent on the next GET /cases call. Age from and age to belong to the same filter set, and an age range the wrong way round is refused before the list reloads (AC5).
RWB-E2-011.6: The team manager opens Team queues from the menu, which is the second screen of this story, SCR-07, built as the React component TeamQueuesPage. The person needs Queue and allocation R with team scope and sees only the queues of their own teams. RW-CAPACITY holds the same right with scope All and opens the same screen. A role without the right is refused with MSG-P4-002, which is access test TC-E2-011-13 with RW-WRITEOFF. The screen starts in Loading with skeleton rows, then moves to the List state once the call of step 7 returns.
RWB-E2-011.7: The front end calls GET /queues, which takes no request parameters. The scope on the endpoint decides what comes back, so the caller receives the queues of their own teams and nothing else. The endpoint already exists and you extend its response with the computed fields of step 8 in build step 3. One call serves the whole screen, so the queue rows and the owner counts arrive in the same response. With the feature flag rwb.p3.queue-views off the endpoint answers with the Epic 1 fields only, which keeps the screen hidden and the API working.
RWB-E2-011.8: The queue service computes the numbers for each queue in scope. QueueSummaryService with QueueSummaryRepository groups counts by queue_id and owner_user_id and returns openCaseCount, the cases whose status is not Closed; oldestEntryDate and oldestAgeDays; breachCount, the open cases whose SERVICE_LEVEL timer has status EXPIRED; and owners, each with their open case count and atCap against queue.capacity_cap, 150 in the examples. The counts have to equal the case list count for the same queue, so MTG-BKK-CO shows 412 on both screens (AC11). A queue is listed even when it has no cap loaded.
RWB-E2-011.9: The team manager selects a queue row, and the front end calls GET /api/recovery/v1/queues/{queueId}/cases with page, size and the service level sort, showing the same case rows as My queue. Build step 4 adds the scope check to this endpoint: a queue of another team is answered with 404 and MSG-P4-003, so SME-NTH-CO is not found for a MTG-BKK manager (AC7). From the list the manager can go on to SCR-05 Transfer case, which story RWB-E2-012 builds. This story reads cases, queues and timers and changes no case.

RWB-E2-024.1: The field collector does this in the field app, and the app itself is out of scope for you. For each file it records the device time of the capture, the GPS position and a client file ID, which is the identifier the app gives that one file. Your side takes those values as sent: the device time is stored with its offset and the server never replaces it (BR2 and the guardrail in section 17). The collector can capture with no signal, so the capture time and the time the file reaches you can be a day apart (AC2). The kinds captured are photos, bills and the checklist.
RWB-E2-024.2: The app sends the captures for one case to POST /cases/{caseId}/field-captures, the new endpoint you build as FieldCaptureController. The request is multipart form data: a JSON manifest holding inspectionRef and one item per file with clientFileId, kind of PHOTO, BILL or CHECKLIST, capturedAt with its offset, latitude, longitude and fileName, plus one file part per item named by its clientFileId. The app sends when a signal is available, which can be hours after the visit. The feature flag rwb.dochub.field-capture is off at first, and the endpoint then answers 404. The endpoint itself is recorded in the additions file.
RWB-E2-024.3: Three checks run before any file is touched. The caller must hold Documents right C, so a phone collector with read only is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002 (TC-E2-024-16). The case must be in the caller scope, which you read through CaseDirectory.findById in P3; a case where the collector has no task gives 404 with MSG-P4-003 and nothing is stored (AC12). The manifest and the file parts must match one to one, and a mismatch gives 422 with MSG-GEN-001 naming the client file ID with no file, again storing nothing (AC14). More files than CAPTURE_MAX_FILES, set to 50, gives 413 with MSG-GEN-002 and stores nothing (AC15).
RWB-E2-024.4: The duplicate check comes next, per item. FieldCaptureService looks up the client file ID among the items already received for that case, and a repeat returns the result of the first attempt with status DUPLICATE and the documentId written then, storing nothing new. The partial unique index ux_document_client_file on case_id and client_file_id, which applies only to rows where client_file_id is filled, backs this up in the database. This makes the endpoint idempotent per item, meaning the app can resend a whole sync after the connection dropped: six items return DUPLICATE and the four that never arrived are accepted (AC5).
RWB-E2-024.5: For an item that is new the service checks the file and the times, then stores and scans it. The file type must be in INTAKE_ALLOWED_TYPES, so a HEIC photo is refused with MSG-P5-001 while the other items of the same sync go on (AC10), and the size limit is INTAKE_MAX_FILE_MB of 25 with MSG-P5-017. A capture time later than the receipt time plus CAPTURE_CLOCK_SKEW_MINUTES of 5 is refused with MSG-GEN-002, and one before the case entry date or older than CAPTURE_MAX_AGE_DAYS of 30 with MSG-GEN-003. The file is written to the intake container and MalwareScanService.scanNow is called; a threat gives status QUARANTINED, MSG-P5-016, an incident and no document (AC11).
RWB-E2-024.6: Storage goes through the existing document hub. Call DocumentStore.store from RWB-E1-024 with a StoreRequest holding the case, the document type, source UPLOAD, the file and its hash. The type comes from the item kind with no classification step: PHOTO to INSPECTION_PHOTO, BILL to UTILITY_BILL and CHECKLIST to INSPECTION_CHECKLIST (BR5), and the case is the one in the path, so no case matching runs (BR6). The store writes the document row, the DOCATT decision log entry and the DocumentStored event.
