When the decision log write fails, that item is refused with MSG-P7-003 and nothing is stored for it (TC-E2-024-17).
RWB-E2-024.7: Five columns on document are new in this story and you set them in the same transaction as the store call, so a document never exists without its capture detail. They are captured_at, capture_latitude and capture_longitude as numeric with six decimals, client_file_id and capture_kind, added by migration V2_5_024__field_capture.sql and written through DocumentHubRepository. A transaction means these writes and the store writes are kept together or dropped together. An item with no GPS position is still stored, with latitude and longitude left empty, and the response carries the warning MSG-P5-015 with the count of such files (AC6).
RWB-E2-024.8: Two components you already have carry the item on, with no further call from your service. DocumentStoredListener from RWB-E1-049 reacts to the DocumentStored event and creates the OCR intake item; your check in build step 4 is that the item carries the type you gave, so classifyStep skips it. For a UTILITY_BILL, extractStep from RWB-E1-053 reads the UTILITY_BILL field list and writes bill_amount and due_date on the document, turning the Thai date 28/12/2569 into 2026-12-28 (AC3). A field read below the confidence threshold of 0.80 goes to state REVIEW, the document joins the review queue on SCR-31, and MSG-P5-003 shows on it (AC13).
RWB-E2-024.9: The endpoint answers 201 with FieldCaptureResult, which holds one entry per item: the clientFileId, a status of ACCEPTED, DUPLICATE, REFUSED or QUARANTINED, the documentId when one was written, and a messageCode. Item level refusals leave the rest of the request working, so a sync of ten items can return nine accepted and one refused. Only the request level failures of step 3 refuse everything. The warning MSG-P5-015 is returned when any accepted item arrived with no position. The field app shows these per item results to the collector, who can then capture a refused photo again.
RWB-E2-024.10: The case owner reads the result on SCR-30 Case documents. You build the React component CaptureDetails for that screen, showing the capture time, the position and a map link for each capture, the bill fields with their confidence, and MSG-P5-015 on captures that have no position. A GPS position and a photo of a home are personal data, so the position is masked for roles without the right to see it (BR9), and positions, file names and bill values are kept out of the logs. The phone collector holds Documents R and reads only. The restructuring officer reads the captures on deed in lieu cases.

RWB-E2-030.1: A person does both actions. The center of excellence analyst, RW-COE, loads the sample LEGAL-S1 through POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/agent-samples and then starts the evaluation through POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/agent-evaluations for agent LEGAL_DOC. Both endpoints come from RWB-E1-058 and need Rules and parameters right C, so RW-LITOFF calling them is refused with MSG-P4-002 (TC-E2-030-10). The sample is the answer key: for 50 Epic 1 litigation cases it holds one row per case and checklist item with the status the legal officers gave, PRESENT, MISSING or DEFECT. The officers supply those packs. A sample with no labeled rows is refused with MSG-P10-002.
RWB-E2-030.2: The run is automatic, once per sample case. Shadow mode means the agent reads and answers while nothing it produces reaches a user or changes a record. LegalPackInputAssembler builds the input: the case, its legal action through S4 LegalActionQueryService.listByCase, the documents and their fields through P5 DocumentQueryService.listByCase and getFields, and the checklist for the case type through getChecklist. Every call runs as the service identity SY-AGENT with read rights only, and field values are masked before the model call. Policy LEGAL_DOC version P1 sets the 60 second timeout and the allowed tools. A call that fails gives the run status TOOL_UNAVAILABLE with fallback true, and that case is scored as not run (AC6).
RWB-E2-030.3: The answer is checked before it is kept, by LegalPackRuleChecks, with no person reviewing it. The checks are that the output matches the schema legal-pack-v1, that every item of the checklist for that case type has a status, that every document ID named belongs to the same case, and that every DEFECT carries a reason. A missing status fails the SCHEMA check (AC5) and a document from another case fails the SCHEMA_RULE check (AC4). Either way the run holds status GUARDRAIL_FAILED and the case counts as wrong for every item in the scoring of step 5. The checklist for case type MORTGAGE_CIVIL has 9 items in the examples.
RWB-E2-030.4: The system writes the result on the agent_run row and nowhere else: the pack as document IDs per checklist item, the completeness list, the autonomy mode, the guardrail result, the latency, the tokens in and out and the cost. No document, legal action, task or case field changes, and no user facing endpoint returns the pack (AC1). SCR-46 Agent monitor shows LEGAL_DOC in state Shadow with its runs, fallbacks and score, which is where the analyst watches the batch. The event EV-28 AgentRunCompleted is published per run. The agent never changes a write once legal document.
RWB-E2-030.5: LegalPackScorer compares each run with the officer answer for the same case and item, and the harness stores the result in agent_evaluation. The agreement rate for an item is the number of cases where the agent status equals the officer status divided by the scored cases, written to four decimals, so 46 agreeing cases out of 50 give 0.9200 for DEMAND_NOTICE_PROOF (AC2). The sample size is stored next to the rate, and a case that did not run is left out of both, which leaves 49 scored after one TOOL_UNAVAILABLE run. Build step 4 asks you to test the scorer first on a 10 case fixture with known agreement.
RWB-E2-030.6: The analyst reads the scores through GET /api/recovery/v1/admin/agent-evaluations and then loads the next policy version, P2, through POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/agent-configs. There are two choices: mode L1 with the conditions under which the agent may act, or mode SHADOW with a review date to keep it in shadow. Your work here is PromotionProposalValidator, extended for this story. It refuses a proposal of mode L1 when fewer than 50 cases were scored, and a proposal of mode SHADOW with no review date, both with 422 and MSG-P10-001 naming the check (AC7, AC8). An L1 proposal is accepted only when the evaluation meets every condition stated in it.
RWB-E2-030.7: A second person closes the decision. RW-RISK, the risk and model risk officer, approves version P2, and the system records the status, the approver and the approval date on the agent_policy row. The person who loaded the version cannot approve it: coe.user01 approving their own load is refused with 409 and MSG-P7-002 (AC9). This is the separation of duty between the center of excellence analyst and the risk officer, the same pattern as a rule load. Until the approval the version in force is unchanged, so the agent keeps running under P1.

RWB-E1-007.1: Migration: creates the tables, columns and keys listed in section 11.
RWB-E1-007.2: Build: creates the entities, repositories, mapper/check/service classes listed in section 13.
RWB-E1-007.3: Build: registers the endpoint and published-interface contracts.
RWB-E1-007.4: Deferred: job scheduling, load execution and validation; see the data load reference.

RWB-E1-019.1: A person starts this. The reference data administrator fills the Queues template, which Shared operations owns, and uploads it. The endpoint already exists from RWB-E1-043, so you build nothing here: it takes multipart form data with the file, a table code of either QUEUE or QUEUE_MEMBER, and a valid from date. Two sheets means two calls, one per table code, both with valid from 2026-11-30. Each call answers 201 with a ReferenceLoad holding the load ID, the table, the date, the status and the row count. The caller needs Reference data right C; without it the call is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002.
RWB-E1-019.2: This happens inside the load call, with no second person involved. What you build is QueueTableChecks, a class implementing ReferenceTableCheck for the table codes QUEUE and QUEUE_MEMBER and plugged into the RWB-E1-043 checks. It adds six checks on top of the row checks that already run: the team code must exist in TEAM, the role code must exist in ROLE, the method must be a value of LOV-ASSIGN, the capacity cap must fall between 1 and 500, the overflow queue must exist and the overflow chain must form no loop, and each member must hold the role of the queue they are listed on. Each check returns a RowCheckFailure naming its row.
RWB-E1-019.3: Code from RWB-E1-043 decides this, so you reuse it rather than write it. One failed row refuses the whole file: no queue row and no member row changes, which is what AC4 checks. The response is 422 and every failed row is listed in Problem.detail, as MSG-P1-002 for the queue checks and MSG-GEN-001 or MSG-GEN-002 for an empty column or a cap out of range. A file with no failed row is stored as a new version with status VALIDATED. VALIDATED means checked and not yet in use: the rows sit in reference_version and reference_row and reach the queue tables only later.
RWB-E1-019.4: A load does not take effect because it passed its checks. A second person has to approve it, and that person is the queues table owner in Shared operations, acting as RW-TEAMMGR with Reference data right A. The approve endpoint belongs to RWB-E1-043; your part is to prove the rule holds for queue loads. When the approver is the same user who uploaded the file, the call answers 409 with MSG-P7-002, and the version stays VALIDATED and out of use. Two people are needed so that no one person can change the team structure alone. A successful call returns the load with status APPROVED.
RWB-E1-019.5: Build QueueVersionApplier as a job. It runs daily at 00:05 and again right after an approval or a rollback, with no one triggering it. It takes the QUEUE and QUEUE_MEMBER versions whose valid from date has arrived and writes them into the queue and queue_member tables. Match each queue by its queue code and update that existing row instead of inserting a new one: this is an upsert, insert when the row is absent and update when it is present. Keeping the queue's record ID is the point, because recovery_case.queue_id points at it and open cases must keep the queue they are in. Member rows are replaced, every row written carries table_version, and the whole version applies in one transaction.
RWB-E1-019.6: No person calls this. Build CapacityService in recovery.casewf.queues.api as a published interface, which means the allocation engine of RWB-E1-020 depends on the Java type and never reads the queue tables itself. check(queueId, userId, onDate) counts the user's open cases in recovery_case against their capacity, where the capacity is the lower of the member's own capacity and the queue's cap. It answers a CapacityAnswer of BELOW_CAP or AT_CAP with the open case count, the capacity and the overflow queue ID. The answer must come from the version applied for the date asked, so a question about 2026-12-14 uses the version in force then, not a version approved for 2026-12-15.
RWB-E1-019.7: Also automatic, and also a published interface. QueueMembershipQuery.membershipOf(userId, onDate) returns a Membership holding the team codes, the region codes and the queue IDs for that user on that date. RWB-E1-037 calls it to work out what a user is allowed to see, so scope checks across the service all come from one place. The team codes come from the queue rows the user is a member of, and the region code from the TEAM row for each of those teams. Build it to answer from the version applied for the date given, the same way the capacity answer does. Return codes only, with no name and no other personal field.
RWB-E1-019.8: A person decides this one. The reference data administrator calls POST /admin/reference-loads/{loadId}/rollback, which is a new endpoint you build, with a reason in the body. Build ReferenceRollbackHandler behind it: it marks the version ROLLED_BACK through the RWB-E1-043 store and then triggers QueueVersionApplier, which writes the earlier approved version back over the queue and queue_member rows in one transaction. One call is enough, and there is no second step for the user. With no earlier version to return to, the call answers 409 with MSG-P3-015 and nothing changes. An empty reason answers 422 with MSG-GEN-001. The Idempotency-Key header makes a repeated call return the first result.

RWB-E1-031.1: A person starts this by opening the screen. SCR-02 Case list already exists, and this story adds to it. Build the Loading state into CaseListPage as skeleton rows, which are gray placeholder rows the same shape as the real ones, so the table does not jump when the data arrives. Loading is one of four states the page must handle, with empty, list and filtered. The page is a React component in src/modules/recovery/casewf/caselist. Put the new queue and owner columns and the export behind the feature flag rwb.p3.caselistqueue, so the screen falls back to its old columns when the flag is off.
RWB-E1-031.2: The page does this itself as soon as it loads. It calls GET /api/recovery/v1/cases with page 0 and size 50, and sends no scope of its own. Scope is applied on the server from the caller's role, as Own, Team, Region or All, with Team the team manager's default. CaseQueryService builds the query with that limit already in it, so a case outside the caller's scope cannot come back even if the request asks for it. The endpoint needs Case record right R and answers 403 with MSG-P4-002 without it. Never filter by scope in the browser, because the response would still carry the rows.
RWB-E1-031.3: The page renders what the response gave it. Seven columns are needed: case number, product, status, stage, queue, owner and entry date. Queue and owner are the new ones in this story. The response carries queueId and ownerUserId, so CaseQueryService joins the queue table to supply the queue code and name, and the owner display name comes from the ACE user directory interface in the common module. A case with no owner still shows, with the owner cell left blank, which AC7 tests. Build the table with the Radix table component. The labels "Export" and "Owner user ID" are set by DL10 and not chosen in the component.
RWB-E1-031.4: The manager chooses the values and the page reacts. Build CaseListFilters with three pickers, queue, team and status, filled from the queues of RWB-E1-019 and the lists LOV-CASE-STATUS and LOV-TEAM through the P4 list interface. On a change, call the same GET /cases with the chosen values. Queue and status already exist as query parameters; team is new and has to be added to the endpoint. The filters combine with AND, so a case has to match every one of them to show. The filtered state keeps the chosen values visible above the list with a control to clear them, and Export uses exactly the filters shown.
RWB-E1-031.5: Server-side work, with no user action. CaseQueryService applies the caller's scope first and the filters after, so a queue of another team returns no row rather than an error, which is what AC6 expects. The response is a CasePage holding the items, the page number, the page size and the total. The total is the count of all matching rows, not of the page, and the table needs it to show how many pages there are. Add the index ix_case_team_status on recovery_case (team_code, status) in migration V031_1__case_team_index.sql; the query uses it along with ix_case_status_queue. The list has to answer in under two seconds on 26,500 cases.
RWB-E1-031.6: A person presses this. Build ExportButton, which calls GET /cases/export with the same query parameters as the list but without page and size, since an export covers the whole filtered set. The endpoint is new in this story. The button also shows what comes back from a refusal: MSG-P3-021 when the filtered set is above the row limit, and MSG-P7-003 when the access log cannot be written. A good call answers with an xlsx file, content type application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet. Hide the button when the feature flag rwb.p3.caselistqueue is off.
RWB-E1-031.7: Automatic, and the order of the three actions is the requirement. First count the rows and compare them with the parameter caselist.export.maxrows, which is 10,000; above it, stop with 422 and MSG-P3-021. Second, publish the access event AC-EXPT through AccessEventPublisher, the P4 interface from RWB-E1-039, with the user, the time, the filters and the row count. If that write throws DecisionLogUnavailableException, make no file and answer 503 with MSG-P7-003. Only then build the workbook, running each column through FieldMasker so the caller's role decides which values appear. Exactly 10,000 rows is allowed, so the check refuses only a count above the limit.
RWB-E1-031.8: The browser handles the download once the response arrives, so there is no code for saving the file. What you do control is the file name, which follows the pattern "Case list YYYYMMDD 1.xlsx" with the date of the export, and the content type on the response, which is what makes the browser offer a download instead of showing the bytes. The file holds one row per case in the filtered set, with the masked columns. Nothing in the export is written back to the database. The only trace of it is the AC-EXPT access log entry from the previous step, which RW-COMPLY reads.

RWB-E1-044.1: A developer does this by hand, once per story that changes the database. Put the file in recovery/src/main/resources/db/migration/recovery, name it V<number>__<description>.sql, and make the first line a comment reading "-- Story: <story key>". A migration is a SQL file Flyway applies once and then remembers, so the database of any environment is the sum of the migrations applied to it. One story gets one file, and no two files may carry the same story key. Write no schema name in the SQL: use the ${schema} placeholder, which Flyway replaces with the value of RWB_SCHEMA for the environment it is running in.
RWB-E1-044.2: The build does this, not a reviewer. Build MigrationLint as a build step with four refusals: a literal schema name written before a table name, a file with no story key in its header, the same story key in two files, and any file whose name begins with U, which would be an undo migration. For the literal name check, compare against every object name in sys_objects. Each failure stops the build with MSG-P3-016 and names the file, and the line as well for a literal schema name. Test each refusal with its own fixture file. The lint is the reason a wrong file never reaches an environment.
RWB-E1-044.3: This runs in the pipeline with no person watching. Start an empty PostgreSQL container, set RWB_SCHEMA, and let Flyway apply every migration from the first to the newest. The result is the schema the repository describes and nothing else, which is why it can be compared against a real environment in the next step. It also proves the placeholder works: the same files build a schema named rwb_case here and in SIT, from files that are byte for byte identical in both runs. Use a clean container every time, because a container that keeps state from an earlier run would hide a migration that only works against an older database.
RWB-E1-044.4: Build SchemaDriftCheck and put it in the pipeline before each deployment to SIT, UAT and PROD. It lists the tables, columns, types, constraints and indexes of RWB_SCHEMA in the clean container, then the same list from the target environment, read through the read-only database account from the key store, and reports every difference. Drift is any object in an environment that the migrations did not produce, such as a column someone added by hand. A difference fails the pipeline with MSG-P3-016 naming the object, and no deployment starts. The feature flag rwb.p3.migration-drift-gate controls this: on in SIT, UAT and PROD, off in DEV, where drift is reported and the deployment continues.
RWB-E1-044.5: Flyway does this inside the service as it starts, with no pipeline step and no person. Configure it with RecoveryFlywayConfig and the properties in section 12, including spring.flyway.table set to flyway_schema_history_recovery, so the recovery module keeps its own history and its version numbers cannot collide with the ACE and collection modules. Pending means present in the repository and not yet in this database. Flyway applies those migrations lowest version first and writes one history row per migration with its version and its checksum, a number computed from the file content. Out of order is off, so a version below the newest applied one is refused.
RWB-E1-044.6: Also automatic, and it happens before anything is applied, because validate-on-migrate is true. Flyway recomputes the checksum of each file that has a history row and compares it with the stored one. A file edited after it ran gives a different number, so validation fails with MSG-P3-016 naming the version and the service does not start, as AC4 describes with checksum 104553219 changed to 88120477. An applied migration is never edited. A mistake in one is corrected by adding a new migration that puts it right. PROD runs forward only: clean is disabled in every profile and an undo file is refused by the lint.
RWB-E1-044.7: A person reads the result here. Build MigrationRunRecorder to write one job record per migration run through the P1 job monitor interface, which is what gives SCR-44 something to show. The administrator then sees each run with its version, its checksum and its drift result, in state running, failed or complete, and the same data comes back from GET /api/recovery/v1/admin/jobs with type MIGRATION. Reading it needs Platform administration right R, and a role without that right is refused with MSG-P4-002. MSG-P3-016 belongs in the pipeline log and on this screen only, and is never shown to a business user.

RWB-E1-056.1: A person owns these rows, and the platform administrator keeps them. Your part is the table and the first rows. Build job_catalog in migration V2026_11_56__p2_job_catalog.sql with job_id as the primary key and a check that it matches ^JOB-[0-9]{2}$, which refuses a job ID in any other shape. Build the JobCatalogEntry entity and JobCatalogRepository over it. The migration inserts the 13 Epic 1 rows from the batch schedule, each with the job name, the owner role, the schedule text, the run book path, the expected minutes, the alert threshold in minutes and first_release. Thresholds are assumed at 1.5 times the expected duration.
RWB-E1-056.2: A person writes these too, one file per job, and the squad that built the job writes its own. The path is docs/operations/runbooks/<job ID>.md and it must match the runbook_path on the catalog row. Six headings are required: purpose, schedule, owner, failure signs, restart steps and escalation. Write the restart steps so that the operations team can follow them without the developer, since that is the whole point of the story. Name roles and service identities in the text, never a person, because the file outlives whoever holds the job today. Thirteen run books are needed for Epic 1.
RWB-E1-056.3: The build does the checking, so a missing run book cannot be merged. Build RunbookCompletenessTest to find every Quartz JobDetail bean and every Spring Batch Job bean in the service and, for each one, assert that a job_catalog row exists and that the file at its runbook_path holds all six headings. A failure stops the build with MSG-P2-005 naming the job and the missing section, as AC4 describes for a job whose run book has no Escalation section. Finding the jobs from the Spring context instead of from a written list means a job added later is caught on its first build.
RWB-E1-056.4: The jobs emit this themselves once you attach the listener. Build JobRunEventListener as a Spring Batch JobExecutionListener and attach it to every Spring Batch job, so no squad writes logging code of its own. It emits an event named rwb.job.run at the start and at the end of a run, carrying the job ID, the business date, the status and the duration. Structured means the fields are separate named values rather than one sentence, which is what lets Log Analytics filter and total them. Put no personal data in the event: job IDs, dates, counts and durations only.
RWB-E1-056.5: A person looks, and both paths have to show the same numbers. Build the Log Analytics workbook named "Recovery jobs" in ops/monitoring, with one line per job holding its last run time, status and duration. For the endpoint, build JobOperationsImpl.lastRun, which reads the last run from the Spring Batch job repository through the framework rather than by querying its tables. GET /admin/jobs then answers with the job ID, type, business date, status, startedAt and endedAt. Reading needs Platform administration right R, which RW-DATASTEW, RW-AUDIT, RW-COMPLY, RW-COE and RW-SECADM hold as well as RW-PLATADM.
RWB-E1-056.6: No one is watching the workbook at 05:00, so two alert rules do it. Build them in ops/monitoring over the rwb.job.run events: one for a run whose status is FAILED, one for a run still going past alert_after_minutes on its catalog row. Each one emails the role in owner_role and RW-PLATADM with MSG-P2-004, which names the job, the time, the business date and the run book to follow. The owner is the role from the batch schedule, so JOB-01 and JOB-02 alert the data steward and JOB-03 the team managers. A job over its threshold is alerted and left running; the rule never stops it. Test each rule with a forced failure in SIT.
RWB-E1-056.7: A person drives the restart, with the run book open. The endpoint takes the ID of the failed execution, not the job ID on the catalog row, and calls JobOperations.rerun. Build it on the Spring Batch JobOperator.restart call. Check first whether the job is running: if it is, throw JobAlreadyRunningException and map it to 409 with MSG-P2-006, and let the running job carry on. An unknown execution answers 404 with MSG-P4-003. The call needs Platform administration right U, so RW-TEAMMGR, who receives the alerts for JOB-03 and JOB-06, cannot make it, and RW-CASEOWN is refused with MSG-P4-002.
RWB-E1-056.8: The service does the rest. Spring Batch restarts the execution at the step that failed instead of at the beginning, so the steps that already completed are not run twice. The jobs that depend on it then run in the order of the daily timeline, which is why AC2 expects JOB-02 after JOB-01. A rerun has to be idempotent for the job and the business date, meaning a second run has no further effect: running JOB-01 again for a date it already completed writes each interface run as DUPLICATE and loads no account record a second time, which the unique key on interface_run from RWB-E1-007 enforces.

RWB-E1-068.1: A person opens the screen, and the panel calls on its own. Build CaseHistoryPanel as a React component on SCR-03 Case record. On load it calls GET /cases/{caseId}/interactions with page 0 and size 50, which is the default page size from the property rwb.dataengine.ledger.page-size-default. The panel needs three states beyond the list: Loading with skeleton rows, Empty with a sentence saying no interaction is recorded on the case, and Error showing the message from section 14 above the panel. SCR-03 is read only in Epic 1, so the panel reads and offers nothing to change. The full timeline screen SCR-04 is Epic 2 work.
RWB-E1-068.2: This is automatic, and it is a change to an endpoint that already exists. InteractionsHandler in P3 keeps the access check it has: without Case record right R the call is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002. What you add is the actor query parameter and the delegation. The handler builds a LedgerFilter from channel, actor, from and to, then calls InteractionLedgerReader.read with it, the page, the size and the caller's UserContext. The handler queries nothing itself. Passing the caller's context down is what lets the reader apply scope and masking for the right user, rather than the handler deciding either of them.
RWB-E1-068.3: The reader does this first, before it touches the ledger. Build LedgerReadService behind the published interface and have it call CaseScopeQuery, the P3 interface from RWB-E1-016, to ask whether this caller may see this case. Scope is the set of cases a role may reach: Own for a case owner, Team for a team manager. A case outside it answers 404 with MSG-P4-003, not 403, so the response does not tell the caller that a case they may not see exists. The interface throws CaseNotInScopeException, which the handler maps to that 404. Make the scope check before the query, never by filtering rows afterwards.
RWB-E1-068.4: Still inside the reader, with no call back to the browser. Three checks on the LedgerFilter: the channel must be a value of LOV-CHANNEL, the from date must not fall after the to date, and the page size must lie between 1 and 200, the maximum held in the property rwb.dataengine.ledger.page-size-max. Each failure answers 422 and changes nothing: MSG-GEN-003 for the dates, naming "to" and "from"; MSG-GEN-002 for the size, naming the minimum and the maximum; MSG-GEN-001 for a malformed channel or date. Size 200 passes and size 201 is refused, so the size check refuses only a value above 200.
RWB-E1-068.5: Automatic. Build the query in InteractionRepository: the interaction rows for the case, narrowed by channel, actor_ref and an occurred_at range when the filter holds them, ordered by occurred_at and then case_seq, earliest first. The second column is the tie-break, so two entries recorded at the same moment always come back in the same order and paging cannot repeat or skip a row. The existing index ix_interaction_case_time serves the case and time part; add an index on (case_id, actor_ref) in a Flyway migration for the actor filter. One read of a case with 5,000 entries has to finish inside two seconds.
RWB-E1-068.6: The reader does this to every row before it answers. Call the P4 masking interface from RWB-E1-037 with the caller's roles for the summary field, which is the one field marked is_personal. When no masking rule allows the caller to see it, the value comes back as "MASKED". Compliance owns those rules and they may be empty, in which case every personal field is masked, so write the code to mask by default rather than to allow by default. The channel, the result, the promise amount and the promise date are returned in full. Masking belongs here so that every consumer of the ledger gets the same treatment.
RWB-E1-068.7: Automatic, and only on the condition named. When a personal field leaves the reader unmasked, write the read to the PII access log; when every personal field was masked, write nothing. Put the write in LedgerReadService after the masking step, so the decision rests on what actually went out. The entry is what lets Compliance show later who read which personal content. Never put the summary text into that entry or into any log: the guardrails say summaries are never logged, and test data uses synthetic text instead.
RWB-E1-068.8: The handler maps the reader's LedgerPage to the API response with no further logic. InteractionPage holds the items, the page, the size and the total, where total is the count of all matching entries. The Interaction type gains six fields in this story: eventCode, caseSeq, actorType, actorRef, sourceRef and decisionLogEntryId. Source matters to the person reading the screen, because each entry has to name the system it came from and its reference, for example "EFS, INT-07" or "WORKBENCH, P3 case and workflow", so a case owner can tell a call loaded from EFS from an entry made in the Workbench. An empty page answers 200 with 0 items and total 0.
RWB-E1-068.9: A person chooses the filter, and the panel repeats the call it made on load with the chosen values added. There is no second endpoint and no filtering in the browser: the three filters go to the server every time, so scope and masking are applied again on each read. Build the controls on CaseHistoryPanel as a channel picker fed by LOV-CHANNEL, an actor field, a from and to date pair, and paging. Reset to page 0 when a filter changes, because the page numbers of the old result mean nothing against the new one. An architecture test proves that no class outside recovery.dataengine.ledger queries the interaction table.

RWB-E2-012.1: A person opens it, and from two places. Build TransferCasePage as SCR-05 in src/modules/recovery/casewf/transfer, reachable from SCR-03 Case record for one case and from a selection on SCR-07 Team queues for up to 50 cases, the limit in transfer.bulk.max. The person needs RW-TEAMMGR or RW-CAPACITY with Queue and allocation right U, and the cases must be in their scope. A case owner may read the result and may not transfer. The feature flag rwb.p3.manual-transfer hides the screen and makes the endpoint answer 403 for every role except SY-CASEWF when it is off.
RWB-E2-012.2: The manager fills the form. One of the two targets is required and only one is allowed: a queue, which leaves the owner to the engine, or a named owner. The reason code is required and comes from LOV-TRANSFER-REASON, with the assumed values R01 Capacity, R02 Customer deceased, R03 Skill, R04 Owner absent, R05 Legal referral and R06 Wrong queue. The note is optional and holds at most 500 characters. Build the reason picker from that list rather than from a fixed set in code, because the center of excellence owns those values. The note is never logged. This is the Form state of SCR-05.
RWB-E2-012.3: The page sends the call when the manager confirms. One request per case, each with its own Idempotency-Key header holding a fresh UUID. An idempotency key is a value that names one attempt, so a request sent twice takes effect once. Build IdempotencyStore to keep the key, a hash of the request and the response for 24 hours, and have the controller return the stored response when the same key arrives again. For a bulk move, BulkTransferRunner sends the requests one after another and collects a result per row, so each case is its own request and its own transaction.
RWB-E2-012.4: Automatic, in ManualTransferService, and the order of the checks is set in the build steps. Check the reason code first: a missing one answers 422 with MSG-P3-001 and changes nothing. Then the case state. A case that is closed, or whose legal_hold flag is true, answers 409 with MSG-P3-005 naming the target and the held state. Then scope: a case the caller may not reach answers 404 with MSG-P4-003. A legal hold is a flag on recovery_case that keeps the case where it is while legal work runs on it. Make every check before any write, so a refusal leaves the case, its assignment and the decision log untouched.
RWB-E2-012.5: No person is involved, and the logic is not yours. Call TransferRules.evaluate from RWB-E1-021 with the case ID, the target queue, the target owner and the reason code. It answers a TransferDecision holding either the rule row that allows the move or the ID of the rule that refuses it. On a refusal, answer 409 with MSG-P3-033 naming that rule, as AC2 expects for rule R-DEV-02 on a case with an open deviation. Keep the allowing rule's ID and version, because both have to appear on the assignment row and in the decision log entry. Write no transfer condition into this service; the rows decide.
RWB-E2-012.6: Two paths, both automatic. For a queue transfer, call AssignmentEngine.pickOwner from RWB-E1-020, which picks by the queue's assignment_method, so ROUND_ROBIN on queue LIT-BKK-01 gives the owner whose turn it is. For a named owner, build OwnerLoadRepository to count that owner's open cases and compare them with the queue's capacity_cap: at or above it, answer 422 with MSG-P3-002 naming the owner, and name every owner when the whole target queue is at the cap. For reason R04, owner absent, also check that the target owner's team matches the case's team, and refuse with MSG-P3-033 naming R-UNI-18 when it does not.
RWB-E2-012.7: Automatic, and the sequence is the rule. Call DecisionLogWriter.record through the P7 interface first; a failed write answers 503 with MSG-P7-003 and nothing else happens. Only after it succeeds, open one transaction holding five writes: set ended_at on the current assignment, insert the new assignment with reason TRANSFER or MANUAL, the rule ID, the queue ID and transfer_reason_code, update recovery_case with the new queue, owner and team_code, and insert the CaseTransferred event into the outbox. The case update uses the version column as an optimistic lock, which means the update names the version it read and fails when another transfer changed the row first, answering 409 with MSG-GEN-004. The status, route state and clocks stay as they were.
RWB-E2-012.8: The page shows the outcome. For a single case, the Saved state with MSG-GEN-005. For a bulk move, BulkTransferRunner keeps the result of each request and the page lists one line per case, so a refused case shows its own message, MSG-P3-005 for a case under a legal hold, beside the cases that moved. Above the list, show MSG-P3-035 with the counts, which for AC11 reads 8 of 10. A refused case is queued nowhere and no retry happens; the manager corrects the reason and sends it again. SCR-09 Exception queue has no part in this story.

RWB-E2-025.1: A person does this, and two more approve it. The reference data administrator loads the document type table version DOCTYPE-2026.12 through the RWB-E1-025 loader with valid from 2026-12-31, after legal counsel and the Head of NPA have signed the type and field list. You write no loader code. Your work is the load file: the five new types with their classify_threshold and their field definitions, each field carrying its data type, its extraction method, its review_only flag and an optional pattern. Prepare it with a test case per new row and validate it in SIT first. The document_hub_parameter row EXTRACT_ACCURACY_PASS, 0.90, is loaded the same way.
RWB-E2-025.2: Automatic, and already built. JOB-12 Document intake runs its steps in order, and the first two, scanStep and ocrStep from RWB-E1-041 and RWB-E1-049, need no change for these documents. OCR turns the scanned page into text that later steps can read, which matters here because these documents arrive on paper and much of their text is Thai. Nothing in this story touches the file itself. A write-once document, one whose stored file may never be altered, keeps its hash, its storage_ref and its write_once flag through everything that follows.
RWB-E2-025.3: Automatic, in the classifyStep of RWB-E1-050, whose code does not change. What changes is the classifier version it uses: one trained on the 60-document labeled sample to tell eleven types apart, the six from Epic 1 plus the five new ones, selected through the agent runtime in P10. For each document it writes predicted_type and classification_confidence on document_intake. Confidence is a number between 0 and 1 saying how sure the classifier is. Below the classify_threshold held on the type's own row, the item goes to the review queue with review_reason LOW_CONFIDENCE. The evaluation run has to show at least 45 of the 50 new-type samples classified correctly.
RWB-E2-025.4: Automatic, and the point of the story is that no Java changes here either. ExtractStep reads the field definitions for the predicted type from DocumentTypeCatalog, taking the table version in force on the extraction date, then calls the extractor named in each field's extraction_method, either TemplateFieldExtractor or ModelFieldExtractor. Both are configured from the type table alone, so a new type is rows and not a class. For JUDGMENT the definitions name court_name, red_case_no, judgment_date and judgment_amount. A document received before 2026-12-31 is read against DOCTYPE-2026.11 and its six types, which is why the judgment in AC6 ends in the review queue with review_reason UNKNOWN_TYPE.
RWB-E2-025.5: Automatic. ValueNormalizer from RWB-E1-053 turns each extracted value into its stored form: "2,400,000.00 บาท" becomes "2400000.00", and a Buddhist Era date becomes an ISO date, so "5 มีนาคม 2570" is stored as 2027-03-05. The normalized value is then matched against the pattern on the field's own row in field_definitions, a text rule the value has to fit, for example two to four letters, a space, digits, a slash and four digits for red_case_no. One document_field row is written per field, with the extracted value, the extractor version, the confidence and the state. The patterns are data, so write none of them into code.
RWB-E2-025.6: Automatic, and three separate conditions lead to the same place. A confidence below the field threshold of 0.80, a value that does not fit its pattern, and a field whose review_only flag is true each set the field state to REVIEW and send the document to the review queue of RWB-E1-054 with that field marked. So "Por345-2570" at confidence 0.9200 goes to review on its pattern, while "Por 345/2570" at the same confidence is OK. SCR-30 shows MSG-P5-003 on the document. The review_only flag is how a field whose accuracy on the sample fell below the 0.90 pass mark is held back, and it takes effect only when the new table version is loaded.
RWB-E2-025.7: Automatic, in the matchStep of RWB-E1-032. The document and its fields are written through DocumentStore, never by this story's code reaching into another module's tables. For a document already attached to a case, the event DocumentFieldsExtracted, EV-17, is written so that the modules waiting on those values learn they exist. The idempotency key is the document ID, the doc_version and the table version, so the same document extracted again under the same version produces no second set of rows. A write-once document gains its document_field rows and keeps its file, its hash and its storage_ref, which AC10 checks with four rows on a judgment.
RWB-E2-025.8: A person reads and corrects here. SCR-30 Case documents lists the new types with their fields and confidences, and shows MSG-P5-003 on any document holding a field in REVIEW. SCR-31 Document review queue, built in RWB-E1-054, is where the officer checks a marked field and either confirms the extracted value or corrects it, which moves the field state to CONFIRMED or CORRECTED. Both screens are existing work, and this story only brings the new types and fields into them. Party names and other personal values are masked unless the officer's role may see them, and a document of another team answers 404 with MSG-P4-003.
RWB-E2-025.9: Automatic, and this is the one new interface you build. DocumentFieldReader.checkedFields(caseId, documentType) in recovery.dochub.extract answers a list of CheckedField holding the document ID, the doc version, the field name, the value, the state and the confidence. Return only fields in state OK, CONFIRMED or CORRECTED; a field still in REVIEW is held back until a person has dealt with it. The caller passes its own service identity, and values come back unmasked only to a module whose purpose needs them, SY-CASEWF or SY-AGENT, and are never logged. Add the index ix_document_type_case on document (case_id, document_type) for this query, and write a contract test from the S4 side.

RWB-E1-008.1: No person does this. The decision log writer, service identity SY-DECLOG from RWB-E1-027, calls your append method. You build DecisionLogStore in the Java package recovery.decision.log with the method append(DecisionLogRecord record) from section 12, declared to throw DecisionLogUnavailableException. Only the writer calls it; other modules reach the log through the writer. The call runs inside the caller's own transaction. A transaction is one group of database statements that either all take effect or none do. BR5 puts the append as the last statement of that group, so the business action and its entry commit together. Do not open your own transaction inside append and do not commit there.
RWB-E1-008.2: Your store code takes the lock; the database does not do it for you. Use a PostgreSQL transaction advisory lock on the key "decision_log_chain". An advisory lock is a lock the application asks for by a name of its own choosing, and the database does not attach it to any row or table; a transaction-level one is released when the transaction ends. It makes the appends line up one after another, so two writers cannot read the same last entry and give two entries the same chain_seq. AC5 is the test: entries after chain_seq 50 take 51 and 52, and the prev_hash of 52 equals the entry_hash of 51.
RWB-E1-008.3: Still inside append, the store reads the last stored entry and works out the two chain columns. chain_seq is the last value plus one, and prev_hash is the entry_hash of that last entry. For the very first entry there is nothing before it, so prev_hash takes 64 zeros. Read that value from the property rwb.decision.chain.genesis-hash rather than writing it into the code, as section 13 requires. The migration V_E1_008__declog_chain.sql adds chain_seq as bigint not null unique, so a repeated value is refused by the database itself. AC2 checks that the first prev_hash is 64 zeros and that each later prev_hash matches the entry before it.
RWB-E1-008.4: The store builds the canonical form and hashes it. A canonical form is one fixed way of writing the entry as text, so the same entry always produces the same hash. BR4 sets it: every field of the entry except entry_hash and the standard columns, as JSON with keys in alphabetical order, UTF-8, no spaces, timestamps in ISO 8601 UTC with microseconds, numbers written as strings and empty fields as null. SHA-256 turns that text into a fixed value, which you write as lower-case hexadecimal. Build this once as CanonicalEntryForm and use the same class in the verifier. Check golden test vectors into the test resources, a fixed entry with its expected hash.
RWB-E1-008.5: The insert is the only write the store makes. Use DecisionCenterAndLogRepository, which has no update and no delete method. Your code does not commit; the caller's transaction does, and it covers both the business action and this entry, so the two are kept together or not at all. The transaction advisory lock from step 2 ends with that commit, which lets the next writer read the new last entry. AC7 tests the other direction: when the append fails inside a transaction that also changes the case owner, no entry is stored, the case owner is unchanged and no chain_seq is used up.
RWB-E1-008.6: The store catches any failure of the lock, the read, the hash or the insert and throws DecisionLogUnavailableException, which section 12 declares on the append method. Do not swallow the error and do not let the caller carry on. Because the append sits inside the caller's transaction, that throw rolls the whole transaction back, so the business action is undone with it. The caller then shows MSG-P7-003, which tells the user the action was not taken because the decision could not be recorded and to try again in a few minutes. This is exception path X5 and acceptance criterion AC7.
RWB-E1-008.7: The database stops this, not your Java code. The trigger tr_declog_append_only already exists from RWB-E1-001. A trigger is code the database runs by itself when a statement touches a table, and this one refuses the statement with the text "decision_log_entry is append only". Your migration also revokes UPDATE and DELETE on decision_log_entry from the service role, so the service role is refused by the missing grant and the schema owner is refused by the trigger. Confirm both paths in the migration test, which is build step 1. The ACE service writes each refused attempt to the ACE audit and SOC log with the table, the operation and the entry ID, as AC1 requires.
RWB-E1-008.8: You build HashChainVerifier with the method verify(fromSeq, toSeq) from section 12. It reads the entries in chain_seq order across the range, in batches of 1,000 as section 13 requires, rebuilds each entry's canonical form with the same CanonicalEntryForm class the store uses, recomputes the SHA-256 and compares it with the stored entry_hash. It also checks that each prev_hash equals the entry_hash of the entry before it. Nothing calls it on a schedule in this story; the nightly run and its daily report are RWB-TE-008. AC2 runs it over 100 entries and AC4 over 10,000 entries with one of them changed in the DEV database.
RWB-E1-008.9: verify returns ChainCheckResult holding the count checked, lastSeq, lastHash, breakSeq and breakEntryId. When every hash matches, the break fields stay empty. When one does not, the first entry in chain_seq order that fails is named, and your code calls ChainBreakNotifier, which raises the incident on the ACE incident path and sends MSG-P7-008 to the Compliance group through the ACE notification path. The notification group is configuration, not a value in code. BR6 and AC4 set the time limit: Compliance is told within 15 minutes of the run start. AC4 expects chain_seq 7,412 and its entry ID reported as the first break.

RWB-E1-020.1: Nobody starts this by hand on a normal day. Quartz is the scheduler inside the service, and you configure it to fire JOB-03 Morning allocation once JOB-02 case creation has completed for the business date. Build AllocationJob as a Quartz job with @DisallowConcurrentExecution, which stops a second copy of the same job running at the same time. The job checks the JOB-02 completion before it does any work: when JOB-02 has not completed, JOB-03 does not start, the job monitor shows it waiting with MSG-P1-001, and the cases keep status NEW. That is exception path X7 and AC10. The run has to be finished by 07:00 Asia/Bangkok.
RWB-E1-020.2: AllocationJob runs the selection with no person involved. Read recovery_case for rows with status NEW whose last_allocation_date is before the business date. last_allocation_date is a new date column added by the migration V020_1__allocation_columns.sql in this story, together with queue.rr_cursor_user_id. That date is what makes the run safe to repeat: a case already allocated for the business date is skipped and the outcome type is SKIPPED, which is build step 5 and AC8. The job then calls AllocationService.allocate with the case ID and the business date for each case, and commits per case, so one failing case leaves the others in place.
RWB-E1-020.3: AllocationServiceImpl does this. Start by locking the case row with SELECT ... FROM recovery_case WHERE id = ? AND status = 'NEW' FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. A row lock held for the length of the transaction keeps a second worker off the same case, and SKIP LOCKED makes that worker pass over it instead of waiting, which is AC11 and exception path X8. Then read deviation_open. When it is true, place the case in the queue named by the parameter allocation.deviation.queue.code, set no owner and leave the status NEW. Rule R-DEV-01 and AC7 cover this branch, and no allocation row is read for such a case.
RWB-E1-020.4: This happens automatically, and the rows are evaluated under the service identity SY-RULES. Your AllocationRuleEvaluator does not read the rule tables itself. It calls RuleTableReader.rowsInForce("ALLOCATION", businessDate), the P4 published interface in section 12, then walks the returned rows in row_order. The first row whose product group, region and exposure band match the case wins, and "any" in a column matches every value, per BR1. When no row matches, the case goes to the queue named by allocation.exception.queue.code, keeps status NEW, gets a decision log entry with final call RULE_GAP and publishes CaseAllocationFailed (EV-03), which is exception path X2 and AC5.
RWB-E1-020.5: AssignmentEngine picks the owner, with no person choosing. Read assignment_method and capacity_cap from the target queue row and the members from queue_member. Build OwnerLoadRepository to count each member's open cases, which BR3 defines as cases in that queue owned by the person with a status other than CLOSED. Implement all four methods named in BR2: ROUND_ROBIN, LOWEST_LOAD, NAMED_OWNER and SKILL. Skip any member at or above the cap, and for round robin carry the turn in queue.rr_cursor_user_id. When every member is at the cap the case goes to the queue's overflow_queue_id, and when the queue has none, to the exception queue with the reason NO_OVERFLOW_QUEUE.
RWB-E1-020.6: All of these writes happen in the one transaction that already holds the case row lock, so they take effect together or not at all. On recovery_case set queue_id, team_code, owner_user_id, status ASSIGNED, stage_clock_start, rule_version and last_allocation_date, and update the optimistic version column. Insert the assignment row with reason ALLOCATION. Write CaseAllocated (EV-02) into the outbox table instead of publishing it directly: the outbox pattern stores the event beside the data in the same transaction and a separate sender delivers it afterward, so no event goes out for a change that rolled back. EV-02 carries caseId, queueId, ownerId, ruleId and ruleVersion.
RWB-E1-020.7: Your service calls DecisionLogWriter.write from the P7 interface of RWB-E1-027, inside the same transaction and after the case and assignment writes, as the last step before commit. Pass the row ID, the table version, the queue, the owner and the inputs used, which AC6 checks as rule ID ALLOC-014 and rule version ALLOC-2026.11. The call can throw DecisionLogRecordInvalidException or DecisionLogUnavailableException. Let either one roll the transaction back, so the case keeps status NEW with no queue and no owner, and record MSG-P3-013 for that case on the job record. The case is tried again in the next run. This is BR7, exception path X3 and test TC-E1-020-15.
RWB-E1-020.8: After the last case, AllocationJob calls AllocationSummaryBuilder, which counts the overflow and exception cases for each team and fills MSG-P3-011 with the overflow count and MSG-P3-012 with the count that matched no allocation row. The job sends each summary to the team manager of that team through the ACE notification path. No case number or customer detail belongs in it; the guardrails allow counts and the team only. A run with no new cases still sends the summary with count 0, which is exception path X6 and AC9. Thai text for both messages follows decision DL10.
RWB-E1-020.9: The job writes its own counts: cases read, assigned, overflow, exception and failed. Write them to the job record that the job monitoring of RWB-E1-056 reads, so the platform administrator sees the result of each run and can rerun JOB-03 through POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/jobs/{jobId}/rerun. Count the cases skipped as already allocated as well, because AC8 expects the job record to show 1 case skipped after a repeated run for 2026-12-01. A rerun by a user without Platform administration U is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002, which is exception path X10 and the access test TC-E1-020-14.

RWB-E1-032.1: No person starts this. JOB-12 Document intake runs every 15 minutes in business hours, and matchStep is one more step inside that job, placed after the extraction step. Your work is the step itself, built as MatchStep in the Java package recovery.dochub.attach. It reads rows the earlier steps left behind, so it needs nothing from the scanners or the mailboxes. The feature flag rwb.dochub.autoattach controls it: with the flag off, matchStep gives every classified item match_status NO_MATCH and reviewers attach them by hand. Items the step leaves untouched are taken by the next run, as the restart behavior in section 12 states.
RWB-E1-032.2: MatchStep runs the selection. Read document_intake for rows with ocr_status DONE, match_status PENDING, no document_id and a predicted type, where review_reason is empty or LOW_CONFIDENCE. Lock each row as you take it, so two runs cannot work on the same item. An item whose review_reason is UNKNOWN_TYPE or MODEL_UNAVAILABLE is not matched at all: give it match_status NO_TYPE and leave it for a person, which is exception path X9 and AC11. match_status is a new varchar(12) column with default PENDING, added together with candidate_case_ids by the migration V1_5_032__intake_match.sql. Items already MATCHED are never read again, so a repeat run writes nothing further, as AC9 requires.
RWB-E1-032.3: CaseMatcher gathers the identifiers automatically, from two places for each kind. Case numbers come from the extracted field case_no of RWB-E1-053 and from the OCR text in document_text.text_content, found with the parameter CASE_NO_PATTERN. Account numbers come from the extracted field account_no and the same text, found with ACCOUNT_NO_PATTERN. Read both patterns through MatchPatterns from document_hub_parameter; no pattern belongs in the code. The scanned text holds Thai and English around the numbers, so build the unit tests on text of that kind, as build step 2 says. Collect every value found, because more than one value is what produces the MULTIPLE and CONFLICT outcomes in the next step.
RWB-E1-032.4: CaseMatcher resolves what it collected through the P3 published interface CaseDirectory, calling findByCaseNo for each case number and findOpenCasesByAccountNo for each account number. Your module never reads the case tables itself. It then returns one of five results together with the candidates it found: MATCHED for exactly one open case, NO_MATCH when nothing resolves, MULTIPLE when an account number gives two or more open cases, CONFLICT when the case number and the account number point to different cases, and CASE_CLOSED when the only candidate is closed. The matcher never picks one of several candidates. Unit test all five against a CaseDirectory stub, which is build step 3.
RWB-E1-032.5: MatchStep calls DocumentStore.store from RWB-E1-024 with the case ID, the predicted type, the intake source, the file, its hash and the extracted fields. The store already exists: it writes the DOCATT decision log entry holding the classifier version, the confidence and the match method, then the document row and the DocumentStored event. Your part is building the StoreRequest in AutoAttachService, including the match method, which AC1 expects as CASE_ID and AC4 as ACCOUNT_NO. When the same file with the same hash is already on the matched case, the item is linked to that existing document and no second document row is written, which is exception path X6 and AC8.
RWB-E1-032.6: AutoAttachService sets these values on the stored document. Write classification_confidence, document_type and type_candidates from the classification of RWB-E1-050. When review_reason is LOW_CONFIDENCE, meaning the confidence is under the parameter CLASSIFY_THRESHOLD of 0.80, also set review_status PENDING and write_once false, so the file is held in rwb-docs. Write-once storage cannot be altered or deleted for its retention period, and a type that is not yet confirmed must not be fixed that way. The document is then listed on SCR-31 for a person to confirm its type in RWB-E1-054. AC10 covers this, with a scan classified APPRAISAL_REPORT at 0.62.
RWB-E1-032.7: MatchStep closes out each intake item itself. For a MATCHED item write match_status MATCHED, case_id and document_id, which is what keeps the next run from processing it again under BR6. For any other result write that result as match_status, one of NO_MATCH, MULTIPLE, CONFLICT, CASE_CLOSED or NO_TYPE, and write the candidates found into candidate_case_ids as JSON. Write no document row for those items, as AC2, AC3 and AC7 require. The partial index ix_intake_held on document_intake (match_status, received_at) covers the held values, so the review list can read them oldest first.
RWB-E1-032.8: A person does this part. A reviewer holding Documents C opens the Unmatched tab of SCR-31, which lists the held items oldest first with source, received time, match status, proposed type and candidate cases. Only items whose candidates are in that reviewer's scope are listed, and items with no candidate are listed only for roles with scope ALL. The reviewer opens one item, sees the scan, the OCR text page by page and the candidate cases, picks the case and the document type and sends the attach request. Build UnmatchedIntakeTab as the React component for the list, the viewer and the two pickers, and IntakeItemController for the endpoints in section 12. Each read of the item text is written to the PII access log.
RWB-E1-032.9: ManualAttachService runs the checks before anything is stored. Confirm the chosen case is in the reviewer's scope, and refuse with 403 and MSG-P4-003 when it is not, leaving the item held, which is exception path X10 and AC13. Confirm the chosen document type is in force, and refuse with 422 and MSG-P5-006 naming the value when it is not. Use the version the client sent as an optimistic lock, a check that the record has not changed since it was read, so the second of two reviewers acting at once gets 409 and MSG-GEN-004. Then call DocumentStore.store with the reviewer as approverUserId, which puts PERSON as the match method on the DOCATT entry, and set the item match_status MATCHED.

RWB-E1-045.1: A person does this, the center of excellence analyst holding Reference data C. Nothing is built here and no screen exists in this story. The analyst prepares two files: a PRODUCT_PARAMETER load with one row for each product group and parameter code, and a SERVICE_LEVEL load with one row for each product group and case status. BR2 names the parameters each product must carry, those the catalog of RWB-E1-042 marks with scope PRODUCT and required yes: ENTRY_DPD, EXCLUSION_LIST, NOTICE_PERIOD_DAYS, CURE_PERIOD_DAYS and EXPOSURE_BAND_SET. The values themselves belong to the product heads, with entry at 90 days from DL16, service levels from DL22 and caps from DL23.
RWB-E1-045.2: A person again, the reference data administrator, who also holds Reference data C. The call is POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/reference-loads, a P4 endpoint that already exists; this story adds checks behind it. The request is multipart form data carrying the file, the table code PRODUCT, PRODUCT_PARAMETER or SERVICE_LEVEL, and the valid from date, and the response is a ReferenceLoad with its id, table, validFrom, status and row count. A load by a role without Reference data C is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002, which is the access test TC-E1-045-09. Two loads of the same table code, valid from date and content are treated as one, as in RWB-E1-043.
RWB-E1-045.3: This runs on its own once the file is loaded. The checks of RWB-E1-043 run first, then the new one you build as ProductCompletenessCheck, added as a table check for PRODUCT, PRODUCT_PARAMETER and SERVICE_LEVEL. It confirms that every product in the PRODUCT version in force on the valid from date has a row for each catalog parameter with scope PRODUCT and required yes, and a SERVICE_LEVEL row for each status in the parameter servicelevel.required-statuses. A missing row refuses the whole load, with MSG-P3-034 naming the product and the item, and the version already in force stays in force. AC3 names SSME and WAITING_PARTNER.
RWB-E1-045.4: The same check does this, with no person involved. Read the type, unit and allowed range the parameter catalog of RWB-E1-042 holds for each parameter code and compare every value in the file against them. A value of the wrong type or outside the range refuses the load in full, with MSG-GEN-002 naming the field and the two ends of the range, which AC4 shows as NOTICE_PERIOD_DAYS, 1 and 365 for a loaded value of 0. Two rows for the same product and parameter also refuse the load, with MSG-P3-027, as does a PRODUCT load that drops a product with open cases. Build OpenCaseCounter for that last count.
RWB-E1-045.5: A second person has to act before any value is used. The approver holds the approve right in Reference data, and for a version where a limit or threshold moves it is the risk and model risk officer, per section 10. A validated version sits unused until that approval, and it then takes effect on its own valid from date rather than on the approval date. AC2 turns on this timing: PRODUCT version 2, PRODUCT_PARAMETER version 3 and SERVICE_LEVEL version 3 all carry valid from 2026-12-05, all three are approved, and the new product group AUTO_LEASE works on that date with no deployment between 2026-12-01 and 2026-12-05.
RWB-E1-045.6: The timer engine of RWB-E1-028 does this when it starts a notice timer, and you change it to take the period from the published interface instead of its own table. The call is ProductParameterService.get(productGroup, "NOTICE_PERIOD_DAYS", businessDate), and the returned ProductParameter carries the value, the unit and the version number. Pass the value and the unit to DueDateCalculator, which you build: a value in CALENDAR_DAYS is added straight, and a value in WORKING_DAYS skips the dates in the HOLIDAY rows in force, per BR7. Write the result to timer.expires_at. When no row is in force the call throws MissingProductParameterException, handled in build step 6.
RWB-E1-045.7: You change two services that already exist, CaseEntryService from RWB-E1-018 and AllocationService from RWB-E1-020, so they call ProductParameterService.get for ENTRY_DPD, EXCLUSION_LIST and EXPOSURE_BAND_SET with the case's product group and the business date. Remove any product group code, period or band written in their code; the done condition is that a search of the recovery module finds no product group code literal outside test fixtures and the generated API types. Where the call throws MissingProductParameterException, place the case in the exception queue and name the gap with MSG-P3-034, which is exception path X5 and AC7.
RWB-E1-045.8: The owning story of each engine writes its own decision log entry, so you add no entry here. What this story requires is that the version number the lookup returned travels into the inputs of that entry, which is why ProductParameter and ServiceLevel both carry versionNo. AC1 checks it on the timer side: each timer start records PRODUCT_PARAMETER version 2. Keep the number the lookup gave at the moment of the call and do not read the version again later, because a running timer keeps the value it started with while new timers take the new value from its valid from date, per BR6 and AC8.

RWB-E1-057.1: Nothing here is done by hand. The job is JOB-12 Document intake, which already exists as the Spring Batch job DocumentIntakeJob from RWB-E1-049, and this story adds intakeStep as its first step, ahead of the malware scan step of RWB-E1-041. The Quartz cron in section 12 is 0 0/15 8-17 in Asia/Bangkok on Monday to Friday, and bank holidays from the reference data holiday table are skipped. Two service instances may be running, so the schedule has to produce one run only: AC12 expects a single run recorded for 09:15 and one document_intake row per file. Outside business hours no run starts, which is exception path X11 and AC15.
RWB-E1-057.2: IntakeStep lists the work automatically through three readers you build behind one interface, IntakeChannelReader, with listNew, open, markProcessed and markRejected. FolderChannelReader covers the branch scanner folders, one per branch code, and the mailroom folder. SftpChannelReader covers each partner subfolder under the SFTP inbound folder. MailboxChannelReader covers each recovery mailbox, read as Exchange Online through Microsoft Graph by the SY-OCR managed identity, which is an identity the platform holds for the service so no password or key is kept anywhere. Every folder path and mailbox address is a property set per environment by the platform administrator, and each channel has its own sub-flag under rwb.dochub.intake.
RWB-E1-057.3: IntakeService does this for each file and each email attachment. A SHA-256 hash is a fixed value computed from the file's bytes, so two copies of one file give the same value and any change gives a different one. Look in document_intake for the same channel_code and file_sha256 with received_at inside the window the parameter INTAKE_DUPLICATE_WINDOW_DAYS sets, loaded as 30 days. A match means no new row: move the file to the processed folder and count it as a duplicate, which is exception path X4 and AC8. The index ix_intake_hash on document_intake (channel_code, file_sha256, received_at) serves this lookup.
RWB-E1-057.4: The same service applies the two limits, with no person involved. Check the type by the file's content as well as its extension and accept only the values in INTAKE_ALLOWED_TYPES, loaded as PDF, JPG and PNG. Check the size against INTAKE_MAX_FILE_MB, loaded as 25. A refused file gets no document_intake row, is moved to the rejected folder of its channel and is counted as refused, with MSG-P5-007 on the job record and MSG-P5-001 or MSG-P5-017 as the reason. Test the boundary exactly as AC6 sets it: a file of 25.1 MB is refused and one of 25.0 MB is taken in.
RWB-E1-057.5: SftpChannelReader applies this check by itself. The subfolder name is the partner_code, and you resolve it through the S9 published interface PartnerDirectory.findByCode, which returns the partner's id, code, type and panel status. Your module never reads the partner table. Take the file in only when a partner is found and its panel_status is ACTIVE, and write that partner's id to document_intake.partner_id. An unknown code and a partner that is not ACTIVE are both refused, with no row written and the file moved to the rejected folder, counted with the reasons PARTNER_UNKNOWN and PARTNER_NOT_ACTIVE. This is exception path X3 and AC7.
RWB-E1-057.6: IntakeService copies the accepted file into the intake container of RWB-TE-012, reached by managed identity only, then writes one document_intake row. The row holds source SCAN, PARTNER or EMAIL per BR1, the channel code, the source reference, the file name, size and hash, the received time, the scanner time in captured_at for scanner files, the partner id for partner files or the sender address for email, and the run id. Leave scan_result empty, because scanStep sets it and ocrStep reads nothing until it says CLEAN, which is AC16. The seven new columns come from the migration V1_5_057__intake_channels.sql, which also widens source_ref to varchar(400).
RWB-E1-057.7: The order matters and your code keeps it: commit the document_intake row first, then move the source file. A file moved before the commit could be lost when the transaction rolls back, so BR6 allows the move only after the commit. Scanner and SFTP files go to the processed folder, emails to the archive folder of their mailbox, and refused files to the rejected folder. When the move fails after a successful commit, leave it: the next run sees the file again, finds the same channel and hash, writes no second row and moves it then, which is exception path X10 and AC14. Build the unit test for this order, as build step 2 says.
RWB-E1-057.8: IntakeStep writes its own counts with no person involved: for each channel, the number taken in, the number refused with the reason, and the number treated as duplicates. Write them to the job record that SCR-44 Interface and job monitor reads, so the platform administrator sees each run. A run where no channel has a new file still writes zero counts for every channel, which is exception path X5 and AC9. No sender address and no email file name may appear in these counts or in any log, because BR9 treats the sender address as personal data, masked by role and never logged.
RWB-E1-057.9: These five steps already exist in other stories and they run after yours inside the same JOB-12 run: scanStep from RWB-E1-041, ocrStep from RWB-E1-049, classifyStep from RWB-E1-050, extractStep from RWB-E1-053 and matchStep from RWB-E1-032. You build none of them. Your work is to place intakeStep ahead of them in DocumentIntakeJob and to leave each new row in the state they expect, with scan_result empty and ocr_status PENDING. scanStep then sets scan_result and quarantines an infected file, and ocrStep reads only a file whose scan_result is CLEAN, which TC-E1-057-16 tests with a delayed scanStep stub.
RWB-E1-057.10: A person does this, the platform administrator holding Platform administration U. SCR-44 shows each JOB-12 run in the states running, failed and complete with the intakeStep counts per channel, and the rerun is POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/jobs/{jobId}/rerun with the job id of a failed run. A rerun while a run is still in progress is refused with 409 and MSG-GEN-004, and a caller without the right is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002, which is the access test TC-E1-057-17. A failed run leaves its files at the channel, so the next scheduled run takes them even without a rerun. Add the intakeStep section to the JOB-12 run book of RWB-E1-056.

RWB-E2-001.1: Nothing is started by hand. JOB-01 publishes LoadCompleted (EV-26) once its load checks pass, and your LoadCompletedListener consumes that event for sources ALS and EFS with the same business date before HandoverJob begins. Put the listener behind IdempotencyGuard from RWB-E1-007, so a redelivered event does not start a second run; events are often delivered more than once, and the guard keeps the work to one time per key. Build HandoverJob as the JOB-02 step in the Java package recovery.integration.handover, and chain JOB-03 allocation after it. The feature flag for the story is rwb.integration.efs-handover.
RWB-E2-001.2: HandoverService makes this check itself. Confirm that both the ALS and EFS data products carry business date D before any account is read. When one is older, hold the run: create no case from the earlier day's data, show MSG-P1-001 against the stale product with the date it holds, and alert the data steward with MSG-P2-007, which names the date and the number of accounts waiting. No case is built from a load that did not pass its checks, per BR4. When a day is missed, the next good load covers it and the run summary names the gap date, which AC6 shows as 2026-12-15 with cases created on 2026-12-17.
RWB-E2-001.3: This runs under the SY-DATALOAD managed identity with no person involved. Call AccountQuery.findAtOrAboveDpd(threshold, businessDate) from the P1 published interface recovery.data.api, and take the threshold from the parameter case.entry.dpd_threshold, in force at 90 per DL16. Do not write 90 into the code and do not read the account tables directly. The call returns the EntryCandidate rows for accounts at or above the threshold on business date D with no open case link. Your module reads loan_account values through that interface only: the product code, the total balance, the days past due and the data as of date.
RWB-E2-001.4: Your code makes this call for each account before any write. IdempotencyGuard from RWB-E1-007 remembers the keys it has already seen, so a second run for the same account and business date does the work only once. Idempotent means running the same request twice leaves the same result as running it once. The key is the fixed text handover with the account id and the business date, exactly as the step writes it, and section 12 gives the job's idempotency key as account ID plus business date. An account whose key is already present is skipped and counted as a repeat in the run summary, which is exception path X1 and AC2.
RWB-E2-001.5: HandoverGroupBuilder does this grouping. Two accounts of the same customer in the same product group belong to one case, per BR2 and decision DL17, so group the candidates by primary customer and product group before any case is created. The product group comes from the account's product code through the loaded product code map, LOV-PRODUCT-CODE to LOV-PRODUCT, which is reference data and not a value in code. Build this with tests for one account and for two accounts per customer and product group, as build step 1 says. An account whose customer is not in the party data is dropped and listed in the data quality exceptions, which is exception path X3 and AC5.
RWB-E2-001.6: Your service calls CaseCreation.createOrLink from the P3 published interface for each group, and P3 does the writing. It writes the decision log entry first, then creates the case with status New, a case number in the form RW-YYYY-NNNNNN and entry date D+1, or links the account to the customer's open case for that product group. For a link it writes the case_account row with linked_from and is_primary false and creates no new case, which is exception path X5 and AC4. The call throws DecisionLogUnavailableException: stop that account, count it as held, raise the incident and leave it for the next run.
RWB-E2-001.7: P3 publishes the event and you build nothing for it. CaseCreated (EV-01) goes out through the P3 outbox in the same transaction as the case row, so the event exists only when the case does. An outbox is a table the event is written to beside the data, with a separate sender delivering it afterward. The event carries the business date, which AC1 checks as 2026-12-14 even though the case was created on 2026-12-15. What your code must get right is passing that business date into the request, and the same date into the inputs snapshot of the decision log entry, which AC1 also checks.
RWB-E2-001.8: SY-DATALOAD does this once the case exists. Read the account's EFS records with EfsHistoryQuery.forAccount(accountId, businessDate) from P1, limited to the action codes of the collection period that DL29 lists, and pass them to InteractionLedger.appendEfsHistory(caseId, records), which returns the number of entries written. Each interaction entry carries the time it occurred, the channel, direction, action code, contact result, promise amount, promise date and source_system EFS, per BR5. AC1 sets the count: 14 contact records and 2 promises give 16 entries with source system EFS. Do not log the content of these entries; the guardrails allow counts and synthetic keys only.
RWB-E2-001.9: HandoverService returns HandoverSummary with the accounts read, the cases created, the accounts linked, the repeats, the held accounts and the gap dates, and HandoverSummaryRepository writes it to interface_run.checks. The data steward reads it on SCR-45 Data quality, together with the accounts held because their customer was missing. Carry MSG-P7-003 on the summary for an account stopped by a failed decision log write, which is AC7. JOB-03 allocation runs after this job, so the new cases get a queue and an owner the same morning. A rerun requested while JOB-02 is still running is refused with 409 and MSG-P2-006.

RWB-E2-013.1: Another module starts this, not a person and not your code. For the first use, the litigation route calls you after rule R-LIT-03 generates a notice. You publish the interface ApprovalRouter in the Java package recovery.decision.approval with the method request(ApprovalRequest), which throws DecisionLogUnavailableException. The request carries the case, the decision code, the regulation item, the product group, the amounts, the recommendation, the preparer, the source type and reference, the rule id and version, and an idempotency key. Keep the preparer, because BR4 forbids that person from approving the item. Keep the rule id and version too, because AC1 expects the routing entry to record R-LIT-03 and LIT-2026.12.
RWB-E2-013.2: ApprovalRoutingService chooses the approver with no person involved, and there are two paths.
