For a decision with delegation rows, call DelegationOfAuthority.lowestLevel through the P4 interface of RWB-E1-038, which returns the lowest level whose row covers the decision, product and amount on the routing date, and assign the item to the holder of that level. AC4 routes a 2,400,000.00 mortgage settlement to L6 holder U-9201. For a decision with no amount limit, read the route role from its parameters, which for D7.1 notices is rwb.approval.route.D7.1.role holding RW-LITOFF, and assign the item to that role rather than to one named person.
RWB-E2-013.3: Both branches are automatic. When the required level has no holder and no substitute, move the item one level up straight away and record the reason on the routing entry, which AC11 expects as NO_HOLDER for L6 with the item assigned to the L5 holder. An item must never wait on an empty level, per BR8. When the lookup returns NOT_COVERED, meaning no delegation row covers that decision and product, store the approval with status HELD_NO_LIMIT, leave the case at Waiting approval and raise an incident to RW-RISK with MSG-P7-010, which names the decision and the product. AC14 uses a hire purchase decision with no rows in DOA-2026.11.
RWB-E2-013.4: Your service does all of this in one transaction. Create the row in the new approval table from the migration V_E2_013__approval.sql with status WAITING, the level, the delegation row id and limit version, and due_at from the service level parameter, one working day for D7.1 notices and three working days by default. Call the P3 task and timer interfaces to open the decision task and start the service level timer. Write the routing entry through the decision log writer, and publish EV-09 ApprovalRequested with the approval id, case id, level and amount. P3 moves the case to Waiting approval, which AC1 checks.
RWB-E2-013.5: A person does this. The approver opens SCR-10 Approval queue, which calls GET /api/recovery/v1/approvals and lists each item waiting on them with the decision, the case, the amount, the level, the limit version, the age and the due time. Build the screen as the React component ApprovalQueueScreen with its loading, list and empty states. The query returns the items assigned to that user and the items routed to a role they hold, and never an item they prepared, which AC1 checks for U-9211. The indexes ix_approval_assignee on (assigned_user_id, status) and ix_approval_role on (route_role_code, status) serve these reads.
RWB-E2-013.6: The approver acts through four endpoints, three of which already exist: POST /approvals/{approvalId}/approve, /refuse and /return, plus GET /approvals/{approvalId} for the detail. This story adds reasonCode from LOV-OVERRIDE-REASON, the changed terms and membersPresent to the approve request. Each call takes an Idempotency-Key header, so a repeated send does not produce a second outcome. Refuse and return both need a reason in text, and a refusal with no reason is rejected with 422 and MSG-GEN-001 for the field reason, which is AC8. A return sets status RETURNED and opens a task for the preparer, which is AC9.
RWB-E2-013.7: ApprovalDecisionService runs the checks before anything is written. Confirm the caller holds the A letter in the decision's capability area, taken from the parameter rwb.approval.area for that decision code, and that they are the holder or substitute of the required level or hold the route role; otherwise refuse with 403 and MSG-P4-002. Refuse the preparer with 409 and MSG-P7-002 even when that person is a substitute at the right level, which is AC6. Require a coded reason where the approver departs from the recommendation, refusing with 422 and MSG-P7-005. Check the record version with the optimistic lock, so the second of two approvers acting at once gets 409 and MSG-GEN-004.
RWB-E2-013.8: The writes happen together in one transaction, the decision log entry among them, so an outcome that cannot be recorded does not take effect. Write the entry with the approver, the approval level, the limit version, the rule id and version and the final call, APPROVED, REFUSED, RETURNED or ESCALATED. Set the approval status and publish EV-08 DecisionRecorded. P3 then moves the case from Waiting approval to In progress, and the source module acts on the outcome, which for a D7.1 notice is release to dispatch in RWB-E2-014. AC5 expects MSG-P7-004 in the response naming the new state. For a committee level, L1 to L3, the entry also holds the resolution reference and the members present.
RWB-E2-013.9: This happens on its own when an approval passes its service level. JOB-05 of RWB-E1-028 publishes EV-19 TimerBreached, and your ApprovalEscalationListener consumes it for approval timers. Move a limit-routed item one level up, and a role-routed item to the escalation role, which for D7.1 is rwb.approval.route.D7.1.escalation-role holding RW-HEADLIT. Raise escalation_level, set a new due time, restart the service level timer, write an entry with final call ESCALATED and tell the new approver with MSG-P7-011. The case stays at Waiting approval. AC2 moves the AC1 item to RW-HEADLIT with escalation level 1 and a new due time of 09:00 on 16 December 2026. Test it with a fixed clock.

RWB-E2-026.1: Either a person or another module starts this. The person is a restructuring officer or case owner holding Documents C, who reaches the engine through the screens of RWB-E2-017; the module is SY-CASEWF for rule-driven generation from Epic 3. Build both doors: the endpoint POST /cases/{caseId}/generated-documents and the published interface DocumentGenerator.generate. The request carries the treatment id, one to ten template codes and the language, TH or EN with TH as the default, and an Idempotency-Key header is required. An empty templateCodes list is refused with 422 and MSG-GEN-001. The whole engine sits behind the feature flag rwb.dochub.generation-engine, which when off makes the endpoint return 404.
RWB-E2-026.2: DocumentGenerationService does this first. Call TreatmentReader.find from S2 and never read the treatment table yourself. The treatment passes only when its type is DEED_IN_LIEU or RESTRUCTURE, its decision_log_id is set, which is what shows it was approved at D6.4, and its outcome is still empty. Anything else is refused with 409 and MSG-P5-011 and nothing is stored, which is exception path X4 and AC6. Check the case scope at the same time: a case outside the caller's scope returns 404 with MSG-P4-003, as AC12 shows for a case of team HP-NE requested by an officer of team FCR-BKK.
RWB-E2-026.3: TemplateSelector does this through the P6 interface TemplateCatalog.current(templateCode, language, productGroup, asOf). For each code it takes the version that is approved by Legal, active and the highest one valid on the request date, and a template for that exact product group wins over a template for all products, per BR1. A current version with approved_by_legal false is refused with 422 and MSG-P5-010 naming the template and version, which is AC4. A withdrawn template with no approved successor is refused with 422 and MSG-P6-003, and a task goes to the officer who asked, which is AC5. No template for the product group or language is MSG-P5-010 as well.
RWB-E2-026.4: MergeFieldResolver does this automatically. A merge field is a named placeholder in the template body, written as {{merge_field_code}}, that is replaced by a value from the case. Read the list for the chosen version with TemplateCatalog.mergeFields(templateId), group the codes by the module that owns them, and call MergeFieldProvider.resolve(caseId, treatmentId, mergeFieldCodes) on each provider listed in your configuration: P3 for the case, S2 for the treatment and P1 for party and collateral. The background of section 7 gives the fields of DIL-CONTRACT version 2 as case_no, borrower_name, title_doc_no, transfer_price and contract_date. A national ID number is filled from the token service at render time only.
RWB-E2-026.5: The same resolver checks completeness and ValueFormatter does the formatting. A required field with no value stops the whole request with 422 and MSG-P5-009 naming the template and the field, and nothing is stored, which is AC2 for a case with no title_doc_no. Formatting follows the format the merge field catalog holds for each field: a Thai long date in the Buddhist Era, an amount with two decimals, and an amount written out in Thai words. AC1 sets the expected output exactly, with "1,250,000.00 บาท (หนึ่งล้านสองแสนห้าหมื่นบาทถ้วน)" and the date 2026-12-10 shown as "10 ธันวาคม 2569". Unit test both conversions.
RWB-E2-026.6: TemplateRenderer does the rendering with no person involved. PDF/A-2b is a PDF profile made for long-term keeping, which requires every font used to be carried inside the file, so embed the Thai font named by the parameter GEN_FONT. Replace each {{merge_field_code}} tag in the body with its formatted value. Write each rendered file and the merge snapshot, the record of the values used, into the draft area of the standard container through BlobStorageAdapter from RWB-E1-024. Do not use DocumentStore.store here, which would place a legal type in the write-once container at once. A body that cannot be rendered returns 503 with MSG-GEN-006, stores nothing and raises an incident.
RWB-E2-026.7: Your service writes one entry for the whole request through DecisionLogWriter.write, and that entry holds the decision code, an inputs reference pointing at the merge snapshot, and the template code and version of each document produced. AC13 checks that one entry names the three template codes and versions for a three-template request. A failed write stops everything: return 503 with MSG-P7-003, remove the draft files from the container, write no document row and raise an incident as R-UNI-39 requires. That is exception path X5, AC7 and the resilience test TC-E2-026-16, which forces the failure during a three-document set.
RWB-E2-026.8: These writes sit in the same transaction as the decision log entry, so the documents and the entry are kept together or not at all. Write one document row per file with source GENERATED, state DRAFT, write_once false, the document type the mapping gives for that template code, and the template and treatment values. The Flyway migration in this story adds the three columns those values need, with the partial unique index ux_document_draft_per_template on document (treatment_id, template_code) where the state is DRAFT, which is what makes the second of two requests at the same moment fail with 409 and MSG-GEN-004. Write one DocumentStored (EV-16) per document to the outbox.
RWB-E2-026.9: The response is 201 with a DocumentPage of the generated documents, and the interface returns GenerationResult with the decision log entry id and, for each document, the document id, template code, template version and document type. A repeated request with the same Idempotency-Key returns that first result and writes nothing further, which is AC8, so hold the key and its result in IdempotencyRepository for the 24 hours the parameter GEN_IDEMPOTENCY_HOURS sets. The documents stay DRAFT until they are sent. No screen belongs to this story: review and send are RWB-E2-017, and the documents also show on SCR-30 Case documents in its list state.

RWB-E1-009.1: Migration: creates the tables, columns and keys listed in section 11.
RWB-E1-009.2: Build: creates the entities, repositories, mapper/check/service classes listed in section 13.
RWB-E1-009.3: Build: registers the endpoint and published-interface contracts.
RWB-E1-009.4: Deferred: job scheduling, load execution and validation; see the data load reference.

RWB-E1-021.1: You build nothing here; the publishing modules already write these events. The outbox is a table a module writes in the same transaction as its own change, so an event cannot exist without the change that caused it, and a listener reads it afterwards. The eight triggers reach you as seven event types: CaseStateChanged (EV-05) for a stage change and also for a route decision, where the rule event code is ROUTE_APPROVED, plus TimerDue (EV-18), DeviationRaised (EV-06), DeviationCleared (EV-07), ApprovalRequested (EV-09), DocumentStored (EV-16) and PaymentMissed (EV-12). Your job is to consume them. A TimerBreached event for a service level is not in that list and never moves a case.
RWB-E1-021.2: Build TransferListener for this; it runs on its own with no person involved. It reads the seven event types from the outbox and calls TransferService.transferByRule with the case ID, the trigger event and the event ID. Deduplicate by event ID, because a message can be delivered more than once. Migration V021_1__transfer.sql creates table processed_event with event_id as its primary key, a consumer column of 60 characters and processed_at. A primary key cannot hold the same value twice, so the second insert fails, you drop the event and count an idempotency hit. One transfer results from one event, however often it arrives.
RWB-E1-021.3: This is automatic and runs under the service identity SY-RULES. Build TransferRuleEvaluator so that it reads the rows of rule table TRANSFER through RuleTableReader in P4, never from the tables of another module. Each row holds a trigger event code, a condition expression, a target queue code and a row order. Take the rows of the version in force, which is TRF-2026.11, keep those whose event code equals the trigger, evaluate the condition against a snapshot of the case, and return the first match in row order. Later matching rows are not applied. When no row matches there is no transfer, and no decision log entry is written at all.
RWB-E1-021.4: TransferService does this check itself before anything moves. Read legal_hold on the case. When it is true, an event-driven transfer stops here under R-UNI-20: the queue, the team and the owner are unchanged, and you write the skip to the job log naming that rule so the reason can be seen later. No decision log entry and no message to a user come out of it. The legal hold placed through the endpoint of step 9 is what sets the flag. This check covers rule transfers; a manual transfer is a person acting with a coded reason and goes through the path of step 8.
RWB-E1-021.5: Three things happen inside TransferService, with no person involved for a rule transfer. First, read the case with its version column and plan the update as UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?. That is optimistic locking: when another transaction has already changed the row, zero rows are updated and you refuse the call with MSG-GEN-004. Second, ask the AssignmentEngine of RWB-E1-020 for an owner in the target queue, using the queue method and the queue capacity_cap. When every member is at the cap, place the case in the queue named by overflow_queue_id with no owner and tell the team manager with MSG-P3-011. Third, refuse the move when the case status does not allow it, as a closed case does not.
RWB-E1-021.6: The service writes all of this in one transaction, so the case and its assignments can never be read half changed. Set ended_at on the open assignment row, insert a new assignment row with reason TRANSFER, the rule ID and, for a manual call, transfer_reason_code. Update recovery_case queue_id, team_code and owner_user_id, and the row version. Write CaseTransferred (EV-04) to the outbox with the case ID, the previous owner, the new owner and the reason code. The partial unique index ux_assignment_open_case keeps one open assignment per case. A partial index applies only to the rows that meet its condition, here the rows where ended_at and task_id are both null.
RWB-E1-021.7: The service writes the decision log entry, through the writer built in RWB-E1-027, as the last write before the transaction commits. The entry holds the rule row ID, the rule version, the queue and owner the case came from, the queue and owner it goes to, and the trigger that fired. A refused transfer is logged too, with the final call TRANSFER_REJECTED. When the entry cannot be written, nothing takes effect: a manual call returns 503 with MSG-P7-003 and the case keeps its queue and owner, and a rule transfer rolls back so the event is retried later. A transfer leaves the case status and the clocks untouched.
RWB-E1-021.8: A person does this one. The team manager calls POST /api/recovery/v1/cases/{caseId}/transfer with a TransferRequest carrying either toOwnerId or toQueueId, reasonCode MANUAL, an optional note and transferReasonCode, a new field holding a value of LOV-TRANSFER-REASON such as R03 Skill. Build the endpoint on CaseAndWorkflowController with an access check for Queue and allocation right U in team scope, and support the Idempotency-Key header so a repeat with the same key returns the first response. Refuse with 422 and MSG-P3-001 when the transfer reason is missing, and with 422 and MSG-P3-002 when the named owner is at the caseload cap. The work of steps 5 to 7 is reused with reason MANUAL.
RWB-E1-021.9: A person does this as well, usually a litigation officer acting on a legal or court instruction, and the caller needs Case record right U. Build POST /api/recovery/v1/cases/{caseId}/legal-hold taking a LegalHoldRequest with action place or lift, a required reason and a reference, and build LegalHoldService behind it. On place, store the current case status in the new column status_before_hold, set legal_hold true and move the status to On hold. On lift, read status_before_hold and return the case to that status under R-UNI-21. A place on a case already on hold, or a lift on a case not on hold, is refused with 409 and MSG-P3-005. Each call writes its own decision log entry.

RWB-E1-033.1: A litigation officer starts this by hand. There is no screen ID for a cross-case search in screens.txt, so you build the page yourself under the Documents menu and the missing ID is recorded in the additions file. Build DocumentSearchPage as a React component in the front end folder recovery/documents, with a criteria form holding the document type, a stored date range, a field condition made of a field name, an operator (eq, gt, lt or between) and one or two values, and a free text term. The field list offered to the user comes from the field_definitions of the chosen document type. The user may fill one criterion or several.
RWB-E1-033.2: The browser does this when the user submits the form. Send the criteria as query parameters: type, dateFrom, dateTo, field, op, value, value2, q for the free text, page and size, where size defaults to 50 and 50 is also the maximum. The response is a DocumentSearchPage object holding items, page, size, total and capped. Each item carries documentId, caseId, caseNo, documentType, storedAt, source, matchedField, matchedValue and snippet. Keep the path you build on the controller and the path the front end calls the same, and hide the menu item when the feature flag rwb.dochub.search is off, because the endpoint then answers 404.
RWB-E1-033.3: DocumentSearchService does this on the server, before any query reaches the database. Four checks. At least one criterion is filled, otherwise 422 with MSG-GEN-001 naming a search criterion. dateFrom is not after dateTo, otherwise 422 with MSG-GEN-003. The free text term is between FREE_TEXT_MIN_CHARS and FREE_TEXT_MAX_CHARS, which are 3 and 100, otherwise 422 with MSG-GEN-002 showing those two numbers. The named field is in the field list of the chosen document type, read from document_type.field_definitions. Read the two length limits from document_hub_parameter rather than writing 3 and 100 in code, because the reference data administrator can change them.
RWB-E1-033.4: The service does this next, still before any query. Call the P4 interface mayReadUnmasked with the role code of the user and the field class, which is PARTY_NAME, ACCOUNT_NO or ID_NO. Masking means a value is replaced by a token for roles that may not see it, so a role that cannot read party names unmasked also cannot search on them: free text runs over document text that holds names, and a condition on a personal field would reveal the value by matching it. Refuse such a request with 422 and MSG-P5-020 naming the field, and run no query at all. Under the assumed rules of DL26, RW-LITOFF, RW-LEGAL and RW-AUDIT may search these; other roles may not.
RWB-E1-033.5: The service does this with no person involved. Call caseIdsInScope on the P3 CaseDirectory interface with the scope filter of the signed-in user, and use the returned set of case IDs as the boundary of the search. For a user whose scope is ALL, pass an empty filter and every case is in range. This is how a litigation officer with scope TEAM on a mortgage team never sees a document on a hire purchase case, even when that document matches every criterion. Take the case IDs from this interface rather than reading recovery_case, because another module owns that table. The result is the only list of cases the query may touch.
RWB-E1-033.6: DocumentSearchRepository runs one SQL query and no person is involved. Select active documents whose case_id is in the scope set, filtered by document_type and by created_at, which is the stored date in Epic 1. Join document_field for a field condition and document_text for a free text term, order newest first, and stop at SEARCH_MAX_RESULTS, which is 1000, with the page size applied on top. Flyway migration V1_5_033__document_search_indexes.sql gives the query its support: the pg_trgm extension and a GIN trigram index on document_text.text_content, which makes an ILIKE search over Thai text fast, a function dochub_to_numeric for numeric comparisons on field values, and two indexes on document_field.
RWB-E1-033.7: The service builds the result rows with no person involved. Each row carries the case number, read through CaseDirectory.caseNumbers, the document type, the stored date, the source, and either the matched field with its value or a text snippet. Build SnippetBuilder for the snippet: 60 characters of the OCR text around the matched term, with the term highlighted and any other personal identifier in that window replaced by a token through the ACE PII service. A result that matched on a field shows the field value instead of a snippet. The masking applies even for a role allowed to search the text, because other people can be named in the same line.
RWB-E1-033.8: The service writes the access event and waits, with no person involved. Build the DOCUMENT_SEARCH event with the user, the role, the criteria, the result count and the case IDs returned, and send it to the PII access log of the ACE common module. The free text term goes in as a SHA-256 hash, which is a one-way fingerprint of the text: the same term always gives the same value and the term cannot be read back out, so the log holds no personal data. Wait for the write to be confirmed. Without a confirmation, return 503 with MSG-P5-019 and no result rows, because a read of personal data is allowed only once it is recorded.
RWB-E1-033.9: The user sees the results and works with them. Render the first 50 rows with paging controls, driven by the page and size values of the response, and show the capped flag with MSG-P5-021 and the count 1000 when more documents matched than the limit allows. Build the other screen states as well: skeleton rows while loading, the empty state with the text No documents match this search and the action Clear the search, and an error state showing the message from section 14 at the top. Clicking a row opens DocumentDetailPanel, built in RWB-E1-024, so you reuse that component rather than building a second detail view.

RWB-E1-046.1: A person does this: the reference data administrator, who holds Reference data right C. They post the merge field catalog file to /api/recovery/v1/admin/reference-loads as multipart form data with the file, the table name merge_field and a valid from date. P4 owns that endpoint and you do not build it. What you build is a table handler: MergeFieldLoadHandler, implementing the P4 interface ReferenceLoadHandler, whose table method returns merge_field and whose validate and apply methods do the checks and the writes. The file holds one row per merge field, each naming the BR Field ID of the case data it draws from in the Logical Data Model.
RWB-E1-046.2: The handler does the checking with no person involved. For every row: merge_code is unique within the catalog version, field_id names a BR Field ID that exists in sys_fields, source_entity and source_field are filled, and is_required is set. Read sys_fields through the P4 reference data interface, not by querying the tables of another module. A single failed row refuses the whole load, so no row of the file is written and the catalog version already in force stays in force; the answer is 422 with MSG-P1-002 naming the failed check. Write the accepted rows to table merge_field, which migration V1_046__template_catalog.sql creates with a unique key on merge_code and catalog_version.
RWB-E1-046.3: The same person does this second load, again through the P4 endpoint, this time with the table name template. The file carries one row per template version: template code, language from LOV-LANG, product group from LOV-PRODUCT, channel, notice type from LOV-NOTICE, signature basis, the body_ref that points at the DOCX body, the list of merge codes the template uses and, where Legal counsel has signed, approved_by and approved_at. Build TemplateLoadHandler as the second ReferenceLoadHandler. Those approval columns are how a version is approved in Epic 1, before the template screen of RWB-E1-034 is live. A row with no template code, language or body reference refuses the load with MSG-GEN-001 naming the field.
RWB-E1-046.4: The handler does this with no person involved. Build MergeCodeScanner to read the merge codes out of the DOCX body, where they are written in the form {{CODE}}, and compare that set with the merge code list declared on the row. Check every code from both places against the merge field catalog version in force. One unknown code refuses the whole load with MSG-P6-006 naming the template and the code, and no version of that template is created. This check is what keeps the letter engine safe: it can only fill a field the catalog knows, so a template cannot ask for data the Workbench has no source for.
RWB-E1-046.5: The handler assigns the version, with no person involved. Count the existing versions for the template code and language and use the next number. Earlier versions are never updated or deleted, because an open case has to keep the version its notice was generated under. Migration V1_046__template_catalog.sql replaces the unique key on template_code alone with uk_template_version on template_code, language and template_version, so one code can hold many versions. Set the state column from the approval columns: APPROVED when both approved_by and approved_at are present, DRAFT when they are not. A check constraint allows only DRAFT, APPROVED and WITHDRAWN, and requires both approval columns when the state is APPROVED.
RWB-E1-046.6: This is the read side, used by other code and not by a person. Build TemplateCatalogService to implement the published interface TemplateCatalog in package recovery.comms.templates. Its current method takes a template code, a language and a date, and returns the Approved version with the highest version number whose valid_from is on or before that date. A version with a valid_from in the future is therefore ignored until that day arrives: version 3 valid from 2026-12-01 leaves version 2 current on 2026-11-30 and becomes current on 2026-12-01. The TemplateVersion returned carries the version numbers, the body reference, the approver, the approval date and the merge codes, and no personal data.
RWB-E1-046.7: The caller is the letter engine built in RWB-E1-052, so this happens in code with no person involved. When every version of the template is still Draft, the catalog throws TemplateNotApprovedException and the refusal carries MSG-P6-005 naming the template and the version, and nothing is generated. When the version that was current has been withdrawn, it throws TemplateWithdrawnException with MSG-P6-003, and generation waits until Legal counsel approves a new version. Build both exceptions as part of the interface, because the engine has to tell the two cases apart: one is a template waiting for its first approval, the other is a template taken out of use.
RWB-E1-046.8: The handler does this at the end of each load, with no person involved. Write the result of the load to the reference load record that P4 keeps: rows loaded, rows refused and the version numbers assigned, with the load status moving to refused or in force. Send the same result to the ACE audit log. The administrator reads it there, because Epic 1 has no screen for it; SCR-40 Reference data shows the template and merge_field versions once it is built. A repeat of a file already loaded for the same table is caught on the SHA-256 hash of the file and answered with 409 and MSG-P1-002, with no new version created.

RWB-E1-058.1: A person does this: a center of excellence analyst holding Rules and parameters right C. They post each file to /api/recovery/v1/admin/agent-configs as multipart form data with the file in JSON, the kind PROMPT or POLICY, the agent code and a valid from date. The policy file carries the values the runtime reads later: model code and version, output schema reference, allowed tools, autonomy mode, confidence floor, timeout seconds, daily cost cap, price per 1,000 tokens, alert role and review date. Build AgentConfigController for the endpoint and AgentConfigService behind it. The agent in this flow is INTAKE; the test agent ECHO is seeded from files in src/test/resources/agent/.
RWB-E1-058.2: The service does this with no person involved. Validate the file against the policy JSON schema file that is versioned with the loader, which holds the limits: timeout seconds between 1 and 120, confidence floor between 0 and 1. A file that fails any check is refused in full with 422 and MSG-P10-001 naming the check, and no version row is created, so the version already in force is untouched. A file that passes becomes a new row in agent_policy or agent_prompt with status LOADED, its valid from date and the loader, and for a prompt the body text and its hash. Earlier versions stay readable through GET /admin/agent-configs with their hashes unchanged.
RWB-E1-058.3: A different person does this: a risk and model risk officer holding Rules and parameters right A. They call POST /admin/agent-configs/{versionId}/approve with an If-Match header carrying the row version they read, and the status moves from LOADED to APPROVED. Build two rules. The loader may not approve their own version, so compare the approver with loaded_by and refuse with 409 and MSG-P7-002. The If-Match value is checked against the current row version, so when two officers approve at the same moment the first succeeds and the second gets 409 with MSG-GEN-004. An approved version takes effect on its valid from date, and the version it replaces is retired with valid_to set to the day before.
RWB-E1-058.4: Another module calls this in code, through the orchestration built in RWB-TE-013, and no person is involved. The entry point is AgentOrchestrator.run with an AgentRunRequest holding the agent code, the case ID, a subject ID, the trigger event, the inputs and an idempotency key. Idempotent means a repeat has no further effect: agent_run carries a unique key on idempotency_key, so a second request with the key ECHO:RW-2026-000101:2026-11-30 writes no second row, makes no second model call, returns the result of the first run and counts the repeat. Build the request and result types in package recovery.agent.orchestrator, so every caller reaches a model by one path.
RWB-E1-058.5: AgentRuntimeService does all of this with no person involved. Resolve the policy and prompt versions with status APPROVED whose valid from date is on or before the run date; a run already open keeps the versions it started with. Gather the inputs through ToolGateway, which executes only the tools on the policy allowed list, acts as the service identity SY-AGENT and reads through the published interfaces of P3 and P5. Pass every input value through PromptInputMasker, which calls the P4 masking service built in RWB-E1-037, so the prompt holds masking tokens in place of names, national ID numbers, phone numbers and account numbers. Then call the INT-23 endpoint through ModelGatewayClient with the policy timeout and no retry inside the step.
RWB-E1-058.6: GuardrailChecker does this on the answer, with no person involved, and the order is fixed. First the output schema: validate the answer against the schema named by the policy, using JSON Schema draft 2020-12, and fail with check code SCHEMA naming the field that is missing. Second the allowed tool list: a tool the agent asked for that is not on the policy list is refused, is not executed and is logged with check code TOOL_NOT_ALLOWED. Third the confidence floor: an answer with confidence 0.79 against a floor of 0.80 gives status BELOW_FLOOR. The first check that fails sets the run status and sets fallback true, and the checks after it are not run.
RWB-E1-058.7: The service writes the record with no person involved. Insert one agent_run row holding the agent code, the agent version, the prompt and model versions, the case and subject, the autonomy mode, the trigger event, the idempotency key, the status, the fallback flag, the guardrail result, the output, the confidence, latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_thb, the data as of date and the run time. Compute the cost as tokens in plus tokens out, divided by 1,000, multiplied by the policy price per 1,000 tokens, rounded to four decimals: 1,050 tokens at 0.0500 baht gives 0.0525. Write the AgentRunCompleted event EV-28 to the outbox in the same transaction as the row, so the event and the record cannot disagree.
RWB-E1-058.8: The orchestrator answers its caller in code, with no person involved. The AgentRunResult carries the run ID, the status, the fallback flag, a fallback reason, the output, the confidence, the agent version and the model version. The fallback reason is the one value the caller acts on: TIMED_OUT when the endpoint did not answer inside the policy timeout, TOOL_NOT_ALLOWED or the schema code from the guardrail, BELOW_FLOOR under the confidence floor, and DISABLED when the feature flag rwb.agent.platform is off and no model call was made. On any fallback the calling step uses its rule result under R-UNI-32. None of these paths shows a message to a user.
RWB-E1-058.9: A person does both of these: the center of excellence analyst. First they post a labeled sample to /admin/agent-samples as a CSV with the columns subject_type, subject_id, label_key and expected_value, and each load creates the next sample version. Then they start the harness with POST /admin/agent-evaluations carrying the agent, the sample code, the sample version and the approaches, which default to AGENT alone. Build two refusals: 422 with MSG-P10-002 when the sample holds no labeled row for that agent, and 409 with MSG-P10-003 when an evaluation of the same agent, sample and sample version is already RUNNING. A partial unique index on agent_evaluation_run enforces the second, applying only to rows whose status is RUNNING.
RWB-E1-058.10: EvaluationHarness does the work with no person involved, after the endpoint has answered 202 with status RUNNING. Run the agent once for every row of the sample in shadow mode, which means the answer is scored and stored and no case is changed by it; each run writes a normal agent_run row with trigger EVALUATION and mode SHADOW. Compare each answer with the expected value of its label key and write one agent_evaluation score row per label key, holding the approach, sample size, true positives, false positives, false negatives, agreement rate, precision and recall. Each score row carries the policy, prompt and model versions, so a score can later be read against the versions that produced it. The run then moves to DONE.

RWB-E2-002.1: No person starts this. JOB-02 already runs once a day and creates cases from the COLLINS load, built in RWB-E2-001. You add PlanStatusStep as a second step of the same job, ordered after the case creation step, so every case created that morning is covered in the same run. Put the step behind the feature flag rwb.integration.ace-plan-status, so it can be switched off without a release. This step is the daily path; the endpoint of step 8 is the live path for a single case. Both read the same stored columns, and the daily step is what keeps them current when nobody opens the case.
RWB-E2-002.2: The step does this, running under the service identity SY-DATALOAD. PlanStatusService asks the P3 CaseQuery interface for every open case with its account numbers. The numbers come from case_account and loan_account.account_no, and the account number is the join key between a Workbench case and an ACE plan under DL21, because the two systems share no case identifier. Read them through the P3 interface rather than querying recovery_case or loan_account yourself, since other modules own those tables. Build PlanStatusService in package recovery.integration.aceplan. The result is the work list for the rest of the step: one entry per open case with the account numbers to ask ACE about.
RWB-E2-002.3: The service does this through AcePlanClient, which you build as a thin wrapper around the ACE published interface RestructurePlanQuery. Call statusFor with a list of account numbers and read back one PlanStatusView per plan, holding planRef, accountNo, status and statusDate. Send the account numbers in batches of 500, set by the property rwb.ace.plan.batch-size, and apply a 2-second timeout from rwb.ace.plan.timeout-ms. ACE is reached this way only, never by reading ACE tables. When ACE does not answer inside the timeout, the whole step changes nothing, writes MSG-GEN-006 naming the ACE common module on the run summary, and leaves every case to the next run.
RWB-E2-002.4: The service compares, with no person involved. For each plan returned, read the stored plan_status and plan_status_as_of on the case and compare them with the status and status date from ACE. An unchanged plan is skipped, which costs nothing and raises no event. The idempotency key for this step is the case ID with the plan reference, the status and the status date, so a rerun on the same day writes no second row and raises no second event. Check the status against the list LOV-PLAN-STATUS, which holds CREATED, APPROVED, BOOKED and BROKEN. A code such as SUSPENDED is not stored and gets a data quality exception with the check Lists of values.
RWB-E2-002.5: The write goes through P3, called by the service and not by a person. CasePlanStatus.update takes the case ID, the plan reference, the status and the status date, and writes plan_ref, plan_status and plan_status_as_of on recovery_case. P3 adds those three columns, varchar(30), varchar(10) and a date, in its own migration for this story; P2 gets no table of its own here. Call the interface rather than updating recovery_case directly, because the case table belongs to P3. After this write the rules component and the case record view both read the stored status, which is what keeps litigation away from a customer who is paying a plan.
RWB-E2-002.6: The service does this when the status has just changed to BROKEN. Read the plan event map, a versioned reference table whose rows hold an ACE status, a route state and a rule event, loaded by the center of excellence analyst. A case in route state PLAN_CURE_PERIOD maps to the event CURE_PERIOD_EXPIRED; any other route state maps to TREATMENT_BROKEN. Then call CaseEvents.raise on P3 with the case ID, that event code and the facts, which include plan_status broken and the break count. Build PlanEventMap as a rule table, so a row can be added without a release. The event, and not this step, is what moves the case.
RWB-E2-002.7: This runs in P3 and P4 after the event, with no person involved, and your work is to handle what comes back. SY-RULES evaluates the rule for the current route state: R-RES-29 moves PLAN_CURE_PERIOD to PLAN_BROKEN, R-RES-30 moves PLAN_BROKEN to BACK_TO_ROUTE_DECISION while the break count is below restructure.max_breaks, which is 2, R-RES-31 bars a further restructure at that limit, and R-LIT-02 returns a litigation case to the legal route. Each move writes a decision log entry with the rule ID and version, and SY-CASEWF places the case in the case owner queue with a task due in 5 working days. CaseEvents.raise throws DecisionLogUnavailableException when the entry cannot be written: catch it, leave the route state alone, raise an incident with MSG-P7-003, and let the next run raise the event again.
RWB-E2-002.8: A person triggers this one by opening the case record view, SCR-03. Build GET /cases/{caseId}/plan-status on PlanStatusController with an access check for Case record right R and the scope check, which answers 404 with MSG-P4-003 for a case outside the scope of the caller. The endpoint tries ACE live with the same 2-second timeout and falls back to the stored status when ACE is slow or silent. The response holds planRef, status, statusDate, a live flag that is true only when the value came from ACE just now, and a message code. Build PlanStatusPanel to show the plan, the status and the date, with MSG-P2-008 and the stored date when live is false. The read writes nothing.
RWB-E2-002.9: The daily step does this with no person involved. A case can hold a plan reference that ACE no longer returns any status for. Keep the stored plan_status and plan_status_as_of as they are, because the last known status is of more use than none, and write a data quality exception naming the plan with product DP04 so the ACE team can follow it up. The data steward and the platform administrator read those exceptions with Platform administration right R. The case record view then shows MSG-P2-008 with the stored date, which tells the case owner the status on screen is from an earlier day.

RWB-E2-014.1: No person does this. Build NoticeGeneratedListener to consume the event EV-13 NoticeGenerated, which the notice module publishes in RWB-E1-052 when it generates a notice from an Approved template. Filter to the notice types DEMAND and RECALL and ignore the rest. For each one, call ApprovalRouter.request with decision D7.1, source type NOTICE, the notice ID, the preparer, and rule R-LIT-03 with its version, for example LIT-2026.12. The routing itself is already built in RWB-E2-013: it creates the approval in status WAITING for role RW-LITOFF with a 1 working day service level and escalates to RW-HEADLIT. Your part is the listener and the call it makes.
RWB-E2-014.2: A person does this. The litigation officer opens SCR-10 Approval queue, which exists from RWB-E2-013, and selects the waiting D7.1 item. Nothing happens to the notice at this point: it keeps the state Generated until the officer decides. Who can see and take the item is set by the routing of RWB-E2-013 and by the right Litigation A for decision D7.1, so a case owner holding Litigation R reads the case and cannot act on the approval. The person who prepared the notice may also hold a role that routes the item to them, and step 8 is where such a call is refused.
RWB-E2-014.3: The front end does this when the item is selected. Build DecisionScreen as the SCR-11 shell and NoticeApprovalPanel as the SCR-18 panel inside it. On open, make three reads: GET /api/recovery/v1/approvals/{approvalId} for the approval with its source reference, rule, version and due time, GET /api/recovery/v1/notices/{noticeId} for the notice, and the document content for the PDF. Read the case facts with their business dates as well: the case number and product group through the P3 interface, and the total balance through the P1 data product interface, which returns the value together with the business date of the load it came from. This story adds no new endpoint.
RWB-E2-014.4: The screen shows this, assembled from the reads of the previous step. Put on one screen the notice PDF, the case number, the product group, the total balance with its business date, the role of the addressee, the postal address, the rule ID and version, the template code and version, and the user who prepared the notice. The address comes from contact_point as a masked value token through the DTO of the owning module, so the officer sees it in the form the masking rules allow and the raw value never reaches the browser. Showing each input with its business date is the point of the screen: the approver sees how old the facts are before deciding.
RWB-E2-014.5: The screen and the service do this together, with no person involved. Build InputFreshnessCheck to compare the business date of each input with its age limit parameter: rwb.decision.input-age-days.TOTAL_BALANCE is 1 day and rwb.decision.input-age-days.POSTAL_ADDRESS is 30 days. Read the current state of the template version the notice was built from as well. The result sets the screen state. Ready means every input is inside its limit and the template is still Approved. Stale input means an input is past its limit: show MSG-P7-006 with the input name and the age in days, and disable approve. A template withdrawn after generation holds the notice under R-LIT-04 and shows MSG-P6-003.
RWB-E2-014.6: A person does this, and it is the decision the story exists for. The litigation officer has three actions on the panel: approve as proposed; pick another Approved template variant, enter a coded reason and approve; or reject with a reason. The variant list offers only Approved variants of the same notice type and product, such as DEMAND-MTG-B beside DEMAND-MTG. The coded reason comes from LOV-OVERRIDE-REASON, which holds TEMPLATE_VARIANT and WRONG_PARTY. A rejection needs free text and is refused with 422 and MSG-GEN-001 when the reason is empty. A variant change with no reason code is refused with 422 and MSG-P7-005, and no new notice version is generated.
RWB-E2-014.7: This runs only when the officer changed the variant, and the service does it. Call NoticeApi.regenerate with the notice ID and the chosen template code. The notice module builds a new notice version from that Approved variant and returns a NoticeRef. Put the new version on the approval in place of the proposed one, so the version the officer looked at is the version approved and the only one that can reach dispatch. The decision entry of the next step records both: the proposed template DEMAND-MTG, the chosen DEMAND-MTG-B and the reason code, under the final call APPROVED_CHANGED. The notice version first proposed is kept and is never sent.
RWB-E2-014.8: NoticeApprovalService calls the approval endpoint, POST /approvals/{approvalId}/approve or POST /approvals/{approvalId}/refuse, with an ApprovalAction holding the reason, the reason code and, for a change, changes.templateCode. The checks come from RWB-E2-013 and you rely on them: Litigation A for D7.1, and the preparer rule, which refuses with 409 and MSG-P7-002 when the approver prepared the notice. The call writes the decision entry with the inputs reference and the business date of each input, the rule version, the template version, the approver and the time. Send an Idempotency-Key header. An item another approver already decided is refused with 409 and MSG-GEN-004, and a failed entry write gives 503 with MSG-P7-003.
RWB-E2-014.9: The service does this straight after the entry is written, with no person involved. On approval, call NoticeApi.approve with the notice ID and the decision entry ID, which moves the notice from Generated to Approved and makes it part of the 16:00 dispatch run, JOB-10 in RWB-E2-021. On rejection, call NoticeApi.hold with the reason code REFUSED_BY_APPROVER and the entry ID, which moves the notice from Generated to Held, and open a task in the case owner queue carrying the reason text of the officer. The approval entry and the notice state change commit in one transaction, so no notice is Approved without its entry.
RWB-E2-014.10: The screen does the last part, with no person involved. Show MSG-P7-004, Approved. The case moves to {state}, and set the screen state to Decided, which shows the outcome, the approver and the decision time and offers no action. A screen loaded before another approver decided reloads into that same state and names the approver who was first. The approval also publishes EV-08 DecisionRecorded for anything downstream that listens to it. The case status returns to In progress on approval, and a rejection leaves the case In progress with the new task in the case owner queue.

RWB-E2-027.1: A person does this: the reference data administrator, holding Reference data right C. They post the file to /api/recovery/v1/admin/reference-loads as multipart form data with the file, the table name payment_match_rule and a valid from date. P4 owns the endpoint. Your work is PaymentMatchRuleLoadHandler, a ReferenceLoadHandler for that table, with its validate and apply methods. A version is a set of rows sharing a rule_version such as PM-2026.12, each row holding a rule code, a priority, a match type, an amount tolerance, window days before and after, and a partial floor. The endpoint takes the SHA-256 hash of the file per table, so a file already loaded is refused with 409 and MSG-P1-002.
RWB-E2-027.2: The handler checks the file with no person involved. For each row: match_type is one of EXACT, WINDOW and PARTIAL; amount_tolerance_pct is between 0 and 100; window_days_before and window_days_after are 0 or more; priority is unique within the rule_version; approved_by is filled, since Credit Administration owns the list and approves the version the administrator loaded. Any failed row refuses the whole load with 422, using MSG-GEN-002 for a value outside its range or a repeated priority and MSG-GEN-001 for an empty value, and the version in force stays in force. Migration V2_027__match_rule_partial.sql adds partial_floor_pct as numeric(5,2), the check constraint on the tolerance, and a unique key on rule_version and priority.
RWB-E2-027.3: JOB-07 does this at the start of its run, with no person involved. The job already exists from RWB-E2-008. For the business date it is matching, read the rule rows whose valid_from is on or before that date and whose valid_to is empty or later, and use that one version for the whole run. This is what lets Credit Administration change a window or a floor without a release: a run on 2027-01-05 under version PM-2027.01 allows 5 window days after the due date, while a match already decided under PM-2026.12 keeps that version on its decision entry and is never recomputed.
RWB-E2-027.4: The job does this per payment, with no person involved. Build MatchRuleEvaluator to take the rows of the version in force, sort them by priority and try each one against every running plan on the case, stopping at the first row that matches. Build one evaluator per match type behind it: ExactMatch for an amount inside the tolerance with a payment date inside the window before the due date, WindowMatch for the same with the window extended after the due date, and PartialMatch for an amount at or above the partial floor and below the installment. When two rows would both match, the lower priority number decides, so a payment of the exact installment amount is matched by EXACT even though WINDOW also fits.
RWB-E2-027.5: The job does this, and the order of the two writes matters. Build MatchDecisionWriter to assemble a D5 DecisionLogRequest holding rule R-RES-26, the rule version equal to the parameter version in force, the row code that matched and the inputs, which are the payment code, the amount, the dates and the row code only, never personal data. Call DecisionLogApi.write on P7 first, then write the proceeds row and call TreatmentApi. A DecisionLogWriteException means no proceeds row is written for that payment: the run summary shows MSG-P7-003 for it, an incident is raised under R-UNI-39, and the next run of JOB-07 for that business date matches the payment again.
RWB-E2-027.6: The job does this when the matching row is PARTIAL, with no person involved. Call TreatmentApi.recordInstallmentPaid on P3 with the treatment ID, the proceeds ID, the due date, the amount paid and the shortfall, which is the installment amount less the amount paid. P3 writes it to treatment.installment_shortfall and holds it on the plan, so the plan shows what is still owed for that due date. A payment of 11,875.00 against an installment of 12,500.00 is 95 percent, above the partial floor of 90 percent, and leaves a shortfall of 625.00 THB on due date 2026-12-15. You build the call and the amounts; holding the shortfall belongs to the treatment interface.
RWB-E2-027.7: The job does this when no row matched, with no person involved. Write the proceeds row with matched_to set to UNMATCHED and write a D5 decision entry under rule R-UNI-03, so even a payment that matched nothing carries a record of why. These are the receipts a person works through: a payment 4 days after the due date where the window allows 3, a payment at 80 percent of the installment against a floor of 90, and a payment above the installment by more than the tolerance. The run summary carries MSG-P8-001 with the count of unmatched payments for the business date, and they come back from GET /proceeds with matched false.
RWB-E2-027.8: A person does this: the Credit Administration officer, or another role holding Write-off and posting right R. They open SCR-28 Proceeds matching, which has the states Loading, matched and unmatched. For each matched receipt the screen shows the row code and the rule version that decided it, and for each unmatched receipt the reason. The data comes from two reads: GET /api/recovery/v1/proceeds for the receipts, and GET /api/recovery/v1/decision-log for the entry behind each one, which is where the row code and the version are held. Until SCR-40 Reference data is built, the administrator reads the result of a parameter load on the reference load record.

RWB-E1-010.1: Migration: creates the tables, columns and keys listed in section 11.
RWB-E1-010.2: Build: creates the entities, repositories, mapper/check/service classes listed in section 13.
RWB-E1-010.3: Build: registers the endpoint and published-interface contracts.
RWB-E1-010.4: Deferred: job scheduling, load execution and validation; see the data load reference.

RWB-E1-022.1: A person does this and no Workbench code runs yet. The user opens the Workbench in a browser. The Workbench is a module folder loaded by the ACE front end, so there is no Workbench login page, no Workbench password and no local account. What you build here is the front end entry: the recovery/access folder in the ACE front end holding the SessionBanner and AccessRequestPage components that later steps use. A user who already holds an ACE session from another module comes straight back from the redirect in step 2. Epic 1 has no business screens, so the first page after sign-in is an administration screen or the access request page.
RWB-E1-022.2: The ACE common module and Entra ID do this, with the person typing their credentials. You configure it rather than code it: the Workbench application is already set up in Entra ID as INT-21, under the bank conditional access policy that requires a second factor. Entra ID is the bank identity provider. What comes back is an OpenID Connect token, a signed set of claims about the person, where a claim is one named value inside the token. Two claims matter here. The groups claim holds the Entra ID group names the person belongs to. The amr claim, authentication methods reference, holds how they proved who they are.
RWB-E1-022.3: This happens on its own and is the first Workbench code in the flow. Build SessionResolver in package recovery.access.signin. Read the amr claim from the verified token and refuse the session unless it holds the value named in property rwb.access.required-amr, which is mfa. A token carrying only pwd fails here. Throw SessionRefusedException with reason code NO_MFA, which the controller maps to 401 with MSG-P4-005 asking the person to sign in again with their second factor, and publish the refusal through AccessEventPublisher. Keep the expected value in the property so the check holds no fixed text in code.
RWB-E1-022.4: This happens on its own inside SessionResolver. For each group name in the groups claim, read the role table for an active row whose entra_group column equals that name, and collect the role codes found. Use index ix_role_entra_group on role (entra_group) where is_active. A group with no active role row is skipped without an error, and the skipped name is written on the sign-in event so an administrator can see it. When no group maps to a role, refuse the session with 401, MSG-P4-001 and reason NO_ROLE, and the person sees the access request page with no data. Group names differ per environment and are data rows, never values in code.
RWB-E1-022.5: This happens on its own. Read the role_conflict rows whose conflict_version is in force by valid_from and valid_to, and test every pair of roles the person now holds. The conflicts_with column holds either a role code or one of the class values ANY_BUSINESS_ROLE and ANY_OTHER_ROLE, so one row can bar a role from every business role at once. On a match, refuse the session with reason ROLE_CONFLICT and MSG-P4-006 naming both roles, and raise an incident to the security administrator queue. You create the table in migration V_E1_022__role_conflict.sql with the RoleConflict entity; RW-REFADM loads version SOD-2026.11 into it.
RWB-E1-022.6: This happens on its own. Build the SessionContext object that every later check reads: the Entra ID object reference for the person, never their name or e-mail, the role codes from step 4, the default_scope of each of those roles from the role table, and the permission matrix version in force at that moment, PM-2026.11 at release. Hold the conflict version on it as well. The session keeps both versions until it ends, so a matrix version that takes effect later in the day does not change an open session and the next sign-in picks the new one up. Build the one-line scope text here too, for example Case owner. Scope: own cases.
RWB-E1-022.7: This happens on its own. Build AccessEventPublisher as a published interface in recovery.access.signin with one method, publish(AccessEvent). In Epic 1 it writes to the ACE audit log and to the SOC log through INT-22. RWB-E1-039 later adds the decision log write behind the same interface, so no caller has to change. Publish a successful sign-in with the roles resolved and any unmapped group name, and publish every refusal with its reason code: NO_ROLE, NO_MFA, ROLE_CONFLICT or NO_RIGHT. The event carries the Entra ID object reference and no personal data. These events are how the bank answers who could see a case on a given date.
RWB-E1-022.8: The front end does this on its own once the session resolves. Build the new endpoint GET /me/session returning userRef, the roles with code, name and default scope, the matrix and conflict versions, the scope line and resolvedAt. It needs only a resolved session and no capability area, because it returns the caller's own session and nothing else. The React component SessionBanner shows the scope line at the top of every page. Menu filtering reads the same response and shows an entry only when at least one session role holds R in that screen's capability area, so RW-CASEOWN sees no Administration menu. Leave the breakGlass field empty until RWB-E1-039 fills it.
RWB-E1-022.9: The person makes the call and the check runs on its own on the server. Every endpoint declares its capability area and right with the x-capability marking in the API file. AccessCheckInterceptor, a Spring method interceptor, reads that marking before the handler runs and calls AccessCheck.check with the session, the area and the right. AccessCheckService unions the permission letters of all the session's roles for that area and tests the right needed; a dash for every role refuses every action in the area. A refusal is 403 with MSG-P4-002 naming the action, plus one refusal event with the area, the right and result REFUSED. Service identities such as SY-RULES go through the same check. Add a contract test that fails any operation with no declared area.

RWB-E1-034.1: A person starts this. The litigation officer opens SCR-33 Template approval, which you build as the React component TemplateApprovalScreen in folder recovery/comms/templates. The screen lists templates by code and language from GET /templates, which needs Documents R and applies the caller's scope. The officer picks an existing pair, for example DEMAND-MTG with language TH, to add the next version, or types a new code for a template that does not exist yet. Show the versions of the chosen pair with their state, approver and valid from date, so the officer can see what is current before uploading anything. The common loading and error states apply to the screen.
RWB-E1-034.2: The same person continues. The screen sends POST /templates as multipart with the DOCX file and the fields templateCode, language, productGroup, channel, noticeType, signatureBasis and mergeCodes. A merge code is a placeholder in the letter body that the generation step later replaces with a value from the case, for example CASE_NO or TOTAL_OUTSTANDING. The caller needs Documents C, which RW-LITOFF and RW-LEGAL hold. Build the upload form with each field required where the contract says so. Keep the allowed file types in property rwb.comms.template.allowed-types rather than in code; DOCX is the only value in Epic 1.
RWB-E1-034.3: This happens on its own in TemplateAdminService, before anything is stored. Refuse a caller without Documents C with 403 and MSG-P4-002. A missing template code or language is 422 with MSG-GEN-001 naming the field. A file that is not DOCX is 415 with MSG-P6-010, and a file above rwb.comms.template.max-size-mb, which is 10, is 413. Then run MergeCodeScanner from RWB-E1-046 over the body and test every merge code it finds against the merge field catalog in force. An unknown code such as LINE_ID is 422 with MSG-P6-006 naming it, no version row is created and no file is kept.
RWB-E1-034.4: This happens on its own. TemplateBodyStore writes the DOCX through the ACE storage pattern into a write-once container and returns body_ref. Write-once means a stored body can never be overwritten, so a correction is always a new version. Then insert the template row with the next template_version for that code and language, state Draft, created_by and the fields from the upload. Assign the number inside a transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the highest existing version of that code and language, so two uploads at the same moment cannot take the same number; the unique constraint uk_template_version from RWB-E1-046 is the backstop. The response is 201 with the Template.
RWB-E1-034.5: A second person acts. Legal counsel opens the Draft version on SCR-33, downloads the body through GET /templates/{templateId}/content and reads the merge codes shown beside it. Offer Approve with a valid from date only in the Draft state and only to a role holding Documents A. The action sends POST /templates/{templateId}/approve with validFrom and an Idempotency-Key header. Idempotency means the same key sent twice returns the first result and changes nothing, so a repeated click leaves one approval in the audit log. Hide the action from roles without Documents A, and check the right on the server as well, because hiding a button is not a control.
RWB-E1-034.6: This happens on its own in TemplateAdminService, as four checks. A caller without Documents A gets 403 with MSG-P4-002. An approver whose user ID equals created_by gets 409 with MSG-P7-002, the separation of duty rule that nobody approves their own work. A version in any state other than Draft gets 409 with MSG-P3-005. A valid from date before today gets 422 with MSG-GEN-003. When all four pass, write state Approved, approved_by, approved_at and valid_from. Use the optimistic lock on the version column, so a second approver acting at the same moment gets 409 with MSG-GEN-004 instead of overwriting the first approval.
RWB-E1-034.7: This happens on its own, with no further action by anyone. The current version is derived, so there is nothing to switch over: TemplateCatalog from RWB-E1-046 picks, for a code and language, the Approved version with the latest valid_from that is on or before the date asked for. A version approved with valid from today becomes current today, and one approved with a later date becomes current on that date. Earlier Approved versions keep their rows, their approver and their approval time, and stay visible on SCR-33 to any role with Documents R. That is how the bank shows which wording was approved when a notice was sent.
RWB-E1-034.8: A person starts this and the system then holds generation. Legal counsel sends POST /templates/{templateId}/withdraw with a reason. An empty reason is 422 with MSG-GEN-001, and a version that is not Approved is 409 with MSG-P3-005. Write state Withdrawn and keep the reason on the row for the screen to show. From then on TemplateCatalog throws TemplateWithdrawnException with MSG-P6-003 for that code and language, so notices wait until Legal approves a new version. Do not fall back to the earlier Approved version. Resuming the held notices once a new version is approved is built in RWB-E2-021.
RWB-E1-034.9: This happens on its own in TemplateAdminService on all three actions. Write one ACE audit entry per action, holding the user ID, the template code, the version number and the time. Hold nothing else: no body text and no personal data, so test bodies carry synthetic wording only. The Idempotency-Key store makes the count exact, because an approve repeated with the same key returns the first response and adds no second entry. These entries are what control CTL-14 rests on, showing for any notice which version was in force and who approved the wording.

RWB-E1-047.1: A person does this through an endpoint you build, POST /admin/feature-flags, which needs Platform administration C. The request body FeatureFlagRequest holds key, description, ownerUserId, ownerTeam, defaultOn and removalDate. There is no screen in this story, so the platform administrator calls the endpoint through the ACE admin console API client; the flag list screen arrives later as SCR-44. A feature flag is a data row that switches one piece of behavior on or off per environment with no new deployment, so unfinished work can ship switched off. The removal date is the date by which the flag and the old code path should both be gone.
RWB-E1-047.2: This happens on its own in FeatureFlagService. Test the key against the pattern rwb.<module>.<short-name>. The same rule is a check constraint in migration V2026_11_47__p2_feature_flags.sql written as ^rwb\.[a-z0-9]+\.[a-z0-9-]+$, so a bad key is refused in the service and in the database. A missing removal date is 422 with MSG-GEN-001, and a removal date before today is 422 with MSG-GEN-003. A key that already exists is 409. Then insert the feature_flag row with dev_on, sit_on, uat_on and prod_on all set to default_on, so a new flag behaves the same in every environment until somebody changes one. The response is 201.
RWB-E1-047.3: This runs on its own inside every module that has work behind a flag. Build the published interface FeatureFlags with the single method isOn(String flagKey) in package recovery.integration.flags.api, and FeatureFlagsImpl behind it. Hold the value per key in a cache refreshed every rwb.flags.cache-seconds, which is 30, so a change takes effect within half a minute with no restart. Read the current environment from property rwb.environment and pick the matching column. Return false for a key with no row and write a warning with the key and no user data to the application log. Other modules call this interface and never read the flag tables themselves.
RWB-E1-047.4: This runs on its own in the browser when the page loads. Build GET /feature-flags returning a map of flag key to boolean for the caller's environment. It needs a resolved session and no capability area, and answers 401 with MSG-P4-001 without one. In front end folder src/modules/recovery/flags build the hook useFeatureFlag, which reads that endpoint once per page load and returns the value for a key, and the component FlagGate, which renders its children only while the flag is on. The queue column on SCR-02 Case list behind rwb.casewf.case-list-queue-column is the reference use. A value read at page load changes only on the next reload.
RWB-E1-047.5: A person does this. The platform administrator sends PATCH /admin/feature-flags/{flagKey} with FeatureFlagChange holding environment, value and reason, plus an If-Match header carrying the version they read. If-Match is how the server learns which copy of the row the caller saw. The endpoint needs Platform administration U. An empty reason is 422 with MSG-GEN-001 and an unknown key is 404 with MSG-P2-016. Setting the value the environment already holds writes no change row. RW-SECADM may also change flags, while RW-COE, RW-DATASTEW, RW-AUDIT and RW-COMPLY may only read flags and their change history.
RWB-E1-047.6: This happens on its own in FeatureFlagService, all in one transaction. Compare the If-Match version with the version on the feature_flag row and refuse with 409 and MSG-GEN-004 when they differ, so of two administrators who both read version 4 one write succeeds at version 5 and the other is refused. Then write the new value into the environment column, insert a feature_flag_change row with flag_key, environment, old_value, new_value, reason, created_by and created_at, and call the ACE audit log with the same change. The change row and the audit entry hold the user ID, never the person's name.
RWB-E1-047.7: This happens on its own, and the step needs no code beyond steps 3 and 4. The browser reloads the page, useFeatureFlag reads GET /feature-flags again, and FlagGate renders the component the flag now allows, for example the queue column on SCR-02. On the server side the cache picks the new value up within 30 seconds. No code is released and no service is restarted, which is the reason for holding the value as a row. Every flag that is off has to run the previous code path, so write a test for both paths of each flag you add.
RWB-E1-047.8: This runs on its own on a timetable, with nobody starting it. Build FlagRemovalReportJob as a Quartz job that fires every Monday at 08:00 Asia/Bangkok. It reads the feature_flag rows where is_active is true and removal_date is before today, and works out how many days each one is overdue. Its idempotency key is the report date, so a rerun on the same date sends nothing new; a restart runs the job from the beginning. The same rows are available on demand through GET /admin/feature-flags with overdue=true, which returns daysOverdue per flag to a caller with Platform administration R.
RWB-E1-047.9: This happens on its own at the end of the job. Send one email per owner, holding that owner's flags, and one email to the RW-PLATADM group, both through the ACE notification path for staff. Write one log line per flag with MSG-P2-003, which names the flag, the date it passed and its owner, and asks for the flag and its old code path to be removed. The owners are the tribe lead and squad members, who receive the report and hold no right to change a flag. The report repeats every week until the flag is retired.

RWB-E1-059.1: No person is involved and nothing in this story does this. The case workflow module, under service identity SY-CASEWF, creates and allocates cases daily and writes event EV-01 CaseCreated to the outbox, all of it built in RWB-E1-030. An outbox is a table the publishing module writes the event into inside the same transaction as the case, so the event cannot be lost when messaging is down. The event carries caseId, caseNo, productGroup, accounts and businessDate. Your work starts on the consumer side in step 2; for this step you only need cases being created in DEV to test against.
RWB-E1-059.2: This runs on its own. Build IntakeShadowListener in package recovery.agent.intake to consume EV-01 from the outbox and call AgentOrchestrator from RWB-E1-058 for agent INTAKE. Build the run key INTAKE:<caseId>:<businessDate> and hold it in agent_run.idempotency_key. Idempotent here means the same event delivered twice leaves one run: the listener checks the event ID and that run key, and counts the repeat. The listener sits behind feature flag rwb.agent.intake-shadow, and with the flag off it ignores CaseCreated, so this work can ship without touching case creation.
RWB-E1-059.3: This runs on its own. Build IntakeInputAssembler to call the five allowed tools through the gateway: read_case, read_accounts and read_contact_points on the P3 CaseQueryService, read_documents on the P5 DocumentQueryService and read_valuations on the P1 CollateralQueryService. Each call runs under service identity SY-AGENT, which holds Case record R and Documents R, so the agent reads no more than its role allows and touches no other module's tables. Mask every personal field before the request leaves, so the model receives masking tokens only. Then call the model with prompt version PR1 and the 60 second timeout from policy P1. Write a test that no personal field reaches the request.
RWB-E1-059.4: This runs on its own in the guardrail from RWB-E1-058. There are three checks on the model's answer. It has to match output schema intake-summary-v1, with summary up to 1,500 characters, gaps holding a gapType from the enum with reason and sourceRef, and confidence between 0 and 1. It may have used only tools on the allowed list. Its confidence has to reach the floor of 0.80. Add the stale input rule here as check SCHEMA_RULE for INTAKE. Write the agent_run row either way, with status ANSWERED, TIMED_OUT, GUARDRAIL_FAILED or BELOW_FLOOR, autonomy_mode SHADOW, the policy, prompt and model versions, output, confidence, latency, tokens, cost and data_as_of.
RWB-E1-059.5: This runs on its own. Publish EV-28 AgentRunCompleted with runId, agent INTAKE, caseId, outcome and fallback. SHADOW mode means the output is stored and shown to nobody, so this step has to leave no other trace: no case field, no task, no queue entry and no decision log entry changes, and the case owner sees nothing. GET /cases/{caseId} and the case timeline return no agent output, and GET /admin/agent-runs returns run metadata without the summary or the gap flags. Write tests that look for exactly those absences, because the agreement rate is only worth measuring while nobody has acted on the output.
RWB-E1-059.6: A person starts this. The center of excellence analyst sends POST /admin/agent-evaluations with agent INTAKE, sampleCode INTAKE-S1 and sampleVersion 1, holding Rules and parameters C. The endpoint comes from RWB-E1-058 and answers 202 with an AgentEvaluationRun, so the comparison runs in the background. One RUNNING run is allowed per agent and sample version, and a second attempt is 409 with MSG-P10-003. A sample with no labeled rows for the agent is 422 with MSG-P10-002, which tells the analyst to load the labels first. The same analyst loaded sample INTAKE-S1, the business analysts' review of 200 Epic 1 cases with one row per case and gap type.
RWB-E1-059.7: This runs on its own inside the evaluation harness from RWB-E1-058. For each of the 200 cases in the sample the agent runs again in SHADOW mode, through the same assembler, guardrail and policy as a live shadow run, and its agent_run row carries the evaluation_run_id. Build IntakeOutputScorer to compare, per case and gap type, the flag the agent returned against expected_value Y or N in agent_sample. Cases with no label are left out of the comparison and listed as unlabeled on the evaluation run, so a sample labeled for 180 of 200 cases is scored on 180. Test the scorer on a small fixture whose counts you already know.
RWB-E1-059.8: This runs on its own at the end of the evaluation. Write one agent_evaluation row per gap type: MISSING_DOCUMENT, NO_VALID_APPRAISAL, NO_CONTACT_POINT and STALE_INPUT. Each row holds evaluation_run_id, label_key, sample_size, true_positive, false_positive, false_negative, agreement_rate, precision_value and recall_value, together with the policy, prompt and model versions. The agreement rate is the count of cases where the agent's flag equals the label divided by the labeled cases, to four decimals, so 182 agreeing cases out of 200 gives 0.9100. Precision and recall come from the same three counts. Move the evaluation run from RUNNING to DONE.
RWB-E1-059.9: A person does this. The analyst calls GET /admin/agent-evaluations with agent, from and to, holding Rules and parameters R; RW-RISK may read the same scores. The response is the evaluation runs with their score rows. No screen is built in this story, so the read happens through an API client, and a role without the right is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002. These numbers are the purpose of the shadow run: the move of the intake agent to autonomy level 1 in RWB-E2-028 rests on the measured agreement rate per gap type, and the report with the level 1 proposal is built in RWB-E1-061.

RWB-E2-003.1: A person does this, on a screen that already exists. SCR-03 Case record went live with Epic 1, and this story adds one panel to it, the React component OtherProductsPanel in src/modules/recovery/case. Build the panel with four states: loading, the product list, the stale banner and the empty state. The case has to be in the caller's scope, which for a case owner means a case they own, and the server tests that in step 3 rather than the screen. Put the panel behind feature flag rwb.integration.customer-products, so SCR-03 can ship without it if the work is unfinished.
RWB-E2-003.2: This happens on its own when the panel loads. Build the new endpoint GET /cases/{caseId}/customer-products with path parameter caseId, authorized by Case record R with scope applied. The response is CustomerProducts, holding dataAsOf, stale, messageCode and items, where each item carries partyId, partyRole, productType, accountNo already masked for the caller, productStatus and dataAsOf. The controller is CustomerProductsController in package recovery.integration.customer. The endpoint is read only, so it needs no idempotency key. Its errors are 401 with MSG-P4-001, 403 with MSG-P4-002, 404 with MSG-P4-003 and 503 with MSG-GEN-006, each returned in the Problem shape.
RWB-E2-003.3: This happens on its own before any data is read. The access check tests that the caller's session holds right R in capability area Case record, and refuses with 403 and MSG-P4-002 otherwise, as for RW-REFADM. Then test the scope: a case owner with scope Own passes only for a case they own. A case outside the scope answers 404 with MSG-P4-003 rather than 403, so the caller learns nothing about a case they may not see. Both checks sit in the controller and the service, and no party or product row is read until they pass.
RWB-E2-003.4: This happens on its own in CustomerProductsService. Call CaseQuery.partiesOf(caseId, partyRoles) on the P3 published interface, passing the party roles from property rwb.customer.products.party-roles, which holds BORROWER and CO_BORROWER.
