RWB-E2-005.5: The Workbench does this on its own. An entry whose recomputed hash, or whose link to the entry before it, does not match is still returned, with chainVerified false and the warning MSG-P7-012 naming the entry, and ChainMismatchNotifier raises one incident to the Compliance queue for it. Raise it once per entry so that a repeated query over the same page does not fill the queue. An entry that fails is never hidden and never dropped from the result, because the auditor has to see that the log has a gap. Test it with one entry changed in the SIT database with the trigger disabled, the database rule that otherwise refuses a change to a stored entry.
RWB-E2-005.6: The Workbench writes this itself, through the access event interface of RWB-E1-039, for every query that runs. One entry per query, carrying the decision code AC-READ, the filter the auditor used and the number of rows returned. The entry goes into the decision log, which is why a query that cannot write its access event returns 503 with MSG-P7-003 and gives the auditor nothing back; test TC-E2-005-12 forces that failure. A refused query writes its own entry as well, with decision code AC-DENY, area DECISION_LOG and right R.
RWB-E2-005.7: The auditor chooses the export, and DecisionLogCsvWriter produces it. Build it to stream the full result instead of one page, with a header row, one row per entry, and chainVerified on every row. The export runs the same filters and the same scope as the query, so an auditor cannot reach an out-of-scope entry through it. Write one more access event for the export, with decision code AC-EXPT, the filter and the row count. Personal fields inside a recommendation or an action are masked under the masking rules before the file is written, and the file otherwise carries references and codes.

RWB-E2-017.1: A person starts this. The restructuring officer, holding RW-RESTRUCT with scope over the case, opens SCR-14 Treatment record for a deed in lieu treatment that was approved at D6.4, and chooses Generate documents. You build GenerateDocumentsPanel, the React component that adds this to SCR-14. The control is available only while the treatment is approved and still open, which the panel reads from treatment.decision_log_id and treatment.outcome: a treatment with no decision_log_id has not been approved, so the panel disables the control and shows MSG-P5-011, and a direct call returns 409 with the same message. The whole panel is hidden while the feature flag rwb.dochub.generation-screens is off.
RWB-E2-017.2: The Workbench does this with no person involved. Read the document set for the treatment type and product group from the template catalog in reference data (RWB-E1-046), and for each template read the current version that Legal approved. DEED_IN_LIEU gives DIL-CONTRACT, DIL-CA and DIL-MORTGAGE; RESTRUCTURE gives RES-AGREEMENT. Show each template with the version the drafts will be made from, which for the deed in lieu set of AC1 is versions 2, 1 and 1. The set and the versions are data owned by Legal, so hold none of them in code. Templates are reached through the published interface of the owning module, never by reading its tables.
RWB-E2-017.3: The officer confirms, and the Workbench then calls the generation engine. Post to POST /api/recovery/v1/cases/{caseId}/generated-documents, the endpoint RWB-E2-026 defines, which fills each template with the case facts and returns the drafts. Show the three drafts with the merge values that were filled, a merge value being one named field in the template, for example the contract date or the transfer price. Each draft is a document of its own type, CONTRACT, CREDIT_APPROVAL or MORTGAGE_DOCUMENT, all three legal types in the document type table, held at doc_version 1 in state DRAFT. The merge rules and the template selection belong to RWB-E2-026.
RWB-E2-017.4: A person reads here, and the work is in the component. Build GeneratedDocumentReview on SCR-30 Case documents: the PDF of the draft on one side and the list of merge values on the other. Each merge field is marked overridable or locked in the merge field catalog, and a locked one is shown read only. Amounts, parties, title numbers and the treatment terms are locked, and the dates of signing and the witness details are overridable. Show the fields read only for a team manager as well, who holds Documents R. Reading the catalog flag in the component keeps the officer from attempting a change that the endpoint would refuse.
RWB-E2-017.5: The officer does this in the review component, which calls POST /documents/{documentId}/regenerate. You build that endpoint, which is new and recorded in the additions file. The request is RegenerateRequest: between one and ten overrides, each holding the merge field, the new value and a reason, plus the version of the document the officer read. An empty reason is refused with 422 and MSG-GEN-001 naming Reason, and a change to a field that the catalog locks is refused with 422 and MSG-P5-014 naming the field. A document already in state SENT is refused with 409 and MSG-P5-002. The second of two officers saving against the same version gets 409 with MSG-GEN-004.
RWB-E2-017.6: The Workbench does all of this in DocumentSetService, in an order you have to keep. Write the decision log entry first, through DecisionLogWriter, carrying the decision code, the old value, the new value and the reason as override_reason. Then call DocumentGenerator.generate with the overrides and store the result as the next doc_version, leaving the earlier version readable. A failed decision log write stops the whole action with 503 and MSG-P7-003, with the document left at its doc_version and no file added. A correction on a REVIEWED document moves it back to DRAFT at the new doc_version, so the officer has to review it again.
RWB-E2-017.7: The officer does this for each draft, and the Workbench records it. The call is POST /api/recovery/v1/documents/{documentId}/review with action COMPLETE, the endpoint that RWB-E1-054 adds. Extend it for generated drafts so that it sets the document state to REVIEWED and review_status to CONFIRMED where nothing was corrected or CORRECTED where something was. Every document of the set has to reach REVIEWED before the send in step 9 is allowed, which is why the Mark reviewed control is per draft and not per set.
RWB-E2-017.8: The officer does this once, on SCR-14 from GenerateDocumentsPanel, and the control is available only while every draft of the set is reviewed. The request goes to POST /treatments/{treatmentId}/signature-requests with the treatment ID, the list of document IDs and a required Idempotency-Key header, which the Workbench keeps for 24 hours under the parameter GEN_IDEMPOTENCY_HOURS. That key is what makes a repeated send safe: the same key arriving again returns the first result, with one signature request for the treatment and no second copy to the container. The send step sits behind its own flag, rwb.dochub.generation-screens.send, until RWB-E2-018 is merged.
RWB-E2-017.9: The Workbench does the whole sequence, and the order is fixed. Check that every document of the set is REVIEWED and was made from the template version that is current now; a document that fails either check gives 422 with MSG-P5-013, naming the document and the reason, and nothing is sent. Then copy each final file to the write-once container through BlobStorageAdapter, which is idempotent by file hash through ContentHashGuard. Then write the decision log entry with final_call SENT_FOR_SIGNATURE. Then call SignatureRequests.start in P6; an answer of UNAVAILABLE gives 503 with MSG-GEN-006 and leaves every document REVIEWED. On an accepted request, set each document to state SENT with write_once true.
RWB-E2-017.10: The Workbench does this once the send succeeds. The screen shows MSG-P5-012 with the count of documents sent, three for the deed in lieu set, and each document appears on SCR-30 Case documents in state SENT. A sent document is read only: SCR-30 shows it without edit controls, and a later attempt to correct it is refused with 409 and MSG-P5-002. The file in the write-once container is never changed after this point, so a correction has to be made before the send. The signature flow itself, the wet ink path and the return of the signed copy belong to RWB-E2-018.

RWB-E2-033.1: A person does this. The team manager, holding RW-TEAMMGR with Team scope, opens SCR-02 Case list. You change CaseListPage, the React component behind that screen, instead of building a new one: add the columns age in state, service level state, service level due, prescription date, prescription clock and deviation, add the breach filter, and mark a breached row with the text Breached so that the mark does not rest on color alone. A paused stage clock shows Paused. Build the Loading, Empty, List and Filtered states. While the flag rwb.casewf.case-list-ageing is off, the screen keeps the columns of RWB-E2-011 and RWB-E1-031.
RWB-E2-033.2: The screen does this with no further action from the manager. It calls GET /api/recovery/v1/cases with the filters the manager chose: product, stage, status, owner, queue, page, size, sort, and the new parameter breached, set to true or false. No new endpoint is added in this story. Add breached and the response field prescriptionClockStatus to the API specification, record the change in the additions file, and regenerate the types through RWB-TE-003 so that the front end and the service agree on the shape. Each item of the CasePage already carries ageDays, serviceLevelDueAt and serviceLevelState from RWB-E2-011.
RWB-E2-033.3: The Workbench does this in CaseAndWorkflowController, before any case is read. The common module access check tests the right R in the capability area Case record and refuses a caller without it with 403 and MSG-P4-002, which test TC-E2-033-12 shows for the reference data administrator. The caller's scope then limits every row to Own, Team or All, taken from the default scope of their roles, so the manager of MTG-BKK sees the cases of that team's queues and no others. A case outside the scope appears on no page and under no filter, and the number of rows left out is never shown.
RWB-E2-033.4: The controller does this next, again before any case is read. Check each filter value against its list of values: the product against LOV-PRODUCT, the status against LOV-CASE-STATUS, the stage against LOV-STAGE, and the queue against the queue codes in force, all read through the P4 reference data interface. A value outside its list is refused with 422 and MSG-GEN-007, which names the value and the field, so a request with product CAR reads nothing. Check the page size against 1 to 200 and refuse a size outside that range with 422 and MSG-GEN-002, which carries the minimum and the maximum.
RWB-E2-033.5: The Workbench does this in CaseListQueryService, which RWB-E2-011 built and which you extend. It reads the cases in scope with their queue and owner and the SERVICE_LEVEL timer row of each, and computes ageDays and serviceLevelState. Age in state is the whole number of calendar days from stage_clock_start to today in Asia/Bangkok, or from entry_date where stage_clock_start is empty. A case is breached when its SERVICE_LEVEL timer has status EXPIRED, or has status RUNNING with expires_at earlier than now; a paused timer is never breached, and a case with no timer gets serviceLevelState NONE. Hold these as pure functions in AgeingCalculator and unit test them without a database.
RWB-E2-033.6: This is the new code of the story, and the Workbench runs it with no person involved. PrescriptionClockReader reads the PRESCRIPTION timer of each case and sets prescriptionClockStatus to RUNNING or EXPIRED from timer.status, or NONE where the case has no such timer. It then applies the breached filter, keeping only breached cases when breached is true and only the rest when it is false. Both clocks appear side by side because a deviation pauses the stage clock while the prescription clock keeps running. Add index ix_timer_case_type on timer (case_id, timer_type) where the status is RUNNING, PAUSED or EXPIRED, through a Flyway migration in the P3 migration folder.
RWB-E2-033.7: The service does this before it returns the page. Order the rows by breach first, then by age in state descending, then by case number. The three cases of AC1 therefore come back as RW-2026-000101, which is breached, then RW-2026-000102 at two days, then RW-2026-000103 at zero days. Case number is what makes the order stable: 120 cases with no breach and the same age in state still split cleanly into pages of 50, with no case on two pages and none missing. Put the order in the query rather than the front end, because only one page of rows is returned.
RWB-E2-033.8: The screen does this from the response. Show the columns case number, product, queue, owner, status, stage, age in state, service level state, service level due, prescription date, prescription clock and deviation, and write Unassigned where a case has no owner. Mark each breached row with text, so that the mark is readable without color. Where no case matches the filters, show the Empty state with MSG-P3-020. The layout itself belongs to the designer under DL31, so keep the component to the columns and states listed in section 15.
RWB-E2-033.9: The manager does this, and the screen calls GET /api/recovery/v1/cases/export with the same filters, including breached, and without page and size. The endpoint comes from RWB-E1-031; this story adds the new columns and the breached parameter, and records the change in the additions file. Keeping one set of filters for the list and the export is what makes the file match what the manager is looking at, as AC3 expects: three filters and one row. The right needed is R in Case record, and the caller's scope applies to the export exactly as it does to the list.
RWB-E2-033.10: The Workbench does this in CaseExportService, which RWB-E1-031 built. Extend it with the columns age in state, service level state, service level due, prescription date, prescription clock and deviation open, on top of the columns it already writes. Two rules control the file. The access log entry goes in first, through the RWB-E1-039 interface that the service already calls, with the user, the time, the filters and the row count; an entry that cannot be written returns 503 with MSG-P7-003 and no file. The row count is checked against caselist.export.maxrows, 10,000 at release, and a larger result is refused with 422 and MSG-P3-021 naming the limit. The file carries no customer personal field.

RWB-TE-001.1: A developer does this by hand, once. Create the back end folder ace-service/src/main/java/<ACE base package>/recovery/ and inside it one package for each of the 19 Workbench modules: dataengine, integration, casewf, access, dochub, comms, decision, payments, reporting and agent for P1 to P10, then valuation, treatment, guarantee, litigation, asset, debtsale, writeoff, deviation and partner for S1 to S9. Each module package holds two child packages. The api package holds the interfaces that other modules are allowed to call. The internal package holds the rest, which only that module may use. Add a package-info file to each one, and create the front end folder src/modules/recovery as well. Every later recovery story places its code inside these folders.
RWB-TE-001.2: You write one file by hand at architecture/recovery-modules.yaml. For each of the 19 modules it gives the module code, its Java package, the packages that count as published, and the client libraries that module is allowed to use. A published package is one that other modules may import. The api package is published for every module, and a story that publishes from a different package, for example recovery.casewf.allocation or recovery.decision.writer, lists that package here too. The boundary test reads this file rather than holding module names in test code, so adding or renaming a module is a change to the file. The TechX tech leads own the file through code owners.
RWB-TE-001.3: You write one back end test class using ArchUnit, a library that checks dependencies between compiled classes as an ordinary unit test. It builds five rules from the module map, which it loads through ModuleMapLoader. BND-1 lets a recovery class reach the collection module only through that module's published packages. BND-2 does the same for the common module. BND-3 lets one recovery module reach another only through a package the map lists as published for it, or through an application event. BND-4 keeps a module's entities and repositories inside that module. BND-5 limits HTTP, SFTP and file transfer clients to the packages the map allows. Write one test-only fixture class per rule that breaks it, kept under src/test.
RWB-TE-001.4: You add a dependency rule file for the front end folder src/modules/recovery, and the front end lint step applies it on every build. Two rules go in it. No file under src/modules/recovery imports anything from src/modules/collection. Imports from src/common go only through its public index file. Dependency rules work on import paths in the source, so this check needs no running application. Write a breaking fixture as well, a component under src/modules/recovery that imports a collection screen, and confirm the front end build fails with rule no-collection-import. That fixture stays in the test code and never ships.
RWB-TE-001.5: You write RecoveryAccessGuard and attach it to every path under /api/recovery/v1/. It offers one method, require(String capabilityArea, Right right, ScopeTarget target), which calls the common module's published access check, interface INT-34. When the caller's role lacks the right, the method throws AccessDeniedException, and the service turns that into a 403 Problem response with messageCode MSG-P4-002. For this story, add a test-only controller that declares Case record R so the guard can be exercised. TC-TE-001-08 calls that endpoint as role RW-REFADM and expects the refusal. The access check inside the common module belongs to the ACE team and is not yours to write.
RWB-TE-001.6: This happens on its own once the wiring is in place. The ACE build already runs the unit test phase on every pull request, so RecoveryBoundaryTest runs there with the other back end tests, and the dependency rules run in the front end lint step. Your work is the change to the pipeline definition that makes both checks part of the pull request build, so a failure blocks the merge. The same two checks also run on every build of main. Neither check keeps state, so the answer depends only on the commit: the same commit always gives the same result, and a rerun after a failure needs no cleanup first.
RWB-TE-001.7: The test decides the build result, so no person judges it. When a rule is broken, the pipeline marks the pull request check as failed. RWB-TE-004.5: The job runs these checks on every file of the extract, automatically. CTL-02 is the set of load checks used for every load: the business date of the file, its structure, its control totals and its keys. A loan_account file with 28,118 rows against a manifest of 28,119 is refused in full with MSG-P1-002 and the check text Control totals loan_account 28,118 against 28,119. A refusal at any check leaves the copy already in the environment in use. Balances, dates and keys are never masked, which is what makes these totals comparable.
RWB-TE-004.6: MaskingVerifier runs inside the job and reuses the verifier built in RWB-E1-065, so you wire it in instead of writing the patterns again. It reads the is_personal tag of each field from sys_fields, field DF-REF-105, and scans every column that carries the tag for values that still look personal: a 13-digit number with a valid Thai national ID check digit, a Thai mobile number, or an email address. One hit refuses the whole load with MSG-P1-002 and a check text naming the table and the column, for example unmasked value in party.id_no_token. RWB-TE-004.7: The job loads the files into the staging schema recovery_next in the target environment, then checks that every foreign key resolves. A foreign key is a column whose value has to exist as a key in another table, for example a case_party row that points at a party row, so this check proves the rows still fit together after masking. Once every check has passed, the job makes the staging schema live in one step, renaming recovery_next to recovery. RWB-TE-006.1: The calling service does this in code. No person is involved. Each business service with something to send calls OutboxWriter.publish from inside the transaction that saves its own change. A transaction is one unit of database work that either commits in full or is undone in full, and publish joins the caller's transaction instead of opening its own. The caller passes the event type, which is an event name from EV-01 to EV-28 or an outbound work request type such as WIN_DISPATCH, the schema version, the case ID, which may be empty, a payload of references and codes only, the actor reference and an idempotency key. publish gives back the event ID and throws DuplicateOutboxKeyException when that key already exists.
RWB-TE-006.2: Automatic, inside the caller's transaction. OutboxWriter inserts one outbox_event row with the event type, schema version, case ID, case sequence, idempotency key, payload, actor reference and occurred time. case_seq is the case's highest sequence plus 1, taken under a lock on the case's latest outbox row so two writers cannot claim the same number. OutboxWriter then asks ConsumerCatalog which consumers take that event type and inserts one outbox_delivery row for each, with status PENDING and attempt count 0. Your work is the Flyway migration for the two tables with UNIQUE on idempotency_key, UNIQUE on case_id and case_seq, UNIQUE on event_id and consumer, the status CHECK, and the partial index on next_attempt_at for open deliveries.
RWB-TE-006.3: The database does this at commit time, with no code of yours running at that moment. Because publish joined the caller's transaction, the business change, the outbox_event row and every outbox_delivery row reach the database in one commit. When the business work fails after publish and the transaction is rolled back, no event and no delivery exist for that item, so the sender has nothing to send. To hold that guarantee, keep publish out of a separate transaction and out of any after-commit hook, which is what BR1 asks for: no event without the change, and no change without the event. Test a commit and a rollback, which is build step 2 of section 13.
RWB-TE-006.4: A Quartz job does this, not a person. JOB-11 already runs every minute for outbound files, and this story adds an event step beside that one. OutboxRepository selects outbox_delivery rows whose status is PENDING or RETRYING and whose next_attempt_at is at or before now, up to the batch size of 200 per run. The select takes a row lock and skips rows another instance already holds, so two running instances share the work and no delivery is picked up twice. Rows are ordered by case sequence, oldest first, and only the lowest open sequence per case and consumer is taken. That ordering keeps events for one case reaching each consumer in the order they were written, and holds later events back while an earlier one is failing.
RWB-TE-006.5: Automatic. For each locked delivery, OutboxSender calls OutboxConsumer.consume on the consumer named in the row and passes an EventHeader with the event ID, the idempotency key, the schema version, the occurred time and the actor, together with the payload. The consumer answers OK or FAILED with a code. Delivery is at least once, so the same call can arrive twice, for example after an instance stops part way. Each consumer therefore calls IdempotencyGuard.firstTime with its own consumer name and the key, and acts only when the answer is true, meaning it has not handled that key before. The consumers themselves belong to other stories, so build a stub consumer that fails on demand for the tests.
RWB-TE-006.6: Automatic, inside the sender. On an OK answer, set the outbox_delivery row to DELIVERED, fill delivered_at and leave attempt_count at the number of attempts made. Then check two things: whether this delivery had already failed at least once, and whether the consumer list marks the consumer as holding the case step, which means the case was paused while waiting for it. When both hold, call CaseEvents.raise for the case with event code RETRY_SUCCEEDED, and R-UNI-35 returns the case from RETRY_QUEUE to the state it paused in. For a consumer that does not hold the case step, such as ledger or reporting-feed, mark the delivery and leave the case route state alone.
RWB-TE-006.7: Automatic. On a FAILED answer, add one to attempt_count, keep the code in last_error_code, set the status to RETRYING and work out next_attempt_at from the retry settings that ConsumerCatalog reads from rwb.integration.outbox.retry, which hold 3 retries at 1, 5 and 15 minutes after the previous attempt. Read those delays for each attempt rather than once at service start, because a change in the configuration service has to apply to the next attempt. On the first failure of this delivery, and only for a consumer that holds the case step, call CaseEvents.raise with SYSTEM_UNAVAILABLE, which moves the case to RETRY_QUEUE by R-UNI-33 so the person waiting on that case can see why it stopped.
RWB-TE-006.8: Automatic, after the last retry fails. Set the delivery to EXCEPTION, then call TaskApi.raiseTask for the case with task code RESOLVE_OUTBOX_DELIVERY and the owner role named for that consumer, and keep the task ID it returns in task_id. For a consumer that holds the case step, also raise RETRY_LIMIT_REACHED, which moves the case to EXCEPTION_QUEUE by R-UNI-36 and writes the decision log entry through the P7 writer. Wrap all of it in one transaction. When the decision log write fails, everything is undone: the delivery stays RETRYING for the next run, MSG-P7-003 goes to the job log, and R-UNI-39 raises an incident. An event with no case gets EXCEPTION and an alert, with no task and no case event.
RWB-TE-006.9: A person does this, the platform administrator, once the consumer behind the failures works again. Build OutboxAdminController with both endpoints. The GET takes status, consumer, eventType, from, to, page and size, returns a page of OutboxDelivery items without the payload, and needs Platform administration right R. The POST needs right U, sets the delivery to PENDING with attempt count 0 and due at the next run, answers 200 with MSG-GEN-005, and is written to the ACE audit log with the user and the time. A delivery that is not in EXCEPTION is refused with 409 and MSG-P2-022, which also covers a second call on a delivery already set back to PENDING. A delivery that cannot be found gives 404.

RWB-TE-007.1: No person triggers the daily runs. Build DailyJobTrigger as a listener on two signals: LoadCompleted (EV-26), which JOB-01 publishes with the business date when the COLLINS load passes its checks, and the completion of JOB-02 case creation for that same date. When both have happened for business date D, it schedules JOB-03 Morning allocation and JOB-04 Daily reconciliation for D on the Quartz scheduler. The date is passed into the job, because a job body never works out its own business date from the clock (section 17). JOB-03 has to finish by 07:00. JOB-01 and JOB-02 belong to P1 and are out of scope here, so treat them as signals you listen for.
RWB-TE-007.2: Automatic and time-based. RecoveryJobRegistry schedules JOB-05 Timer check with the cron expression 0 0/5 * * * ? in the Asia/Bangkok zone. A cron expression is a schedule written as fields for second, minute, hour, day, month and weekday, and this one fires at second 0 of every fifth minute. Take the expression from jobs.timer-check.cron in the configuration service rather than writing it into the code. The idempotency key of JOB-05 is its fire time slot rather than a business date. Its misfire instruction is to do nothing, so a fire missed while the service was down is never repeated, and the next run picks up the timers that are due by then.
RWB-TE-007.3: The scheduler does this, with no code of yours running at the moment of locking. The ACE service runs on more than one instance, and all of them share one Quartz job store in PostgreSQL with isClustered set to true. The job store hands each fire to a single instance, so the same job does not run twice. BusinessDateJobRunner carries @DisallowConcurrentExecution, which holds back a second run of the same job while one is still going, and requestsRecovery, which lets another instance pick the job up when the instance running it stops. That pair gives AC4, where a JOB-05 run of 7 minutes delays the 10:05 fire, and AC8, where ACE-2 takes over inside the 20 second check-in interval.
RWB-TE-007.4: Automatic, as the first check inside BusinessDateJobRunner. Call JobRunRecorder.lastSucceeded with the job ID and the business date. When it answers with a run, do no work: write a SKIPPED entry to the P1 job run log and return. This is what makes a repeated fire for a date that already succeeded harmless, so JOB-03 allocates no case a second time. The job bodies are also idempotent for their business date (BR8), meaning a second run for the same date leaves the same result, and this check keeps them from being called at all. The job run log belongs to the P1 job monitor of RWB-E1-056 and is reached only through JobRunRecorder, never by reading its tables.
RWB-TE-007.5: Automatic, as the second check. Each BusinessDateJob names its dependencies through dependsOn, for example JOB-02 for JOB-03. The runner asks JobRunRecorder.lastSucceeded for each named job ID and the same business date. When one of them has not succeeded, write the run as WAITING with MSG-P3-031 naming the job that is missing, and stop without calling the body. Nothing retries from inside the runner. The run happens later, when the dependency succeeds for that date and DailyJobTrigger fires the job again, which is what AC7 asks for after JOB-02 succeeds at 08:10. The platform administrator can also start a WAITING run through POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/jobs/{jobId}/rerun.
RWB-TE-007.6: Automatic. Call JobRunRecorder.start with the job ID, the business date and the instance name, keep the run ID it gives back, then call run with that business date on the BusinessDateJob. The body itself comes from another story: allocation from RWB-E1-020, reconciliation from RWB-E1-011 and the timer check from RWB-E1-028. Whatever the outcome, call JobRunRecorder.finish with the run ID, the status SUCCEEDED or FAILED, and the counts the body produced. Put the finish call in a finally block, so a failure is recorded rather than lost. Those entries are what the platform administrator reads on SCR-44 with the business date and status. Logs carry job IDs, dates and counts, with no personal data.
RWB-TE-007.7: Automatic at service start, in CatchUpOnStart. Find every business date whose COLLINS load passed and that has no successful run of JOB-03 or JOB-04, then run the job for each of those dates in date order, oldest first, so an outage of three days gives three runs one after another. The number of dates is capped by jobs.catch-up.max-dates, which is 5 in the configuration service. When more dates than that are missing, start no automatic run and send an alert with MSG-P3-031 naming the job and the dates, which leaves the decision to the platform administrator. Pass each date into the job body, because the body takes the date it is given.
RWB-TE-007.8: Automatic, and separate from the allocation job. DeadlineWatcher is its own Quartz job on a cron at 07:00 Asia/Bangkok, with the time taken from jobs.allocation.deadline in the configuration service. It asks JobRunRecorder.lastSucceeded for JOB-03 and the current business date. When there is no successful run, it sends an alert with MSG-P3-031 naming JOB-03, the date and 07:00 to the operations channel through the alert route of RWB-E1-056, and that alert has to arrive within 15 minutes, so by 07:15. The watcher only reports. It does not start JOB-03 itself and it does not change any run status.
RWB-TE-007.9: A person does this. The platform administrator opens SCR-44 Interface and job monitor, in its Running, Failed and Complete states, and reads each run of JOB-03, JOB-04 and JOB-05 with its business date and status. The screen reads GET /api/recovery/v1/admin/jobs, which gives back id, type, businessDate, status, startedAt, endedAt and checks, and needs Platform administration right R. A rerun calls POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/jobs/{jobId}/rerun with right U and runs the job again for its own business date when that run is FAILED or WAITING. A run that already succeeded answers 409 with MSG-GEN-004 and runs nothing. A role without the right is refused with 403 and MSG-P4-002, and a run that cannot be found gives 404.

RWB-TE-008.1: Quartz is the job scheduler added to the ACE service in RWB-TE-007, and it starts this run with no person involved. Add JOB-14 to it using the cron expression 0 0 2 * * ? in the Asia/Bangkok time zone. A cron expression is the schedule text the scheduler reads to work out the next fire time. Mark the job DisallowConcurrentExecution so that only one run is active at a time. Take the start time from the parameter rwb.decision.chaincheck.start rather than writing 02:00 into the code. Each firing works on the business date of the previous day, because those are the entries the check covers, so pass that date into the job and keep it on the run record.
RWB-TE-008.2: The job makes this check itself, with no operator involved. JOB-13 is the nightly decision log copy, scheduled at 01:00 in RWB-E1-014, and the check has to run after it for the same business date. Build code that looks up the JOB-13 run for that date and sees whether it has ended. When it has not, sleep and look again every five minutes, up to the latest start held in rwb.decision.chaincheck.latest-start, which is 04:00. At 04:00 begin the check anyway and write a note on the run record that JOB-13 had not ended. When JOB-13 ends earlier, start at that moment and keep its end time. Use a clock you can replace in tests, because AC6 needs fixed times.
RWB-TE-008.3: The job reads this value on its own at the moment it begins. chain_seq is the running sequence number on each decision log entry, and the log only grows, since RWB-E1-008 blocks updates and deletes in the database. Query the highest chain_seq once, hold it in the run, and treat it as the last entry of this run. Every entry written after that point falls outside the run and is covered the following night. Reading the end point once keeps the result stable: the count of entries checked, the last chain_seq and the last entry_hash all match the same fixed end, even while the service keeps appending entries during the time the run takes.
RWB-TE-008.4: The job calls HashChainVerifier, which already exists from RWB-E1-008. The hash chain works like this: each entry carries entry_hash, computed from the canonical form of its own fields, and prev_hash, which holds the entry_hash of the entry before it. Recompute entry_hash for every entry and compare prev_hash with the hash you computed for the preceding one. Any difference means the entry changed after it was written. Read the entries in chain_seq order through the unique index on that column, in groups of 1,000 taken from rwb.decision.chaincheck.batch-size, so that millions of entries do not load into memory at once. Use the same canonical form implementation as the store, never a second copy.
RWB-TE-008.5: The verifier from RWB-E1-008 stops at the first problem, so extend it for this job. Keep going after a failing entry, count every entry whose entry_hash or prev_hash does not match, and hold the chain_seq and entry ID of the lowest failing one as the first break. AC7 shows what this gives: with chain_seq 12,001 and 40,350 both changed, the first break is 12,001 and the failing count is 2, and one report names both entry IDs. The counting happens inside the run with no person involved. Do not repair anything and do not write to decision_log_entry; the job only reads and reports.
RWB-TE-008.6: JobRunRecorder writes this through the scheduler interface built in RWB-TE-007, automatically at the end of the run. The record goes to the ACE job run record in the Job schema, not to a recovery table. Fill type JOB-14, the business date, status, startedAt and endedAt, and the checks block: entriesChecked, lastSeq, lastHash, result, breakSeq, breakEntryId and failingCount. Result is INTACT or BROKEN, and status is COMPLETED or FAILED. A failed run still writes what it reached, as AC3 shows with 20,000 entries checked. These records are what GET /api/recovery/v1/admin/jobs lists for the job monitor, so internal audit and the platform administrator can read any night's result.
RWB-TE-008.7: ChainCheckReporter sends this on its own as the run ends, through the ACE notification path to the Compliance and PDPA officer group. Build it with the three messages of section 14. On an intact chain send MSG-P7-007 with the entry count and the last hash. On a break send MSG-P7-008 with the entry ID, and raise an incident at the same time; the security administrator receives that incident with Compliance. An empty log counts as intact, with count 0 and the genesis hash, so MSG-P7-007 goes out. When the run is a rerun, mark the report as a rerun. Each message needs Thai text as well as English, following DL10.
RWB-TE-008.8: This path runs by itself when the run cannot finish, for example when the database connection is lost part way. Catch the error, write the run record with status FAILED and the entries checked so far, alert the platform administrator group, and send MSG-P7-013 to Compliance with the date the chain was last confirmed. That last date comes from earlier run records, so your query has to find the most recent completed run. A failed run is never resumed from the point where it stopped. Compliance learns the same night that the check did not complete, which is why this message names the last confirmed date in place of a result.
RWB-TE-008.9: A person does this. The platform administrator, holding RW-PLATADM, calls POST /api/recovery/v1/admin/jobs/{jobId}/rerun from the job monitor, which needs Platform administration U. Internal audit may read the run records and may not rerun, so a caller without that right gets 403 with MSG-P4-002. The rerun starts again from chain_seq 1 and writes a second run record for the same business date with rerun true, leaving the first record in place. Business date plus run number is the key, so the history shows both attempts. Return 409 with MSG-GEN-004 when a run is already active, and keep the scheduler guard so that no scheduled start begins while the rerun works.

RWB-TE-009.1: Either the pipeline starts this or a person does. Add a performance stage to the release pipeline that runs in SIT before the UAT exit, so that a build reaches the gate without anyone asking. Also allow a squad member holding RW-TRIBE to start the same stage by hand, which is how a run happens outside a release. The build under test must already be deployed to SIT with the feature flags planned for the release, and an SIT slot must be booked, so the stage works against a known deployment. This is a pipeline stage, so it gets no entry in the job list and no Quartz schedule. The harness code sits in perf/recovery and does not ship inside the service.
RWB-TE-009.2: The harness takes the lock itself at the start of a run. Build RunLock so that only one run is active in SIT at a time: the second caller is refused with run already in progress, while the first run carries on. The reason is shared data; two loads at once on the same masked copy would make both sets of numbers meaningless. Give each run its own run ID. Release the lock when the run ends, and release it after 90 minutes at most, so a run that stops part way does not block SIT; that run is marked failed. The limit matters because a full run is 10 ramp minutes plus 60 steady minutes.
RWB-TE-009.3: DataVolumeCheck does this automatically before any load. Call GET /api/recovery/v1/cases and count the open cases in SIT. When the count is below 23,600, refuse the run and write data volume below the test base with the count found and the base, as AC4 shows with 9,800 of 23,600. The check exists because response times depend on data volume; a screen that is fast on a small set can be slow on the real one. RWB-TE-004 loads the masked copy that holds at least 23,600 open cases, so a low count means the SIT data was not loaded or was reduced. No load starts and nothing else is reported.
RWB-TE-009.4: The harness signs in by itself, using the named SIT test users listed per role in its configuration, with Entra ID groups per DL40. The mix covers RW-CASEOWN, RW-TEAMMGR, RW-LITOFF and RW-PHONECOL, and each simulated user calls the API with the rights of its own role. That matters for the expected refusal: a RW-PHONECOL user calling postCasesCaseidTransfer gets 403 with MSG-P4-002, which the run counts as expected. Hold the sign-in tokens for the length of the run so that sign-in work does not appear in the measured steady period. Read the user list from configuration rather than writing names into the load script.
RWB-TE-009.5: The harness drives this load with no person watching. Build BusiestHourSimulation to raise the number of virtual users to 410 across 10 minutes, then hold that level for 60 minutes with each user making 3 requests a minute. A virtual user is a simulated session the script drives, and it represents one of the 370 staff and 50 partner users online in the busiest hour. Pick each request from the weights in the mix file, so with MIX-2026.12 about 30 percent are getCases and 15 percent are getCasesCaseidTimeline. The steady hour is the part that gets measured, and the ramp only brings the load up to that level. Read the user count, rate, durations and weights from configuration.
RWB-TE-009.6: The harness records every request as it runs. Store the operation name, the response time in milliseconds and the HTTP status of each call, with the run ID and the mix file version. Treat status 403 as expected when the mix file marks that operation as a refusal for that role, so the planned refusal of postCasesCaseidTransfer for RW-PHONECOL does not count toward the error rate. That refusal still has to answer inside the 2 second target, which is what the access test proves. Keep the ramp requests apart from the steady ones, because the percentiles and the error rate are computed on the 60 steady minutes only. Hold operation names and numbers, with no personal data.
RWB-TE-009.7: The harness computes these numbers after the steady period, with no person involved. For each of the 7 operations in the mix, work out the 50th, 95th and 99th percentile response time, the throughput and the error rate. A percentile is the time that a share of requests came in under: a 95th percentile of 1,800 ms means 95 of every 100 calls answered within 1,800 ms. Compute them for each operation on its own, because one slow operation would otherwise hide behind six fast ones. Use only the 60 steady minutes. At 410 users and 3 requests a minute that is about 73,800 requests, which is the sample the report and the gate work from.
RWB-TE-009.8: PerformanceGate decides this in code, with no human judgment. It passes when every operation's 95th percentile is below 2,000 ms and the error rate over the steady period is below 1 percent. Both limits are exclusive: 2,000 ms exactly fails and 1,999 ms passes, and 740 errors in 74,000 requests is 1.0 percent and fails. A failing gate fails the release stage, and the report names the operation with its 95th percentile and the limit. Read both limits from the harness configuration so that they can change without code. Write this component first and test it against result fixtures, which are saved result files in place of live runs, so the boundary cases are quick to prove.
RWB-TE-009.9: ReportPublisher does this at the end of the run. Attach the report to the release record with the build ID and the mix file version, so that the release team can see which configuration produced the numbers. A repeated run for the same build adds another report and leaves the earlier one in place, and the gate result for that build comes from the latest run, as AC6 shows with a failed run at 10:00 and a passing run at 14:00. Then release the SIT lock so that another run may start, and trigger the reload of the masked copy, because the run wrote interaction rows through postCasesCaseidInteractions and SIT has to go back to a known set.

RWB-TE-010.1: The pipeline starts this on its own, in two places. Add a browser stage that runs after the front end build on each pull request, so that a developer gets the result before merge, and schedule the same stage nightly against SIT. No person starts it in normal work, though a squad member holding RW-TRIBE may run it. The tests live in ace-web/e2e/recovery in TypeScript with their configuration in ace-web/e2e/recovery/config, and they do not ship inside the service, so there is no feature flag. The stage holds no state of its own, which is why a rerun is the same stage run again. The runner needs a test deployment with the synthetic data set of RWB-E1-065 and test users per role.
RWB-TE-010.2: BrowserGuard does this check first, automatically, before any test. browsers.json is the configuration file that lists the browser names and versions under test: Chrome N, Chrome N-1, Edge N and Edge N-1, where N is the current major version in the runner image. Read that file and confirm each listed browser is present in the image. When one is missing, fail the stage at once with browser not available and the browser and version, as AC5 shows for Chrome N-1. A missing browser is always a failure and is never skipped, because a silent skip would let a screen ship untested on a browser the bank supports. Keep the version list in the file, never in the test code.
RWB-TE-010.3: The runner signs in by itself, with no person at the keyboard. screens.json gives the roles for each screen, and the runner uses the SIT test user of each of those roles: RW-CASEOWN, RW-TEAMMGR, RW-PLATADM and RW-PHONECOL. Each user sees the screens with its own rights, which is what makes the refusal test real: a RW-PHONECOL user opening SCR-05 sees MSG-P4-002 and no Save control at all. Build the sign-in as a reusable step the suite calls for each role and each browser, since every browser session needs its own sign-in. Take the user list from configuration rather than writing names into the tests.
RWB-TE-010.4: The runner opens the screens and drives them automatically. Build ScreenSuite to work through the six main screens of screens.json, SCR-02, SCR-03, SCR-04, SCR-05, SCR-07 and SCR-09, and for each one through every state listed for it, for example SCR-03 in Loading, Read only, Editable and On hold. Run each screen's functional test on all four browsers, so the suite covers six screens by their states by four browsers. A fault on one browser alone still fails the stage, and the report names the screen, the browser version and the failed check, as AC3 shows for SCR-02 on Edge N-1. The states come from the configuration file, so adding a state needs no new test code.
RWB-TE-010.5: AccessibilityScan runs this without a person looking at the screen. For every screen and every one of its states, run the scan engine twice, once with the English labels and once with the Thai ones, and select the rule tags for WCAG 2.1 level A and level AA. WCAG 2.1 AA is the accessibility level the bank's screens have to meet, and a rule tag is how the scan engine groups its checks, so selecting those tags runs the checks that belong to that level. Any violation gives the screen, the state, the language, the rule and the element, for example rule button-name on SCR-02 in state List. Both languages are needed because Thai text changes layout and label length.
RWB-TE-010.6: KeyboardCheck runs this automatically as part of the stage. For each primary action named in screens.json, prove that the action can be reached with the Tab key, that it can be used from the keyboard, and that the focus is visible when it is reached. Focus is the browser's mark of the control that keyboard input reaches, and a user with no mouse depends on seeing it. A failure fails the stage with keyboard access, the screen and the action, as AC8 shows for Save on SCR-05. Build the check to walk the tab order rather than clicking, since a control that answers only a mouse click can pass a functional test and still block a keyboard user.
RWB-TE-010.7: The runner applies the exception list itself, with no review during the run. a11y-exceptions.json holds each excused violation with the screen, the rule, an owner, an expiry date and a reason. For every violation the scan reports, look for an entry matching that screen and rule. When the entry exists and its expiry date is still ahead of the run date, the violation does not fail the stage. When the expiry has passed, the violation fails the stage and the report says exception expired with the screen, the rule and the date, as AC6 shows for color-contrast on SCR-07 in a run on 4 January 2027. Reject any file entry that has no owner or no expiry date.
RWB-TE-010.8: The runner handles the retry on its own. When a functional test fails, run that one test a second time. A test that passes on the second run goes into the flaky list of the stage report with its screen and name, for example the SCR-04 filter test. Flaky means the test gives a different result on the same code, which usually comes from a timing problem in the test rather than a defect in the screen. Only one retry is allowed, so a test that fails twice is a real failure. Build the retry around the single failing test rather than the whole suite, and keep the flaky list in ReportWriter so that the squad can see which tests need fixing.
RWB-TE-010.9: The pipeline does this, with no person deciding. Fail the stage when any WCAG 2.1 A or AA violation remains after the exception list is applied, when any functional test fails on any browser, or when a listed browser is missing from the runner image. Attach the report either way, covering each screen, state, language and browser with its functional result, its violations with rule and element, the keyboard result and the flaky list. A failed stage blocks the merge of the pull request, which is the reason the stage runs before merge. Developers read that report in the pipeline, so name the screen, the state, the language and the element in plain text.

RWB-TE-011.1: No person types this list by hand. The build reads it, through the PersonalFieldReader service you write under tools/pdpa-lint. It takes two sources: the is_personal column of the sys_fields metadata seed in the schema, and the x-personal-data: true marking in the API specification. A seed here is a file of starting rows for a table, and this story adds no database access, so the lint opens the file itself. Rule BR1 says the personal field list is never written inside the lint, so when Compliance marks a new field in the dictionary the next build picks it up with no code change.
RWB-TE-011.2: The build generates the rules, and nobody edits the generated file by hand. Write RuleGenerator, which turns each personal field name into the forms a developer would really write in code: the snake case name from the schema, the Java getter, the camel case property used in JSON and TypeScript, and the class name of an entity that holds such a field. It writes them to pdpa-rules.yaml, which carries the six rules listed in section 12: PDPA-LOG-FIELD, PDPA-LOG-ENTITY, PDPA-EXCEPTION, PDPA-TOSTRING, PDPA-FIXTURE-FIELD and PDPA-FIXTURE-ID. Generating the file on every run is what makes scenario AC5 work. When contract_no is marked personal, the next build already has a rule for contract_no and for getContractNo.
RWB-TE-011.3: The scan runs on its own in the pipeline. Your work is the Java and TypeScript rules of build step 2 in section 13. They read the back end source under src/main and the front end source, and they look at every place that writes text out: a logger call, a string joined together inside a logger call, and the message given to an exception. A finding is raised when such a place uses a personal field, as in party.getFirstName() for AC1 and console.log(party.lastName) for AC7, or passes a whole personal entity object, as in a PartyEntity for AC2. An exception message built with getCifNo() is rule PDPA-EXCEPTION in AC9.
RWB-TE-011.4: This scan is also automatic. Write the fixture rules and the CheckDigitMatcher service. They read src/test, the end-to-end tests, the SQL seed files and the JSON fixtures. Two kinds of finding come out. First, a literal sitting in a personal field position that does not begin with the synthetic prefix SYN-, so last_name set to TESTNAME fails and last_name set to SYN-LAST-0001 passes, as AC4 shows. Second, a value anywhere that looks like real contact or identity data: a Thai national identifier whose check digit is valid, a Thai mobile number, or an email address outside the example domains. A check digit is an extra digit computed from the other digits, which lets the lint test a number for validity instead of counting its length.
RWB-TE-011.5: A rule does this for you at build time. The text form of an entity is the string the class returns when it is printed, usually from its toString method, and anything in it reaches a log line as soon as the object is printed. The rule reads each entity class that holds a personal field and checks the field is left out of that text form. When ContactPointEntity keeps value_token in its text form, the build fails with rule PDPA-TOSTRING and names value_token, which is scenario AC10 and rule BR5. Removing the field from the text form is the fix, and the masking helper remains the way to print a value when a log line has to name a record.
RWB-TE-011.6: The comparison is automatic, and the entries behind it are written by people. Each finding is matched against pdpa-allow.yaml, where an entry carries the rule, the path, a line or pattern, an owner, a reason and an expiry date. Only an entry whose expiry date has not passed excuses a finding. With an entry for PDPA-FIXTURE-FIELD that expires on 30 November 2026, a run on 1 December 2026 fails and prints allow entry expired with the rule, the path and the date, as AC6 and section 14 set out. Adding or changing an entry needs a pull request approved by the TechX tech leads as code owners. The repository host refuses the merge when someone else approves it.
RWB-TE-011.7: The pipeline does this, on every pull request and every build of main. Write PdpaLintStep and add it to the pull request pipeline. One finding is enough to fail the build, and the output gives the rule, the file, the line and the field name in the form of section 14: the rule, then file and line, then the personal field used, then the advice to remove it or use the masking helper. The value found is never printed, which is rule BR7. The step keeps no state of its own, so the same commit with the same dictionary gives the same findings every time, and a failed run can be repeated by starting the pipeline again.

RWB-TE-012.1: A person starts this. The platform administrator applies the infrastructure template for one environment, and you write that template in the ACE infrastructure folder, in the format the ACE team already uses. It sets the storage account: shared key access off, public network access off, TLS 1.2 as the lowest version, and a private endpoint, which is the network route that keeps the account reachable only from inside the bank network. It then creates four containers, rwb-intake, rwb-docs, rwb-docs-legal and rwb-quarantine. A container is a named space inside a storage account that holds files, called blobs. Build step 1 of section 13 asks you to apply the template in DEV and SIT.
RWB-TE-012.2: The same template carries these settings, so they apply when it runs and nobody switches them on later. For rwb-docs it turns on blob versioning, which keeps the earlier blob readable after an overwrite, and soft delete, which keeps a deleted blob restorable for the softDeleteDays parameter of 30. For rwb-docs-legal it sets a time-based immutability policy of the legalRetentionDays parameter, 3,650 days, which makes the storage service refuse any overwrite or delete inside that period. The policy is locked in PROD and unlocked in DEV, SIT and UAT so test files can be removed. It then assigns the Storage Blob Data Contributor role: the ACE service identity on rwb-intake, rwb-docs and rwb-docs-legal, and SY-OCR on rwb-intake, rwb-docs and rwb-quarantine, and nothing else, as AC5 checks.
RWB-TE-012.3: This runs by itself when the service starts. Build StorageReadinessIndicator and join it to the ACE health endpoint, as build step 5 says. A readiness check is the answer a module gives the platform about whether it can take work. This one asks the storage account two questions: do the four containers exist, and does rwb-docs-legal carry its immutability policy. The document hub reports ready only when both answers are yes, which is rule BR5. When the policy is missing in DEV, AC9 expects the document hub to report not ready and to name rwb-docs-legal, an upload to POST /api/recovery/v1/cases/{caseId}/documents to return 503 with MSG-GEN-006, and no document row to be written.
RWB-TE-012.4: The document store of RWB-E1-024 writes the file, so this happens in code and not by hand. It goes through BlobStorageAdapter with a managed identity, which is an identity the platform gives the service so that no key or password is held in code or configuration. Your part in this story is the published DocumentContainers interface and DocumentContainersConfig, which builds the container clients with DefaultAzureCredential limited to managed identity and with the 10 second timeout, reading the account URL and the four container names from the properties listed in section 13. A write-once document type goes to rwb-docs-legal and any other type to rwb-docs. The blob name is {caseId}/{documentId}/v{docVersion}, and storage_ref holds the container in front of it.
RWB-TE-012.5: The storage service refuses the write or the delete, because the immutability policy is enforced inside the account. Any client meets that refusal, including one using the ACE service identity. Your work is StorageErrorMapper: it turns BlobImmutableDueToPolicy and conflicts on rwb-docs-legal into WriteOnceViolationException, turns a timeout into StorageUnavailableException, and writes the audit event for the refused overwrite or delete with the identity and the time, as AC1 expects. The document store turns that exception into 409 with MSG-P5-002, which tells the user that legal documents cannot be changed and that a new version should be added. The stored blob keeps its hash, so DOC-0701 in AC1 is unchanged after the attempt.
RWB-TE-012.6: The document store does this in code. Because the write-once policy protects a name that already holds a blob, a changed document is written as a new blob at the next version number, v{n+1}, and the earlier blob stays readable. AC3 shows v1 and v2 of DOC-0701 both readable in rwb-docs-legal. Build ContentHashGuard for the case where the same name is written again: it compares the SHA-256 hash of the file with the hash of the blob already there, returns the existing blob reference when they match, and raises WriteOnceViolationException when the content differs, which is rule BR7 and scenario AC12. The doc_version field gives the number used in the blob name.
RWB-TE-012.7: A person reads this. The platform administrator opens SCR-44 Interface and job monitor and sees whether the document hub is ready. No screen is built here, and the monitor itself belongs to another story. What this story owes it is the readiness value from step 3, published through the ACE health endpoint, with rwb-docs-legal named when its policy is missing. The platform administrator also applies the template and holds Platform administration CRUD. The security administrator is the second person involved: build step 6 asks you to run the SIT tests, including the role listing of AC5, and hand the list of assignments over for review, which is part of the done when.

RWB-TE-013.1: The calling module does this before it reaches your code. A case step such as the case workflow, running under its own service identity SY-CASEWF, works out its own answer first and packs it into a rule result: the rule ID, the rule version and the next state the case should move to. The RuleResult record in section 12 is that package, with ruleId, ruleVersion, toState and the result itself as JSON. Rule BR1 fixes this order, because the rule answer has to exist before the agent is asked anything, and it stays the applied answer in both SHADOW and L1 mode. Your work in this step is publishing the record so callers can build it.
RWB-TE-013.2: The calling module makes this call, and your job is the thing it calls. Write AgentStepClient in the package recovery.agent.api with the single method runStep, together with the records AgentStepRequest, RuleResult and AgentStepOutcome exactly as section 12 lists them. The request carries the agent code, the case ID, the decision code, the step key, the rule result and the inputs. A published interface is the one type other modules are allowed to depend on, and build step 1 asks for an ArchUnit test that proves other modules import only recovery.agent.api. The method can throw DecisionNotRecordedException, so a caller has to handle a failed decision log write.
RWB-TE-013.3: The client does this by itself, inside AgentStepClientImpl. Build AutonomyModeResolver, which reads the agent policy in force for that agent and that date and takes autonomy_mode, status and valid_from from agent_policy, together with timeout_seconds. The autonomy mode says how far the agent answer may be used. When the mode is OFF, or the feature flag rwb.agent.client is off, the client makes no orchestrator call and creates no agent run row, applies the rule result, sets fallback false, and the decision log entry holds agent version null, which is scenario AC8. When no approved policy exists on the business date, the rule result is applied with fallback true and reason NO_POLICY.
RWB-TE-013.4: The client makes this call on its own. Build the timed call with a CompletableFuture and the timeout from the policy, 60 seconds in the approved policy, and pass AgentOrchestrator.run an idempotency key built from the step key. Idempotent means that repeating the same call with the same key produces one run and returns the first outcome, so a step that arrives twice does not start a second agent run or write a second decision log entry, which is rule BR5 and scenario AC7. The client waits no longer than the timeout, and build step 3 asks you to test this with a stub that sleeps 61 seconds on a fake clock.
RWB-TE-013.5: The client decides this with no person involved. Shadow mode means the agent runs beside the live path and its answer is recorded only, with no effect on the case. The applied result stays the rule result, the agent answer is stored on the agent run, and the outcome handed back to the calling step carries the rule result and no agent output, as AC1 requires. The decision log entry for that step holds the agent version in the form INTAKE@P1/PR1, the rule ID and version, recommendation null and fallback false in its actions. The mapping in section 12 sets recommendation to null outside L1 mode, so your mapper has to read the mode before it fills that field.
RWB-TE-013.6: The client does this automatically, and a person acts on the result afterwards. In L1 mode the applied result is still the rule result, so nothing in the case moves on the agent answer. The outcome returns the checked agent answer in its recommendation field, which is the JSON the person who decides reads before making the call. The decision log entry holds that answer in recommendation together with its confidence, 0.91 in scenario AC3. The guardrails of this story say the client never applies an agent answer as the case result in SHADOW or L1, so your code keeps the applied result path and the recommendation path apart.
RWB-TE-013.7: The client handles this on its own. Two causes lead here: the agent does not answer inside timeout_seconds, and the answer fails a guardrail check. In both cases the client keeps the rule result as the applied result, sets fallback true, and carries the reason, TIMED_OUT for the timeout in AC2 and the check code such as SCHEMA in AC4. The step continues to the next state the rule asked for, so the case is not held up by an agent. The agent run holds status TIMED_OUT and fallback true. Rule R-UNI-32 is the source of this behavior, and the fallback rate is the measure for the story, with a target below 10 percent per month.
RWB-TE-013.8: The client writes the entry itself, through the P7 interface and never straight into the table. Build DecisionLogMapper to fill the entry from section 12: case ID, decision code, rule ID and version from the rule result, agent version as agent, policy and prompt joined, model version from the run, the reference to the masked inputs snapshot, the recommendation, the final call from the rule result next state, and the actions holding the agent run ID, the mode, the fallback and its reason. DecisionLogWriter throws when the write fails. After the write, AgentRunRepository sets agent_run.decision_log_id. That column is added by migration V10_002__agent_run_decision_link.sql, a numbered SQL file the pipeline applies to the schema.
RWB-TE-013.9: The calling module waits, which is the point of the order in rule BR3: the entry is written first, the step acts second. When the write succeeds, the step moves the case on the applied result, which is always the rule result in this story. When DecisionLogWriter throws, the client raises DecisionNotRecordedException carrying MSG-P7-003, so the user reads that the action was not taken because the decision could not be recorded and can try again in a few minutes. The step takes no action, case RW-2026-000201 keeps its state in AC6, an incident is raised under R-UNI-39, and agent_run.decision_log_id is left empty.

RWB-E1-001.story: Recovery data sits in many places today. It sits in the core bank, EFS, LIT, CCMS, SVAF, AMIS and team spreadsheets. No single target table exists. No one person owns each set of data. The team creates the recovery tables in the ACE database. The team also creates a data dictionary held as table rows. It also creates a catalog of the 14 data products DP01 to DP14. Each data product then names one system of record and one owner. It works when the database build script runs clean in DEV and SIT. The dictionary must match every column, and the catalog must hold 14 rows.

ac.AC1: This checks the database build script. The pipeline runs it in DEV first and then in SIT. After each run the schema must hold all 44 tables. That means the 41 data product tables, the two dictionary tables and the catalog table. The test also counts the columns of loan_account. It compares every field with the dictionary rows, without fixing a total that a later decision could change. If a table or a column is missing, every later load has no place to write its data. The dictionary also stops matching the database.
ac.AC2: This checks that a developer can look up one field and get its full description. The query goes to v_data_dictionary, which is a view. A view is a saved query that reads other tables and looks like a table itself. For the field days_past_due in loan_account, the answer must carry the field ID and both types. It must also carry the source system and source field, the data product, its refresh cycle and its owner. Developers need this to map a source system field to the right column. Without it each team guesses and the loads disagree.
ac.AC3: This checks a good catalog load file with 14 rows, one per data product. After the load the catalog table holds 14 rows for the valid-from date. Each row names exactly one system of record and one owner user ID. The date here is a test value. One system of record per data product means one place to ask when a number looks wrong. One owner means one person answers for it. The test does not assert which system each product names, because the product-to-source mapping is confirmed separately by the data steward.
ac.AC4: This test breaks the build script on purpose. One statement that creates a table is made to fail. The whole script runs in one transaction. That means all of its changes count as one piece of work. Either every change holds or none does. So the schema must end with none of these tables. The pipeline must fail and name the statement that broke. A half built schema is the risk. Later loads would write into some tables and fail on others. Nobody could then tell which parts were created.
ac.AC5: This checks the test that compares the database with the dictionary. The check runs in both directions. A branch adds a column to loan_account with no dictionary row, so the test must fail and name that column. A dictionary row whose column type no longer matches must also fail, with both types in the message. The column name here is test data. Without this check the dictionary slowly stops matching the database. Anyone reading it then gets the wrong types and the wrong source fields.
ac.AC6: This checks what happens when the pipeline runs the same build script again on a schema that already has it. Flyway keeps a list of the script versions it has applied, so it reports version 1.001 as already applied and changes nothing. The dictionary row counts stay the same before and after. Work that can be repeated with no further effect is called idempotent. Deployments are repeated often. Without this, the second run would try to create tables that already exist, fail the pipeline, or write the dictionary rows twice.
ac.AC7: This checks a catalog load file with two faults: one row names two systems of record, and another row names no owner. The whole file must be refused with MSG-P1-003 naming both rows. The catalog must keep the rows of the version already in use. The product codes here are test values. Accepting part of a file would leave some data products with two places to ask and some with nobody to ask. Refusing the whole file lets the loader fix it and load it again.
ac.AC8: This checks a catalog file that holds only 13 rows, with no row for DP09. The system must refuse the whole file with MSG-P1-004. It must also name the product that is missing. No row at all may be written. The row count and the product code here are test values. The catalog must always hold all 14 data products. A load for a product with no catalog row has no owner and no system of record. Naming the missing product tells the loader what to add.
ac.AC9: This checks two values that sit outside the lists allowed for them. One row names an owner role that is not a real role code. Another row names a refresh cycle that is not one of the four allowed values. The system must refuse the whole file with MSG-P1-007. The message must name the row number, the column and the allowed values. The role and cycle values here are test data. Free text in these columns would break every later read of the catalog. The reading code expects only the agreed values.
ac.AC10: This checks what happens when the same catalog file is loaded a second time. The system compares the file content with the version already in use. It does this with a hash. A hash is a short value worked out from the content. Two files with the same content give the same hash. Nothing is written. The answer carries MSG-P1-011, which says the load is already done. Loads get repeated after a slow answer or a lost connection. Without this check the second load would write the same rows again.

RWB-E1-010.story: This story now covers creation only. It builds the tracker row table, the file reader, the upload and sign-off endpoints and the sign-off service. File loads and validation are deferred.

ac.AC1: The migration creates tracker_row and adds the tracker, load-run and sign-off columns and the file hash key.
ac.AC2: The file store and reader are created, and the upload and sign-off endpoints are registered.
ac.AC3: TrackerSignOffService exposes the separation-of-duty, team-scope and count checks.

RWB-E1-020.story: New recovery cases are allocated from team spreadsheets today. Ownership is agreed by email, so a case can wait days with nobody working it. The team builds the morning allocation job. For each new case it reads the allocation rule table. It places the case in the queue the matching row names. It then picks an owner from that queue by the queue's own method and caseload cap. Every allocation is written to the decision log with the rule row and the rule version. It works when every new case has a queue and an owner before 07:00 the next morning.

ac.AC1: This checks the rule match. A new test case carries a product group, a region and an exposure band. The job reads the allocation rows in force. It takes the first row, in row order, whose values match the case. One row matches on product group and region and accepts any exposure band. The case goes to the queue that row names and takes that queue's team. The case numbers and codes here are test data. Placement by rule removes the team spreadsheets and keeps the queue out of one person's head.
ac.AC2: This checks how the owner is picked. The test queue uses round robin. Round robin gives the next case to the owner after the one who got the last case. The job works around the list in turn. The last owner was U-02, so the case goes to U-03. U-03 holds 140 open cases and is under the cap of 150. The case then moves to assigned. An assignment row records the reason and the rule row. These user codes and counts are test data. One owner from the first day is the point of the story.
ac.AC3: This checks the caseload cap. The cap is the largest number of open cases one owner may hold in a queue. The owner next in turn already holds 150 open cases, which equals the cap. That owner is skipped, and the case goes to the next owner under the cap. These counts are test values. Without the cap, round robin would keep giving work to a person who is already full. That work would sit untouched while another owner in the same queue has room for it.
ac.AC4: This checks a queue where nobody has room. All three test owners hold 150 open cases, so no owner can take the case. The case goes to the queue's overflow queue, keeps the status new, and gets no owner. The team manager then gets a summary that counts the cases waiting there. These counts are test values. A full team is a real condition, and the case must still be visible to someone. The summary is how the team manager learns that work is waiting and that the team needs help.
ac.AC5: This checks a case that no allocation row covers. The test case has a product group and a region that match no row. The case goes to the exception queue and keeps the status new. A decision log entry records the gap with the values that found no row. The system also publishes an event saying the allocation failed, and the summary counts the case. Those codes are test data. A case that matches no row must never be dropped in silence. The logged gap tells the analyst which row the rule table still needs.
ac.AC6: This checks the decision log entry that goes with each allocation. One entry per case records the rule row, the rule table version, the queue, the owner and the values used. The entry is written inside the same transaction as the case change. A transaction is a group of changes that either all hold or all fail together. So when the log write fails, the test case stays new with no queue. The job record carries the message for that case. An allocation nobody can explain is then never made.
ac.AC7: This checks a case that already carries an open deviation. A deviation means something about the case sits outside the normal rules. A specialist must look at it first. The test case goes to the deviation handler queue named by its own rule. No case owner is set, and the status stays new. Giving such a case to a regular owner would start normal work on a case that first needs a decision. Sending these cases to one queue also keeps them together where the specialist can see them.
ac.AC8: This checks a second run of the job for the same business date. A case already allocated that day keeps its owner and its one assignment row. No second decision log entry is written. The job record counts the case as skipped. The date here is test data. Reruns happen after a failure, and a person may start one from the job monitor. Without the skip, a case would be given to a second owner. The decision log would then hold two entries for one day.
ac.AC9: This checks an empty run. No case has the status new on the test business date. The job reads nothing and finishes. Each team's summary reports zero in overflow and zero in the exception queue. A run with no work must still finish and still report. On a quiet day a silent job tells the team manager nothing. A day with no new cases would then look the same as a job that never ran. A real failure would go unnoticed.
ac.AC10: This checks the order of the jobs. Case creation has not finished for the test business date, because the load from the source system was refused. The allocation job must then not start, even after its usual time. The job monitor shows it waiting on the earlier job, and every new case keeps no queue and no owner. Running on half created cases would allocate part of the day's work and leave the rest. Nobody could then tell which cases the job had seen.
ac.AC11: This checks two runs working at the same moment. The first run holds a lock on the case row. A lock means it has reserved that row, so another worker cannot change it. The second run skips the locked case. The case ends with exactly one assignment row and one decision log entry for the date. Two workers on one case would give it two owners, and the later write would quietly undo the earlier one. The lock also lets a rerun start safely while the first run is still going.
ac.AC12: This checks the edge of the cap. The owner next in turn holds 149 open cases against a cap of 150, which is one below. So this owner may still take the case, and ends the run holding 150. These counts are test values. The rule is that an owner at or above the cap is skipped. So 149 must pass and 150 must not. A test at the edge catches code that compares the wrong way round. Such code skips an owner with room, or loads an owner who is full.
ac.AC13: This checks a queue whose owners are all full and which names no overflow queue. The case goes to the exception queue with a reason that says there was no overflow queue. The status stays new. The queue code here is test data. Not every queue will have an overflow queue set, especially while the queue data is still being filled. Without this path the case would have nowhere to go and the job would fail. One missing setting would then stop the whole morning run.
