RWB-E1-029.story: Collection and recovery rules sit in procedure documents today, so the system cannot apply them. Audit found the procedure not followed. The team builds the rule load. It has one spreadsheet template for the five rule tables, with checks that run on load. It also has an approval by Risk, a start date, and a rollback in one call. The checks cover the columns and values, rows that overlap, rows that can never match, and a missing default row. They also cover 50 test cases and a dry run against open cases. It works when a rule version loads, is approved, takes effect on its date, and rolls back by one call.

ac.AC1: This checks the whole good path in one test. A template for the allocation table holds 26 rows and 50 test cases and passes every check. The analyst loads it with a start date. A second person with the Risk role approves it. The version is then in force from that date. The change log holds the author, the approver, both times, the test result and the dry run counts. These labels and counts are test values. A rule change that moves from a file to production this way needs no code release.
ac.AC2: This checks the overlap test. Two rows sit at the same row order. Both match the same product group and region. So for one case the system could not say which row wins. The whole load is refused. The message names the check and both row IDs. The version already in force stays in force. The row IDs here are test data. Two rows that both match would make the result depend on the order the rows happen to be read. One case could then be allocated differently on two days.
ac.AC3: This checks the 50 test cases the analyst supplies with the rows. Each test case names a case and the queue it should reach. Two test cases expect one queue, and the new rows send them to another queue. The whole load is refused, and both failing test case IDs are named. These IDs are test data. The test cases are how the analyst says what the change is meant to do. Running them on load catches a row that was typed wrong, before the new rules reach live cases.
ac.AC4: This checks the rollback. Version 7 is in force and version 6 was in force before it. One call rolls back version 7, and version 6 is in force again. The change log records who rolled back, the time and the reason. A case allocated while version 7 was in force keeps that version label on its decision log entry. These labels are test values. A bad rule version can be undone in one step instead of a release. Old cases keep the version they were decided under, so their records stay true.
ac.AC5: This checks the column and value test. One row holds an assignment reason that is not one of the allowed values for that column. The whole load is refused, and the message names the check, the row number and the column. The value here is test data. These columns may only hold values from an agreed list, because the engines that read the rows expect those values. A free text value would load without complaint and fail later. It fails when a real case reaches that row and the engine cannot read it.
ac.AC6: This checks for a row that can never match. An earlier row covers one product group in any region, and a later row covers the same product group in one region. Because the first matching row wins, the later row is never reached. The load is refused and the row that can never match is named. The row IDs here are test data. Such a row is a sign the analyst meant something else, usually that the two rows are in the wrong order. Refusing the load makes them fix the order first.
ac.AC7: This checks that the allocation table ends with a row that matches every case. The test rows have no such row, so the load is refused. A default row is what keeps a case from falling through the table with no result. Without it, a case with a new product group or region would match nothing. It would then have to be handled by hand in the exception queue. Asking for the default row on load means the analyst finds the gap, before a case waits with no queue.
ac.AC8: This checks separation of duty on the approval. The person who prepared a change may not approve it. The analyst who loaded the version tries to approve it and is refused. The version stays loaded and does not take effect. Risk has to sign a rule change, because these rules decide how cases are treated and how much money is written off. One person loading and approving their own rows would let a change reach production with nobody else reading it.
ac.AC9: This checks rollback on a table that has only one version. There is nothing to go back to, so the call is refused with a message that says so. The single version stays in force. The table and version label here are test data. Rolling back with nothing behind it would leave the table with no rows at all. Every engine that reads it would then stop. Refusing the call and saying why tells the analyst to load a corrected version instead.
ac.AC10: This checks the version label. A label already loaded for a table cannot be loaded again. The second attempt is refused. The label here is test data. Each label has to point at one set of rows. The decision log on a case names the label it was decided under. If two different files could carry one label, nobody could say which rows applied to a case. The change log would also hold two loads with the same name.
ac.AC11: This checks the start date. The analyst loads a version with a start date that has already passed. The load is refused with a message about that date. The dates here are test values. A date in the past would mean the new rows applied to decisions already made under the old rows. Cases decided yesterday could then no longer be explained. A version starts today or later. That keeps every past decision tied to the rows that were in force at the time.
ac.AC12: This checks a template with no rows in it. The load is refused and the message names the missing rows. An empty file usually means the wrong sheet, the wrong file, or an export that failed. Accepting it would store a version with nothing in it. On its start date, every engine reading that table would find no rows and stop. Catching it at load time costs one message, and the analyst can send the right file straight away.

RWB-E1-043.story: The values that drive allocation, timers and approval limits live in team spreadsheets and procedure documents today. So nobody can say which value applied to a case on a given day. The team builds the reference data service. Each load of a reference table creates a numbered version with a start date, an author and a different approver. The service gives the engines the approved version that was in force on the business date. Each engine writes one log line naming the table and version it read. It works when a load, an approval and a dated change all hold for the 13 tables.

ac.AC1: This checks that two versions of one table can live side by side and that each business date gets the right one. An approved version 3 already exists with four rows. A new load adds a fifth row and is approved. That creates version 4 and closes version 3 on the day before version 4 starts. The service then answers with version 3 for the earlier date and version 4 for the later one. These codes and dates are test values. Old versions stay readable, so a case decided last week can still be explained.
ac.AC2: This checks that the person who loads a table cannot approve it. The same user loads 24 rows and then tries to approve the load, and the system refuses. The version stays at validated, which means it passed the checks but has no approval. The service keeps serving the previous version, even after the new start date arrives. The counts and codes here are test values. Approval limits are among the most sensitive values in the service. A second person has to read them before they take effect.
ac.AC3: This checks that the engines read their values from the service and say which version they used. Three tables have approved versions in force. The case service and the allocation engine start for a business date. Each one reads every table it needs from the service. Each one then writes one log line per table, with the table code, the version number and the date. The test also checks that no log line holds a party identifier. Those log lines are how a question about a past case gets an answer about the values that applied.
ac.AC4: This checks the column and type test on load. One row in the test file holds the word five where the column expects a number of days. The whole load is refused. The message names the row number and the column. No version and no rows are written. The row and column names here are test data. Refusing the whole file keeps a table from going half new and half old. A half old table would leave some service levels counted in days and one in text.
ac.AC5: This checks a version that was loaded and checked but never approved. Its start date arrives, and the service still answers with the earlier approved version. The unapproved version stays at validated and is never served. The table and dates here are test values. A start date on its own must not put values into use. The approval is what says a second person read them. A forgotten approval then shows up as values that did not change, rather than as values nobody signed.
ac.AC6: This checks the start date against the business date of the service. The load carries a start date one day before the current business date. It is refused, and no version is written. The dates here are test values. A start date in the past would change the values that applied to work already done. Cases decided this morning could no longer be explained. Keeping the start date today or later ties every case to the version in force when it was decided.
ac.AC7: This checks a repeated load of the same file for the same table and start date. The service works out a hash of the rows. A hash is a short value calculated from their content, so the same rows always give the same hash. On the second load it finds the same hash and returns the load it already has. No new version is created. Loads get repeated after a slow answer or a lost connection. Without this check the table would gain a second version holding the same rows.
ac.AC8: This checks two approvals of one version arriving at the same moment. Exactly one approval is recorded. The other is refused with the message that tells the user someone else changed the record. The user codes here are test data. Two approvals held at once could record two approvers. They could also leave the version with an approval time from one person and an approver from another. Writing one and refusing the other keeps one named approver per version, which is what the control asks for.
ac.AC9: This checks what an engine does when a table it needs has no approved version for the business date. The engine does not start its run, and an alert names the table and the date. The table code here is test data. An engine that carried on would use old values or no values and would decide cases on them. Nobody could see that from outside. Stopping and raising the alert turns a missing load into something the platform administrator fixes before the day's work runs.
ac.AC10: This checks a load file that holds only a header row and no data rows. The load is refused with a message that names the missing rows. No version is written. The table code here is test data. An empty file usually means the wrong sheet or an export that failed. Storing it would create a version with no rows. On its start date, every engine reading that table would find nothing and stop its run.

RWB-TE-001.story: Three teams build in one ACE service. Without a checked boundary, one team's change breaks another team's code. A direct call to a core system could also get around the agreed load path. The team creates the recovery folders and packages, each split into a published part and an internal part. It also adds a module map file naming every module and its published packages. A test in every build refuses a call into another module's internal part. It refuses a read of another module's tables. It also refuses an outside call from anywhere except the integration adapters. It works when the build fails on each of these and passes on a published call.

ac.AC1: This checks the first boundary rule with a class written to break it. The test class sits in the recovery code and imports a class from inside the collection module. The build must fail, and the build log must name the rule and both class names. The class names here are test classes, written to be refused. A rule that is only written down gets broken, usually by someone in a hurry. A failing build stops the call before it is merged, and naming both classes tells the developer what to change.
ac.AC2: This checks that the rule is not too wide. The same kind of test class calls an interface in the common module's published package. That call is allowed, so the build passes. Modules do have to work together, and the published package is the agreed way in. A check that only proves the build can fail is not enough. A rule written slightly too wide would block normal work. Developers would then start switching the check off or working around it.
ac.AC3: This checks the same rule between two recovery modules. A class in the integration module imports a repository from inside the decision module, and the build fails. The same class then imports that module's published writer interface instead, and the build passes. The class names here are test classes. Reaching into another module's internal classes ties the two together, so the owning team can no longer change its own code freely. The second half shows developers the way to fix such a call.
ac.AC4: This checks that each module reads and writes only its own tables. A class in the integration module uses an entity class from inside the case and workflow module. The build fails on that rule. An entity class is the code that maps one database table. Using another module's entity reads that module's tables around its published interface. A change to those tables then breaks code the owning team cannot see. The class names here are test classes, written to be refused.
ac.AC5: This checks that only the agreed packages may call outside systems. A class in the case and workflow module uses an HTTP client, and the build fails. An HTTP client is code that calls another system over the network. The same use inside the integration adapter package passes. A direct call from business code would get around the agreed load path. Data would then arrive with no load run, no checks and no record of where it came from. Keeping these clients in one place also keeps outside calls where they can be reviewed.
ac.AC6: This checks the same idea in the screen code. A recovery component imports a component from the collection screens. The front end build fails on its own rule. The folder names here are test files. The front end needs the check as much as the back end. A shared import ties the two sets of screens together. The collection team could then not change their own screen without breaking a recovery one. The check runs in the same pull request as the back end rules.
ac.AC7: This checks the module map itself. A new package is added that the map does not list. The build fails with a message naming that package. The package name here is a test value. The boundary rules are built from the map. A package the map does not name would be covered by no rule at all. Anyone could then put code there. Failing the build makes a new package a decision the tech leads approve in the map.

RWB-TE-011.story: Names, identifier tokens, dates of birth, contact values and case summaries are personal data under Thai law. A log line that prints a party puts that data where the masking rules do not reach. A test file copied from a real record does the same. The team builds a lint step in the pipeline. A lint is a check that reads source files and reports faults without running the program. It reads the personal fields from the data dictionary. It then fails the build when code, test files, log lines or error messages carry them. It works when each rule fails its own test file and prints no value.

ac.AC1: This checks a log line that prints a personal field. The test class logs a party's first name, which the dictionary marks as personal. The build must fail. The log must name the rule, the file, the line and the field, without printing the value it found. The class name here is a test class. Log stores are read by more people than the screens are, and the masking rules do not apply to them. A logged name then sits outside every control that protects it.
ac.AC2: This checks a log line that prints a whole object instead of one field. The object is a party record, which holds several personal fields, so the build fails on its own rule. Printing an object usually prints all of its fields at once. That is the easiest way to put a full customer record in a log. The rule that looks for field names would miss this, because no field name appears in the code. The object type here is a test class.
ac.AC3: This checks test data that looks like a real Thai national identifier. The lint tests the 13 digits with the check digit rule. That rule is a calculation the last digit of a real number has to satisfy. A test file whose identifier token passes that calculation fails the build. The test itself makes the number when it runs. It is never taken from a record. A test file holding a real identifier would spread personal data into the repository and the build output. It would also reach any prompt a coding tool is given.
ac.AC4: This checks that values in personal fields in test data carry the agreed prefix. A seed file sets a last name to a plain word with no prefix and fails the build. The same file with the prefix passes. The prefix makes made up data easy to tell apart from real data. It works both for a person reading the file and for this check. Without it, nobody can say whether a name in a test file was invented or copied from a customer record.
ac.AC5: This checks that the rules follow the dictionary. Compliance marks one more field as personal in a new version of the dictionary. The build makes its rule set again from that list. A log line that passed before now fails, because it prints the newly marked field. The field name here is test data. The list of personal fields changes over time, and a list copied into the lint would soon be out of date. Reading it from the dictionary means one change by Compliance reaches every rule at once.
ac.AC6: This checks the allow list, which holds the few findings the tech leads agreed to let through. Each entry carries an owner, a reason and an end date. The test entry ended on 30 November, and the build runs on 1 December. So the finding fails the build again, and the log says the entry has expired. These dates are test values. An end date keeps the allow list from growing into a list of faults nobody ever fixes. That is how a check like this quietly stops working.
ac.AC7: This checks the screen code as well as the back end. A recovery component writes a party's last name to the browser console. The build fails on the same rule as a back end log line. The folder name here is a test file. Browser output is collected by front end logging tools in the same way. A name written there leaves the bank, the same as one in a server log. The field name is spelled differently in screen code, so the rules cover both spellings.
ac.AC8: This checks the one allowed way to name a record in a log. The log line writes the contact point through the masking helper. That helper is shared code that hides most of a value before it is printed. The lint passes that line. Some log lines do have to name the record they are about, or support cannot follow what happened. With no allowed path, developers would meet a check they cannot satisfy. They would ask for allow list entries instead, which is worse for the same data.
ac.AC9: This check covers error messages as well as log lines. The test code builds a message by joining text to a customer identifier and then throws it. The build fails and names the field. Error messages reach more places than logs. They reach the pipeline output, support tickets and sometimes the screen. A developer who removes a field from a log line can easily leave the same field in the message beside it. So the check has to cover both. The identifier here is a test class.
ac.AC10: This checks the text form of a class that holds a personal field. The text form is the short text a class returns when something prints it. The test class includes a contact value in its text form, and the build fails. This is what makes printing a whole object dangerous. So the check closes it at the class instead of at each log line. One class fixed this way protects every log line, error message and debug output that ever prints it.

RWB-E1-002.story: Each recovery team keeps its own list of accounts today. The lists do not agree with each other, and they do not agree with ALS. The team builds one case list for each working day. A batch step reads the open cases, joins them to the account data, and writes one row for each case and account. It then writes an extract file to the data lake, and Power BI shows the list at 07:30. It works when the row count at 90 days past due or more matches the ALS count. The ten columns also appear on the report.

ac.AC1: This checks the daily count check. The test data holds 28,140 accounts at 90 days past due or more. The case module left 21 of them out when it created cases, so the count to match from ALS is 28,119. The open cases also hold 37 accounts below 90 days past due. The table therefore holds 28,156 rows, and only the rows at 90 days past due or more are compared with ALS. Without this check, accounts can be missing from the list and no one would see it.
ac.AC2: This checks the content of each row and of the report. The ten columns must appear in the order the story gives. Each row also carries the team, the business date and the refresh time. The example case RW-2026-000123 is test data, with a test account number, balance and days past due. The test confirms those values arrive in the right columns. The report must also offer filters on team, queue and product. If a column is missing or out of order, teams cannot read the file and the report the same way.
ac.AC3: This checks the two times carried with the data. The run for business date 30 November 2026 finishes at 07:12 on 1 December 2026. Every row carries that time. The report shows both times: when the list was refreshed, and which day the data covers. A team manager needs both. A list built from old account data looks current when only the refresh time is shown. The team then plans work on old numbers.
ac.AC4: This checks what happens when the count does not match. The tolerance parameter is 0.00 percent, so any difference fails. In the test data the case list holds 28,094 accounts at 90 days past due or more. The ALS count is 28,119, a difference of 25 accounts, or 0.09 percent. The list is still built and published, and the COUNT check is marked FAIL. The data steward and the team managers receive a message. The teams keep working, and they know the list is short before they trust it.
ac.AC5: This checks the step when today's account data has not arrived. The INT-01 load brings the account and arrears data. When that load is not COMPLETED for the business date, the step does not run. It writes no rows for that date. The earlier extract file stays in the data lake. So the teams still have the list from the previous working day in the test data. The run is recorded as REFUSED, and the team managers are told the data is old. A list built from missing account data would show wrong balances and wrong days past due.
ac.AC6: This checks the step when the morning allocation job has not finished. JOB-03 sets the owner and the queue on each case. The step waits until 07:15, which is a parameter. It then builds the list with the owners and queues that exist at that time. The run records the allocation check as NO, and the report warns that owners and queues may be incomplete. The list reaches the teams on time, and a manager who sees an empty owner knows why.
ac.AC7: This checks a repeated run for the same business date. The step deletes the rows of that date and writes them again in one transaction. A transaction is one piece of work that either finishes in full or leaves the data as it was. The row count stays at 28,156 in the test data, and no case and account pair appears twice. Only the refresh time changes. Without this, a second run would double the rows. Every count and every total on the report would then be wrong.
ac.AC8: This checks a failure in the middle of the run. CaseQueryApi is the published interface that the case module offers for reading open cases. In the test it raises an error after 12,000 accounts are read. The step then writes no rows for the business date. The run is marked FAILED, and the rows of the earlier date are left as they were. A platform administrator can run it again. A half-written list is worse than no new list, because the teams cannot tell which part is missing.
ac.AC9: This checks the hand-off of the extract file to the data lake. The outbound file adapter tries the transfer and, in this test, fails every retry. The run is still marked COMPLETED, because the rows were written, and the publish check is set to NO. The failed transfer goes to the exception queue with a task for the platform administrator, so one person owns the problem. Without that task, the rows would exist in the database while Power BI still showed the list from the day before.
ac.AC10: This checks a case whose account has no row in the account table. The test uses account ACC0000456, which is test data. The row is still written to the case list, with an empty total balance and empty days past due. The case therefore stays visible to its team. The system also writes one data quality exception row with check code CL-01 and the account number. The gap can then be chased. Dropping the row instead would hide the case from the team that owns it.

RWB-E1-011.story: No one can say today whether the teams' lists cover every account at 90 days past due. Missing accounts are found late. The team builds a daily step that compares the case list with ALS for each product. The compare is by account count and by balance. It lists every account that does not match. It holds the publishing of the case list when a product is outside the tolerance. It writes the results and the data quality failures to one Power BI report. It works when the report shows each product as green, red or not run. A product with a difference holds the publish.

ac.AC1: This checks a day when everything matches. The test data holds 12,256 mortgage, 12,960 hire purchase and 2,903 SSME accounts at 90 days past due or more. That count is taken after the accounts left out at entry are removed. The case list holds the same counts and the same balance sums. The step writes six result rows, one count check and one balance check for each of the three products. Each result row has variance 0 and result PASS. The case list is then released for publishing, and all three products show green on the report.
ac.AC2: This checks a day when one product does not match. The case list holds 2,891 SSME accounts against 2,903 in ALS. That is a difference of 12 accounts, 0.41 percent. The SSME count result is marked BREAK. The system writes one data quality exception row for each of the 12 account numbers. The data steward can then see which accounts are missing. The system holds the publishing of the case list for that date, so the data lake keeps the earlier list. It alerts the data steward, the platform administrator and the team managers. Teams then never work from a list known to be short.
ac.AC3: This checks the edge of the tolerance. A reference load changes the tolerance for the count check to 0.10 percent from 30 November 2026. A mortgage difference of exactly 0.10 percent passes, and an SSME difference of 0.11 percent breaks. The rule is that a result breaks only when the difference is above the tolerance. A value equal to the tolerance still passes. The parameter and the comparison must be read the same way every day. Otherwise the same number would pass one day and fail the next.
ac.AC4: This checks the step when today's account data has not arrived. The INT-01 load for the business date is late and not COMPLETED, so no comparison can be made. The step writes no result rows and holds the publishing of the case list for that date. The report shows every product as not run, with the reason. A reader then sees that the check did not happen. A green or empty report would look like a day with no difference, and a short case list would be published.
ac.AC5: This checks the path after a fix. The SSME count result broke and the publishing was held. The case module has since created the 12 missing cases, and the case list has been built again. The platform administrator runs the step again for the same date. The step replaces the six results for that date, and all six pass. It sets the 12 exception rows to CLEARED with the date they were cleared. It then releases the case list for publishing. A day that has been fixed must be able to publish without waiting for the next morning.
ac.AC6: This checks two runs of the same job for the same date starting on two servers at once. The result table allows only one row for each check, product and date, so both runs together leave six rows in all. This is what idempotent means here: running the step twice gives the same result as running it once. Double rows would double the counts on the report and could show a difference where there is none.

RWB-E1-021.story: Cases change hands between the TDR, litigation, NPA and debt sale teams by email today. A case can wait between teams with nobody holding it. The team builds a transfer engine with a rule table. When one of eight events arrives, the engine takes the first matching rule row. It picks an owner in the target queue, ends the old assignment and writes the new one. A team manager can transfer a case by hand with a coded reason. Every transfer is written to the decision log with the rule row and its version. It works when each of the eight events moves a case.

ac.AC1: This checks a transfer made by rule, with no person asking for it. Test case RW-2026-000301 sits in a TDR queue with owner U-21. Rule row TRF-007 says a case goes to queue LIT-BKK-OFF when route R4 is approved. When the route decision arrives, the case moves. The engine picks U-31, because that member holds the fewest cases. The old assignment is given an end time. The new one carries the reason TRANSFER and the rule row ID. The decision log entry carries the row ID and the rule version. A later reader can see which rule moved the case.
ac.AC2: This checks a transfer asked for by a person. A team manager calls the transfer endpoint, which is a web address the system offers for one action. The call gives the test case number, the reason code MANUAL, the transfer reason R03 and the target owner U-22. The case owner becomes U-22. Both the new assignment and the decision log entry carry the reason R03. The coded reason lets a manager answer later why the work moved. Teams need this before the Epic 2 screens exist.
ac.AC3: This checks two transfers reaching the same case at the same time. The test case holds record version 7. The first transfer to be saved is kept. The second is refused, because the version it read is no longer current. The case ends in exactly one queue with one open assignment. The refused transfer is still written to the decision log, with the final call marked as rejected. Without the version check, two writes could leave a case in two queues. They could also leave it with two owners who each think the other holds it.
ac.AC5: This checks the two endpoints together. A team manager with the queue and allocation right moves the test case to owner U-23 with the transfer reason R04. A litigation officer with the case record right then places a legal hold with a reason and a court reference. The officer lifts it again. The case status goes to ON_HOLD and comes back to IN_PROGRESS, the status it paused in. Each of the three calls writes its own decision log entry with its reason. A hold must pause a case without losing where the case was.
ac.AC6: This checks a manual transfer sent with no transfer reason. The system refuses the call with code 422 and shows the message asking for a reason. Code 422 means the request was read and rejected because its content is incomplete. The case keeps its queue and its owner, so nothing is half done. The reason list is short and fixed, so every move can be counted later by reason. A transfer with no reason would leave a move that nobody can explain.
ac.AC7: This checks a transfer to an owner who is already full. The test owner U-24 holds 150 open cases, which is the caseload cap for the queue. The call is refused with code 422 and a message that names U-24. Nothing changes on the case. The manager can then pick another owner or the team queue. Without the check, a manager could push work onto a person who cannot take it. Those cases would then sit untouched with an owner's name on them.
ac.AC8: This checks a transfer of a case that is already closed. The test case has status CLOSED, and the call is refused with code 409. Code 409 means the request does not fit the current state of the case. Closed work must stay closed. A closed case given a new owner and a new queue would appear in queue counts and in a person's caseload. The team would then spend time on work that is already finished.
ac.AC9: This checks the rule that a transfer is never made unless it can be recorded. The decision log store is unavailable in this test. The manual transfer is refused with code 503, which means the service cannot answer now. The case keeps its queue and its owner. The log write is the last step before the change is saved, so the whole change is dropped when the write fails. A move with no log entry cannot be explained to audit later.
ac.AC10: This checks a legal hold stopping an automatic move. The test case has the legal hold flag set to true. A timer event arrives and matches a rule row, and the engine makes no move. The case keeps its queue and its owner. The skip is written to the job log with the rule that caused it. A case under a court or legal instruction must stay where the people handling that instruction expect it. Moving it could put the case with an owner who has no part in the legal work.
ac.AC11: This checks the same event arriving twice. The test event ID EVT-88120 already moved a case. When the same ID arrives again, the case still has one transfer for that event. The repeat is counted as an idempotency hit. Idempotent means that handling the same message twice gives the same result as handling it once. Message systems do deliver the same message more than once. Without this check, one missed payment could move a case twice and end the wrong assignment.
ac.AC12: This checks the case where the target queue has no room. Every member of queue LIT-BKK-OFF holds 150 open cases, which is the cap. The case is placed in the overflow queue LIT-BKK-OVF with no owner. The team manager is told how many cases are waiting there. The move still happens, so the case reaches the right team. Leaving the case in its old queue would hide it from the team that must work it. Nobody would know it is waiting.
ac.AC13: This checks a second legal hold on a case that is already on hold. The call is refused with code 409. The message says the move is not allowed from the current status. The first hold stays as it is. When the first hold is placed, the system saves the status the case paused in. A second hold could overwrite that saved status with ON_HOLD. The case would then never return to the status it was really in.
ac.AC14: This checks an event with no matching rule row. The document stored event arrives for the test case, and no transfer row matches it. The case keeps its queue and its owner. No decision log entry is written. Doing nothing is the right answer here, because no rule asked for a move. A log entry for an event that moved nothing would fill the decision log with entries that say nothing. Real moves would then be harder to find.

RWB-E1-030.story: Team managers rebalance work by hand today. They count queues from spreadsheets that do not match each other. The team builds a daily job, JOB-06. It assigns cases that have no owner. It takes the newest cases off any owner above the caseload cap. It then takes one snapshot of each queue: depth, cases with no owner, age, owner spread and service level breaches. The snapshot is published only when each queue depth equals the case count for the same queue at the same time. It works when the job logs an entry for each case it moves. The Power BI queue page must also show the snapshot.

ac.AC1: This checks the normal morning run. Queue TDR-BKK-CO holds 12 cases with no owner. Members U-61 and U-62 hold 140 and 144 open cases against a cap of 150. These are all test data. The job gives 8 cases to U-61 and 4 to U-62, which leaves both at 148. The queue uses the lowest load method. When two members hold the same number, the one listed first in the queue takes the case. Each new assignment carries the reason REBALANCE and has its own decision log entry.
ac.AC2: This checks that the queue numbers agree with the case list. The snapshot is taken at one moment, 06:52 in the test data. The depth of each queue must equal the case count for that queue at that same moment. Queue TDR-BKK-CO shows depth 296, no cases without an owner and an average age of 41 days. Managers compare their queue numbers with the case list every day. Two sets of numbers from the same system would send the teams back to counting from spreadsheets.
ac.AC3: This checks the alert when a case passes its service level. A service level is the time agreed for a step on a case. The timer check raises the breach for the test case. The team manager of TDR-BKK is told the queue and the count. The next snapshot shows one breach for that queue. The case itself does not move. The manager decides what to do with a late case. The count on the report lets the team see whether late work is growing.
ac.AC4: This checks a run where no member has room. Every member of queue TDR-BKK-CO holds 150 open cases, which is the cap. 5 cases have no owner. The job moves nothing, the 5 cases keep no owner, and the team manager is told the count of 5. The job does not break the cap to place the work. The manager can then add people or raise the cap. The 5 cases stay visible, and no one who is already full gets them.
ac.AC5: This checks a queue with no caseload cap loaded. Queue WO-BKK-CO has no cap, so the job cannot tell who is above it. It moves no case in that queue. The queue still appears in the snapshot with its numbers. Guessing a cap could move work onto people who cannot take it. Reporting the queue keeps it visible, so a missing cap shows as a gap in the reference data. The queue also does not disappear from the report.
ac.AC6: This checks one failed log write inside a run of many moves. Owner U-63 holds 153 open cases, so the 3 newest cases should move. The decision log write fails for the second of the three. That one case stays with U-63 and the other two move. The job record names the case that stayed, with the reason. The run carries on. One failure must not stop the whole morning rebalance. The case that did not move is named, so a person can deal with it.
ac.AC7: This checks running the job twice on the same day. The queues are already balanced from the first run. So the second run finds no owner above the cap and no case without an owner. It moves nothing and writes no decision log entry. The job can be run again safely after a failure. A job that moved cases on every run would change owners for no reason. The decision log would then fill with moves that no rule asked for.
ac.AC8: This checks cases that must not move. Owner U-64 holds 152 open cases, so 2 should move. The 2 newest have an open deviation. Those 2 stay with U-64, and the next 2 newest move instead. A case with an open deviation or a legal hold is being handled by a named person for a reason. Moving it would lose that work. The job still brings the owner back inside the cap, by taking the next cases in order.
ac.AC9: This checks what happens when the snapshot does not match the case list. For queue DIL-BKK-CO the snapshot depth is 88. The case count at the same moment is 87, a difference of one. The snapshot is not published, and the data steward is told which check failed. One wrong number is enough to hold the whole snapshot. The queue report and the case list must show the same figures. A report that is nearly right is still used, and the error is passed on.
ac.AC10: This checks the boundary at the cap. Owner U-65 holds exactly 150 open cases, which is the cap. No case is moved off U-65, because the rule only takes cases from an owner above the cap. An owner at the cap is inside the agreed load. Moving a case from an owner who is exactly at the cap would create work. It would change owners every morning for no gain.

RWB-E1-044.story: The recovery tables share one database with the collection module, and two squads change that database from one repository. A column added by hand in one environment makes SIT and UAT test a database that PROD does not have. The team makes every database change a migration: a numbered SQL file that the tool applies once and never again. There is one file per story, and no schema name is written inside the file. The pipeline checks the files, builds a clean database from them, and compares it with each environment. It works when a clean build and every environment hold the same objects.

ac.AC1: This checks that a migration is applied once only. The test file V12 carries a header line naming the story it belongs to. When the service is deployed, the file runs, and its version number and its checksum are written to the history table. A checksum is a number worked out from the content of the file, so any change to the file changes the number. A second deployment finds nothing pending and changes no object. Services restart often, and a file that ran twice could add a column twice or lose data.
ac.AC2: This checks for drift, which is a difference between the database the migration files produce and the database an environment really holds. A column named note_x was added by hand to the queue table in SIT. The pipeline builds a clean database from the files, compares the object lists, fails, and names the exact object. No deployment to SIT starts. Tests that pass against a hand-changed database say nothing about PROD, where that column does not exist.
ac.AC3: This checks that the schema name comes from a parameter. The same test file V13 runs in DEV and in SIT, with the parameter set to the same value. The timer table is created in that schema in both runs. The file itself is the same bytes in both runs. The name goes in through a placeholder. A placeholder is a marker in the file that the tool replaces with the real value when it runs. One file per change then serves every environment. A review of that file is a review for all of them.
ac.AC4: This checks the rule that an applied file is never edited. The test file V12 ran in SIT and its checksum was recorded. Someone then changes the file, so its checksum is different. The tool compares the two at the next start. It fails, names version 12, and the service does not start. The database already holds what the old file did. Letting the service start would leave the history saying one thing while the database holds another. The next change would then be built on a wrong picture of the structure.
ac.AC5: This checks the lint, which is an automatic check on the text of the files. The test file V14 has a create index statement with a schema name typed into it. The build fails and names the file and the line. A typed name works in the one environment where that name happens to be right and breaks everywhere else. Keeping the name out of the file is what lets the same file run in DEV, SIT, UAT and PROD.
ac.AC6: This checks the rule of one migration file per story. Two test files carry a header naming the same story. The lint fails the build and names both files and the story key. One file per story means a reviewer sees the whole database change for a story in one place. A story can also be traced from its key to the change it made. Two files for one story breaks that link. A file with no story key breaks it too.
ac.AC7: This checks that PROD only moves forward. The pipeline calls the tool's clean command, or an undo file is present in the folder. Both are refused, and no object in PROD changes. Clean removes every object in the schema, and an undo file reverses a change that has already run. A mistake in PROD is fixed by writing a new migration that puts it right. Clearing or reversing a live database would destroy recovery data that no file can rebuild.
ac.AC8: This checks a migration that fails part way. The second statement of the test file V17 names a table that does not exist. The first statement is rolled back, which means the database returns to the state it was in before the file started. The history records version 17 as failed, the service does not start, and the run shows as failed on the job monitor. A half-applied file would leave a structure that fits neither the old code nor the new code.
ac.AC9: This checks two service instances starting at the same moment with one migration pending. The tool takes a lock on the history table. One instance applies the file. The other waits, then finds nothing pending. Both instances start. Services run on more than one node, and they start together after a deployment. Without the lock, two instances could run the same file at once and leave the change half applied, or fail both starts.

RWB-TE-002.story: The recovery squad, the collection squad and the ACE team all merge into one repository. Without named owners for each folder, a change can be merged without the team that answers for it. That holds for the recovery module and for the shared common module. The team writes a code owners file that maps each folder to the team that must review it. It adds a pipeline check on that file. It asks for a rule on the main branch that blocks a merge until a code owner approves. It works when every merged pull request on a recovery folder carries an approval from a code owner.

ac.AC1: This checks that a change to a recovery file asks the right reviewers. A pull request changes a Java file inside the recovery folders. The repository asks a TechX recovery tech lead to review it. An approval from any other squad member leaves the merge blocked. The folder owners are the people who know what that code must do. If any approval counted as the required one, a change to recovery code could merge without the team that answers for it.
ac.AC2: This checks the shared folder. A pull request changes a file under the common module folder, which both squads and the ACE team use. The ACE team is asked to review it. The common module belongs to the ACE team. A change there can break the collection module as well as the recovery module. The team that carries that risk must see the change before it is merged.
ac.AC3: This checks a pull request that touches both modules. One changed file is in a recovery folder and one is in the common module folder. An approval from a TechX tech lead alone is not enough. The merge stays blocked until a member of the ACE team also approves. Each owning team sees the part it owns. A single approval for a change that crosses both modules would let one team decide for the other.
ac.AC4: This checks the folders that are easy to forget. One pull request changes a front end page, a migration file and the module map file. All three belong to the TechX recovery tech leads, so all three ask for the same reviewers. The front end, the database changes and the map of the modules are part of the recovery module. They matter as much as the Java code. Leaving any of them without an owner would let a change merge with no review.
ac.AC5: This checks that an author cannot approve their own pull request. A TechX tech lead opens a pull request on a recovery folder and approves it. The merge stays blocked until a second member of the team approves. The purpose of review is that someone other than the author reads the change. A self approval would make the rule easy to pass and would find nothing.
ac.AC6: This checks what happens after new work is pushed. A pull request on a recovery folder has been approved, and then a new commit is pushed to it. The approval is dismissed, and a code owner must review again. The approval was given for the code as it was at that time. Keeping it would let any amount of new, unreviewed code merge under an approval that was given for something else.
ac.AC7: This checks the code owners file itself. The file names a team that does not exist in the repository, because of a spelling mistake. The pipeline check fails and names the owner it could not find. A misspelled team is worse than no entry at all. The repository then asks nobody to review, and the merge is allowed. The check finds the mistake on the pull request that makes it, not months later.

RWB-TE-012.story: A notice or a contract held in a shared folder can be replaced with no trace. Audit findings record that the records behind decisions were incomplete. The team sets up four containers, which are folders in cloud storage that hold files. The four are intake, standard documents with version history, a write-once container for legal documents, and quarantine. The write-once container refuses every overwrite and delete inside its retention period. All four are reached only by managed identity, so a service proves who it is without a key or a password. It works when an overwrite of a legal document is refused and recorded.

ac.AC1: This checks the write-once rule. A test court notice is already stored in the legal container with a hash. A hash is a short value worked out from the content of a file. The same content always gives the same value. The service tries to overwrite the file, and storage refuses. The stored file is unchanged. The attempt is written to the audit log with the identity and the time. The document store turns the refusal into a 409 error for the caller. A legal document that can be replaced proves nothing later.
ac.AC2: This checks delete as well as overwrite. The same test court notice is in the legal container, and the service tries to delete it. Storage refuses, and the file is still readable. A rule that blocked only overwrites would leave an easy way around it. Someone could delete the file, then write a new one at the same name. Both paths must be closed for the retention period. A notice or a contract then stays as it was filed.
ac.AC3: This checks that the write-once container still accepts new files. A new version of the same test document is written at a new name ending v2, and the write succeeds. Both v1 and v2 can be read. Write-once protects the files that are already there, and it still allows new ones. Documents are replaced in real work, for example a corrected notice or a signed contract. The history is kept by adding versions, so a reader can see what was filed and when.
ac.AC4: This checks the standard container, which holds the documents that are not legal types. A file is overwritten in SIT. The version before the overwrite can still be read, because blob versioning keeps the earlier copies. A deleted file can be brought back within 30 days, because soft delete holds it for that long. Not every document needs the write-once rule. These two settings give a way back from a wrong upload or a wrong delete.
ac.AC5: This checks that each identity holds only the roles it needs. The template gives the ACE service identity write access on intake, standard and legal, and nothing on quarantine. It gives the OCR identity write access on intake, standard and quarantine, and nothing on legal. The test lists the assignments and compares them. A quarantine file may hold malware, and the legal container is the one place where files cannot be changed. Extra access on either would remove the reason for keeping them apart.
ac.AC6: This checks that keys cannot be used. Shared key access is turned off on the storage account. A client calling with the account key or with a shared access signature is refused. A shared access signature is a link that carries its own permission. Keys and links of that kind get copied into configuration files, scripts and messages. Anyone holding one has the access it carries. Managed identity can be given and taken away per container and per environment. It also leaves a record of who did what.
ac.AC7: This checks access by an identity that has no role on a container. The test identity has no role on the legal container and tries to read a document there. Storage refuses the read. Being inside the network is not enough. Being a known identity is not enough. Each read is checked against the roles given for that container. A new service added to the environment cannot read legal documents until someone grants it that access.
ac.AC8: This checks the network path. Public network access is turned off on the storage account, so a client calling from outside the private endpoint is refused. A private endpoint is a network address inside the bank's own network. Customer documents must not be reachable from the public internet, whatever the caller holds. This check and the identity checks work together: one closes the route, the other closes the access.
ac.AC9: This checks the readiness check made when the service starts. The immutability policy is removed from the legal container in DEV, and the service starts. The readiness check reports the document hub as not ready and names that container. An upload then returns 503, and no document row is written. Without this, the service would keep taking legal documents and write them to a container that allows overwrites. Those files would look protected on the screen while anyone with write access could replace them.
ac.AC10: This checks a storage account that does not answer. The adapter waits 10 seconds for a write to the standard container and then raises its unavailable error. The upload endpoint, which is the web address the user's upload is sent to, returns 503 to the caller. The timeout is short and fixed. A slow storage account cannot hold user requests open and use up the service's threads. The user gets a clear answer and can try again.
ac.AC11: This checks the quarantine container. A test file sits in quarantine, and the ACE service tries to read it for a case owner. The read is refused. Only the OCR identity can write there. A file in quarantine is one that failed the malware scan, or one that has not been scanned yet. Letting a user open it would pass a possibly harmful file to a person's computer. That is the one thing the quarantine container exists to prevent.
ac.AC12: This checks a repeated write of the same file to the same name. The guard reads the hash of the file already stored and compares it with the hash of the file being written. When the two match, no overwrite is attempted and the reference to the existing file is returned. When they differ, the write-once error is raised. A retry after a timeout or a dropped connection is common, and the caller cannot always tell whether the first write succeeded. A retry of the same content must be safe, and a different file at the same name must still be refused.

RWB-E1-003.story: This story now covers creation only. It builds the load tables, the check runner, the source mapper and the batch step classes. The full load and its validation are deferred until the COLLINS delivery is confirmed.

ac.AC1: The migration creates the four load tables and the keys that keep one active run per interface and date.
ac.AC2: The check runner exposes the seven DQ checks and the mapper exposes the listed transformations; both are Spring beans.
ac.AC3: The batch configuration defines the INT-01, INT-02 and run-closure steps in the right order.
ac.AC4: The four entities and their repositories map the four tables.

RWB-E1-012.story: This story now covers creation only. It builds the retirement columns, the retirement and report services and the two endpoints. Retirement execution and validation are deferred.

ac.AC1: The migration adds the four retirement columns and the mappedTo entry in the field list.
ac.AC2: TrackerRetirementService exposes the four checks and TrackerRetirementReportService builds the per-team report.
ac.AC3: The retire and retirement-report endpoints are registered, and the Tracker response carries the retirement fields.

RWB-E1-022.story: Access to recovery data is granted system by system today. The bank cannot show who could see a case on a given date. The team builds the sign-in path. The person signs in through Entra ID with a password and a second factor. The Workbench then turns their Entra ID groups into Workbench roles, a scope and the permission matrix version in force. The Workbench holds no password and no local account. It works when a test user for each Epic 1 administration role signs in. Each test user sees only the screens and actions their role allows.

ac.AC1: This is the normal sign-in. A test user sits in one Entra ID group and signs in with a password and a second factor. The Workbench builds a session. The session holds the role and the scope that limits which cases the person sees. It also holds the permission matrix version in force at that moment. The front end shows one line naming the role and scope. The menu holds only the areas the role can read, with no administration menu. The user ID and group name in the test are test data.
ac.AC2: A role with no letter in a permission area may take no action in that area. Here the test user holds only a phone collector role, which has no rights in platform administration. That user calls the admin roles endpoint. An endpoint is one web address the system answers on. The system answers 403, which means the caller is not allowed this action. It also writes one refusal event with the user, the area, the right asked for and the result. The refusal event is what lets the bank show later who tried what.
ac.AC3: A person can have a bank account in Entra ID and still hold no Workbench role. Here the test user is in no Workbench group. The Workbench refuses the session. It shows the access request page with a message telling them to ask their team manager. It returns no case, queue or reference data. Every Workbench web address answers 401 for that token, which means there is no valid session. A refusal event with the reason NO_ROLE is written. Showing a part-working screen with empty lists would make people think the system is broken.
ac.AC4: The sign-in token carries a claim that lists how the person proved who they are. Here that claim shows a password only and no second factor. The Workbench refuses the session with 401 and asks the person to sign in again with their second factor. A refusal event with the reason NO_MFA is written. The Workbench checks this itself and does not rely only on the bank policy. A policy change or a wrong setting in one environment would otherwise let password-only sign-in reach recovery data.
ac.AC5: A person can hold two roles at once. Here the test user is in two groups, so the session holds both roles. In each permission area the rights are added together. In the documents area one role allows create, read and update. The other allows those three and approve, so the session allows all four. No right comes from a role the user does not hold. Adding rights by hand, or picking the first role only, would block work the person may do. It could also allow work they may not do. That is why this is tested.
ac.AC6: Some role pairs may not be held by one person. Here the test user holds a security administrator role and a business role. The conflict table says the security administrator role may not be held with any business role. The system refuses the whole session and names both roles in the message. It raises an incident to the security administrator queue, and writes a refusal event with the reason ROLE_CONFLICT. One person who can both grant access and work cases could give themselves rights and use them. So the check runs at every sign-in.
ac.AC7: Some parts of the system sign in as themselves rather than as a person. These are service identities, and each one holds a role row like a person does. Here a service identity calls the admin roles endpoint. The system refuses it with 403 and writes a refusal event naming that identity. The identity name in the test is test data. Service identities are often given wide access because they are hard to test by hand. Checking them the same way keeps one set of rules and one place to look for refusals.
ac.AC8: A person may be in Entra ID groups that have nothing to do with the Workbench. A person may also be in a group whose role row has been switched off. Here the user is in one group that maps to an active role and one that maps to none. The session holds only the mapped role. The unmapped group name is written on the sign-in event. The group names in the test are test data. Refusing the whole sign-in over an unrelated group would block real users. Dropping the name silently would hide a group that should have mapped.
ac.AC9: The permission matrix has versions, and a new version can take effect while people are signed in. Here a user signs in under one version. A later version removes a read right from their role an hour later. The call still goes through in the open session. After the user signs in again, the same call is refused. The version names and times in the test are test data. Fixing the version at sign-in means a person's rights do not change mid-task. The bank can also say which version a past action was checked against.

RWB-E1-031.story: A team manager today asks each collector for their list to see who holds which case. Every case now carries a queue, a team and an owner. The team builds the queue and owner columns on the existing case list. It adds filters by queue, team and status, and an export to Excel. The list and the export show only the cases the manager's scope allows. Each export is written to the access log before the file is built. It works when the filters return the right cases. Every export must also appear in the access log with its filters and row count.

ac.AC1: This is the normal path. The manager filters the case list by one queue of their own team. The manager sees the 64 cases in that queue, each with its owner and status. No case from another queue shows. The queue name and the count of 64 are test data. Two things are tested together. The filter returns every case in the queue, and it returns nothing extra. A filter that quietly drops cases would leave work unowned. A filter that lets other queues through would show the manager cases they do not run.
ac.AC2: The manager filters the list and chooses Export. The system writes the export to the access log first. The entry holds the user, the time, the filters used and the row count. It then builds an Excel file holding the same 51 rows the screen showed. The count of 51 is test data. The access log entry is needed under PDPA, the personal data law. An export takes customer data out of the system. Matching the file to the filters shown on screen is what makes the row count in the log meaningful.
ac.AC3: A filter can be correct and still return nothing. Here the chosen queue and status match no case. The list shows an empty state with a plain sentence telling the user to change a filter. The queue and status in the test are test data. An empty table with no words looks the same as a screen that failed to load. The manager would then retry or call support. The message tells them the query worked and the answer is zero. A blank table cannot say that.
ac.AC4: An export holds at most the number of rows set in a parameter, here 10,000. The test gives a filtered list of 10,001 rows for a user whose scope covers every case. The system builds no file and shows a message naming the maximum. The counts are test data. A limit keeps one user from pulling the whole case book into a spreadsheet. That is both a data protection risk and a load on the service. The message tells the user to narrow the filters, so they can still get the data they need.
ac.AC5: The access log entry is written before the file is built. Here the access log store cannot be reached. The system builds no file, and tells the user to try again in a few minutes. This order matters. If the file were built first, a user could take customer data out of the system. There would be no record of it. Refusing the export is the safe answer. The bank can explain a late export to a manager. It cannot explain an export nobody can find.
ac.AC6: A team manager sees only their own team's cases. Here the manager filters by a queue that belongs to another team. The list returns no case. It shows the same empty state as any filter with no match. The queue and team names in the test are test data. The scope is applied in the query itself, so a filter cannot reach past it. That holds even when the user types a queue they learned about elsewhere. Showing the other team's cases would break the scope rule that the whole access model rests on.
ac.AC7: A case can sit in a queue with no owner yet. Here one such case is in the filtered queue. The row shows with the owner cell blank, and the case is still counted in the list. The case number in the test is test data. Cases with no owner are the ones a team manager most needs to see. They are the work nobody has picked up. Dropping them from the list, or failing on the blank owner, would hide exactly the cases the screen was built to show.
ac.AC8: The export limit of 10,000 rows is a maximum that is still allowed. Here a filtered list of exactly 10,000 rows exports, and the file holds all 10,000 rows. This test and AC4 together fix the boundary, so the check reads as more than the limit. The counts are test data. An off-by-one here would refuse a valid export. The user would then narrow filters and run two exports for data they were allowed to take in one.

RWB-E1-045.story: Mortgage, hire purchase and SSME follow different notice periods, service levels and bands. Each difference sits in a team procedure today. If the engines hold these values in code, every product change waits for a release. The team builds one read service. It returns the value for a product group, a parameter code and a date from the versioned reference tables. The team also builds a completeness check that refuses a load leaving a product without a required value. It works when a product is added or changed by an approved reference load, with no deployment.

ac.AC1: Two cases, one mortgage and one hire purchase, get their notice timer set on the same day. A timer is a due date the system holds against a case. The mortgage case gets 30 calendar days and the hire purchase case 60, so their due dates differ. Each timer start records the parameter version it used. The product groups, dates and day counts are test data. This is the core of the story. One piece of code sets both timers, and the difference comes only from the reference rows for each product.
ac.AC2: A new product group is added by three approved reference loads. There is one load for the product, one for its parameters and one for its service levels. All three are effective on the same date. The daily load then brings in an account of that product. The system creates a case for it, and the timers come from the new rows. No deployment happens in between. The product name and dates are test data. This is the measure the story is judged on. A new product reaches the Workbench through a reference load that a business owner approves.
ac.AC3: Every product in force must have a service level row for each required case status. Here the load has no row for one product and one status. The system refuses the whole load and names both in the message. The version already in force stays in use. The product and status in the test are test data. Refusing the load is the point. A gap found at load time is one message to the person loading the file. The same gap found at run time is a case with no timer and a person waiting.
ac.AC4: Each parameter in the catalog carries the type and the range its value may take. Here the notice period is loaded as zero against an allowed range of 1 to 365. The system refuses the load and names the parameter and both limits. The numbers in the test are test data. Holding values as data means a typed mistake can reach the engines. A notice period of zero would expire every timer at once. The range check is what keeps a wrong value out before it is approved.
ac.AC5: A product group and parameter code together must appear once in a load. Here one product has two notice period rows with different values. The system refuses the whole load and names the product and the parameter. The values in the test are test data. With two rows in force, the read service would return whichever row it met first. Two cases of the same product could then get different due dates on the same day. A refusal at load time keeps the reference data to one answer per product.
ac.AC6: A product load lists the products in force, so leaving a product out removes it. Here three cases of that product are still open. So the system refuses the whole load and names the product and the count of open cases. The product name and the count of 3 are test data. A removed product would leave those cases with no parameter rows. No timer could then be set, and no rule could read their bands. The check makes the load wait until the open cases are closed or moved.
ac.AC7: A gap can still reach run time. One case's product may have no notice period row in force on the date the timer starts. The system writes no timer and puts the case in the exception queue. It names the product and the missing parameter. The product and case number in the test are test data. Guessing a value or using another product's value would hide the gap. It would also set a due date nobody agreed. The exception queue makes the case visible, so a person decides what to do with it.
ac.AC8: A running timer keeps the value it started with. Here a mortgage notice period changes from 30 to 45 days, two days after one timer started. That timer's due date does not move. A timer started on the new date uses 45 days. The dates and day counts are test data. Recalculating running timers would move due dates that staff and customers have already been told. It would also change a date a past decision was based on. New values apply from their effective date forward only.

RWB-TE-003.story: The recovery API has 79 operations written in one OpenAPI file. Keeping the server code, the front end code and that file in step by hand brings problems. A renamed field breaks a screen in SIT. An operation can ship without the access check its specification states. The team builds generation of the server interfaces and the front end types from the file. It also builds one contract test and one access test for each operation the current release implements. A contract test calls the operation and checks the answer against the file. It works when the build fails on any mismatch.

ac.AC1: A property is added to one schema in the OpenAPI file, and the build is run. Both the generated server model and the generated front end type hold the new property. Both sides compile against them. The schema and property names in the test are test data. This is the base of the story. The file is the one source, and the types on both sides come from it at build time. Writing the same type twice by hand is how the front end and the service start to disagree.
ac.AC2: An operation is changed so it returns a number field as text. The contract test calls the operation and compares the answer against the file. The build fails, and the message names the operation and the exact place in the answer where the mismatch is. The operation and field names in the test are test data. Naming the place matters, because a developer reading a failed build needs to find one field in a large answer. Without this test the mismatch would reach SIT. A screen would fail there, and the cause would be far from the change.
ac.AC3: The file is linted before anything is generated. To lint is to check a file against a set of rules without running it. Here an operation has no capability setting. That setting names the permission area and right the operation needs. The build stops at the lint step and names the operation. Generating code from a file with a missing capability would produce an operation that no access test could check. The gap would only show when someone called it with the wrong role.
ac.AC4: The file lists the response statuses each operation may return. Here the operation returns 400 for an unknown case, while the file lists other statuses only. The contract test fails the build and names the status and the operation. The status numbers in the test are test data. Front end code is written against the statuses in the file. An extra status falls into whatever the client does by default, often a blank screen. Either the file or the code is wrong, and the build makes someone decide which.
ac.AC5: Each operation in the file names the release it first appears in. Here an operation belongs to the release being built and has no controller method, so the build fails and names it. The operation name and the release in the test are test data. This catches the case where the file and the plan say an operation is in this release and nobody wrote it. Finding it in the build is cheaper than finding it when a screen calls the address and gets nothing back.
ac.AC6: The same check must not fail on work that belongs to a later release. Here an operation first appears in a later release and has no controller method. So the build passes, and the report lists that operation as pending. The operation name and the release in the test are test data. The whole file is written ahead of the build, so most operations are not implemented yet. Without this rule the build would fail from the first day. The team would then switch the check off.
ac.AC7: A property is removed from a schema in the file while a screen still reads it. The front end build runs its type check and fails. The message names the file and the line that reads the removed property. The schema, property and screen in the test are test data. The type check is the only place that finds this before run time. The field would otherwise arrive as nothing, and the screen would show a blank value. Failing the build turns a quiet wrong display into a change the team must handle.
ac.AC8: Every operation must call the access check before it does its work. Here one operation does not. The access test calls it as a role with no right in the declared area. The operation answers 200 instead of 403. The build fails and names the operation. The role and operation in the test are test data. An endpoint is one web address the system answers on. An endpoint without its access check is a hole that no screen reveals. The screen hides the menu entry while the web address still answers. The test calls the address directly, so the hole shows.

RWB-E1-004.story: This story now covers creation only. It builds the EFS history table, the step configuration and the published history API. The full EFS load and its validation are deferred.

ac.AC1: The migration creates collections_history, the case-list columns and the approval_ref column.
ac.AC2: The EFS step configuration exposes the DQ checks, the mapping version and the named action-code filter.
ac.AC3: CollectionsHistoryService implements the published CollectionsHistoryApi.

RWB-E1-013.story: Today the recovery measures are counted by hand from spreadsheets at month end. Each team counts a case a different way. The team builds a measure definition table. It holds each measure's formula, data product, unit and approver. The team also builds a nightly job that computes six measures from Workbench records. It builds a frozen snapshot for the baseline business date that later epics are compared against. The job also writes a nightly extract to the data lake for the Power BI data set. It works when the six approved definitions are in force. The baseline values must also match the known totals of the test case set.

ac.AC1: This checks the definition load. A file of six rows names the measure code, data product, formula, unit and approver for each measure. The approval date sits on the row. After the load, one definition version is in force and holds all six measures. The catalog returns each measure's data product and formula to the job that computes it. Every measure must have one agreed meaning before any value is published. A formula may live only in code or in someone's spreadsheet. Two teams would then report a different number for the same measure name.
ac.AC2: This is the baseline run itself. The test set holds 120 open cases with known totals. After the nightly job, the snapshot rows for the baseline business date are marked baseline and frozen. They carry the definition version used. The case count by route must total 120 cases with 60 Mortgage. Realized recovery must equal the sum of the test payments since entry. The baseline is the number every later epic is measured against. If it is wrong or not frozen, every later improvement figure is wrong too.
ac.AC3: This checks the nightly extract that feeds the report. The job writes the extract files for the previous business date into the data lake. Each file carries a freshness stamp and the record count in the trailer. The trailer is a summary line at the end of the file. The baseline rows stay unchanged inside the extract. The job monitor records the run with its row count, start and end time. Power BI reads the extract. It does not read the Workbench. Without the stamp and the count, nobody can tell whether the report is complete and current.
ac.AC4: A definition row is missing its formula. The whole file is refused, the message names the missing field, and no definition version is put in force. Loading the good rows and dropping the bad one would leave a measure with no agreed formula. The other five would be live. The report would then show five measures and a gap. The team would not know whether the sixth was forgotten or refused. Refusing the whole file keeps the six definitions together as one approved set.
ac.AC5: The baseline is published a second time. The job is rerun for the baseline business date. The frozen rows do not change, and the run record carries the message that names the date. Frozen means the rows can never be written again. A database rule refuses the change as well as the service. If the baseline could be recomputed, every comparison made against it would move whenever the job ran. No one could then say which figures an earlier report used.
