ac.AC6: The loads for the baseline date did not pass their checks. In the test data the COLLINS load was refused at its control total. The job writes no baseline rows for that date. The run record carries the message naming the data product and the date it is from. The baseline is published by the first run after the load for that date passes. A baseline computed from an incomplete load would be too low. Freezing it would lock that error into every later comparison.
ac.AC7: The data lake does not answer. The job still writes its measure snapshot rows inside the Workbench. It holds the extract files. It sends an alert to the operations channel naming the data lake. The next run sends the extract. The measures must survive a problem in a system the Workbench does not own. Keeping the snapshot means no day of measures is lost. Holding the extract instead of failing the whole job keeps the report one day behind. The day is not missing for good.
ac.AC8: A measure is listed in the extract configuration but has no definition in force. In the test data this is the measure code COST_PER_CASE. The job writes no value for it, and the run record names it in a message. A number with no approved definition would be read as agreed once it reaches the report. Nobody looking at the report could tell the difference. Naming it in the run record tells the Tribe lead that a definition is needed before that measure is published.

RWB-E1-023.story: A case owner opens EFS, ALS, shared drives and team spreadsheets today to answer one question about a case. The team builds one read-only screen for a case, SCR-03. It holds the header and the Accounts, Parties, Contact history and Documents sections. Each section shows the business date of the data it reads. Personal fields show masked by role, and every read of personal data is written to the access log. It works when the screen opens in under two seconds and each section shows its own data date. A case outside the user's scope shows nothing, and one failing section does not hide the rest.

ac.AC1: This is the speed check. The test case holds 50 documents and 120 contact history entries, which is a heavy case. The header, accounts, parties, contact history and the first page of documents must appear in under two seconds. The measure is taken over 50 openings, and 95 percent of them must meet it. The screen only saves time if it is fast. A case owner may wait longer than it takes to open the old system. Those owners will keep using the old systems, and the case record screen will be ignored.
ac.AC2: This checks that the figures on the screen come from the data product. A person does not type them. For the test account, the Accounts section must show the days past due and the total balance. These must match the values the account data product holds. The section must also show the business date of that data. The header must show queue, owner, status and entry date from the case. A figure with no date beside it cannot be trusted. The case owner needs to know both the number and the day it was true.
ac.AC3: This checks the customer facts and the contact history. The borrower profile arrived in the daily COLLINS load. The Parties section must therefore show the party role, the segment and the business date of that load. The contact history must show the EFS entries with channel, direction, result and time. These are the facts the case owner needs before calling a customer. If the party role or the segment were missing, the owner would open another system to find them. That is the problem this story removes.
ac.AC4: A section is older than the rest. In the test data the next day's load was refused, so the account data product is still from the day before. The Accounts section shows that earlier business date and a stale banner above it. The banner message names the product and the date. The data is still useful, so the section is shown. The banner stops the case owner from treating arrears from yesterday as arrears from today. It also tells them a load has not arrived.
ac.AC5: The case belongs to another team, and the user may only see their own cases. The answer is 404, the code for not found. The message says the case is not in the user's scope, and no case data appears on the screen. A scope rule only works if it hides the case completely. An answer that said the user has no right would confirm that the case exists and which team holds it. So 404 is used for both an unknown case and a case outside the scope.
ac.AC6: The document hub is a separate module. In this test it does not answer within three seconds. The Documents section shows its own section message. The header, accounts, parties and contact history all appear as normal. Each section is read separately for this reason. One slow neighbor system could otherwise blank the whole screen. The case owner would then lose the case facts because of a problem with documents. The owner would go back to opening the other systems.
ac.AC7: The access log cannot be written. Every read of personal data must be recorded. The screen therefore shows the borrower name and customer number masked, and puts a section message on the personal details. The rest of the case still shows. Showing personal data while the log is down would leave reads of customer data with no record. Nobody could say who read them, and the bank cannot accept that. Masking the fields, instead of failing the screen, keeps the case owner working on the parts that hold no personal data.
ac.AC8: Masking depends on the role. The test user is a phone collector who may not see the customer number. It appears with only its last digits visible. The access log records the read with the user and the fact that the result was masked. Two people on the same case may see different fields, and the rule is held as data for each role. The system logs masked reads as well as full reads. The access log then answers who opened the case, and not only who saw unmasked data.
ac.AC9: The case is on hold for a deviation. The screen shows an on hold banner with the deviation code and the prescription date held on the case. A case on hold must not be worked like a normal case. If the banner were missing, a case owner could take an action that the hold forbids. The banner holds the deviation code and the prescription date. The owner then sees why the case is on hold and which date applies, without opening another screen.
ac.AC10: A new case has no documents and no contact history. Each of those two sections shows a short sentence saying nothing is recorded yet. An empty panel with no text looks like a screen that is still loading or broken. The case owner would then reload it, or ask someone whether the data is missing. The sentence says that the Workbench holds nothing for that section. That is a real answer, and it lets the owner move on to the next question.

RWB-E1-035.story: A case that changes owner today arrives with no history except what the last owner remembers. The team adds a Timeline panel to the case record screen. It merges the contacts, documents, assignments, transfers and status changes of one case into one list in time order. For each event it shows the person who did it, or the rule row and version that caused it. A transfer item also opens its coded reason and the owner it moved from and to. It works when the merged order is always the same. The list must page by 50 with a total, and one failing source must not hide the others.

ac.AC1: This checks the merge and the order. The test case holds four events of four different types. They are a transfer made by a rule, two stored documents and a status change made by a user. All four must appear in the agreed time order, and each must show what caused it. The rule transfer shows the rule row and its version. The status change shows the user. A new owner reads this panel to learn what happened. Without the cause on each event, the owner sees that the case moved and cannot see why.
ac.AC2: This checks the detail of a manual transfer. When the event is opened, the panel shows the transfer reason with its code and label. It also shows the owner the case came from and the owner it went to. It shows the version of the transfer rules in force. A manual transfer is a decision made by a person, so the next owner needs the reason to carry on correctly. The rule version tells a later reviewer which set of transfer rules applied on that day. That matters when the rules change.
ac.AC3: One of the four sources does not answer. In this test the decision log query times out after three seconds. The interactions, documents and assignments still show in time order. The panel shows a section message for the decisions. A part of the history is still worth reading. If the whole panel failed because one source was slow, the case owner would see nothing. That owner would ask the previous owner instead, which is what the panel is meant to replace.
ac.AC4: A case was just created, and its only record is the creation entry. The panel shows one item with the type for a created case, its date and the version of the entry rules. An empty panel on a new case looks like a fault. The case owner would then reload the screen or report a problem. Showing the creation item says that the panel works and the case has no history yet. It also shows which rule version put the case into the Workbench.
ac.AC5: Two events carry the same time to the second. A fixed order by event type decides which comes first. The decision log entry appears before the assignment. The order is the same every time the panel opens. The list is read page by page. If two events swapped places between two calls, an event could appear on two pages or on none. The case owner would then see a history that changes each time they look at it.
ac.AC6: A long case history is read in pages. The test case holds 132 events. The first page returns 50 events with the total of 132, and the third page returns the remaining 32. Loading every event at once would make the panel slow on old cases. The case owner usually needs only the recent events. The total tells the owner how much history exists. They then know there is more to read, and the paging controls can be shown correctly.
ac.AC7: The case belongs to another team, and the user may only see their own cases. The timeline answers 404, the code for not found. The message says the case is not in the user's scope. The timeline must follow the same scope rule as the rest of the case record. Without that, a user could read the history of a case they may not open. Using not found rather than a refusal means the answer does not confirm that the case exists.

RWB-E1-056.story: Epic 1 runs its loads, case creation, allocation, timers and copies as jobs that nobody watches. A failed job that only its developer can restart delays the case list and the morning allocation. The team builds a catalog row for each job with its owner role, schedule, run book path and alert threshold. The team writes a run book for each job. It adds a test in the pipeline that fails the build when a row or a run book section is missing. It shows each job's last run, status and duration. It works when the operations team restarts a failed job from the run book alone.

ac.AC1: This is the pipeline test. The build checks every job it finds in the service against the job catalog. It also checks that each of the 13 Epic 1 jobs has a run book file. The run book must hold six headings: purpose, schedule, owner, failure signs, restart steps and escalation. A run book that is missing a section fails the operations team at the moment they need it. Checking it in the build means a job cannot reach production with no written restart steps and no named owner.
ac.AC2: This is the restart the story is for. A load job fails early in the morning on one of its steps. A platform administrator follows the restart steps in the run book and calls the rerun endpoint. An endpoint is a web address the system answers. The job restarts from the step that failed and finishes. The next job in the daily order then runs, and the case list shows the data of that business date. No developer is involved. Without this the case owners start the day on yesterday's case list.
ac.AC3: This checks that the monitoring exists and agrees. Every job has run once in the test environment. The monitoring workbook then shows the last run time, status and duration for each of the 13 jobs. The admin endpoint returns the same values. The platform administrator must be able to see quickly which job failed and how long each one took. If the workbook and the endpoint gave different answers, the operations team would trust neither. The team would go back to asking the developer.
ac.AC4: A developer adds a job whose run book has no escalation section. The pipeline fails the build and the message names the job and the missing section. A check that only warns is ignored under time pressure, so the build has to stop. Naming the job and the section means the developer knows what to write without reading the test. Escalation matters most at night: without it, the person on duty knows the job failed but not who to call next.
ac.AC5: A rerun is asked for while the job is still running. The answer is 409, the code for a request that does not fit the current state. The message says the job is already running, and the running job continues. Two runs of the same job would write the same rows at the same time. The results would then depend on which run finished last. Refusing the second request and leaving the first alone keeps one clear run for that business date.
ac.AC6: A job runs longer than the threshold on its catalog row. In the test the threshold is 45 minutes and the job reaches 46 minutes. The owner role group and the platform administrator group get a message. The job is not stopped. A slow job may still finish correctly, and stopping it could leave work half done. The alert gives the operations team time to read the run book and decide. Without it, the team would find out hours later that the morning jobs never finished.
ac.AC7: A job that already finished for a business date is run again. Each interface run for that date is written as DUPLICATE and no account record is loaded a second time. This is what idempotent means: running the job twice leaves the same result as running it once. The operations team must be able to rerun a job without checking first whether it already finished. If a second run could load the same rows again, balances and counts would double and the fix would take a day.

RWB-TE-004.story: SIT and UAT must show that the loads, allocation, reconciliation and reports work at production volume and with production data shapes. Made-up data cannot show that. Production data is not allowed in these environments. The team builds a loader. It takes the masked copy and its manifest from the bank's PII service, and checks the manifest. It scans every field marked personal for values that still look real. It loads the files into a side schema. It swaps that schema in only after every check passes. It works when a clean copy loads with counts and balance sums equal to the manifest. Any copy holding a real personal value is refused.

ac.AC1: This is the clean load. After it, every column marked as personal in the party and contact point tables holds a token or a masked value, and a scan of those columns finds no value that matches the national ID, mobile or email pattern. A token is a replacement value that takes the place of the real one. The row counts and the balance sums per product must equal the manifest, which is the summary file delivered with the extract. Each party token must still join to the same case and account rows as in the extract. Tests of volume and reconciliation only mean something when the totals and the links match production.
ac.AC2: A personal value was left in the copy. In this test one party row holds a 13-digit value with a valid national ID check digit. That value sits in a column that should hold a token. The whole load is refused, and the message names the column that failed. The copy already in the environment stays in use. One real customer ID in a test environment is a data breach. Test environments are open to more people than production. Loading the clean rows and skipping that one would leave the real value in place, with nobody seeing it.
ac.AC3: The file does not match its manifest. In this test the account file holds one row fewer than the manifest states. So the control total check fails, and the whole load is refused with the message naming both counts. A control total is a count or a sum that the loader recomputes and compares. A missing row changes every count, balance and reconciliation result in the test environment. A test that then fails would send the squad looking for a defect in the code when the data was short.
ac.AC4: The load is aimed at the wrong environment. When the target is DEV the loader refuses before it reads any file, and the load report records that no file was read. Masked copies are allowed only in SIT and UAT. Even masked production data must not reach development, where access is wider and the rules are looser. Checking the environment first, before any file is opened, means that a wrong start copies nothing at all. The allowed environments are held as a property, so this limit does not depend on who starts the load.
ac.AC5: The same extract is loaded twice. The loader recognizes the extract ID from its own record of earlier loads. It skips the load and names the earlier load in the report. The extract ID is what makes each delivery unique. Reloading the same files would replace the whole environment with the data it already holds. Any test data the squad added since would be lost. Naming the earlier load in the report tells the team the environment already holds that copy. No action is needed.
ac.AC6: The manifest names a masking rule version that is not the version in force. The whole load is refused. The masking rules belong to Compliance, and they change. An older version may leave fields unmasked that the current rules require to be masked. A copy made under that version is not safe to load, even though the PII service produced it. The system compares the version in the manifest with the version in force. The check then does not depend on anyone reading the manifest.

RWB-E1-005.story: This story now covers creation only. It builds the tracker inventory table, the reference handler and the read endpoint. File loading and validation are deferred.

ac.AC1: The migration creates tracker_inventory with its unique key, check constraints and team index.
ac.AC2: TrackerInventoryHandler implements the reference table handler and is registered for tracker_inventory.
ac.AC3: GET /admin/trackers is registered with the three filters and the documented Tracker response.

RWB-E1-015.story: Recovery data arrives in nightly batches and in weekly or monthly file loads. A fact on a case can be one day or one week old, and today nobody can see how old it is. The team builds a freshness stamp for each data product and business date. The stamp holds the time the source data was taken, the time the Workbench loaded it, and a status. A product whose load has not arrived by its expected time is marked stale. It works when the case record view and the saved inputs of each decision both show the stamp.

ac.AC1: This checks the normal case. A daily product is loaded in the morning from an extract taken the night before. An extract is the copy of data that the source system hands over. The test reads the stamp through the published interface and through the read endpoint. Both return the same two times: the source time and the load time. The status is loaded. The two times answer different questions. The load time says when the Workbench received the data. The source time says how old the facts themselves are.
ac.AC2: This checks what happens when a daily load does not arrive. At the expected time the system looks for a load for the expected business date. With no load, it marks the product stale and writes a data quality exception with check freshness. It also alerts the operations channel. The case record view then shows a short warning in its data panel. Without this check, a person would read yesterday's arrears and payments as if they were today's. They would make a call, an offer or a legal step on old facts.
ac.AC3: This checks that the freshness of every data product a decision read is kept with that decision. Each decision log entry points to a saved set of its inputs. The test reads one entry for one case and finds one stamp per product, each with its load time and status. This matters for review later. Months after a decision, audit and the team need to see how old the data was at the time, without guessing. Without the saved stamp, a later load replaces the numbers and nobody can see what the person actually saw.
ac.AC4: This checks a load that was refused at one of its checks. The system marks the product stale at once, without waiting for the expected time. The stamp of the last good load stays in use. The case record still shows data with its own date. A refused load leaves the product with no new data. People must see at once that what they read is older than they expect. Marking it stale immediately also starts the operations work earlier in the day.
ac.AC5: This writes the same stamp twice for one product and one business date. Only one row may exist for that pair. The second write changes nothing and is counted instead. Load jobs get restarted after a failure, so the same commit can report itself twice. Two rows for one product and date would give two load times and two statuses, and reports would count the load twice. The count of repeats is kept so the team can see how often jobs run again. Those repeats change nothing that anyone reads.
ac.AC6: This checks a load that arrives after the product was marked stale. The late load sets the status back to loaded with its own load time. It closes the freshness exception for that day. The stale mark must not hold once the data is there. A product left stale after a good load would send people to look for a problem that is already fixed. The open exception would also stay on the data quality list. Clearing it takes the stale warning off the case record.
ac.AC7: This checks the moment just before the deadline. A load commits one minute before the expected time, and the check then runs at the expected time. The product must not be marked stale. This is a boundary test, which checks the behavior right at the edge of a limit. An off-by-one error in the comparison would mark on-time loads as stale every day. That would send false alerts and put a warning on case records that hold current data. It would teach the team to ignore the stale warning.
ac.AC8: This checks a weekly product on a day between its loads. The weekly product loaded on its expected day. The check then runs on a later day of the same week, and the product must not be marked stale. The refresh cycle and the expected time of each product are data rows, not code. Without this test, the daily check would mark every weekly product stale on the days between loads. People would see warnings on data that is as current as that product ever gets. Real stale products would be lost among them.

RWB-E1-024.story: Recovery documents sit today in folders, shared drives and with couriers. Originals go missing, and the evidence is built again for each audit. The team builds one document store and one index. Every file gets one document record held against its case, with its type, date, source and the fields taken from it. Legal types go into a write-once container, which is storage that refuses any change to a file once it is written. Every later change makes a new version, and older versions stay readable. It works when a document is found by case, type and date, and a legal document cannot be changed.

ac.AC1: This stores one scanned court notice against a case, then reads it back. The record must hold the case, the type, the source, version 1 and today's date. The field taken from the document must be in the index, so the document can be found by that value. The file must sit in the write-once container under a path built from the case and the document. An event must be written so other parts of the system learn the document exists. The read returns the same hash as the stored file. A hash is a short value computed from the file content, so an equal hash means equal content.
ac.AC2: This attempts to delete a legal document and to replace its content, both through the service and directly on the storage container. Each attempt is refused with the message that legal documents cannot be changed. The file content and the record stay the same. Each attempt is written to the audit trail with the document and the caller. Court notices and other legal types are used as evidence, so a changed or deleted file costs a case. Testing the direct attempt on the container matters because the service is not the only way in.
ac.AC3: This stores a document of a type that is not write-once. The record must carry the retention class that the document type table gives for that type. The retention class says how long the document is kept. The file goes to the standard container rather than the write-once one. The type table is the only source of the write-once flag and the retention class, so the caller cannot choose them. If a caller could set them, a legal document could be stored as changeable. A short-lived document could be kept for ten years.
ac.AC4: This adds a second file to a document that already has version 1. The new row is version 2, is active, and points back to version 1. Version 1 becomes inactive, and its content is still returned when asked for. A read of version 2 lists both versions with their dates and sources. Documents get revised, for example after a new valuation. Keeping the old version readable lets anyone see what the case held at the time of an earlier decision. Overwriting would lose that, and the audit trail would break.
ac.AC5: This stores a file with a document type that is not in the type table in force. The system refuses the call and writes nothing: no document record, no decision log entry and no event. The type table in force is the list of types allowed on that date. A free-text type would break the index, the retention rules and the write-once rule. None of them would know what the type means. Refusing early also keeps the case clean, since no half-stored document is left for someone to find later.
ac.AC6: This sends a Word file for storage. The system reads the file content to find its real type, rather than trusting the file name. Only three types are allowed, and Word is not one of them. The call is refused, and nothing is written to the storage containers or the tables. A file renamed to look like a PDF is refused in the same way. This matters for safety and for the later work. Office files can carry code, and the reading and extraction steps later in the system handle only the three allowed types.
ac.AC7: This checks the file size limit at its edge. Two test files are used. One is exactly at the limit and one is a single byte above it. The file at the limit is stored. The larger one is refused with a message that names the limit. This is a boundary test, which checks the behavior right at the edge of a limit. An off-by-one error here can refuse files that are allowed, which blocks real work. It can also accept files above the limit, which slows every later step that reads or copies them.
ac.AC8: This stores the same file a second time on the same case with the same type. The system returns the document that already exists. The case keeps one document record, one decision log entry and one event for that file. Users scan or upload the same page twice, and jobs retry. A second record would show the case two court notices where one arrived. Counts, searches and the document list would all be wrong. A person would not know which record to open or which file to work from.
ac.AC9: This has two users add a new version of one document at the same time. One request succeeds and returns the next version number. The other is refused with a message that asks the user to reload the record. Exactly one new version exists afterward. Without this check, both writes could take the same version number, or both could point back to the same earlier version. The version history would then show two rows with one version number, and nobody could tell which file is the current one.
ac.AC10: This adds a new version to a version that has already been replaced. The system refuses the request and tells the user to open the latest version first. No new row is written. Only the latest version takes a new version. Without this rule, two chains of versions would grow from one document, and the case would hold two current files. People reading the document could open either one, and the Workbench could not say which file the case runs on.
ac.AC11: This makes the storage container refuse writes while a document is stored. The record is written with a state that says the copy is still to come. A request for the file content is answered with a message that storage is not available. The request is queued. When the container accepts writes again, the next document intake run copies the file and sets the state to stored. The record and the file are written in two steps. This test proves a failed copy neither loses the document nor returns a broken file.
ac.AC12: This has a phone collector ask for a document on a case that this person does not own. The person's scope is own cases only. Scope is the set of records a role may reach. The request is refused, and neither the details nor the file content come back. Recovery documents hold borrower data, so every read is checked against the role and the scope. Returning the details while refusing the file would still tell the caller that a court notice exists on that case. That is itself data they may not see.

RWB-E1-037.story: Audit found unsuitable user access and staff sending debtor data outside the bank. Today rights are set inside each system. Nobody can show who could do what on a past date. The team holds three things as versioned data. The first is the rights each role has in each capability area. The second is how far each role may see. The third is which personal data fields each role sees unmasked. Every screen and API applies them. A rights change becomes a file load with an approver, in place of a code release. It works when a rights change takes effect with no deployment and personal data is masked by default.

ac.AC1: This changes one right by loading a file. The administrator loads a new permission matrix version in which one role gains read rights in one capability area. A capability area is a group of actions, for example queue and allocation. A second person, holding the security role, approves the load. After the start date, a user with that role signs in. The call that was refused before now succeeds, with no software release. One decision log entry records the approval, its version, its row count and who approved it. The change can then be shown later.
ac.AC2: This has a user with one role open a case, and checks what the user sees. The identity number and the phone number come back with only their last digits visible. The system must not ask the personal data service for the clear values at all, because this role may not see them. The view is written to the access event stream with the case and the fields shown masked. Asking for clear values and then hiding them on the screen would put real personal data into logs, memory and network traffic. This role should never reach that data.
ac.AC3: This has a user call an action that the user's role may not perform. The request is refused before the handler runs. The handler is the code that would carry out the action. The case owner and the queue stay unchanged, and one refusal event is written with the capability area and the missing right. Checking before the handler matters because a check inside the handler can run after part of the work is done. The refusal event also gives audit a trail of attempts, and not only of successful actions.
ac.AC4: This has a user whose role sees only the cases that user owns. A list call returns only those cases, and the total shown equals that same number. A request for one case outside the scope is refused and returns nothing about it. Scope is applied to the query first, so out-of-scope rows never reach the permission check or the screen. The count of excluded records is never shown either. A total higher than the list would tell the user about cases they may not see. A different answer for a case that exists would do the same.
ac.AC5: This loads a permission matrix file that holds two faults. One role is repeated in the same capability area, and one letter is not an allowed right. The system refuses the whole file. It names the repeated row and the wrong letters, and keeps the version already in force. Nothing from the new file is saved. Loading part of the file would leave the matrix with gaps. A person could then gain or lose rights that nobody approved. Naming both faults in one answer also lets the administrator fix the file in one pass.
ac.AC6: This checks two rules about who may approve a load. The person who loaded the file tries to approve it and is refused, and the load stays waiting. Then a person with a different role tries to approve it and is refused as well. Only the role named in the parameter for that table may approve. Two people must take part in a rights change, so one person cannot give themselves new access. Checking the approver's role separately also stops anyone with load rights from acting as the approver.
ac.AC7: This makes the decision log store unavailable, then approves a load. The call fails, the load stays waiting, and the version already in force keeps running. The decision log is the record of who decided what. A rights change that took effect without that record would leave audit unable to say who approved it. The record and the status change must succeed together or neither happens. Failing the call also tells the approver to try again, instead of leaving them to believe the change is live.
ac.AC8: This removes a user from their access group while that user has an open session. The user's rights come from groups held outside the Workbench, and the Workbench rechecks them at a short interval. On the first request after that recheck, the session ends and the call is refused. A new sign-in is refused as well. Leavers and movers keep working sessions open. Without this check, a person who left the team could keep reading and changing cases. That access would last until their session timed out on its own.
ac.AC9: This asks for a personal data field that no masking rule covers. The field comes back masked. The default is to mask. A field is shown clear only when a rule in force allows it for one of the session's roles. This matters while the masking rules are still being set. With the opposite default, every field that Compliance has not yet ruled on would be shown to every role. The first missing rule would then expose borrower data. A masked field can be opened up later, once the rule exists.
ac.AC10: This has two approve calls for the same load arrive at the same time. One succeeds and writes one decision log entry. The other is refused and writes nothing. One load may be approved once. Without this check, two entries could record the same approval, or two approvals could set different start dates on one version. Audit would then see one change approved twice, and the version in force could depend on which call finished last.

RWB-E1-064.story: The recovery tables hold 1,256 fields. They come from 13 source systems or from the Workbench itself. 108 source mappings still say the system owner has to confirm them. With no confirmed agreement, a source system can rename or change a field. The load then breaks or loads the wrong value. The team builds the data dictionary as versioned data. Each field carries its type, source system, source field, refresh, owner and behavior when the data is late. The mapped fields are grouped into one data contract per source system. A contract is published only after its system owner confirms it.

ac.AC1: This reads one field and then checks all of them. A read of one named field returns its type and its database type. It also returns the source system, the field name in that source, and how often it refreshes. It returns the owner role and what to do when the data is late. A second check reads every field in the dictionary. It finds none with any of those six attributes empty. Developers build loads and screens from these entries. An empty source field or refresh leaves the developer to guess. A wrong guess shows up only when production data is wrong.
ac.AC2: This publishes a data contract after its confirmation is recorded. The steward first records who confirmed it, on which date, and which stored document holds the confirmation. Publishing then sets the contract to published at contract version 1, with that confirmation date on it. The contract is the written agreement about what the source system sends. Publishing only after the owner confirms means the Workbench never depends on a mapping that the owning system never agreed to. That is how silent breaks start.
ac.AC3: This changes one field definition and checks the history. The steward changes the field name in the source system and gives a reason and a date. The field moves to version 2 with that date and reason. Version 1 stays readable with its own date. Field definitions change because source systems change. Keeping each version readable lets the team see what the definition was when a load ran. A wrong value in old data can then be traced to the definition used then, rather than the current one.
ac.AC4: This publishes a contract for which no confirmation was recorded. The system refuses the call, names the source system in the message, and leaves the contract in draft. The confirmation is the whole point of the contract. The check belongs in the publish step, not in a review habit. A contract published without it would look agreed to everyone reading the dictionary. Loads would be built on a mapping the source system never accepted. The gap would show up only when a field changes.
ac.AC5: This changes a field with an empty reason. The system refuses the call, names the reason field, and leaves the field at its current version. Every change must carry a reason, because the reason is what a later reader uses to judge the change. A history of dates with no reasons tells nobody why a type or a source field moved. Refusing the change outright, instead of saving it with an empty reason, keeps the history complete for every field in the dictionary.
ac.AC6: This loads a set of dictionary attributes in which one field has no refresh cycle. The system refuses the whole load and names the missing attribute and the field it belongs to. The dictionary already in force stays unchanged. Accepting the other rows would leave one field without that attribute. The load jobs and freshness checks that read it would then have nothing to use. Naming the field and the missing attribute in the message also lets the steward fix that one row and load again.
ac.AC8: This changes a field that belongs to a published contract. The system creates a new draft version of that contract. The published version stays in force. A published contract is never edited where it sits. The source system owner agreed to a fixed set of field definitions, so a change needs their confirmation again. The published version stays in force until the new one is confirmed and published. Loads then keep running on the agreed definitions while the new confirmation is collected.

RWB-TE-005.story: Case routing runs on 448 rule rows in ten route sets, held as data instead of code. A wrong condition, owner or target state in one row moves every case that reaches it. Today nothing proves a row does what its owner expects. Every rule row already names a test case. The team builds a harness that runs those test cases. A harness is code that feeds set inputs to the rules and compares the result with the expected result. It runs on every rule load and in every build. It works when a version with any failing test cannot take effect.

ac.AC1: This runs the harness over a route set whose rows all have their test cases. One test runs per rule row, so the test count equals the row count. Each result names both the rule it tested and the test case it used. A reader then goes straight to the row and the data behind it. All tests pass, and the version is marked validated. Only a validated version goes on to approval. The count per row also proves that no row was skipped, which a single pass or fail answer would hide.
ac.AC2: This uses a version in which one row's target state no longer matches what its test case expects. The harness runs, that one test fails, and the message names the expected state and the state the row actually gives. The whole version is marked failed and cannot be approved. The target state decides where a case goes next. A changed target state would send every case that hits this row to the wrong queue or team. Naming expected and actual together tells the analyst which of the two is wrong.
ac.AC3: This uses a version in which one row names a test case that the Tests sheet does not hold. The harness marks the version failed and names both the row and the missing test case. Every row needs its own test case, so an untested row is treated the same as a failing one. Without this check, an analyst could add a row and name a test that was never written. The version would pass with that row never run. That row would then move cases with nothing proving what it does.
ac.AC4: This uses a version in which two rows both match one test input. Exactly one row may match any input. The harness fails the test and names both rows. Two matching rows mean the result depends on which row the rules component reaches first. The same case could then be routed differently from one run to the next. Naming both rows points the analyst at the pair of conditions that overlap. That is faster than reading the whole route set to find the overlap.
ac.AC5: This uses a version in which one row's condition was changed so that no row matches its test input. The harness fails the test, names the row it expected to match, and reports that no row matched. A case that matches no row stops moving and waits with no owner and no timer. Nobody is told, because the case was never routed to anyone. Catching this at load time, with the row named, is far cheaper. Finding the stuck cases weeks later in a queue report costs much more.
ac.AC6: This uses a test case that gives no value for one of the facts its rule reads. A fact is one piece of case data that the condition uses. The harness fails the test and names the missing fact. An unset fact would be treated as empty or zero. The test could then pass or fail for a reason that has nothing to do with the rule. Failing with the fact named tells the analyst which column of the Tests sheet to fill. The next run then tests what the rule really does.
ac.AC7: This runs the harness twice on one version and checks that both runs give the same results. The system keeps one set of results for the version and does not add a second set. Loads get retried, and builds run again. Different results from the same inputs would mean the harness itself depends on something outside the test data. Every result would then be unreliable. One stored result set also keeps the change log clear. A reader sees one answer for the version, instead of a list of runs to compare.
ac.AC8: This runs the harness inside the build over the rule files held in the repository. The build runs one test per rule row across all ten route sets. Each test is named by its rule. A failing rule test fails the build. Rules are data, so a rule change can reach production with no code release. The same checks run in the build. A rule file edited in the repository is then checked the same way as code. The named tests also appear in the build report.

RWB-E1-006.story: Today a wrong case owner, one account on two cases, or a balance that does not add up stays hidden. A case owner finds it only when working the case. The team builds a rule runner for ten checks on single rows. The runner starts after every data load and after the daily case list build. Each row that fails is written to the exception list with its rule code and the business date. The data steward reads those rows through one read address the system answers on, or in the Power BI report. It works when every failed row carries a rule code before a case owner meets the case.

ac.AC1: This tests that the ten rules start on their own after the daily case list is built. The test data holds three accounts, each linked to two open cases. One rule looks for an account that sits on more than one case, so three rows fail. The test checks three things. The failure rows are written, the read address returns them, and the count per rule is kept with the load result. Without this, duplicate work is found only when two case owners call the same customer on the same day.
ac.AC2: This tests that the day's failures reach the reporting extract. The extract is a set of rows copied out for Power BI. The test data holds 3, 14 and 2 failures of three rules, so 19 rows. Each row carries the rule code, the rule name, the data product, the business date and the record key. The record key says which record failed. Without the extract, the data steward can read failures only one query at a time. Nobody can see which rule fails most often, or on which day.
ac.AC3: This tests that a new rule starts working after a load, with no new software release. The test adds one rule that checks an interest rate against a top value of 30. Two test accounts hold 32.5, so two rows fail. The rule starts only on its valid from date, and only after the data steward approves the version. The test also checks that the first ten rules keep working. Without this, every new check waits for a code change, and the bank cannot answer an audit point in days.
ac.AC4: This tests the check on a new rule version before the version is used. The test rule names a column that the data dictionary does not hold. The data dictionary is the list of tables and columns the system knows about. The whole load is refused, and the version already in force keeps running. Without this check, a rule would build its query against a column that does not exist. Loads would fail every night, or the rule would pass every row and hide real problems.
ac.AC5: This tests that a rule may read only the tables this module owns. The test rule names a case table that another module owns. The load is refused in full, and the message lists the tables a rule may name. Without this limit, the data engine would read another module's tables directly. A change in that module would then break the rules with no warning. The same data would also be held in two shapes, and the two copies would stop matching.
ac.AC6: This tests what happens when one rule cannot finish. In the test, one rule runs past the 60 second limit set for each rule. That rule is marked ERROR with the load result. The other rules still run and write their failures. The data steward group gets a message naming the rule, the date and the reason. Without this, one slow rule would stop every other rule. The day would then end with no data quality result at all, and nobody would know why.
ac.AC7: This tests that running the rules again for the same load adds nothing. The test writes two failures, then runs the rules again for that load. The count stays at two. The database holds one key made of the load, the rule code and the record key. A second write of the same row is dropped. Work that gives the same result when it is repeated is called idempotent. Without this, a rerun after a failed load would double the counts. The data steward would then chase the same rows twice.
ac.AC8: This tests that a rule runs only inside its own dates. Each rule row carries a valid from date and a valid to date. The test rule has a valid to date of 30 November 2026, and the load is for that same date. The test expects the rule to stay out of the run and out of the load result. Without date control, an old rule would keep writing failures after the bank stopped using it. The exception list would then fill with rows that nobody owns.
ac.AC9: This tests that a failure is closed when the data is fixed. The test has one open failure for an account from 27 November, raised because the case had no owner. The case now has an owner. When the rules run for 30 November, the system sets that failure to CLEARED and writes the date. Without this step, the exception list would only grow. The data steward could not tell a problem that is still live from one that a team fixed last week.

RWB-E1-016.story: Today staff can hold read access to data they do not need. Personal data can also be read with no trace left. The team builds an access check in front of each data product, plus masking for personal fields. It also builds a log of every read and one catalog entry per product. A data product is one named set of data with one owner. The check runs in order: the user's right, an access row for their role, then the case in their scope. It works when a role with no access row is refused, personal fields come back masked, and every read is logged.

ac.AC1: This tests a read that is allowed. The test user holds a read-only role that may read one data product. The data comes back with personal fields hidden. The mobile number shows only its last four digits, and the national ID comes back as MASKED. The system also writes one entry to the personal data access log. The entry holds the user, the product, the case and the time of the read. Field values are never logged. Without the log, the bank cannot answer who read a customer's personal data. That is the audit finding behind this story.
ac.AC2: This tests the catalog, which holds one entry per data product. The test expects 14 entries. Each entry names the owner role, the system of record, the refresh cycle and the time the data is expected by. It also names the retention class and every field. The system of record is the system the data comes from. Each field says whether it holds personal data. The test data has one product with 20 fields, of which 9 are personal. Without the catalog, a developer or an auditor has to ask people where data comes from and how fresh it is.
ac.AC3: This tests a read that must be refused. The test user holds a phone collection role with no access row for the product asked for. The call is refused with the message that the role does not include this action, and no data row is read. The refusal is also written to the access log with the user and the product. Without logging refusals, repeated tries to reach data a person has no right to would leave no trace. The security administrator could not see them.
ac.AC4: This tests the check on a new access version before it takes effect. Access rows arrive as a file load. The test file holds a role code that the bank does not use. The whole file is refused, the message names that role code, and the version already in force keeps working. Without a whole-file refusal, part of a file would load. Some roles would gain new access while others kept their old rows, and nobody could say which version is live.
ac.AC5: This tests the third check, the user's scope. Scope says which cases a user may see. The test user holds a case owner role that may see only their own cases. The user asks for a case owned by someone else. The answer is 404, the same answer as a case that does not exist, and no data row is read. The same answer keeps the caller from learning that the case exists. Without the scope check, any case owner could read the personal data of every customer in the bank.
ac.AC6: This tests the safe default. Compliance has not yet given the rules that say which role may see which personal field. Until those rules arrive, every personal field is masked for every role. The test reads a product with a role that has access. It expects the name fields, the customer number, the date of birth and the contact value all masked. Without this default, an empty rule table would mean no masking at all. Personal data would then be open to every role with an access row.
ac.AC7: This tests the system when the personal data access log cannot be written. The log in the test refuses every write. The read is then refused with a service unavailable answer, and no personal field is returned. The rule is short: no log, no personal data. Without it, an outage in the log would become a window in which reads of personal data leave no trace. An auditor could not later show who read a customer's data during that time.
ac.AC8: This tests that an access row starts on its valid from date. The test gives a role read access to a product from 15 December, and the test clock is set to 14 December. The read is refused on 14 December. Without this date control, an approved change would take effect as soon as the file loaded. A change prepared in advance would open access early. The bank could also not say which access version applied on a date in the past.

RWB-E1-025.story: Today the bank has no signed list of which document types are read and which fields come out of each. Classification and extraction cannot be built or measured against a list that may still change. The team builds one versioned reference table holding six document types, their fields, a write-once flag and a retention class. The rows arrive as a file load, are checked as a whole, and are approved by a second person. It works when the file with both sign-offs loads and is approved. It then takes effect on 30 November 2026 for every team that reads it.

ac.AC1: This tests the load of the agreed list. The test file holds the six document types and their 26 fields. Every row carries a sign-off from a legal user and from an NPA user, each with a date. After the load the file sits at status LOADED with six rows. Every row holds both sign-off users and both dates. Nothing is in force yet. The sign-offs sit on the row itself. Without them, nobody could later show that Legal and NPA agreed the field list the models were built against.
ac.AC2: This tests the approval and the read. A second user approves the load from the first test, and the version takes effect on 30 November 2026. The test checks the six type codes, then two types in detail. One holds four named fields, a ten year retention class and the write-once flag set. That flag means a stored document cannot be changed. The other holds a five year retention class, four fields and the flag clear. Without one approved table, each team would code its own type list, and the lists would stop matching.
ac.AC3: This tests the check for a missing sign-off. The test file has one type row with no NPA sign-off. The whole file is refused, and the message names the row and the missing sign-off. No row of that file is written, and the version in force keeps working. Without a whole-file refusal, five types would load and one would be missing. Extraction would then be built against a list that Legal and NPA never agreed in full.
ac.AC4: This tests two more checks in one file. One row holds a retention class that the list of allowed values does not hold. A seventh row repeats a type code that is already in the file. The whole file is refused, and the message lists both rows, so the loader can fix everything in one pass. The version in force keeps working. Without the duplicate check, two rows for one type code would load, and readers could not say which row applies.
ac.AC5: This tests the version name as the key that stops a second load. The test loads a version that is already there. The request is refused with a conflict answer, and the first load stays as it was. Without this, a second upload of the same file would replace rows that are already approved. It could also add a second copy of them. The version in force would then change with no approval, and with no record of who changed it.
ac.AC6: This tests the date boundary between two versions. A new version adds one field to a type. It is approved with a valid from date of 1 January 2027. The test reads the table on 31 December 2026 and again on 1 January 2027. The first read returns the old version. The second returns the new version with the new field. Without this rule, an approved change would take effect as soon as it loaded. Work done last week could not then be read with the version it used.
ac.AC7: This tests separation of duty. That means the person who prepares a change is not the person who approves it. In the test the loader also holds the approval right, then tries to approve their own load. The call is refused with a conflict answer, and the load stays at status LOADED. Without this check, one person could put any type list into force alone. The sign-offs from Legal and NPA would carry no weight, because one person would control both steps.

RWB-E1-038.story: Today approval limits for problem loans sit in a bank regulation and in people's heads, and approval authority is an audit finding. The team builds a versioned limit table and one lookup that the approval router calls. The lookup takes the decision, the regulation item, the product, the amounts, the conditions and the decision date. It returns the lowest approval level whose limit covers the request, the rows used and the version name. Limits change by an approved file load, never by a code change. It works when a lookup for a past date returns the level and version that applied then.

ac.AC1: This tests the load of the first limit version. The test file comes from the bank regulation and holds 95 limits. Those become 218 rows, 109 for each of the two products in the file. One decision code can cover several regulation items. The test checks that every row has a decision code, an approval level and a product. It also checks that no two rows repeat the same combination. One item at one level is stored as two rows with different amounts. Either row can be met, so both are needed to describe that level.
ac.AC2: This tests the normal lookup. The router asks who may approve one decision for a mortgage case. The question carries a principal amount, a loss percentage, a loss amount and a date in December. The answer is the lowest approval level whose row covers all of those values. The answer also gives the row used and the version name. The row and the version matter later. An auditor can then check the approval against the limit that applied on the decision date. The limit table may already have changed since then.
ac.AC3: This tests a limit change. A new version adds one row for a regulation item at a lower approval level, and takes effect on 1 January 2027. The old rows stay readable with an end date of 31 December 2026. A lookup on 2 January returns the new level and the new version name. The approval of the new version writes one entry to the decision log. The log is the record of who decided what and when. Without the old rows staying readable, past approvals could no longer be checked.
ac.AC4: This tests two checks on a limit file. One row gives a lower authority level a higher principal limit than the level above it, which cannot be right. Another row holds a decision code the bank does not use. The whole file is refused, the message names both problems, and no row is stored. Without the order check, a junior level could approve a larger amount than a senior level. The system would then route large decisions to the wrong people while staying inside its own rules.
ac.AC5: This tests two limits on who may approve a version. First the person who loaded the file tries to approve it, and is refused. Then a product head tries, and is refused because only the Risk officer approves this table. Each refusal has its own message. Without the first check, one person could set the bank's approval limits alone. Without the second, a role with an interest in a higher limit could approve the file that raises it.
ac.AC6: This tests the approval when the decision log is down. The decision log is the record of who decided what and when. The test switches the log store off, then approves the load. The call comes back as service unavailable, and the load stays at status Loaded. Without this rule, a limit version could be in force with no record of who approved it. Every approval routed under that version would then be hard to defend to an auditor.
ac.AC7: This tests a request the table does not cover. The loaded version holds no row for hire purchase. Those limits come from another chapter of the regulation and are not supplied yet. The lookup returns NOT_COVERED, and the system raises an incident to the Risk queue naming the decision and the product. Without this, a request with no limit would fall to some default level, or pass with no approval at all. A gap in the table has to stop the item and be seen by Risk.
ac.AC8: This tests the two days on either side of a version change. The same request is looked up on 31 December 2026 and on 1 January 2027. The first returns one level and the old version. The second returns a different level and the new version. Date logic usually breaks at these two days, by one day at each end. A decision taken on the last day of a version could be approved at the level the next version sets. Without this test, nobody would catch that.
ac.AC9: This tests one rule that overrides the amounts. Some write-offs are for a director, a senior executive, a major shareholder or a related party. For those, the lookup returns the highest level. The amount does not change that. The test uses a small principal amount to show that the amount does not matter. The answer also carries the reason. Without this rule, a small write-off for a person close to the bank would be approved at a low level. That is the kind of finding an auditor looks for.

RWB-E1-065.story: Squads start work on 2 November, and the real data loads and the masked test copy are not ready. Production data is not allowed in development. The team builds a sandbox database in development. The same migrations that build the real schema create it. A generator fills it with made-up recovery data. A migration is one versioned change to the database. The generator reads the data dictionary, so a new column is filled with no code change. It works when every squad can query and extract the sandbox from the first day. The sandbox holds no personal data.

ac.AC1: This tests the built sandbox. The counts come from the test properties: 1,226 mortgage, 1,296 hire purchase and 290 SSME cases, which is 2,812 in total. Ten more examples are added for each unusual shape the rules must handle. The test checks that every entity table except decision_log_entry holds at least one row. It also checks that one named test case has its accounts, parties and interactions linked to it. Without linked records, a developer can read single tables. That developer still cannot test a screen or a rule that needs a whole case.
ac.AC2: This tests the access a squad member gets. A member of the development group runs a grouping query and sees the three product groups with their counts. The export script writes one table to a CSV file. The same database role is then refused an UPDATE. Read-only access keeps one developer from changing rows that another developer is testing against. Changed rows would make a test result impossible to repeat.
ac.AC3: This tests the generator against a schema change. A migration adds one column to the case table. The column has its row in the data dictionary and its own list of allowed values. After the rebuild, every case holds a value from that list in the new column, and the generator module is unchanged. Without this, each schema change would need hand-written code for the new column. The sandbox would fall behind the schema, and squads would test against tables that no longer match the real ones.
ac.AC4: This tests the generator when a column is missing from the data dictionary. The data dictionary is the list of tables and columns, with the type of each one. A migration adds a column with no entry there. The build fails and names the table and the column, and the sandbox already in use stays as it is. Guessing a value for an unknown column would hide the real problem. The problem is that the dictionary and the database no longer agree.
ac.AC5: This tests that a build gives the same result every time. The generator starts from one fixed number, called a seed, so the same seed and the same commit produce the same rows. The test builds twice for the same commit and checks that the row counts match. It also checks that one named case still holds the same opening balance. Without this, a rebuild would change the data under a failing test. A developer could not tell a real bug from new data.
ac.AC6: This tests the build when the seed lists are wrong. The test empties the list of product values. The generator then has nothing to put in the product column of the case table. The build fails and names that table and column, and the sandbox in use stays as it is. Without a clear failure, the build would write an empty value, or stop with a database error that names nothing useful. The team would then spend hours finding the cause.
ac.AC7: This tests the check that runs before a sandbox is published. The checker scans every column marked as personal data. In the test, one value matches the shape of a real 13 digit national ID, with a valid check digit. The build fails, names the table and the column, and publishes no sandbox. Development data has to stay made-up. One real identifier in a database that every squad can read and export breaks the bank's own rule.
ac.AC8: This tests the data around the 90 days past due line, which is where a case is opened. The build creates ten accounts at 89 days past due with no case. It creates ten at 90 days past due with one open case each. Without rows on both sides of that line, a developer testing the entry rule has nothing to test with. The usual bug there is one day out, and only accounts at 89 and 90 days past due show it.

RWB-TE-006.story: Today a message to another system can be sent for a change that is then undone. It can also be lost when the other side is down, and nobody sees it. The team builds an outbox. It is a table that holds each event and each outbound request, written in the same transaction as the change. A transaction is one unit of work that saves in full or not at all. A job every minute delivers each row to its consumers in order, and retries on a schedule held as configuration. It works when no delivery is lost and none is sent for a change that did not save.

ac.AC1: This tests the normal path, from approval to delivery. When the approval saves, the outbox holds one outbound request for that case, with one delivery row for its consumer. A consumer is a system or component that takes the event. The header carries the event ID and a key that marks this request as one of a kind. It also carries the schema version, the time and the actor. The payload holds references only, with no name, address or identifier in it. At the next minute run the delivery goes out and is marked DELIVERED.
ac.AC2: This tests a consumer that stays down. The settings allow one attempt and three retries. The test fails at four set times and expects no fifth attempt. The delivery ends at status EXCEPTION with four attempts. The system raises a task for the owner role on the case. It moves the case to the exception queue with one decision log entry. Without a limit, a delivery would retry forever. The failure would stay there with nobody told, and with no owner to fix the consumer.
ac.AC3: This tests the rule that ties the event to the change. The approval writes to the outbox, then fails, so the whole unit of work is undone. Afterwards no event and no delivery exist for that notice. The outbox row is written in the same unit of work, so it disappears with the change. Without this, another system would act on an approval that the bank never saved. It would dispatch a notice for a case that holds no approved notice.
ac.AC4: This tests recovery after one failure. The first attempt fails. This consumer holds a step of the case, so the case moves to the retry queue and waits. The next attempt succeeds, and the delivery is marked delivered with two attempts. A success event then returns the case to the state it was paused in. Without that return step, the case would sit in the retry queue after the problem was over. A case owner would then have to move it by hand.
ac.AC5: This tests the key that stops duplicates. The same approval is submitted twice with the same key, and both units of work commit. The outbox ends with one event for that key. The second submission gets an error and changes nothing. Work that gives the same result when it is repeated is called idempotent. Without this key, a double click or a retried call would put two outbound requests in the outbox. The other system would then act on the same notice twice.
ac.AC6: This tests the job with two copies of the service running. Both start in the same minute with 200 deliveries due. Each delivery is made once, and the delivery log holds 200 calls. The job selects rows with a lock that skips rows another copy already holds. Without that, both copies would pick up the same rows. Each consumer would get the same event twice, and the bank would depend on every consumer catching the duplicate.
ac.AC7: This tests order inside one case. Two events for one case carry sequence numbers 11 and 12. The consumer fails on 11. The test checks that 12 is not delivered to that consumer until 11 is delivered. Order matters because a later event often depends on an earlier one. A state change can be sent before the transfer that caused it. The other system would then hold a case history that makes no sense. It would also have no way to put it right.
ac.AC8: This tests one event going to two consumers. One fails and one succeeds. The one that succeeded is delivered, and the other is left at RETRYING with its next attempt a minute later. Each consumer has its own delivery row and its own status. The case route state does not change, because neither consumer holds a step of the case. Without separate rows, one slow consumer would hold back all the others, and a delivery that already succeeded might be sent again.
ac.AC9: This tests the admin action that sends a failed delivery once more. A delivery at status EXCEPTION is sent again. It returns to PENDING with zero attempts, due at the next run. A delivery that is already DELIVERED is refused with a conflict answer and its own message. Only a delivery in the exception queue may be sent again. Without that limit, an administrator could resend a delivery that already worked. The other system would act on the same event twice.
ac.AC10: This tests a failing delivery for an event that has no case. After the retries are used, the delivery goes to EXCEPTION, and an alert reaches the platform administrator within 15 minutes. No task and no case event are raised, because there is no case to put them on. Without the alert, this kind of failure would be silent. A task on a case is the usual way a failure is seen, and that path is closed here.
ac.AC11: This tests that the retry delays are read when they are needed. The delays are changed in the configuration service before the failure, from one minute to two minutes for the first retry. The delivery then fails, and its next attempt is set two minutes later. Without reading the current settings, the delays would be fixed in code. A change after an incident would need a release, and operations could not slow the retries down while another system recovers.

RWB-E1-007.story: This story now covers creation only. It builds the four adapter tables, the adapter classes and the exception queue endpoints. File loads and validation are deferred.

ac.AC1: The migration creates the four P2 tables and their unique keys and index.
ac.AC2: The adapter, outbound, guard and SFTP classes implement the published interfaces, and the boundary rule holds.
ac.AC3: The two exception queue endpoints are registered with the documented contract.

RWB-E1-018.story: Today each recovery team keeps its own list. One account can appear on several lists under different references, and some accounts at 90 days past due have no owner. The team builds a daily job. It reads the account data after the load passes. It applies the entry rule and the exclusion rows, and creates one case per customer and product group. Each case gets a number in the form RW-YYYY-NNNNNN that is issued once and never used again. It works when every account at 90 days past due has one case, and the daily check shows no unexplained difference.

ac.AC1: This is the main path. One test account reaches 90 days past due in the load and matches no exclusion rule. The job creates a case with the next number in the year, status NEW, no stage code and the entry date. The account is linked as the primary account, and the customer is linked as the borrower. The job then publishes an event, a message other parts of the system listen for, so later work knows the case exists. If this fails, accounts pass 90 days past due with no case. No team owns them, and no letter can name one reference.
ac.AC2: This checks that an excluded account gets no case. The test account is 92 days past due and its tdr_flag is true. The exclusion rule therefore gives it the reason ACTIVE_PLAN. The job writes an exclusion record instead of a case. The record holds the account, the reason code, the rule ID and the rule version in force. Keeping the reason and the version lets a reviewer see later why the account was left out. It also shows which rule row decided it. Without this check, the system would start recovery work on accounts the bank has agreed to treat another way.
ac.AC3: This checks the grouping. One test customer has two hire purchase accounts, both at 95 days past due. The job creates one case for that customer and product group, and links both accounts to it. The total outstanding at entry is the sum of the two balances, THB 412,350.00 in the test data. One case per customer and product means one owner, one history and one set of letters for both accounts. Two cases would mean two officers calling the same customer about the same product.
ac.AC4: This checks that a case number is never given to a second case. A closed case keeps its number, and the next new case takes the next number from the yearly sequence. In the test the closed case is still found by a search on its number. Case numbers appear on letters, court files and payment records, so a reused number would point to two different cases. Keeping a closed case readable by its number also lets staff answer a question about an old letter years later.
ac.AC5: This checks that case status values come from a list in the database rather than from code. In the test a new value is added to the status list with a start date. A case moves to that value the next day. The case service accepts the value with no code change and no release. The decision log entry for the move records why the system acted. It holds the list version in force, so a reader can see which list applied. If statuses lived in code, every new status would need a build and a release.
ac.AC6: This checks a second exclusion reason, so the rule table works for more than one reason. The exclusion rows include OPEN_DISPUTE. The test account is at 90 days past due and has an open dispute. The job creates no case and writes an exclusion record with that reason. Running a second reason through the same path proves the reasons are data rows and not special code for one reason. A customer in dispute would otherwise receive recovery letters while the bank is still answering the complaint.
ac.AC7: This checks the edge of the entry rule. One test account is at 89 days past due and one is at 90. The job creates a case for the 90-day account and none for the 89-day account. The 89-day account is read again the next day, when it reaches 90. Boundary errors are easy to write. A rule that reads "more than 90" instead of "at or above 90" would delay every case by one day. The threshold itself is a parameter, so the number can change without new code.
ac.AC8: This checks that running the job twice for the same business date changes nothing. In the test the job already created a case for an account on that date. The second run finds the account is already linked and skips it. The account keeps one case link, and no case number is issued in the second run. Operations staff do rerun a failed job, so a second run has to be safe. Without this, a rerun would create a second case for the same account and would use up case numbers for nothing.
ac.AC9: This checks that the job waits for good data. In the test the daily load for the next date was refused at the control total check. The case creation job does not start for that date. The job monitor shows the message that today's load has not arrived, so staff know why no case was made. The job runs for that date once a later load passes. Cases built from a refused file would place accounts in recovery on wrong figures. Those cases would have to be canceled by hand.
ac.AC10: This checks that a case is created only when its decision record is also written. The decision log holds why the system acted. In the test the decision log store cannot be written. No case is created for the account. The job record lists the account as failed with its message, and the next run takes the account again. Both writes sit in one transaction, one unit of work that saves everything or nothing. A case with no decision record could not be explained to an auditor. The bank would also not know which rule version created it.
ac.AC11: This checks the end of the yearly number range. In the test the last number issued in 2026 is the highest the six-digit format allows. The job creates no case for the next account. It writes its message with the year on the job record, and raises an incident to the platform administrator. Stopping is safer than issuing a number outside the agreed format, because the number is printed on letters and court files. The accounts are not lost. They wait until the range is extended and are taken in a later run.
ac.AC12: This checks that the grouping is per customer and per product group. One test customer has a mortgage account and a hire purchase account. Both are at 91 days past due. The job creates two cases, one for each product group. Recovery work differs by product, with different teams, letters and legal steps. One case holding both would have no single owner and no single set of rules. This also shows the grouping does not pull every account of one customer into a single case.

RWB-E1-027.story: Without one writer, each module would build its own record of why it acted. Some actions would go unrecorded. The team builds one writer that every module calls to record a decision. The writer checks the record is complete. It writes the record in the same transaction as the action.
