A transaction is one unit of work in the database that saves everything or saves nothing. The writer ignores a repeat of the same event and publishes an event for other modules. It works when every case created, owner assigned, case transferred and document attached has one complete record. No action happens without one.

ac.AC1: This checks the main path for two events. A test case is created by the case creation job and then given an owner by an allocation row. Two entries exist for the case, one per event, each with its final call. The owner entry carries the rule ID, the rule version, the actor and a reference to the inputs used. Both entries pass the field check, and two events wait in the outbox, a table that holds events until they are sent. Holding the rule ID and version lets a reviewer see which rule row chose the owner, even after the rules change.
ac.AC2: This checks that an incomplete record is refused. The test record names a case transfer but carries no rule version, model version or agent version. At least one of the three is required, because every decision must say what decided it. The writer refuses the record, names the missing group in its message, and logs the case ID and the field. The transfer then rolls back in the same transaction, so the case is not transferred. A transfer with no record of what decided it could not be explained later. A refused write has to stop the action.
ac.AC3: This checks a narrower rule. The test record names a rule but leaves the rule version empty. The writer refuses it and names the rule version field. A rule ID alone is not enough. Rule rows change over time, and the same ID can hold different conditions in different versions. Without the version, nobody could rebuild the decision as it was made on the day. Naming the exact missing field in the message also lets the calling team fix its code quickly.
ac.AC4: This checks the behavior when the store is down. In the test the allocation job tries to give a case to an owner while the decision log store cannot be written. The write raises its unavailable error, the case owner stays empty, and the case status stays New. An incident goes to the platform administrator queue so someone looks at the store. The action and its record are one unit of work, so a half-done result is not possible. The job takes the case again later, once the store is back.
ac.AC5: This checks that one event gives one entry. Each record carries an idempotency key, a value that names the event so a repeat can be found. In the test a document attached event was already written, and the same event arrives again with the same key. The writer adds no second entry. It returns the first entry's ID and adds one to the repeat count, so the team can see how often repeats happen. Two entries for one event would show two decisions in the log where only one was made.
ac.AC6: This checks that the writer refuses to work on its own. A caller with no open transaction calls the writer. The call is refused with a transaction state error, and nothing is written. The point of the writer is that the record and the action save together or not at all. That holds only inside the caller's transaction. A record written outside one would stay in the log even when the action it describes was rolled back. The log would then show a decision that never took effect.
ac.AC7: This checks the decision code. Codes come from a list in the database. The test record uses a code that is not in the list. The writer refuses the record and names the decision code field. Codes are how reports and audit queries find entries of one kind. A free-text code would hide the entry from every later query. Checking the code at write time keeps the log readable by code. It also stops a typing error in a calling module from reaching the log.

RWB-E1-039.story: Today the bank cannot answer who read a debtor's record on a given date. Administrators also hold full access to production data all the time. The team writes every sign-in, refusal, record read, document read and export into the decision log store, which is append only. It also builds emergency access, called break-glass. That access works only with a request approved in the bank IAM against an open incident. It ends on its own, and it marks every action it covers. IAM is the bank's own system for granting access. It works when every read of the case store and the document store has a log entry.

ac.AC1: This checks that opening a case record writes one entry. The test user opens a case. The system writes a single entry with the read code, the user, the case ID and the time. The entry lists the field IDs that were returned, and two personal fields show as masked. Masked means the value was hidden from the reader. Field IDs and the masking position are written, never the values. The log therefore holds no personal data of its own. Without this entry, the bank could not answer who saw a debtor's record on a given day.
ac.AC2: This checks the whole emergency access path. The incident is open, and the security administrator approved the request in the bank IAM. The IAM put the test user in the break-glass group until 18:00. The user activates the grant at 10:30, so it ends at 14:30. That is the earlier of the four-hour window and the group end. The banner shows the end time. Every entry for that user until 14:30 carries the grant and the incident. A change at 14:20 is allowed and marked. The same change at 14:31 is refused, with nobody having to close the grant.
ac.AC3: This checks that an export of a list is logged like a read. The test user filters the case list and exports 37 rows. One entry is written with the export code, the user, the filter used and the row count. It carries no case ID, because a list covers many cases. An export takes data out of the system, so it needs its own entry. The filter and the count tell a later reviewer how much was taken and which cases were in the result. The log does not hold the data itself.
ac.AC4: This checks that reads of document contents are logged as well as reads of case records. The test user opens a document on a case. One entry with the read code, the case ID and the document ID is written before the file is returned. Writing first matters. If the entry came after, a reader could get the file and leave no record when the write failed. Documents hold statements, contracts and letters. A document read is as sensitive as a case record read.
ac.AC5: This checks that the workbench does not grant emergency access on its own. The test user holds the platform administrator role but is not in the break-glass group in the bank IAM. The call is refused with status 403, and an entry with the denied code and the reason is written. The approval has to come from the bank IAM, so one person cannot give themselves extra rights. Writing the refusal to the log also shows later who tried to take emergency access and was turned down.
ac.AC6: This checks the two required inputs on the activation call. With no incident reference the call is refused with status 422, and the message names that field. With an incident and a reason of 12 characters the call is refused again. The reason must be 20 to 1000 characters. The incident ties emergency access to real, open work. The reason length stops entries such as "fix" that tell a reviewer nothing. Both limits are parameters, so the bank can change them without new code.
ac.AC7: This checks what happens when the log store is down. The test user opens a case while the decision log store cannot be written. The call returns status 503 with its message and no case data, and an incident goes to the platform administrator queue. A read with no log entry would leave access unrecorded, which is the gap this story closes, so the read fails instead. Staff see a clear message and can try again once the store is back.
ac.AC8: This checks the query internal audit needs. One case was read three times on one day, once under emergency access. The auditor asks for that case, the read code and the one date. Three entries come back in time order with the user, the time and the fields shown. The 11:02 entry carries its incident reference. The reader can then see that this access was emergency access, and why. This is the question the bank cannot answer today, so the query is part of the work, alongside the writing.
ac.AC9: This checks that a refused call is logged too. The test user holds only the phone collection role and calls an admin endpoint. An endpoint is one address in the system that a program can call. The call is refused with its message. One entry is written with the denied code, the area, the right asked for and no case ID. Refusals matter as much as successful reads. Repeated refusals can show an account being probed, or a person given the wrong role.
ac.AC10: This checks two kinds of repeat on the activation call. The call carries an idempotency key. The caller sets that value so the system can tell a repeat from a new request. The same request with the same key returns the first answer and writes no new entry. That covers a lost reply or a double click. A new key while a grant is active returns status 409 and opens nothing. Two active grants would give one person two windows and two incident references, and the log would be hard to read.

RWB-E1-066.story: Today the history of a recovery case sits in several systems, in letters and in team spreadsheets. An officer rebuilds it by hand before each decision. The team builds one ledger per case and one writer that every recording path calls. A contact, letter, promise, payment or hand-over is written when it happens, in the same transaction as the action. A transaction is one unit of work in the database that saves everything or saves nothing. Entries are append only and carry a gap-free number per case. It works when every recorded action lands in the ledger and a failed write stops the action.

ac.AC1: This checks the main write. The test case already holds six entries. The case owner records an outbound call with a result and a promise. The new entry takes the next number for that case, seven. It holds the event code, the time with its time zone, the user, the channel and the direction. The promise amount and promise date sit on the same entry as the call they were made in. Keeping the promise on its own contact means a later reader sees what was agreed. They also see which conversation it was agreed in, with no joining of other records.
ac.AC2: This checks the order and the numbering. The test case holds four entries loaded from EFS, one case created entry and one case allocated entry, six in all. Read together they form one sequence in time order, and the per-case numbers run 1 to 6 with no gap. One ordered history is what lets an officer or a court see the case as it happened. A gap would raise the question of a lost entry. Loaded history kept apart from new entries would leave the officer joining two lists by hand.
ac.AC3: This checks the split between the two records. One owner reassignment is written to both. The decision log entry holds why the system acted. It holds the decision code, the rule, the rule version, the inputs reference and the approver. The ledger entry holds what happened. It holds the event, the time, the actor and the ID of the decision log entry. The ledger carries no rule, version or inputs. Keeping rule detail in one place keeps the history short and readable. A reader who needs the reason follows the link to the decision log.
ac.AC4: This checks that a failed ledger write is never silent. In the test the insert fails with a database error. The call returns status 503 with its message, the ledger still holds its six entries, and no contact is saved. The system raises an incident naming the failure code and the case. The action and the entry are one unit of work, so neither is saved alone. A contact saved with no ledger entry would leave a gap in the history, and nobody would know the gap exists.
ac.AC5: This checks the field check on the writer. A service calls the writer with no event code. The call is refused with the missing value message naming that field, and no entry is written. Every entry must carry the case, the event, the time, the actor and the source. An entry missing one of these cannot be read or sorted later. Refusing early also keeps the ledger clean, since an entry cannot be changed or deleted once it is written.
ac.AC6: This checks the numbering when two writes land at once. Two separate writes append to the same case at the same moment, and both commit. The entries take the next two numbers, seven and eight. None is missing and none is repeated. The writer locks the case ID while it works out the number. Two writes therefore cannot read the same highest number. Without the lock, both entries would claim one number, and one write would fail. The sequence could also show a gap that looks like a lost entry.
ac.AC7: This checks an unknown case. The case owner posts an interaction for a case ID that is not in the system. The call returns status 404 with the out-of-scope message, and no entry is written. The same answer covers a case that exists but sits outside the reader's scope. The response therefore does not reveal whether that case exists. An entry for an unknown case would leave history that no case can show. It would also let a caller add records by guessing IDs.
ac.AC8: This checks that the database itself refuses a change. Any update or delete on an existing entry is refused by a trigger on the table. A trigger is a rule in the database that runs on every write. A mistake is fixed by writing a new entry with event CORRECTION that names the original entry. The old entry stays readable, so the history shows both the first record and the fix. If code could change an entry, the history could be rewritten after a complaint or a court date. It would then carry no weight.

RWB-TE-007.story: The ACE service runs on more than one instance. An instance is a running copy of the service. Without a shared schedule, a job runs twice or not at all, and an outage loses a day's run. The team puts the timer check, the morning allocation run and the daily reconciliation run on the clustered Quartz scheduler. The schedule gives one run per business date and catch-up after an outage. It also gives a check on the 07:00 deadline and a run book for each job. It works when each job shows one successful run per business date. The allocation run must also finish by 07:00.

ac.AC1: This checks the basic promise of the shared schedule. Two service instances share one job store, and the morning allocation is due for one business date. The job runs once, on one of the two instances. The run log holds the job, the business date, the instance, the start, the end, the status and the case counts. Two instances running the same allocation would give cases two owners or allocate one case twice. The run log is also how staff see later that the day's run happened at all.
ac.AC2: This checks the catch-up after an outage. Both instances were down for part of the day. When the service starts again, the allocation and reconciliation jobs run for that business date. They run once the case creation job has succeeded for that date. Each run is logged with the message that names the job and the date. A late run is therefore visible and is not read as a normal one. Without catch-up, a day of cases would wait for a person with nobody noticing. The daily check against the core bank would also be missing for that date.
ac.AC3: This checks that firing a job twice for one business date is safe. The allocation job already succeeded for the date, and it is fired again. No case is allocated a second time, and the run log holds a skip for that job and date. Operations staff do fire jobs again by hand after a problem, so a second run has to change nothing. Without the check, a rerun would move cases to other owners after the morning work had started. It would also send a second set of allocation messages.
ac.AC4: This checks the five-minute timer job when one run takes longer than the gap. A run starting at 10:00 takes seven minutes, so the 10:05 fire falls due while it works. The next run starts only after the first one ends, and two runs are never in progress together. Two runs at once would read the same due timers and send the same warning or escalation twice. Waiting is safe here, because the next run picks up every timer that is due by then.
ac.AC5: This checks the order of catch-up runs. Three business dates have passed loads and no allocation run, because both instances were down. On restart the job runs for the earliest date first, then the next, then the latest. Each run is logged with its own business date. Each run works on the cases of its own business date. Running the dates out of order would mix the days. It would also make the counts per date hard to read.
ac.AC6: This checks the limit on catch-up. Seven business dates have passed loads and no allocation run, and the limit is five. No catch-up run starts on its own. An alert names the job and the seven dates, so a person decides what to do. A long outage usually needs a decision about which dates still matter. Seven days of allocation runs at once would move a large number of cases with nobody watching. Stopping and asking is the safer behavior.
ac.AC7: This checks the order between jobs. The case creation job failed for a business date, so the allocation job must not run for that date. The allocation run is recorded as WAITING with a message naming the job it waits for. When the case creation job succeeds later that morning, the allocation job runs for the date. Allocating before the cases exist would place only part of the day's work and would leave the rest until the next day. The WAITING record also tells staff why the run has not happened.
ac.AC8: This checks recovery when the instance running a job stops. One instance is part way through the reconciliation run for a business date and stops. The other instance takes the job and runs it again for that date. It does this within the 20-second check-in the cluster uses. The run log shows the failed run on the first instance and the successful run on the second. Without this, a job that stopped part way would leave the day's reconciliation missing. The case list would never be compared to the core bank for that date.
ac.AC9: This checks the deadline on the allocation run. The run has not succeeded by 07:00 for the business date. The deadline check at 07:00 sends an alert to the operations channel, naming the job, the date and the time. The alert arrives by 07:15. The deadline exists so officers find their new cases waiting when they start work. A late run with no alert would leave a team idle in the morning. Nobody would know why until someone asked.
ac.AC10: This checks the run books. A run book is a short document about one job. It tells an operator what the job does and what to do when it fails. The test folder holds run books for two of the three jobs. The build fails and names the job with no run book. Failing the build keeps the documents up to date with the jobs. A missing run book would otherwise be found only during a night-time failure. The check is also why a new scheduled job cannot reach production without someone writing down how to restart it.

RWB-E1-008.story: Today the reason for a recovery route, the approver and the figures sit in e-mails and files. Nobody can show the full record later. The team builds the decision log store. Every decision becomes one row holding seven groups of fields. The database refuses any change or delete of a stored row. Each row carries a hash of the row before it. A hash is a short fingerprint computed from the row content. A separate checker recomputes the hashes and reports the first row that does not match. It works when every Epic 1 decision can be rebuilt from the log.

ac.AC1: This test checks that a stored decision row cannot be changed or removed. The test tries an update and a delete twice: once with the service database role and once with the schema owner role. All four statements must fail. The service role fails because it has no grant for those statements. The schema owner fails because of a database trigger. A trigger is code the database runs on its own when a statement arrives. The refused attempts are written to the audit log with the table, the operation and the entry ID. Without this, someone could rewrite history and the log would prove nothing.
ac.AC2: This test checks the math of the chain on 100 test rows. The checker reads the rows in order and recomputes each hash from the row content. Each recomputed hash must equal the hash stored on the row. Each row must also hold the hash of the row before it. The first row holds 64 zeros, because no row comes before it. The result reports the count checked, the last sequence number and its hash. If the chain is wrong here, later checks cannot tell a real change from a coding mistake.
ac.AC3: This test checks that a decision row really holds all seven groups of fields. The test writes one row with a rule and rule version, and a reference to the inputs. The same row holds the recommendation, the approver and approval level, the final call, the actions and the outcome. The test then reads the row through the single entry endpoint. An endpoint is one web address the service answers on. The read must return every group, plus the decision time and the two hashes. If one group is missing, the decision cannot be rebuilt later. Audit would then have to ask people what happened.
ac.AC4: This test proves the checker finds a change made outside the service. The test holds 10,000 rows, which are test data. One row, number 7,412, has its actions changed directly in the DEV database with the trigger switched off. The checker runs over the whole range and must name that row as the first break. It must raise an incident and send the break message to Compliance within 15 minutes of the run start. Without this, a change by someone with database access would stay hidden and the log could not be used in audit.
ac.AC5: This test checks what happens when two writers append at the same moment. Each writer works inside its own database transaction. A transaction is a group of statements that all succeed or all fail together. The store takes a lock, so one writer waits for the other. The two new rows must get sequence numbers 51 and 52, with no gap and no repeat. Row 52 must hold the hash of row 51, and row 51 the hash of row 50. Without the lock, two rows could claim the same place and the chain would break.
ac.AC6: This test checks how a wrong decision is fixed. The stored row keeps its wrong owner. A new row is appended that names the row it corrects and gives the right owner. Reading the case must return both rows in chain order, with the correction pointing at the first row. Nothing is overwritten. This keeps the record of what was decided at the time, and the record of the fix. If corrections overwrote the first row, the chain would break and the earlier decision would be lost.
ac.AC7: This test checks that a failed write leaves no trace. The connection for the store is closed in a test double, which is a fake object used only in tests. A writer then appends a row inside the same transaction that changes the case owner. The store must raise its unavailable error. No row may be stored, the case owner must stay as it was, and no sequence number may be used up. This keeps the action and its record together. A changed owner with no decision row would leave a case nobody can explain.
ac.AC8: This test checks the read right on the decision log. The test user holds only the phone collection role. That role has a dash for the decision log, which means no right at all. The user calls the single entry endpoint and must get status 403 with the no-right message. The log holds who approved what and on which figures. Giving every role sight of it would spread decision data wider than the bank allows. The check also proves the endpoint applies rights, and does not rely on the screen to hide the data.

RWB-E1-019.story: Queues, team structure and who works which list live in spreadsheets today. Changing a team needs a change request to IT and a code release. The team builds queues and queue membership as versioned reference data, loaded from one Excel template. Each queue carries its team, its role, its assignment method, its capacity cap and its overflow queue. A load is checked in full, approved by someone other than the author, and takes effect on its valid from date. One call returns the earlier version. It works when a six-team queue set loads, is approved and rolls back without a release.

ac.AC1: This test loads a full queue set and checks the result. The test data is one template with 12 queues and 48 member rows for six teams. After the load is approved, 12 queue rows must be in force as version 1. Each queue must carry its team code and the role that works it. All 48 member rows must be in force. The version must also keep the author, the approver and the approval time. Those three fields show that the separation of duty was followed. Without them, nobody can say later who changed the organization.
ac.AC2: This test checks the one-call return to an earlier version. Queue version 3 holds an error, so rollback is called once for it. Every queue row must then come from version 2. Each queue must keep the same record ID it had before. Cases point at a queue by that ID, so a new ID would leave cases pointing at nothing. The system must also record who called the rollback, when, and why. A wrong queue load can stop work across a team, so the fix must be fast and must be traceable.
ac.AC3: This test checks the capacity answer that allocation depends on. Member U-11 of a test queue has capacity 40 and already holds 40 open cases. A 41st case is offered for that member. The capacity service must answer that the member is at capacity. It must also name the overflow queue for that case. Without this answer, allocation would keep piling cases on one person while the overflow queue stays empty. The numbers 40 and 41 here are test values, not real team limits.
ac.AC4: This test checks the team code check on a load. The test file has a queue on row 7 whose team code is not in the team table. The whole load must be refused, and the message must name row 7 and the failed check. No queue row and no member row may change. A part-loaded file would leave some queues pointing at a team that does not exist. Cases in those queues could not be allocated. Refusing in full also means the earlier version stays in use while the file is fixed.
ac.AC5: This test checks the range on the capacity cap. A queue in the test file has a cap of 0, which is below the allowed minimum of 1. The load must be refused with the range message naming minimum 1 and maximum 500. A cap of 0 would mean no case can ever be given to that queue, and work would quietly stop. Checking the range at load time keeps a typing mistake out of the live tables. The cap range comes from a parameter, so the values are data and not written in code.
ac.AC6: This test checks separation of duty on approval. User U-90 loaded queue version 4 and then tries to approve it. The approval must be refused with the author message. Version 4 must stay in the checked state and must not come into force. One person who can both load and approve could change the team structure alone, with no second pair of eyes. The queue tables decide who sees and works which cases, so this is the control that keeps that change reviewed.
ac.AC7: This test checks rollback when there is nothing to go back to. Queue version 1 is the only version, and rollback is called for it. The call must be refused with the no-earlier-version message. Version 1 must stay in force. An unguarded rollback here could leave the queue tables empty, and no case could be allocated. A clear message also tells the administrator that the fix is a new load. The refusal is a 409 response, which means the call clashes with the current state.
ac.AC8: This test checks that loading the same file twice does no harm. The file was already loaded as version 5 for the same valid from date. Loading it again must return version 5 and must write no new version. This behavior is called idempotent: the same call repeated gives the same result. Network timeouts and double clicks do happen, so the same file does arrive twice. Without this check, the system would hold two versions of the same content, and it would not be clear which one applies.
ac.AC9: This test checks that a version waits for its date. Version 2 is in force and version 3 is approved with a valid from date of 15 December 2026. Asked on 14 December, the capacity service must answer from version 2. Asked on 15 December, it must answer from version 3. Team changes are planned ahead, so a load must be able to sit ready without affecting today's work. If an approval took effect at once, a change prepared for next month would move cases today.
ac.AC10: This test checks the role check on queue members. Member U-12 on row 22 of the member sheet is listed on a litigation queue without holding the role that works it. The whole load must be refused, and the message must name row 22 and the failed check. A member without the queue role would receive cases they have no right to open. Every call would then fail, and the work would sit in the queue unseen. Catching it at load time keeps the role rules and the queue tables in agreement.
ac.AC11: This test checks the overflow loop. In the test file, one queue overflows to a second queue, and that second queue overflows back to the first. The whole load must be refused with the loop message. An overflow chain that returns to its start would send a case around the two queues without end. That could use up the allocation run and leave cases unassigned. The check walks the overflow links at load time, so the loop never reaches the live tables.
ac.AC12: This test checks a required column. A queue on row 3 of the test file has no assignment method. The whole load must be refused with the required-field message naming the assignment method and row 3. The assignment method decides how cases are handed to people in that queue, so there is no safe default. An empty value would leave the allocation engine with no rule for that queue. Naming the field and the row lets the administrator fix the file in one pass, without reading the whole check output.

RWB-E1-028.story: Deadlines sit in personal diaries today. Audit found cases that met the criteria for litigation and were never filed. The team builds timers on cases. A service level timer starts each time a case enters a queue and status, counting working days from the holiday table. The owner gets a warning at the warning point. At expiry the breach goes to the named escalation role, and the case keeps its queue and owner. A prescription timer is set at case creation from the legal period for the product. It works when every case and every legal claim shows a due date.

ac.AC1: This test checks the start of a service level timer. A hire purchase case is placed in a queue with status assigned at 09:00 on 1 December 2026. The service level is 5 working days, so the timer must expire at 09:00 on 9 December. December 5 to 7 are marked as non-working days in the test holiday data, so they are skipped. The warning time is 80 percent of the service level, which is 4 working days, giving 8 December. The timer must also be readable through the case timers endpoint, an address the service answers on.
ac.AC2: This test checks the warning and the escalation on one timer. The timer passes its warning time first, and its expiry time later. At the warning point the case owner must get the warning message. At expiry the breach must go to the team manager of the queue's team, with escalation level 1. The case must keep its queue and its owner. Escalation asks the manager to act; it does not move the case. Both the warning and the breach must be written to the decision log, the breach with its rule. Without the log entries, nobody can show later that the deadline was raised.
ac.AC3: This test checks the prescription date on a new case. The prescription date is the last day on which the bank can still bring a legal claim. The test case has one account with a last payment date of 15 March 2026. The legal period for the product is 2 years, so the prescription date is 15 March 2028. A prescription timer must expire on that date, with its warning 180 days earlier. The case read must show the date. A claim that expires unnoticed cannot be recovered at all, so this date has to be set at creation.
ac.AC4: This test checks what happens when no service level applies. No service level version is in force for the product group and status on the date. No timer may start, because the system has no limit to count against. The case must appear on the exception queue with the message naming the missing item and the scope. Silence here would be worse than an error. The case would look fine with no clock on it and could sit for weeks. The exception queue gives the team a list of cases to fix, and the message says what is missing.
ac.AC5: This test checks the missing legal period. The legal period table has no row for the SSME product, and an SSME case is created. The prescription date must stay empty, because guessing a legal period could lose a claim or file one too early. The case must appear on the exception queue with the message naming the missing item and the product. Legal owns these rows and loads them, so the list tells the team which product still needs one. An empty date with no entry on that list would leave the case with no deadline.
ac.AC6: This test checks the fallback when no payment was ever made. The test account has no last payment date and a contract date of 30 June 2025. The prescription date must then be 30 June 2027, counting the 2-year legal period from the contract date. Accounts that never paid are the ones most likely to need litigation, so they cannot be left without a date. Without the fallback, the calculation would have no start date. The case would go to the exception queue for no good reason.
ac.AC7: This test checks the catch-up after a missed run. The timer job normally runs every 5 minutes. In the test it does not run from 10:00 to 10:40, and three timers pass their expiry time in that period. The run at 10:45 must raise all three breaches, one for each timer. A job that only looked at the current moment would miss the three, and those cases would never be escalated. The run must also raise each one once, so a long outage does not produce a flood of repeats.
ac.AC8: This test checks that a breach is raised only once. The timer is already expired with escalation level 1, and the job runs again. No second breach event may be published, and the escalation level must stay 1. The job runs every 5 minutes, so it sees the same expired timer many times. Without this guard, a manager would get the same breach every 5 minutes and would soon ignore all of them. The job keeps a key per timer and point, so each warning and each breach happens once.
ac.AC9: This test checks what the job does when the decision log cannot be written. The breach and its log entry belong together, so neither may happen alone. The timer must stay running with escalation level 0, and the job record must carry the log failure message. The first run after the log store is back must raise the breach. A breach raised with no log entry would leave an escalation nobody can account for later. Holding the timer running means the deadline is still live and the breach is only delayed.
ac.AC10: This test checks that a deviation stops the stage clock only. A deviation is a problem on the case that pauses normal work. The test raises one on 2 December and clears it on 4 December. The service level timer must be paused for those 2 working days. Its expiry must move by the same 2 working days. The prescription timer must keep running with the same expiry, because a legal period does not pause for an internal problem. The case record must also show the hold message with the prescription date while the deviation is open.
ac.AC11: This test checks the exact moment the warning is sent. A 5 working day timer starts on Monday 14 December at 08:00. The warning point falls at 08:00 on Friday 18 December. The run at 08:05 that Friday must send the warning once, showing the end date of Monday 21 December. The run at 07:55, ten minutes earlier, must send nothing. Warnings sent early lose their meaning, and a warning sent twice in one morning annoys the owner. The dates here are test data chosen to cross a weekend.

RWB-E1-042.story: Thresholds such as the 90-day entry point are written into code and spreadsheets today. A change needs a release, and nobody can say who owns a value. The team builds one configuration service and a parameter catalog. The catalog lists every parameter with its name, type, default, owner, environments and where it is used. Values are held as approved, dated versions per environment and served to every engine at run time. Two build checks fail the build when code holds a business value or reads a key the catalog does not list. It works when the build on main reports no findings.

ac.AC1: This test checks that an engine reads its threshold from the service. The entry parameter is set to 90 in production as version 1. When the case service decides entry, it must take 90 from the configuration service. It may not use a number written in the code. The decision must also record which version of the parameter it used. Reading from the service is what lets the business change the value without a release. Recording the version is what lets someone explain months later why a case entered on the figure it did.
ac.AC2: This test checks the build check for business values in code. The test uses a small fixture module with the number 90 written into the entry rule. A lint rule runs in the build. A lint rule is an automatic check on source code. The build must fail, and the output must name the file, the line and the parameter whose default equals that number. Naming the parameter tells the developer what to use instead. Without this check, values would drift back into the code, and the catalog would show an owner for a value nobody reads.
ac.AC3: This test checks that the catalog covers every parameter in use. The fixture code reads a key that the catalog does not list. The build compares the keys the services read with the keys in the catalog file. It must fail and name the missing key. Every other key in use must appear in the catalog with an owner and a default. A parameter with no catalog entry has no owner, no range and no default, so nobody can approve a change to it. The check keeps the catalog complete while the code grows.
ac.AC4: This test checks start-up when a required value is missing. The test sets up one required parameter with no value and no default for the UAT environment. The service must fail its health check with the missing-value message naming the key and the environment. It must take no traffic. A service that starts without a required value would fall back on something unknown and behave differently from production. Failing at start-up makes the problem plain at deployment time. The team can still fix it then, rather than during a live run.
ac.AC5: This test checks the range check on a value load. The catalog gives the entry parameter a range of 1 to 365. The load sets it to 400 for production. The load must be refused with the range message naming minimum 1 and maximum 365. The range is the guard that keeps a typing mistake from changing how cases enter recovery. A value of 400 days would stop cases entering at all, and the effect would show up only days later. Catching it at load time keeps the live value safe.
ac.AC6: This test checks the type check on a value load. The entry parameter is an integer, which means a whole number. The load gives it the text value ninety. The load must be refused with the failed-check message saying the value is not an integer. A text value in a numeric parameter would either stop the service or be read as something unintended. The catalog holds the type for every parameter, so the check needs no extra setup. Refusing the load leaves the earlier value in use while the file is corrected.
ac.AC7: This test checks separation of duty on a value version. The user who loaded version 3 then tries to approve it. The approval must be refused with the author message. Parameters set thresholds and limits that change how money is collected, so one person must not be able to change one alone. The approver is the parameter owner, and Risk approves where a threshold or a limit moves. Refusing the author's own approval is the check that keeps a second person in the path.
ac.AC8: This test checks that values can differ per environment. One parameter is 30 in SIT and 300 in production. Read in SIT the service must return 30, and in production 300. Environments need different values. Test environments want short cache times so a change shows at once. Production wants longer ones for speed. Holding both in the same catalog entry means the parameter has one owner and one range, with a value row per environment. Without this, teams would patch environment files by hand and the two would stop matching.
ac.AC9: This test checks how secrets appear in the catalog. One entry is marked as a secret, which means its value is held only in the secret store. When the catalog is read, the entry must show the owner, the environments and where it is used. No value may come back for it. Listing the secret gives it an owner and shows which services need it. Returning the value through a read would put a password into logs, screens and anyone's reach. The catalog and the secret store keep separate jobs here.
ac.AC10: This test checks rollback of a value version. Version 2 is in force, and version 1 was in force before it. One rollback call must put version 1 back in force. The service must then return 90. A wrong parameter value can change how every case is treated, so the way back has to be a single call. A new load with fresh approvals would take too long. The test also proves the service picks up the change. A rollback that only changed the table would leave every running instance on the old value.
ac.AC11: This test checks that a value waits for its date. Version 2 sets the entry parameter to 91 for production, with a valid from date of 10 December 2026. It is approved on 5 December. On 9 December the service must still use 90. On 10 December it must use 91. No instance may be restarted for the change. Business changes are agreed ahead of the date they apply, so approval and effect are separate steps. Each instance refreshes its cache on the approval event, or at the latest after the cache time to live.

RWB-E1-067.story: The Workbench creates, allocates, transfers and escalates cases, attaches documents and records decisions, often with nobody involved. The case owner sees customer contacts in the history and none of this. The team builds a listener on the event outbox. Each of six events becomes one ledger entry with its event code, time, actor and source. Events are delivered at least once, so a repeat with the same key is refused and counted instead. A failed write is retried, then sent to the exception queue with an incident. It works when the case history shows every Workbench action without reading other systems.

ac.AC1: This test checks that six Workbench actions all reach the ledger. The test publishes one event for each action on a test case. The actions are creation, allocation, transfer, document attachment, timer breach and a recorded decision. A listener picks up each event. A listener is code that waits for events and handles each one as it arrives. The ledger must then hold six entries with the matching event codes. Each entry must carry the case, the event, the time and the actor. Missing entries would leave gaps in the history, and the owner would go back to the source systems.
ac.AC2: This test checks the source fields on an entry. The allocation entry must name the source system, the owning module with the event ID, and the service that acted. The transfer entry must show an actor type of user and the user ID. Both are needed because most Workbench actions have no person behind them. Someone reading the history has to be able to tell an automatic step from one a colleague took. The source reference also points at the module and event, which is what support needs when an entry looks wrong.
ac.AC3: This test checks that one event never produces two entries. The allocation event was already written, and the same event arrives again with the same idempotency key. An idempotency key is a value that marks one event, so a repeat can be spotted. Only one allocation entry may exist, and the hit count for that key must be 1. The outbox delivers at least once, so repeats are normal and are not a fault. Without this check the history would show the same step several times, and no reader could tell which one was real.
ac.AC4: This test checks the schema version check. The event has a schema version the consumer does not accept. A consumer accepts the current version and the one before it. No entry may be written. The event must go to the exception queue, owned by the platform administrator, with the reason naming the version. Writing an entry from a payload the consumer does not know could store wrong fields or lose fields. Keeping the event on the exception queue means nothing is thrown away. The platform team can replay it after the consumer is updated.
ac.AC5: This test checks the failure path for a ledger write. Every insert is forced to fail in the test. The delivery must be tried four times in all: the first attempt and three retries. The event must then go to the exception queue with the platform administrator as owner. The write failure incident must be raised for that case. The event may never be dropped, because a lost event is a hole in the case history that nobody would notice. The incident brings a person to look at it.
ac.AC6: This test checks the order of entries for one case. Creation and allocation are written to the outbox in that order. After both are processed, creation must hold case sequence 1 and allocation sequence 2. The sequence number is what the case history is sorted by. Entries out of order would show a case allocated before it was created. Anyone reading the history would doubt all of it. The outbox delivers events for one case in the order they were written, and this test proves the listener keeps that order.
ac.AC7: This test checks two consumer threads handling the same event at the same moment. Only one entry may exist afterwards, and the hit count for its key must be 1. A unique key in the database means the second write fails, and that failure is caught and counted. The count is recorded in its own transaction, so it survives even though the entry write rolled back. A transaction is a group of statements that all succeed or all fail together. Without this, a restart under load could double every entry.
ac.AC8: This test checks an event that names a case that does not exist. The test uses a case ID with no row behind it. No entry may be written. The event must go to the exception queue with the reason that the case was not found. An entry on a missing case could never be read through the case history, so it would sit in the table unseen. Sending the event to the exception queue puts it in front of the platform team. They can find out why the publishing module sent an unknown case.

RWB-TE-008.story: The database refuses changes and deletes on decision log entries. A change made directly in the database is found only by recomputing the chain. Each entry carries a hash, a short fingerprint computed from its content. The team builds a nightly job. It waits for the decision log copy to finish. It fixes the highest sequence number as its end point, then recomputes every hash in batches. Each run is recorded with the count checked, the last sequence number and the last hash. Compliance gets a message for an intact chain, a break, or a run that stopped. It works when every night has a check and a same-day report.

ac.AC1: This test checks a clean nightly run. The test log holds 48,210 synthetic entries and none has been changed. The job runs at 02:00. It must record a run with its job type, the business date, a completed status and an intact result. The run record must hold the count checked, the last sequence number and that entry's hash. The pass message with the count and the last hash must go to Compliance. The recorded last hash is what lets a later run or an auditor confirm the chain has not moved since that night.
ac.AC2: This test checks that the job finds a changed entry. One entry in the test database had its actions changed with the trigger switched off. A trigger is code the database runs on its own when a statement arrives. The run result must be broken, naming that sequence number and its entry ID as the first break. The job must raise an incident and send the break message to Compliance before 08:00 the same morning. Compliance needs the report before the working day starts. Every entry from the break onward cannot be relied on until it is reviewed.
ac.AC3: This test checks a run that stops part way. The database connection is closed in a test double after 20,000 entries. A test double is a fake object used only in tests. The run must be recorded as failed with 20,000 entries checked. The platform administrator group must be alerted. Compliance must be told the check did not complete, with the date the chain was last confirmed. A failed run that nobody reported would look the same as a night with no break. Compliance would believe the log was checked when it was not.
ac.AC4: This test checks a rerun by hand. A run for the business date failed at 02:20, and the platform administrator reruns it at 08:30 from the job monitor. A second run record must be written for the same business date, marked as a rerun. The report to Compliance must also say it is a rerun, so the two reports for one date are not confused. While the rerun is running, a second start of the job must be refused by the scheduler. Two runs at once would read the same range twice and could report a break twice.
ac.AC5: This test checks the empty log. The log holds no entry, and the job runs. The result must be intact with zero entries checked. The last hash must be given as 64 zeros. Those zeros represent the point before the first entry. Early environments and new deployments start with an empty log, so the job meets this case on its first night. A job that failed or reported a break on an empty log would raise an incident on day one. It would also teach the team to ignore its reports.
ac.AC6: This test checks the wait for the decision log copy. The copy job for the business date is still running at 02:00 and ends at 02:25. The check must start at 02:25 and must record the copy job's end time. If the copy job has not ended by 04:00, the check must start anyway at 04:00 with a note saying so. Checking while the copy runs could read a moving range and report a break that is not there. Waiting without a limit would be worse, because some nights would get no check at all.
ac.AC7: This test checks a run with more than one changed entry. Two entries in the test database were changed. The first break must be the lower of the two sequence numbers, and the failing count must be 2. One incident and one message must go to Compliance, naming both entry IDs. Stopping at the first break would hide the size of the problem. Compliance would review one entry while a second stayed unknown. One report per run, rather than one per break, also keeps a widely changed log from flooding the group.
ac.AC8: This test checks entries written while the job runs. The log holds 48,210 entries when the job starts, and 37 more are appended during the run. The run must report 48,210 entries checked and that same number as its last sequence number. The next night's run must then check 48,247 entries. Fixing the end point at the start means the count and the last hash in the run record describe one known range. Without it, the job would chase new entries and its recorded last hash would not match any fixed point.
